### 5.6.2 Extension of Tender Validity Period
The entire process of scrutiny and evaluation of tenders, preparation of ranking statement and notification of award must be done expeditiously and within the original tender validity period. The validity period should not be unreasonably long as keeping the tender unconditionally valid for acceptance for a longer period entails the risk of getting higher prices from the tenderers.

If, however, due to some exceptional and unforeseen reasons, the purchase organisation is unable to decide on the placement of the contract within the original validity period, it may preferably request, before expiry of the original validity period, all the responsive tenderers to extend their tenders up to a specified period. While asking for such extension, the tenderers are also to be asked to extend their offers as it is, without any changes therein. They may also be told to extend the validity of the EMD for the corresponding additional period (which is to be specified in the request). A tenderer may not agree to such a request and this will not lead to forfeiture of its EMD. But the tenderers, who agree to extend the validity, are to do so without changing any terms, conditions, and so on, of their original tenders. Reasons for seeking extension of bid validity should be recorded by the procuring officers.

### 5.6.3 Reasonableness of Prices
In every recommendation of the TEC for award of contract, it must be declared that the rates recommended are reasonable. The comparison maybe made with the similar contracts awarded elsewhere. The Last Purchase Price (LPP) maybe updated taking into consideration inflation during the interim period and geographical conditions etc.

### 5.6.4 Consideration of Abnormally Low Bids
An Abnormally Low Bid is one in which the Bid price, in combination with other elements of the Bid, appears so low that it raises material concerns as to the capability of the Bidder to perform the contract at the offered price. Procuring Entity may in such cases seek written clarifications from the Bidder, including detailed price analyses of its Bid price in relation to scope, schedule, resource mobilization, allocation of risks and responsibilities, and any other requirements of the bids document. If, after evaluating the price analyses, procuring entity determines that the Bidder has *substantially failed* to demonstrate its capability to deliver the contract at the offered price, the Procuring Entity may reject the Bid/ Proposal. However it would not be advisable to fix a normative percentage below the estimated cost, which would automatically be considered as an abnormally low bid.

As a safeguard, it should be closely monitored by the EIC that final payments in such cases do not abnormally increases due to extra items. Further, there is no abnormal increase in quantities of the item for which contractors have initially quoted very high rates.

In case of abnormal rates (both low and high), the L1 bidder's confirmation to bridge the gap by providing necessary discount in case of any vitiation of L1 position after execution, should be sought before finalization of the contract.

### 5.6.5 Cartel Formation/ Pool Rates
It is possible that sometimes a group of bidders quote the same rate against a tender where they were at liberty to quote any competitive price. Such pool/ cartel formation is against the basic principle of competitive bidding and defeats the very purpose of an open and competitive tendering system. A warning clause may also be included in the bid documents to discourage the bidders from indulging in such practices.

question_text: What are the possible bases for valuing materials to be disposed of?
answer:
The valuation of materials to be disposed of shall be based on one or more of the following:

- prevailing market price of such used items, metal index etc.  
- book value of the materials.  
- price from earlier successful auction or sale with escalation.  
- third‑party valuation, if required, depending on the cost of valuation relative to the assumed worth of the items.  
- price from successful auction or sale of other PSUs as intimated by the e‑auction service provider.  
- moving‑average cost or last purchase price of non‑hydro‑carbon (NHC) materials, whichever is higher, plus 15 % administrative charges (applicable when surplus is sold to PSUs).  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 167)
cot:
First, I consider what it means to place a value on materials that have been identified as condemned, scrap or surplus before they are disposed of – the goal is to establish a reserve price that reflects what the items are worth in the current situation, so that the disposal process is both transparent and financially sound.  

Next, I think about the kinds of information that are normally available to an organization when it needs to price such items: there are external market indicators, the internal accounting record, historical sale prices, expert appraisals, benchmark transactions from similar entities, and special rules that apply when the buyer is another public sector undertaking.  

Then, I work through each of these sources one by one. The most direct external signal is the prevailing market price for comparable used goods or the relevant metal index, which tells us what buyers are willing to pay today. Internally, the book value – the amount still carried in the fixed‑asset register – provides a baseline that reflects the original cost less depreciation. Historical transaction data are also useful; if there has been a recent successful auction or sale of similar material, that price can be taken and adjusted for any expected escalation to reflect current conditions. When the internal data are thin or the item is highly specialised, commissioning a third‑party valuation becomes an option, but only if the cost of that appraisal is justified by the presumed worth of the material, otherwise it would be uneconomical. Another practical reference is the price achieved in auctions or sales conducted by other public sector undertakings, which the e‑auction service provider can relay as a benchmark. Finally, there is a specific rule for transfers between PSUs: the valuation should be based on either the moving‑average cost or the last purchase price of non‑hydro‑carbon materials, whichever is higher, and then a 15 % administrative charge is added to cover handling and processing expenses.  

Looking at these points together, I see that the valuation exercise does not have to rely on a single method; any one of the above bases, or a combination of them, can be used depending on what information is accessible, reliable and cost‑effective at the time of disposal.  

Bringing the reasoning to a close, the permissible bases for valuing materials to be disposed of are therefore: prevailing market price of such used items or metal index, book value of the materials, price from earlier successful auction or sale with escalation, third‑party valuation when justified by cost versus worth, price from successful auction or sale of other PSUs as communicated by the e‑auction service provider, and, for sales to another PSU, the higher of moving‑average cost or last purchase price of non‑hydro‑carbon materials plus a 15 % administrative charge. This set matches the required answer.

question_text: Can an external expert’s report alone decide the technical evaluation
answer: No. Even if an external expert’s advice and report is obtained, the Technical Recommendation Committee (TRC) must still review that report and decide whether to accept, reject or modify the evaluation; the report by itself cannot determine the technical outcome. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 121)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: it wants to know if a report from an outside expert can by itself determine the outcome of the technical evaluation in a procurement process.  

Looking at how technical evaluation is described, the responsibility for judging the technical suitability of the offers lies with the technical members of the Technical Recommendation Committee (TRC). They are the ones who examine the description, specifications, drawings and other technical terms and conditions.  

The reference also mentions that an external expert’s advice and report may be sought, but it explicitly states that even when such a report is obtained, it remains the TRC’s duty to accept, reject or modify the evaluation contained in that report. In other words, the TRC cannot simply delegate its judgment to the expert; it must still review and decide on the expert’s findings.  

If the TRC must still review and potentially change the expert’s evaluation, then the expert’s report cannot serve as the sole basis for the technical decision. The report can inform the TRC, but the final determination rests with the committee.  

Putting these points together, the only logical conclusion is that an external expert’s report alone cannot decide the technical evaluation; the TRC must still intervene to accept, reject or modify it. This matches the given answer that the report by itself cannot determine the technical outcome.

question_text: What type of equipment is excluded from the exemption described in paragraph 4.3.5(a) for educational and research institutes?
answer: Routine equipment used in offices is excluded from the exemption described in paragraph 4.3.5(a) for educational and research institutes. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 61)
cot:
I start by asking what the exemption in paragraph 4.3.5(a) actually allows. It says that for educational and research institutes the Secretary can approve global tender enquiries for the procurement of specialised equipment needed for research, together with its spares and consumables, up to a certain financial limit.  

Next, I notice the condition that follows the description of the exemption: the equipment must be of a specialised nature required for research purposes and **not** the routine equipment used in offices. This clause is a direct limitation on what can be covered by the exemption.  

Thinking about that limitation, I realise that any item that does not qualify as specialised research equipment falls outside the scope of the exemption. Routine office equipment—such as desks, chairs, standard computers, or ordinary office supplies—clearly does not serve a specialised research function; it is ordinary, non‑specialised gear meant for everyday administrative work.  

Because the exemption explicitly excludes routine office equipment, I conclude that the type of equipment barred from the exemption described in paragraph 4.3.5(a) for educational and research institutes is precisely the routine equipment used in offices.

question_text: What record‑keeping responsibilities exist for tenders published on the Procuring Entity's website
answer:
- Collect and retain records of all tenders published on the Procuring Entity’s website to serve as proof of publicity.  
- Document the precise dates on which each advertisement actually appeared on the website.  
- Provide these date details when forwarding tender cases to higher authorities for review.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 94)
cot:
First, I consider why any record‑keeping would be required for tenders that are posted on the Procuring Entity’s website. The main reason is to have verifiable proof that the tender was actually publicized, which supports transparency and can be used to demonstrate compliance with procurement rules.

Next, I think about what would constitute such proof. Simply having a copy of the tender notice is not enough; we need to show that the notice was indeed displayed on the website at a specific time. Therefore, the record must capture the fact of publication together with the timing of that publication.

Then, I focus on the timing aspect. The reference material emphasizes that the complete details of the dates on which the advertisements actually appeared on the website should be indicated. This means that for each tender we need to note the exact day—or days—when the notice was live and accessible to potential bidders.

After establishing what must be recorded, I consider how these records are handled internally. They are not just filed away; they serve as supporting documentation when the tender case is reviewed by higher authorities. Consequently, the records must be retained in an organized manner so they can be retrieved and submitted whenever a case is forwarded for approval or audit.

Finally, I synthesize these points into the concrete responsibilities: the Procuring Entity must collect and keep a record of every tender published on its website, document the precise dates of each website appearance, and make those date details available to higher authorities when sending the tender case for review. This fulfills the proof‑of‑publicity requirement and aligns with the procedural guidance.

question_text: What actions can the Procuring Entity take if the consultant fails to correct unsatisfactory performance?
answer:
**A:** The Procuring Entity can first advise the consultant to take necessary measures to address the poor performance, such as improving team performance or replacing underperforming staff. If the consultant does not act adequately, the Procuring Entity may escalate the matter to the consultant’s top management, issue a formal notice to rectify the situation, and, as a last resort, consider terminating the contract. (<Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 61>)  

**Rationale:** These steps follow the contract provisions for handling unsatisfactory performance, giving the consultant a chance to correct the issue before more serious actions are taken.
cot: I’m trying to figure out what the Procuring Entity can do when a consultant’s performance remains unsatisfactory even after being asked to improve. The first thing that comes to mind is that the contract must lay out a graded response—starting with a mild reminder and moving toward stronger measures if the problem persists. So I think about the initial step: the Procuring Entity would likely point out the specific shortcomings and tell the consultant to take the necessary corrective actions, such as boosting the team’s overall performance or swapping out any staff members who aren’t meeting the required standards. If the consultant ignores or inadequately follows that advice, the next logical move is to bring the issue to the attention of the consultant’s senior leadership, because top management has the authority to enforce changes that the project team might resist. Should even that escalation fail to produce results, the Procuring Entity would probably issue a formal notice demanding that the situation be rectified within a defined period, making it clear that further inaction will have consequences. Only after those attempts—advice, escalation, and a formal notice—have been exhausted would the Procuring Entity consider the ultimate sanction: terminating the contract, which serves as a last resort to protect the project’s interests. This progression mirrors the contract’s approach of giving the consultant every reasonable chance to correct unsatisfactory performance before resorting to more severe actions.

## 8.5 Reporting of Progress
The timing, nature, and number of reports that the consultant/ service provider should provide are normally contained in the Consultancy and other services contract. If the assignment is of a routine nature over a long period (for example, implementation supervision), then monthly, quarterly, and annual progress reports may be required. On the other hand, if the assignment is to prepare a study or to implement a particular task, a more specific type of reporting may be required.

## 8.6 Monitoring a Time-based Contract
As indicated earlier, the performance of a time-based contract may depend on the progress in other contracts (for example, the progress of a construction supervision contract depends on the progress of a construction contract). In such situations, the mobilisation and demobilisation of resources/ key experts and time employed by them should be mobilised and monitored carefully as it is possible that the contract period and the total amount under the contract are spent fully and construction work being supervised is not even half complete. These situations could lead to claims and disputes.

## 8.7 Monitoring a Lump-sum Contract
As Lump-sum contract is based on output and deliverables, it is important that the quality of draft reports is checked carefully before release of stage payment as subsequent dispute after completion of the task could lead to disputes. In this form of contract, if there are extra additional services, there should be timely amendment to the contract to reflect these increases and to regulate payment. In general, in a lump-sum contract, the increase should not be more than 10-15 (ten to fifteen) per cent.

## 8.8 Unsatisfactory Performance
Poor performance may involve one or more particular staff from the consultant/ service provider's team, or the whole team or non-participation by the main qualifying JV member. Based on the provisions of the contract, the Procuring Entity will advise the consultant/ service provider to take the necessary measures to address the situation. Poor performance should not be tolerated; therefore, the consultant/ service provider should act quickly to comply with a reasonable request to improve the performance of the team or to replace any particular staff member who is not performing adequately. If the consultant/ service provider fails to take adequate corrective actions, the Procuring Entity may take up the issue with the top management of the consultant/ service provider and issue notice to rectify the situation and finally consider terminating the contract.

## 8.9 Delays
Consultancy and other services may be delayed for a variety of reasons. The consultant/ service

provider should notify the Procuring Entity and explain the causes of such delays. If corrective action requires extra work and the delay cannot be attributed to the consultant/ service provider, the extra work should be reimbursed in accordance with the contract.

## 8.10 Issuing Contract Variations
8.10.1 The formal method of making and documenting a change in the Consultancy and other services contract is through a contract variation.

Contract variations are issued when there are agreed-upon changes in the scope of work, personnel inputs, costs, timing of the submission of reports, or out-of-pocket expenditures. There are few Consultancy and other services contracts of any type that do not require a contract variation at one time or another. Normally, these relate to changes that have a cost implication, but when there is a significant change in the timing of an activity or a particular output, these should also be recorded through a contract variation. Normally, the request for contract variation is prepared by the consultant/ service provider or Consultancy/ service provider firm and submitted to the Procuring Entity.

question_text: How should the Engineer-in-Charge plan the work after reviewing the time allowed for completion?
answer:
The Engineer‑in‑Charge should plan the work in consultation with the contractor, ensuring it can be completed within the stipulated time, making the work front available on schedule, and drawing up a time‑schedule for each stage of the work that is signed by the contractor’s representative.  

This approach coordinates expectations, prevents delays, and formalizes the timeline as required by the contract monitoring procedure. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 77)
cot:
First, I consider what the Engineer‑in‑Charge has just done: reviewed the total time allowed for completing the work. The natural next step is to turn that time allowance into a concrete plan that can be followed on site.  

Then, I recognize that the plan cannot be drafted in isolation; the contractor who will actually carry out the activities must be involved, because only they know the practical constraints of their resources and methods. So the Engineer‑in‑Charge should sit down with the contractor to discuss how the work can be sequenced.  

Next, within that consultation, the Engineer‑in‑Charge checks whether the proposed sequence of tasks fits comfortably inside the stipulated duration. If any activity looks like it would overrun the available time, adjustments are made—perhaps by overlapping certain tasks, adding shifts, or revising the method—until the whole program can be completed by the deadline.  

Further, to keep the contractor from waiting for access or materials, the Engineer‑in‑Charge makes sure that the work front—the area, utilities, and any prerequisite installations—is ready exactly when the schedule calls for it. This prevents idle time and avoids cascading delays.  

Finally, the agreed‑upon sequence is written up as a detailed time‑schedule that breaks the work into discrete stages, and the contractor’s representative signs off on it. This signature formalizes the commitment, creates a reference point for monitoring progress, and satisfies the contract‑monitoring requirement for an approved program.  

Putting these steps together, the Engineer‑in‑Charge plans the work in consultation with the contractor, ensures it can be finished within the allowed time, has the work front ready on schedule, and draws up a signed stage‑by‑stage timetable. This approach aligns expectations, prevents hold‑ups, and locks the timeline into the contract’s monitoring procedure.

question_text: Can I rely on the rate from a previous indent of the same goods to estimate cost, and what condition must it meet
answer: Yes, you can use the rate from a previous indent of the same goods to estimate the cost, but only if that indent is the most recent one that has not yet been converted into an order. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 38)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is really asking: it wants to know whether a rate from an earlier indent for the same item can be used as a basis for cost estimation, and if there is any specific requirement that must be satisfied for that to be valid.  

Next, I think about how cost estimation is typically handled in procurement. The reference material lists several ways to arrive at an estimated cost, and one of them is explicitly mentioned as “estimated rate in past indents of the same goods.” This tells me that using a previous indent’s rate is indeed a recognized method, so the answer to the first part is likely affirmative.  

Then I look closely at how that method is qualified. Right after the bullet point there is a parenthetical note: “[Latest, which had not been converted to order].” This note is not an optional comment; it is attached directly to the method and therefore acts as a condition that must be met for the method to be applicable. In other words, the rate can only be taken from the most recent indent that has still not been turned into a purchase order.  

I now verify that this condition makes sense in practice. If an earlier indent had already been converted into an order, its rate would be tied to a completed transaction and might not reflect current market conditions or the specific circumstances of the new requirement. By limiting the source to the latest unconverted indent, the estimate stays as current as possible while still relying on historical data.  

Finally, I combine these observations: the method is permissible, but only when the indent used is the most recent one that has not yet been converted into an order. This matches exactly the statement that the answer provides.

question_text: What is a consortium of consultants or service providers according to the manual
answer:
**A:** A consortium is an association of two or more consultants or service‑providing firms that join together—either as a joint venture (JV) or as a sub‑consultancy—to combine their expertise, increase technical responsiveness, and make a larger pool of experts available for an assignment. The association may be ongoing or limited to a specific task. In a JV all members sign the contract and are jointly and severally liable; after short‑listing, any JV or sub‑consultancy among the short‑listed firms is allowed only if the Request for Proposal permits it, and one of the short‑listed firms must act as the lead member, with the procuring entity dealing solely with the lead. Bid documents must state whether JVs are allowed, limit the number of partners (commonly three), specify how qualifications are to be met collectively and individually (e.g., each partner must meet at least 25 % of the required experience or turnover, with the lead meeting at least 50 %). A firm may submit only one proposal—either on its own or as a JV partner; participating in more than one proposal leads to disqualification, although a firm may act as a sub‑consultant or team member in multiple proposals if the RfP allows it. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 17)  

**Rationale:** This explanation outlines the purpose, structure, liability, procedural rules, and qualification requirements that the manual sets out for consortia, giving new staff a clear picture of when and how such associations can be used.
cot:
First, I need to pin down what the manual means when it talks about a consortium of consultants or service providers. The core idea is that two or more firms can come together to work on an assignment, and the reason they do this is to bring together different strengths—each firm contributes its own expertise, which makes the group technically stronger and gives the client access to a broader pool of specialists than any single firm could offer on its own.  

Next, I consider the possible structures this association can take. The manual distinguishes between two main forms: a joint venture, where the firms create a separate legal entity for the work, and a sub‑consultancy arrangement, where one firm leads and the others support it under its direction. Both forms serve the same purpose of pooling resources, but they differ in how liability and contractual responsibilities are handled.  

Then I think about the duration and scope of such a consortium. It isn’t limited to a single project; firms may choose to stay associated for the long term, treating the consortium as a standing partnership, or they may come together only for a particular assignment and dissolve afterward. This flexibility lets them adapt to the nature of the work and the client’s needs.  

After that, I look at the contractual and procedural rules that govern how a consortium operates in a procurement process. If the consortium is set up as a joint venture, every member must sign the contract and each is jointly and severally liable for the whole assignment—meaning the procuring entity can hold any one member responsible for the full performance. Once the shortlist is established and the request for proposal is issued, any joint venture or sub‑consultancy among those shortlisted firms is allowed only if the request for proposal explicitly permits it. In that case, one of the shortlisted firms must be designated as the lead member, and the procuring entity communicates with and receives deliverables solely through that lead, simplifying contract management.  

I then turn to the details that the bid documents must spell out when joint ventures are allowed. The documents should state clearly whether joint ventures are permitted to bid, especially for large or complex assignments above a certain threshold. They also need to limit the number of partners in a joint venture—commonly to three—to keep the arrangement manageable. Moreover, the documents have to explain how the required qualifications are to be satisfied: some criteria, like specific experience or financial turnover, can be met collectively by the partners, while each partner must still meet certain individual thresholds. Typically, each partner must fulfill at least 25 % of the collective requirement, with the lead partner expected to meet at least 50 % of that share.  

Finally, I recall the rule about conflicting associations to avoid any misunderstanding. A firm may submit only one proposal—either on its own or as a partner in a joint venture. If a firm appears in more than one proposal, whether as a solo bidder or as a joint‑venture member, all of those proposals are disqualified. However, the manual does allow a firm to act as a sub‑consultant or as a team member in multiple proposals, provided the request for proposal explicitly permits such participation.  

Putting all these pieces together, the consortium is essentially an alliance of two or more consulting or service‑providing firms that join forces—either as a joint venture or a sub‑consultancy—to combine expertise, boost technical responsiveness, and enlarge the expert pool for an assignment. The alliance can be enduring or project‑specific, liability is shared in a joint venture, a lead member handles all interactions with the procuring entity, and the bidding process is governed by clear rules on permissions, partner limits, qualification sharing, and proposal exclusivity. This captures exactly what the manual describes as a consortium of consultants or service providers.

### 2.1.1 Consortium of consultants/ service providers
In large and complex assignments consultants/ service providers may associate with each other to form a consortium to complement their respective areas of expertise, to increase the technical responsiveness of their proposal, and make larger pools of experts available or for other reasons. Such an association may be for the long term (independent of any particular assignment) or for a specific assignment. The consortium may take the form of a Joint Venture (JV) or a sub consultancy. In case of a JV, all members of the JV shall sign the contract and shall be jointly and severally liable for the entire assignment. After the short list is finalised, and the Request for Proposal (RfP) is issued, any association in the form of a JV or sub consultancy among the short-listed firms shall be permissible in accordance with provisions stated in the RfP. Under such circumstance, one of the shortlisted consultants/ service providers must become the lead member of the consortium. The Procuring Entity only deals with the lead member of consortiums for all the purposes. Bid documents should clearly specify whether JVs are allowed to bid (in case of complex and large assignments, say above certain values (say - Rupees five crore). Maximum number of partners in JV shall be limited (say - three). In case JVs are permitted to bid, it should be clarified what qualifications are to be collectively (clubbed together) met by the JV partners (say experience of particular consultancy, Financial Turnover etc) and what each partner has to individually and separately meet (financial soundness). In this case it should also be specified that each partner should meet at least 25% (and the lead partner at least 50%) out of the qualifying limit in case of experience of particular consultancy and financial turnover, if any.

**Conflicting Association:** A firm shall submit only one proposal, either individually or as a JV partner in another proposal. If a firm, including a JV partner, submits or participates in more than one proposal, all such proposals shall be disqualified. This does not, however, preclude a firm from participating as a sub-consultant or an individual consultant to participate as a team member in more than one proposal when circumstances justify but only if permitted by the RfP document.

### 2.1.2 Consultancy or Service Providing Firms
The main source of consultants and service providers is Consultancy or Service providing firms of diverse specializations that provide teams to Clients. These firms provide project preparation services, project implementation supervision services, training, advisory services, and policy guidance. Such firms are normally classified as either international - firms that have international experience and are capable of undertaking work at international level at international rates; or national - firms that may not have international exposure and normally undertake assignments only within that country, usually at significantly lower rates.

question_text: What alternative to the STP criteria can be prescribed for technical qualification under the LCS method?
answer:
**Alternative to the Simplified Technical Proposal (STP) Criteria for Technical Qualification under the LCS Method**  
*Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 40*

---

### Step‑by‑Step Instructional Guide  

**1. Determine When an Alternative Is Needed**  
- Review the assignment characteristics (see Section 6.2.2).  
- If the work is routine, low‑risk, or does not require detailed consultant experience, consider using a simpler qualification approach instead of the STP.

**2. Define Simpler Fail/Pass Pre‑Qualifying Criteria**  
- Adopt criteria that are analogous to those used for procuring non‑consultancy services (e.g., supplies, works).  
- Typical elements include:  
  - Minimum legal registration or licensing status.  
  - Basic financial standing (e.g., minimum annual turnover or solvency ratio).  
  - Evidence of no serious adverse legal judgments (e.g., no pending disqualifications).  
  - Confirmation of compliance with basic health, safety, or environmental requirements, if applicable.  
- Each criterion is expressed as a **fail/pass** threshold; bidders must meet **all** thresholds to proceed to financial evaluation.

**3. Insert the Criteria into the RfP Document**  
- Place the fail/pass criteria in the **Data Sheet** of the Request for Proposal (RfP) under the “Technical Qualification” heading.  
- Clearly label them as “Pre‑Qualifying Criteria (Fail/Pass)” to avoid confusion with scored technical evaluation.

**4. Communicate the Requirements to Bidders**  
- Include a brief instruction in the Letter of Invitation (Loi) or the RfP cover letter stating that only bidders who satisfy all fail/pass criteria will be considered technically qualified.  
- Provide a checklist or annex (e.g., Annex X) that bidders can use to self‑assess before submission.

**5. Execute the Evaluation**  
- **Screening Phase:** The evaluation committee checks each bidder’s submission against the fail/pass list. Any bidder failing one or more criteria is eliminated at this stage.  
- **Documentation:** Record the outcome of each check in an evaluation worksheet to ensure transparency and auditability.  
- **Proceed to Financial Opening:** Only bidders that pass all pre‑qualifying criteria have their financial bids opened and evaluated.

**6. Monitor and Review**  
- After each procurement cycle, review whether the fail/pass criteria were appropriate (e.g., too restrictive or too lax).  
- Adjust thresholds for future tenders based on lessons learned, while maintaining consistency with the LCS method’s objective of minimizing unnecessary technical scoring.

---

### Practical Example  

*Scenario:* Procurement of routine audit services for a small‑scale project.  

- **Fail/Pass Criteria:**  
  1. Valid practicing certificate from the national accountancy body.  
  2. Minimum annual turnover of USD 200,000 in the last two fiscal years.  
  3. No unresolved disciplinary actions in the past three years.  

- **Process:** Bidders submit copies of their certificate, audited financial statements, and a self‑declaration of disciplinary status. The committee verifies each item; any missing or unsatisfactory item results in disqualification before financial bids are considered.

---

### Common Pitfalls to Avoid  

| Pitfall | Why It Occurs | How to Prevent It |
|---------|---------------|-------------------|
| **Vague thresholds** (e.g., “adequate financial standing”) | Leads to inconsistent judgments and potential challenges. | Use specific, measurable values (turnover amount, ratio, etc.). |
| **Over‑loading the list** with many criteria | Defeats the purpose of simplification and slows screening. | Limit criteria to those essential for basic eligibility; mirror the streamlined approach used for non‑consultancy procurements. |
| **Failing to document decisions** | Undermines auditability and can cause disputes. | Keep a simple pass/fail checklist signed off by each evaluator. |
| **Applying scored technical weights inadvertently** | Confuses bidders and violates the LCS method’s intent. | Clearly state that the criteria are fail/pass only; avoid any point‑based scoring language. |

By following these steps, procurement officers can reliably implement an appropriate alternative to the STP criteria—namely, a set of simpler fail/pass pre‑qualifying criteria modeled after those used for non‑consultancy services—while maintaining compliance with the LCS method and reducing procedural errors.
cot:
I start by asking what the LCS method actually requires for technical qualification when a full technical proposal isn’t needed. Since the LCS approach does not rank or weight technical scores, the goal is simply to establish a clear pass‑or‑fail benchmark that tells us whether a consultant is capable enough to move on to the financial evaluation.  

Looking at the description of the Simplified Technical Proposal, I see it is meant for assignments that are routine, low‑risk, and where the terms of reference already spell out the tasks, so detailed scoring of experience or methodology adds little value. This tells me that the alternative must be even more streamlined—something that mirrors the kind of basic eligibility checks used when buying goods or works rather than consultancy services.  

With that in mind, I think about what basic, measurable conditions would be enough to deem a firm technically qualified without going into a full proposal. The first thing that comes to mind is confirming that the firm is legally allowed to operate—valid registration, licence or practicing certificate relevant to the service. Next, a simple financial health check, such as a minimum annual turnover or a solvency ratio, ensures the firm can sustain the contract. Then I consider any serious legal or disciplinary issues that would disqualify a bidder, like unresolved judgments or bans from professional bodies. Finally, if the work has any health, safety or environmental implications, a basic compliance statement can be added. Each of these items is expressed as a clear threshold: the bidder either meets it or does not, with no partial credit or scoring.  

Having identified the substance of the criteria, I turn to how they would be placed in the procurement documents. They belong in the data sheet of the request for proposal, labelled explicitly as pre‑qualifying fail/pass criteria so bidders know they are not part of a scored technical evaluation. I would also include a short note in the letter of invitation or cover letter reminding bidders that only those who satisfy every threshold will have their financial bids opened, and perhaps attach a self‑assessment checklist to make the process transparent.  

During evaluation, the committee would screen each submission against the list, eliminating anyone who fails any one check, record the outcome in a simple worksheet for auditability, and then proceed to open the financial proposals of the remaining bidders. After the procurement cycle, I would review whether the thresholds were appropriately set—neither too lax to admit unfit firms nor too restrictive to exclude competent ones—and adjust them for future tenders while keeping the LCS principle of minimal technical scoring intact.  

Putting all of this together, the alternative to the STP criteria under the LCS method is therefore a set of simpler fail/pass pre‑qualifying criteria modelled on those used for procuring non‑consultancy services, covering legal standing, basic financial capacity, absence of serious legal or disciplinary problems, and any essential health, safety or environmental compliance, inserted into the RFP data sheet, communicated to bidders, applied as a screening step, and monitored for effectiveness. This reasoning leads directly to the answer that outlines exactly such an alternative.

question_text: How must the procuring entity handle the opening of priced bids in a two‑bid system to ensure participation of qualified bidders
answer: - Prior intimation of the priced bid opening date, time, and venue shall be sent to the techno‑commercially qualified bidders so that they or their representatives may remain present during the priced bid opening. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 61)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know the specific action the procuring entity must take when opening priced bids in a two‑bid system so that qualified bidders can actually participate in that opening.  

Next, I recall how a two‑bid system works: there are two separate envelopes—one containing the technical‑commercial proposal and another containing the price proposal. The technical‑commercial bids are evaluated first, and only those bidders who pass that evaluation move on to the priced‑bid stage.  

Because the priced bids are opened at a later date, after the technical evaluation is complete, the procuring entity cannot assume that all bidders will automatically know when and where this second opening will happen. If the qualified bidders are not informed, they might miss the opening, which would defeat the purpose of giving them a chance to be present.  

Therefore, to guarantee that the techno‑commercially qualified bidders (or their representatives) can attend, the procuring entity must proactively communicate the details of the priced‑bid opening. This means sending out a prior notice that specifies the exact date, time, and venue for the opening of the priced bids.  

By doing so, the qualified bidders receive the information they need to plan their attendance, and the procuring entity fulfills the requirement of ensuring their participation in the priced‑bid opening.  

Putting this together, the required handling is that prior intimation of the priced bid opening date, time, and venue shall be sent to the techno‑commercially qualified bidders so that they or their representatives may remain present during the priced bid opening.

question_text: What does the contract say about the contractor's liability for consumable materials supplied by the owner?
answer: The contractor must reimburse the owner for any consumable materials supplied under the contract and is liable for loss or damage to those materials; the contractor has no right, title, lien, or claim over them, and the owner may take full possession and remove the materials at any time. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 140)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the agreement says about the contractor’s responsibility when the owner provides consumable materials. The question is focused on liability, so I’ll look for any clause that ties the contractor to payment or compensation for those items.  

The Procurement of Works Manual includes a provision where the contractor agrees to pay sums that may become due to the owner for “controlled items of consumable materials” as well as for any loss or damage to the owner’s equipment, materials, construction plant and machinery. This makes it clear that the contractor is expected to cover the cost of the consumables supplied by the owner and to compensate the owner if those materials are lost or damaged while under the contractor’s control.  

Next, I examine what rights the contractor retains over those materials. Another section states that the contractor shall have no right, title or interest in the goods, articles, materials, etc., brought onto the site unless they specifically belong to the contractor, and that the contractor shall not have or be deemed to have any lien. This tells me that, despite using the owner‑supplied consumables, the contractor cannot claim ownership, cannot assert a lien, and has no proprietary claim over them.  

Putting those two ideas together, the contractor’s obligation is two‑fold: first, to reimburse the owner for the value of the consumables provided, and second, to bear the risk of any loss or damage to those items, since the contractor must pay for such loss. Because the contractor lacks any title, interest, or lien, the owner retains full ownership and control.  

Finally, I note that the owner is granted an absolute and unfettered right to take full possession of the site and to remove the contractor’s servants, agents, and materials belonging to the contractor. While this clause is framed around the contractor’s own belongings, the principle of the owner’s unilateral right to possession extends to any owner‑supplied items that remain on site; the owner can therefore reclaim the consumables at any time.  

Synthesizing these points, the contract requires the contractor to repay the owner for consumable materials supplied, holds the contractor liable for any loss or damage to those materials, denies the contractor any right, title, lien, or claim over them, and allows the owner to take full possession and remove the materials whenever desired. This matches the answer we need to reach.

Step‑by‑Step Operational Checklist – Contractor’s Rights Regarding Site, Structures, and Materials  

1. Verify that the contractor acquires **no right, title, or interest** in the Owner‑provided site.  
2. Confirm that the contractor has **no claim** to any building, structure, or work erected on that site.  
3. Ensure that goods, articles, materials, etc. brought onto the site are **not owned by the contractor** unless they are specifically the contractor’s own property.  
4. Recognize that the contractor **cannot assert a lien or any charge** for unpaid bills on the site, structures, or materials.  
5. Understand that the contractor **may not assume or retain possession or control** of the site or any structures thereon.  
6. Acknowledge that the contractor’s right to be on the site is limited to a **bare license (licensee simpliciter)** for executing the works.

8. Remember that the Owner retains an **absolute and unfettered right** to take full possession of the site and to remove the contractor, their servants, agents, and any contractor‑owned materials remaining on the site.  

These points summarize the contractor’s lack of rights regarding the site, structures, or materials unless they specifically belong to the contractor (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 140).

question_text: What are the consequences if I do not participate in the reverse auction after agreeing to do so
answer: If you have agreed to take part in the reverse auction and submitted the required compliance form but then do not actually join the live auction, NRL treats this as a failure to participate. As a result, your bid will be disqualified and will not be considered for any further technical or commercial evaluation (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 262). In addition, NRL may impose penal action, which can include placing your company on a blacklist or holiday list in line with its current rules (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 262). Even simply logging into the system counts as participation, so not logging in at all is seen as non‑participation and triggers these consequences (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 261).
cot: I begin by considering what it means to have agreed to take part in the reverse auction. The agreement is formalized when the bidder submits the compliance form during the un‑priced bid stage, which signals acceptance of the auction as part of the tender’s terms. Once that form is filed, the tender documentation makes participation in the live auction mandatory, and it even clarifies that simply logging into the bidding system counts as having participated. Therefore, if a bidder who has submitted the form then fails to log in at all, the only logical interpretation is that they have not fulfilled the mandatory participation requirement. Because participation is a condition for a bid to stay eligible, the next step is to examine what the procuring entity does with a bid that fails to meet that condition. The rules state that such a bidder is treated as disqualified for the tender and their offer is removed from any further technical or commercial evaluation. Beyond disqualification, the procuring entity retains the right to impose penal measures, which can include placing the firm on a blacklist or holiday list in line with its internal policies. Putting these pieces together, the consequence of agreeing to the auction, submitting the compliance form, and then not actually joining the live reverse auction is that the bidder’s submission is disqualified and they may face penal action such as blacklisting or holiday listing.

question_text: Under what circumstances can expenditure from public money be incurred for the benefit of a particular person or group?
answer:
**A:** Such expenditure is permitted only when either (1) a claim for the amount could be enforced in a court of law, or (2) the spending is made in pursuance of a recognized policy or custom.  

**Rationale:** This rule protects public funds from being used for private gain while still allowing legitimate payments that are legally enforceable or aligned with established policies and practices. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, pp. 11-13)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: it wants to know when it is acceptable to use public funds to advantage a specific individual or group, given that the default rule is to avoid such preferential treatment.  

Looking at the guiding norms for handling public money, the overarching idea is that officers must treat public funds with the same care they would their own and must not let spending become a source of private gain. This sets a strong presumption against any expenditure that benefits only a particular person or section of society.  

The next step is to see where the rules carve out exceptions to that presumption. The financial propriety standards spell out that the prohibition is not absolute; it lifts only when one of two specific conditions is met.  

The first condition is that a claim for the amount could be enforced in a court of law. In other words, if the government owes a debt or has a legal obligation to pay, then paying that claim is not a gratuitous gift but the discharge of a duty, and thus it does not violate the propriety principle.  

The second condition is that the spending is made in pursuance of a recognized policy or custom. When a long‑standing, accepted practice or an official policy authorizes the payment, the expenditure is no longer an ad‑hoc favor but part of an established framework that applies uniformly, preserving the spirit of fairness and order.  

If neither of these conditions holds, paying out public money to a particular person or group would be a pure benefit without legal backing or policy justification, which the standards explicitly forbid because it would amount to using public resources for private advantage.  

Putting these pieces together, the only circumstances under which such expenditure can be justified are exactly those two: a legally enforceable claim, or compliance with a recognized policy or custom. This matches the answer that expenditure from public money for the benefit of a particular person or group is permissible only when a claim could be enforced in court or when the spending follows a recognized policy or custom.
chunk_content:
## 1.5 Basic Aims of Procurement - Five R's of Procurement
In every procurement, public or private, the basic aim is to achieve just the right balance between costs and requirements concerning five parameters called the five Rs of procurement. The entire process of procurement (from the time that need for an item, facility or services is identified till the need is satisfied) is designed to achieve following basic aims. Although couched in jargon of procurement of Goods, it's equally applicable to procurement of Consultancy and other services. The

term 'Right' is used here in the sense of being optimal:

- i) Right quality;
- ii) Right quantity;
- iii) Right price;
- iv) Right time and place; and
- v) Right source.

*(For more details on basic aims of procurement, please refer to Chapter 1 of the Manual for Procurement of Goods).*

## 1.6 Principles of Service Procurement
Over and above the basic aims of procurement, the obligations of procuring authorities can be grouped into following five fundamental principles of service procurement, which needs to be followed:

- i) Transparency principle;
- ii) Professionalism principle;
- iii) Broader obligations principle;

*(For more details on principles of procurement, please refer to Chapter 1 of the Manual for Procurement of Goods).*

## 1.7 Standards (Canons) of Financial Propriety
Public Procurement like any other expenditure in Government must conform to the Standards (also called Canons) of Financial Propriety.

**Standards of financial propriety:** Every officer incurring or authorizing expenditure from public moneys should be guided by high standards of financial propriety. Every officer should also enforce financial order and strict economy and see that all relevant financial rules and regulations are observed, by his own office and by subordinate disbursing officers. Among the principles on which emphasis is generally laid are the following:-

- i) Every officer is expected to exercise the same vigilance in respect of expenditure incurred from public moneys as a person of ordinary prudence would exercise in respect of expenditure of his own money.
- ii) The expenditure should not be prima facie more than the occasion demands.
- iii) No authority should exercise its powers of sanctioning expenditure to pass an order which will be directly or indirectly to its own advantage.
- iv) Expenditure from public moneys should not be incurred for the benefit of a particular person or a section of the people, unless -
  - a) a claim for the amount could be enforced in a Court of Law, or
  - b) the expenditure is in pursuance of a recognized policy or custom.
- v) The amount of allowances granted to meet expenditure of a particular type should be so regulated that the allowances are not on the whole a source of profit to the recipients.
- vi) While discharging the duties of financial concurrence of any public expenditure, such

authorities subsequent to such decision, shall not be involved in any future audit responsibilities which may create conflict of interest.

## 1.8 Public Procurement Infrastructure at the Centre


### 1.8.1 Procurement Policy Division
Procurement Policy Division (PPD) in Department of Expenditure; Ministry of Finance has been created to encourage uniformity and harmonisation in public procurement processes by dissemination of best practices, provision of guidance, oversight and capacity building and issuing of procurement manuals. However, Centralisation of procurement or involvement in procurement processes is not the intended purpose of creation of PPD.

question_text: Under the EDI system, where must the Bill of Entry be presented for registration for examination?
answer: Present the Bill of Entry at the counter for registration for examination in the import shed. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 224)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is asking: under the EDI (Electronic Data Interchange) system, where exactly should the Bill of Entry be taken so that it can be registered for the examination of goods.

Next, I recall the part of the Procurement of Goods Manual that talks about the EDI system and the registration step. The manual explains that once the Bill of Entry has been assessed—whether through the regular appraising group or after a first check appraisement—it must be brought to a specific place for registration before the shed appraisal can occur.

Then, I note the exact wording used in that section: “the Bill of Entry … needs to be presented at the counter for registration for examination in the import shed.” This tells me both the action (presenting the Bill of Entry) and the location (the counter in the import shed).

After that, I consider why this step is necessary. The registration at the counter triggers the subsequent flow: the Bill of Entry is passed to the shed appraiser, who examines the goods, records the findings, and eventually releases the cargo. Without this registration, the examination cannot proceed in the EDI workflow.

Finally, I synthesize the information: under the EDI system, after assessment the Bill of Entry must be taken to the counter in the import shed to be registered for examination. This matches precisely the required answer.
chunk_content:
#### 4. Examination of goods:
4.1 All imported goods are required to be examined for verification of correctness of description given in the Bill of Entry. However, ordinarily only a part of the consignment is selected on random selection basis and examined. Also, the goods may be examined prior to assessment in case the importer does not have complete information with him at the time of import and requests for examination of the goods before assessing the duty liability or, if the Customs Appraiser/Assistant Commissioner feels the goods are required to be examined before assessment. This is called First Check Appraisement. The importer has to request for First Check Appraisement at the time of filing the Bill of Entry or at data entry stage giving the reason for the same. The Customs Appraiser records on original copy of the Bill of Entry the examination order and returns the Bill of Entry to the importer/CHA for being taken to the import shed for examination of the goods. Thereafter, Shed Appraiser/Dock Examiner examines the goods as per examination order and records his findings. In case appraising group has called for samples, he forwards sealed samples accordingly. The importer is required to bring back the said Bill of Entry to the assessing officer for assessing the Bill of Entry, which is countersigned by Assistant/Deputy Commissioner if the value is more than Rs.1 lakh.

4.2 The imported goods can also be examined subsequent to assessment and payment of duty. This is called Second Check Appraisement. Most of the consignments are cleared on Second Check Appraisement basis. In this case whole of the consignment is not examined and only those packages which are selected on random basis are examined.

4.3 Under the EDI system, the Bill of Entry, after assessment by the appraising group or first appraisement, as the case may be, needs to be presented at the counter for registration for examination in the import shed. A declaration for correctness of entries and genuineness of the original documents needs to be made at this stage. After registration, the Bill of Entry is passed on to the shed Appraiser for examination of the goods. Along with the Bill of Entry, the CHA is required to present all the necessary supporting documents. After examination of the goods, the Shed Appraiser enters the report in EDI system and transfers first appraisement Bill of Entry to the appraising group and gives 'out of charge' in case of already assessed Bills of Entry. Thereupon, the system prints Bill of Entry and order of clearance (in triplicate). All these copies carry the examination report, order of clearance number and name of Shed Appraiser. Two copies each of Bill of Entry and the order are to be returned to the CHA/importer, after the Appraiser signs them. One copy of the order is attached to the Customs copy of Bill of Entry and retained by the Shed Appraiser.

#### 5. Execution of bonds:
5.1 Wherever necessary, for availing duty free assessment or concessional assessment under different schemes and notifications, execution of end use bonds with Bank Guarantee or other surety is required to be furnished. These have to be executed in prescribed forms before the assessing Appraiser. For instance, when the import of goods are made under Export Promotion schemes, the importer is required to execute bonds with the Customs authorities for fulfilment of conditions of respective notifications. If the importer fails to fulfil the conditions, he has to pay the duty leviable on

those goods. The amount of bond of bond and bank guarantee is in terms of the instructions issued by the Board from time to time as well the conditions of the relevant Notification etc.

question_text: Which national carrier must be used for airlifting imported goods from abroad, wherever applicable?
answer:
- **National Carrier Requirement:** Airlifting of imported goods from abroad must be conducted exclusively through the national carrier, Air India, wherever applicable (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 98).  

- **Strategic Implication for Procurement:** Mandating Air India ensures adherence to government directives, reduces compliance risk, and promotes transparent, cost‑effective logistics that align with corporate value‑for‑money objectives.
cot:
I begin by asking what the question is really seeking: it wants to know which airline is required by government policy to handle the air transport of goods that are brought into the country from abroad, whenever such airlifting is feasible.  

Next, I consider what kinds of rules would dictate a specific carrier for import air freight. Typically, such a rule is issued to promote the national airline, to keep strategic transport capacity under domestic control, and to simplify compliance monitoring for procurement officers.  

I then recall the procurement guidance that addresses airlifting of imported goods. It states that, as per the extant government directive, the airlifting of imported goods from abroad must be carried out only through the national carrier, and it identifies that carrier as Air India, with the proviso “wherever applicable.”  

From this, I deduce that the answer to the question is Air India – the national carrier that must be used for airlifting imported goods from abroad when air transport is chosen.  

To deepen the analysis, I think about the rationale behind mandating Air India. Doing so ensures that every import contract automatically follows the government’s shipping directive, which reduces the risk of non‑compliance and the administrative burden of seeking exceptions. It also supports the domestic aviation sector by guaranteeing a steady stream of cargo business for the national airline, and it allows procurement entities to predict freight costs and arrange insurance more transparently, thereby aligning with broader value‑for‑money objectives.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the question’s answer is the national carrier Air India, and the strategic implication of this requirement is that it guarantees adherence to government policy, lowers compliance risk, and promotes cost‑effective, transparent logistics that support the organization’s value‑for‑money goals.

question_text: Is it permissible to refund the security deposit during the execution of the contract for any reason
answer: - Refund of the security deposit, whether full or partial, during the execution of the contract for any reason is not admissible. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p.44)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: it wants to know if, at any point while the contract is still being performed, the security deposit can be returned to the contractor for any reason whatsoever.  

Next, I look for the rule that governs when and how the security deposit may be released. The policy explains that the deposit is held by the organization until the contract work is finished—or until the defect liability period ends, if that period applies—whichever comes later.  

Reading further, the same rule explicitly states that a refund of the deposit, whether in full or in part, is not allowed at any time during the execution of the contract, and this prohibition applies regardless of the reason for the request.  

Putting those pieces together, because the policy bars any refund during the execution phase for any reason, the answer to the question must be that such a refund is not permissible.  

Thus, the conclusion follows directly: refunding the security deposit while the contract is still being executed, for any reason, is not admissible.

##### 1. Release/refund of security deposit.
(a) The security deposit amount deposited by the contractor against a particular contract or work order (WO) or purchase order (PO) will be retained by NRL till completion of execution of the contract or till end of defect liability period whichever is later as per the terms and conditions of the particular contract. Refund of security deposit amount whether full or part, during any time of execution of the contract and due to any reason will not be admissible.

(b) In the cases **where defect liability period is not applicable** as per contract terms and conditions the security deposit will be refunded to the contractor's bank account as provided by the contractor and registered in the NRL vendor master database, within 30 days from date of completion of contract as certified by the respective Engineer In-Charge (EIC) of NRL and after adjustment of recoveries (if any) as per procedure.

(c) In the cases **where defect liability period is applicable** as per contract terms and conditions the security deposit will be refunded to the contractor's bank account as provided by the contractor and registered in the NRL vendor master database, within 60 days from date of expiry of defect liability period as certified by the respective Engineer In-Charge (EIC) of NRL and after adjustment of recoveries (if any) as per procedure.

(d) **Wherever defect liability period is not applicable**, in case the contractor has deposited the security deposit amount in full as per original PO and successfully executed the work as per contract terms and condition without any recoverable from security deposit amount, however the scope of work / quantity / time period has been extended or increased with increase in total contract value through an amendment over original contract, then security deposit equivalent to 10% of the additional / increased contract (PO) amount will be retained by NRL and the balance amount (if any) of security deposit will be refunded to the contractor period as certified by the respective Engineer In-Charge (EIC) of NRL. This provision will not be applicable for the service / work contracts **where defect liability period is applicable**, and in such cases an additional amount equivalent to 10% of the increased value of contract will be deposited by the contractor immediately after acceptance of amendment of original contract, either in full or in installments.

**Note:** For one time jobs, 80% of SD may be released; balance 20% of the SD to be released after the contract is closed (*Closing may be with/without formal approval, as applicable for individual cases*).

question_text: What process can be initiated after the issuance of the completion certificate?
answer:
**Step‑by‑Step Operational Checklist – Post‑Completion Certificate Actions**

1. Verify that the Engineer‑in‑Charge has issued the Completion Certificate confirming that the works are complete in accordance with the contract documents.  
2. Confirm that the applicable Security Deposit or Performance Guarantee is being retained as required.  
3. Initiate the contract closing process to prepare for the release of the balance/final bill to the contractor.  
4. Carry out all necessary recoveries and adjustments before any payment is made.  
5. Obtain a “No Claim Certificate” from the contractor using the format in Annexure 7, if required.  
6. Complete the required departmental reconciliations (materials, works, and payment) as detailed in sections 6.7.3‑6.7.5.  
7. Once the above steps are satisfied, proceed with the release of the balance/final bill and, subsequently, the Security Deposit/PBG release after defect liability obligations are fulfilled.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 109)
cot:
First, I consider what the issuance of a completion certificate actually signifies: the Engineer‑in‑Charge has confirmed that the works have been finished in full accordance with the contract documents and to his satisfaction. That tells me the contractual obligation for the physical work is done, but the financial and administrative closure of the contract is still pending.  

Next, I think about what typically needs to happen before any final money can change hands. The contract usually requires that any security deposit or performance guarantee held as a safeguard be retained until all outstanding matters are settled, so I note that the deposit/PBG must be kept in place for now.  

From there, the logical next move is to start the contract‑closing procedure itself—preparing the final bill, gathering the necessary documentation, and making sure all dues are accounted for. This means I have to look at any recoveries or adjustments that might be due, such as liquidated damages, price reductions for shortfalls, or variations, and settle them before releasing payment.  

I also recall that a “no claim certificate” is often requested as a safeguard against future claims, so obtaining that from the contractor using the prescribed format becomes a necessary step.  

Then I consider the reconciliation activities outlined in the Procurement of Works Manual. I need to verify that all materials, machinery and assets issued to the contractor have been returned or accounted for, including any scrap or off‑cuts. I also have to check that the works themselves have been taken over in good condition and that performance standards, installation, commissioning, as‑built drawings, and the return of loaned items like ID cards, protective gear, and equipment have been satisfied.  

On the payment side, I must ensure there are no outstanding liabilities: any liquidated damages, price reductions, variations, overpayments, duplicate payments, or charges for services such as accommodation, electricity, water, security, transport, cranes, demurrage, insurance, statutory duties paid on the contractor’s behalf, and so on, are all cleared.  

Only after these verifications—completion certificate confirmed, deposit/PBG retained, recoveries/adjustments made, no claim certificate secured, and all departmental reconciliations (materials, works, payment) completed—can I move forward to release the balance/final bill.  

Finally, once the defect liability period has been satisfied and the defect liability certificate or security‑deposit/performance‑guarantee release certificate is issued, the retained deposit/PBG can be returned to the contractor, bringing the contract to a full close.  

This line of thinking naturally yields the operational checklist: verify the completion certificate, retain the security deposit/PBG, initiate contract closing, make recoveries/adjustments, obtain the no claim certificate, conduct the required reconciliations, then release the final bill and later the deposit/PBG after defect liability is cleared.

question_text: What exactly does the statutory auditor or cost auditor have to certify about my local content
answer:
The statutory auditor, cost auditor, practicing cost accountant or practicing chartered accountant must certify two things about your local content:

1. **They have reviewed the local content** in your offer (the specific offer number and date) as required by the purchase‑preference policy linked to local content.  
2. **They certify your bidder’s status and the actual local‑content percentage** in that offer, stating either:  
   - *Class‑I local supplier*: your offer contains **local content equal to or greater than 50 %**, **or**  
   - *Class‑II local supplier*: your offer contains **local content greater than 20 % but less than 50 %**.  

They must also confirm that they are independent (not an employee or director of your company) and that the certification is signed with their seal, membership number, UDIN, etc. This certification is uploaded along with your unpriced bid. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 255)
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question is really after: it wants to know the exact content that a statutory auditor, cost auditor, practicing cost accountant or practicing chartered accountant must put in their certification when they are verifying a bidder’s local‑content claim.  

The first thing I notice is that the reference material provides a specific format—Format‑2B—that is meant to be filled out and signed by those professionals. Scanning that format, I see a clear statement that the auditor must begin by confirming that they have examined the local‑content details in the particular offer being submitted. That tells me the very first item they have to certify is a review of the local‑content information.  

Moving on, the format continues with a clause where the auditor states the bidder’s status and the measured local‑content percentage. It gives two mutually exclusive options: either the offer qualifies as a Class‑I local supplier, meaning the local content is 50 % or higher, or it qualifies as a Class‑II local supplier, meaning the local content is above 20 % but below 50 %. The instruction to strike out the inapplicable option makes it clear that the auditor must choose one of these two classifications and explicitly state the corresponding percentage range.  

Beyond the substantive statements, the format also reminds the auditor that they must be independent—neither an employee nor a director of the bidding company—and that the certification must be signed with their seal, membership number, UDIN and other identifying details. This reinforces that the certification is not just a statement about the numbers but also a declaration of the auditor’s eligibility and authenticity.  

Putting these pieces together, I see that the auditor’s certification has two core parts: first, an affirmation that they have reviewed the local‑content data in the offer; second, a declaration of the bidder’s local‑content class—either Class‑I (≥ 50 %) or Class‑II (> 20 % and < 50 %). The additional requirements about independence, signature and supporting details are procedural safeguards that accompany those substantive certifications.  

Thus, the exact answer to the question is that the statutory or cost auditor must certify (1) that they have reviewed the local‑content in the bidder’s offer as required by the purchase‑preference policy, and (2) that they certify the bidder’s status and the actual local‑content percentage, indicating either Class‑I (≥ 50 %) or Class‑II (> 20 % but < 50 %), while also confirming their independence and providing the necessary sign‑off details. This matches the explanation that the certification is uploaded with the unpriced bid.

question_text: Where does the Project Import Group keep a note of the description and value of goods for each project
answer: The Project Import Group records the description and value of goods for each project in the Project Contract Register and in the project‑specific file maintained by the Group. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 228)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know where the Project Import Group stores a record of the description and value of goods for each project.  

Next, I consider the process described for handling project imports. The registration step explains that after the contract is approved, the details of the contract are entered into a register kept for that purpose and a registration number is issued. This tells me that the Group maintains a register where the contract particulars—including description and value—are recorded.  

Then, I consider the clearance stage. When a Bill of Entry is submitted, the Group checks the description, value, and quantity of the goods against what was registered. To perform this check, the Group must have those details readily available. The Group keeps a note of the description and value of the goods in the Project Contract Register and also in the file maintained in the Group for each project.  

Putting these pieces together, the place where the description and value are noted is not just the register used at registration but also a project‑specific file that the Group keeps for ongoing reference.  

Therefore, the Project Import Group records the description and value of goods for each project in the Project Contract Register and in the project‑specific file maintained by the Group.

question_text: What does the Supplied by column reveal about the equipment source
answer:
- The **Supplied by** column identifies the actual source delivering the equipment to the buyer: either the **Equipment Manufacturer (OEM)** or an **Integrator / Sole Service Provider / Licensor** operating locally.  
- When the entry reads **Equipment Manufacturer**, the procurement is sourcing directly from the original equipment maker, ensuring a clear OEM provenance.  
- When the entry reads **Integrator / Sole Service Provider / Licensor (in country or region)**, the equipment is supplied through a value‑added intermediary that may perform further processing, customisation, or localisation.  
- This distinction enables senior management to verify supply‑chain transparency, assess risk associated with intermediary involvement, and confirm that procurement practices align with corporate goals for value‑for‑money and strategic sourcing.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 186)

That tells me the column is meant to pinpoint the exact party that delivers the equipment to the buyer, rather than just who designed or built it.  
When the entry reads “Equipment Manufacturer”, the logical inference is that the buyer is dealing directly with the original maker—there’s no middle‑hand involved, so the provenance is a pure OEM source.  
When the entry reads “Integrator / Sole Service Provider / Licensor (in country or region)”, the implication shifts: the equipment is reaching the buyer through a local intermediary that may have added further processing, customisation, or localisation before delivery.  
Thus, the column distinguishes between a straight‑from‑OEM supply chain and a supply chain that includes a value‑added intermediary.  
Having that distinction visible lets senior management see exactly who is in the delivery path, which helps them verify supply‑chain transparency, gauge any risk introduced by intermediaries, and confirm that the procurement approach matches corporate objectives for cost‑effectiveness and strategic sourcing.  
Putting those pieces together, the “Supplied by” column reveals the actual source delivering the equipment—either the OEM directly or a local integrator/sole service provider/licensor—and clarifies whether the equipment arrives as‑is or after additional processing/customisation.

question_text: How can a government modify the procurement guidelines for certain procuring entities
answer: The government can adjust the procurement guidelines for particular procuring entities by issuing a general or special notification that authorizes those entities to adopt detailed, approved procurement procedures. These procedures may differ in certain details from the standard guidelines but must remain aligned with the essential elements of the Procurement Guidelines.
