Scanning that part, I see a statement that the government can, by issuing a general or special notification, allow certain procuring entities to adopt their own detailed approved procurement procedures.  

I then note that these entity‑specific procedures are permitted to differ in some details from the standard guidelines, but they must still conform to the essential elements of the overall Procurement Guidelines.  

Putting those points together, I conclude that the government modifies the guidelines for particular entities through a general or special notification that authorizes those entities to follow tailored, approved procedures, provided the procedures stay aligned with the core requirements of the Procurement Guidelines.

question_text: What happens if no bids are received in the last five minutes before the auction closes
answer: If no bids are received in the final five minutes before the auction closes, the reverse auction will end automatically at the scheduled closing time and will not be extended. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 264)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what actually causes the auction to be extended. The rule says an extension only happens when a bid is placed in the final five minutes and that bid is accepted as the lowest offer. So the extension is conditional on two things: a bid arriving in that window and that bid being the winning one.  

Next, I consider the opposite situation: what if no bid shows up in those last five minutes? Without a bid, the first condition isn’t met, and therefore the trigger for an extension can’t fire. Since the rule explicitly states that the auto‑extension occurs only if a bid comes in those last five minutes and is accepted, the absence of any bid means the condition fails outright.  

Because the trigger fails, there is no mechanism that would lengthen the auction; the system simply follows the default schedule. The original close time remains unchanged, and the auction proceeds to shut down at that moment.  

I also note that the instructions warn bidders not to wait until the last seconds precisely to avoid missing the window, which reinforces that the window is the only chance for an extension—if it’s unused, the auction ends.  

Putting it together, when no bids are received in the final five minutes, the auction does not get extended and closes automatically at the scheduled time. This matches the given answer: the reverse auction ends automatically without any extension.

question_text: Can I get a refund if the duty I paid was later judged to be excessive by an appellate authority
answer: Yes, you can apply for a refund if an appellate authority later judges that the duty you paid was excessive. The refund claim must be filed within the applicable time limit – six months from the date of the judgment (or one year if the import was for personal use, government, educational, research, charitable or hospital purposes). You need to submit the refund application with supporting documents such as the assessment copy, sales invoice and any other evidence showing that the duty was paid in excess and that the burden was not passed on to anyone else. Once the application is complete, Customs will acknowledge it and process the claim; if the duty is found refundable, an order for refund will be issued (subject to the Consumer Welfare Fund rules). (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 230)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the rules say about getting a refund when a duty payment is later found to be too high by an appellate body. The core of the question is whether such a judgment creates a right to reclaim the excess amount.

Next, I recall that the law sets a deadline for filing a refund claim, and that deadline isn’t always calculated from the day the duty was paid. Instead, when the right to a refund arises because of a judgment, decree, order or direction from an appellate authority, the limitation period starts from the date of that judgment. So the appellate decision itself triggers the clock.

Then I consider which limitation period applies. Normally the window is six months from the date the duty becomes refundable, but if the import was for personal use, by the government, or by an educational, research, charitable institution or hospital, the period stretches to one year. Therefore, after the appellate judgment I would have either six months or a year, depending on my status as the importer.

After establishing the timing, I think about what the refund application must contain. To succeed, I need to show that the duty I paid was indeed in excess of what was legally due, that I have not shifted that cost onto anyone else, and that I haven’t already obtained a refund for the same amount. Supporting documents like the assessment copy, sales invoice and any other proof of over‑payment would be required.

Once the application is submitted, Customs first checks whether it’s complete. If it is, they issue an acknowledgement; if not, they return it with a note on what’s missing and I would resupply the deficient items. A complete application is then examined to determine whether any part of the duty paid is actually refundable.

If the examination finds that the duty was excessive, Customs will pass an order for refund. However, the law also directs that any amount found refundable must, in most cases, be transferred to the Consumer Welfare Fund, unless a specific exception applies at the time of the claim.

Putting these points together leads to the conclusion: yes, a refund is available when an appellate authority later judges the duty excessive, provided the claim is filed within the appropriate time limit (six months from the judgment, or one year for certain importer categories), accompanied by the necessary evidence showing excess payment and no passing on of the burden, and after Customs processes the claim and issues a refund order (subject to the Consumer Welfare Fund rule).

### 3. Relevant dates for submission of a refund application:
3.1 In terms of Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962 an application for refund is required to be filed within six months from the date of payment of duty and interest and in case of any import made by an individual for his personal use or by Government or by an educational, research or charitable institution or hospital, application for refund is to be filed within one year from the date of payment of duty and interest. Normally, the time limit of six months or one year is computed from the date of payment of duty; however, in following situations, such time limit is computed differently:

(a) In case of goods which are exempt from payment of duty by an ad-hoc exemption order issued under Section 25(2) of the Customs Act, 1962 the limitation of one year or six months, as the case may be, is to be computed from the date of issue of such order;

(b) Where duty becomes refundable as a consequence of judgment, decree, order or direction of the appellate authority, Appellate Tribunal or any court, the limitation of one year or six months, as the case may be, is to be computed from the date of such judgment, decree, order or direction

(c) Where any duty is paid provisionally under Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1962 the limitation of one year or six months, as the case may be, is to be computed from the date of adjustment of duty after the final assessment thereof; and

(d) The date of payment of any duty and interest in relation to a person, other than the importer shall be 'the date of purchase of goods' by such person.

3.2 The limitation of one year or six months, as the case may be, for claiming refund does not apply where any duty and interest has been paid under protest.

#### 4. Processing of refund claim:
4.1 The application for refund is required to be filed with documentary or other evidence including documents relating to assessment, sales invoice and other like documents to support the claim that the duty and interest was paid in excess,

· incidence of duty or interest has not been passed on by him to any other person, and the refund has not been obtained already.

4.2 Where on scrutiny, the application is found to be complete in all respects the Customs issues an acknowledgement in the prescribed Form. However, in case the application is found to be incomplete, the Customs will return the same to the applicant, pointing out the deficiency. The applicant has to then re-submit the application after making good the deficiency.

4.3 The application of refund found to be complete in all respects by Customs, is processed to see if the whole or any part of the duty and interest paid by the applicant is refundable. In case, the whole or any part of the duty and interest is found to be refundable, an order for refund is passed. However, in view of the provisions of unjust enrichment enshrined in the Customs Act, the amount found refundable has to be transferred to the Consumer Welfare Fund except some situations for which relevant custom provisions as applicable during the time of claim are to be referred.

question_text: How does the policy’s loading of advance costs in bid evaluation safeguard against unnecessary financial exposure
answer:
Advance payments are discouraged; when they are unavoidable, the financing cost of the advance is loaded into the bid price during evaluation (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 109).  
- This loading makes bids that require advances less competitive, encouraging suppliers to offer terms without advance or to absorb the cost.  
- By internalizing the cost of advance financing, the evaluation process aligns supplier incentives with the organization’s risk‑management objective of limiting unnecessary financial exposure.  
- The approach preserves transparency, supports value‑for‑money decisions, and safeguards corporate funds from inadvertent advance‑related risk.
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: how does adding a cost for advance payments into the bid evaluation actually protect the organization from taking on needless financial risk.  
Then I look at the policy backdrop: advance payments are normally discouraged because they put money out before any work or delivery occurs, and they are only allowed under special conditions that must be approved.  
When an advance is unavoidable, the policy says that the financing cost of that advance—essentially the interest or opportunity cost of tying up funds—should be loaded into the bid price during evaluation.  
By doing this, any bid that includes an advance becomes more expensive in the evaluation score, which makes it less competitive compared to bids that offer standard payment terms or that absorb the financing cost themselves.  
This creates a clear incentive for suppliers either to avoid asking for advances or to internalize the cost, thereby shifting the financial burden away from the procuring entity.  
As a result, the evaluation process aligns supplier behavior with the organization’s risk‑management goal of limiting unnecessary exposure, preserves transparency in comparing bids, and safeguards corporate funds from inadvertent advance‑related risk.

question_text: Is there a ceiling on how much the price can increase, and how can that limit be set
answer: Yes, the price variation clause can include a ceiling on how much the price may increase. That limit can be defined as a percentage per year, an overall ceiling, or a combination of both, depending on what the parties agree to. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 111)
cot:
First, I consider what a price variation clause is meant to do: it adjusts the contract price in line with changes in input costs or indices, but left unchecked it could allow the price to rise indefinitely as those indices fluctuate.  
Then, I think about why the parties would want to limit that exposure—especially the buyer, who needs protection against runaway escalation, and the supplier, who may also benefit from predictability. This leads naturally to the idea of inserting a ceiling that caps how much the price may be increased under the clause.  
Looking at how such clauses are typically drafted, I see that the ceiling itself can be expressed in a few standard ways: it might be a maximum percentage increase allowed each year, a total ceiling that applies over the life of the contract, or a combination of both an annual cap and an overall cap.  
Next, I note that the exact formulation is not prescribed by law or regulation; it is left to the negotiators to decide what best balances risk and flexibility for their particular situation.  
Finally, I bring these points together: because the clause can expressly provide for a ceiling, and because that ceiling can be set as a yearly percentage, an overall limit, or both, the answer to the question is affirmative—the limit exists and is defined by the parties’ agreement in those terms.

question_text: What specific role does the Independent External Monitor play in the tender process and contract execution?
answer:
- The Independent External Monitor (IEM) is appointed by NRL to monitor the tender process and the execution of awarded contracts for compliance with the Integrity Pact principles of legality, fairness, transparency and economic use of resources. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 244)  
- The IEM receives and records bidder disputes or complaints, requiring a signed written submission to establish the date of receipt, and follows up via telephone, email or written correspondence. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 245)  
- By overseeing both stages, the IEM helps NRL identify non‑compliance early, thereby protecting the organization from procurement‑related risk, safeguarding value for money and reinforcing strategic procurement objectives.
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is asking: it wants the exact function of the Independent External Monitor during both the tender phase and the subsequent contract execution.  

Looking at the description of the Integrity Pact, I see that the Principal partners with Transparency International and appoints an Independent External Monitor specifically to oversee the tender process and the execution of the contract for compliance with the pact’s core principles—legality, fairness, transparency and economical use of resources. This tells me the monitor’s primary duty is surveillance: watching how bids are handled and how the contract is performed to make sure those principles are upheld.  

Next, the note about bidder disputes clarifies another facet of the monitor’s role. It says bidders may raise complaints with the Independent External Monitor by telephone and email followed by a written document, but the official date of receipt is only when a signed written document is received. This indicates the monitor acts as a grievance receiver, logging complaints and insisting on a formal written submission to establish a clear, traceable record.  

The same passage also notes that after receiving a complaint, the monitor follows up via telephone, email or written correspondence. So beyond just recording, the monitor actively engages with the parties to address the issue, ensuring that concerns are communicated and tracked.  

Putting these pieces together, the monitor’s oversight and complaint‑handling work together to spot any deviation from the Integrity Pact early in the procurement cycle. By catching non‑compliance quickly, the Principal can avoid costly procurement‑related risks, preserve value for money, and stay aligned with its broader strategic procurement goals.  

Therefore, the Independent External Monitor’s specific role is to monitor the tender process and contract execution for Integrity Pact compliance, to receive and record bidder disputes requiring a signed written submission, to follow up on those complaints through various channels, and by doing so to help the organization detect problems early, mitigate procurement risk, safeguard value for money and reinforce strategic procurement objectives.

question_text: Within what timeframe must a subsequent award be made to the next eligible agency in case of refusal by the selected L1 bidder
answer: The subsequent award to the next eligible agency must be made within the original offer’s validity period, or, if that period has been extended, within the extended offer validity. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 76)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is asking: it wants the specific time limit for making a follow‑on award to the next eligible agency when the originally selected L1 bidder refuses to take up the contract.  

Next, I scan the provided material for any mention of what happens after a refusal by the L1 bidder. The section dealing with lottery selection and the consequences of refusal or failure contains the relevant rule.  

Reading that rule, it states clearly that in the event of a “refusal”, the job—or the remaining part of it—may be offered to another L1 agency, and that this subsequent award must be made “within original or extended offer validity.”  

This tells me that the clock for the next award is tied to the validity period of the original offer: if the original offer is still valid, the award must occur before it expires; if the procuring entity has already extended that validity, the award must occur within the extended period.  

Putting those pieces together, the timeframe for the subsequent award is therefore the original offer’s validity period, or, if that period has been extended, the extended offer validity.  

Finally, I verify that this conclusion matches the answer given and that no extra conditions or alternatives have been introduced. The reasoning flows naturally from the question to the specific clause and then to the precise time limit.

question_text: How will you refer to your registered contract in all future communications with customs
answer: When you need to communicate with Customs about your contract, simply use the Project Contract Registration Number that was assigned to you when your contract was registered. This number should be mentioned in every subsequent correspondence or document you send to Customs. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 227)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: it wants to know the specific identifier I should use whenever I write to Customs about the contract I have already registered.  

Next, I recall the registration process itself—once the contract is submitted and accepted, Customs does not keep referring to the original document; instead, they create a reference point for that contract in their system.  

Then, I think about what that reference point looks like in practice. The procedure tells me that after the documents are checked and the contract is deemed eligible, the Customs officer enters the details into a register and issues a unique number tied to that contract.  

After that, I realize that this number is meant to replace the need to re‑attach the full contract or any of its annexes in later dealings; it serves as a shorthand that both parties can instantly recognize.  

Finally, I conclude that in every future Bill of Entry, letter, email, or any other communication with Customs concerning the project, I must quote that Project Contract Registration Number so that Customs can quickly locate the registered contract and proceed with assessment or clearance. This matches the instruction to mention the number in all subsequent correspondence.

question_text: If I sell drugs that have an expiry date at a reduced price, is the fall clause triggered?
answer: No. The fall clause does not apply when you sell drugs that have an expiry date, even if you reduce the price. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 138)
cot:
First, I need to understand what activates the fall clause in a rate contract. It kicks in when the contract holder lowers the price—or even offers to sell—the contracted goods or services under the same conditions as the original contract, and that lower price is extended to any other buyer during the contract’s term.  

Next, I look at the specific situation: I am selling drugs that carry an expiry date, and I am doing so at a reduced price. The key question is whether this price reduction falls under the fall clause’s scope.  

To answer that, I examine the exceptions listed for the fall clause. The provisions explicitly state that the clause does not apply to sales of goods such as drugs that have an expiry date. This means that even if the price is cut, the special rule for expiry‑dated drugs removes the transaction from the fall clause’s reach.  

Since the sale I am considering matches exactly one of those excluded categories—drugs with an expiry date—the fall clause cannot be triggered by the price reduction.  

Putting it together, the fall clause remains inactive in this case, and the rate contract price stays unchanged for subsequent supplies. Therefore, the answer is that the fall clause is not triggered.

question_text: How does the presence of a defect liability period change the refund timeline for the security deposit
answer:
The presence of a defect liability period (DLP) directly extends the timeframe for security‑deposit refund. When the contract does **not** include a DLP, NRL will return the deposit to the contractor’s bank account within **30 days** of the contract‑completion date, as certified by the Engineer‑In‑Charge (EIC), after any applicable recoveries are deducted.  

Conversely, if a DLP **is** stipulated in the contract, the security deposit is retained until the DLP expires. Refund is then made **within 60 days** of the DLP‑expiry date, again certified by the EIC and after adjustment of any recoveries.  

Thus, the DLP shifts the refund trigger from contract completion to the end of the defect liability period and adds an additional 30‑day window to the refund schedule. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p.44)
cot:
To start with, I need to understand what the question is really asking: it wants to know how the existence of a defect liability period alters the schedule for returning a contractor’s security deposit.  

First, I consider the two possible contract structures. One type of contract does not include a defect liability period at all; the other type explicitly requires a defect liability period after the work is finished.  

Next, I look at what governs the refund in each case. When there is no defect liability period, the contract is considered complete as soon as the work is finished and certified by the Engineer‑In‑Charge. The security deposit can then be released, but only after a set waiting period that allows for any final recoveries to be calculated—this waiting period is 30 days from the certification date.  

Then I turn to the situation where a defect liability period is stipulated. Here, the deposit is not released at the moment the work ends because the contractor remains liable for any defects that might appear during the liability period. The deposit is held until the defect liability period itself ends and is certified by the Engineer‑In‑Charge. Only after that point does the refund process begin, and the applicable waiting period is longer—60 days from the certification of the defect liability period’s expiry—again to accommodate any recoveries or adjustments.  

Building on this, I see that the presence of a defect liability period shifts the trigger for the refund from the date of contract completion to the date the defect liability period ends. At the same time, it adds an extra 30 days to the refund window (moving from a 30‑day window to a 60‑day window).  

Taking this further, the extra time reflects the need to cover the liability period itself and to give the administering authority sufficient time to verify that no recoverable amounts remain before releasing the funds.  

In sum, the defect liability period changes the refund timeline by moving the start point from contract completion to the expiry of the defect liability period and by extending the allowable refund period from 30 days to 60 days after that point. This matches the description that, without a defect liability period, the deposit is refunded within 30 days of contract completion, whereas with a defect liability period it is retained until the period ends and then refunded within 60 days of its expiry.

question_text: Which department receives the surplus list for assessing future maintenance requirements
answer:
- The Project Department distributes the surplus list to all Maintenance Departments so they can assess future requirements and reuse excess materials (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 163).  

This practice supports corporate goals by minimizing idle inventory costs, enhancing transparency, and ensuring that procurement decisions align with strategic value‑for‑money objectives.
cot:
The question is asking which department gets the surplus list so that it can evaluate what might be needed later for maintenance work.  
First, I recall the procedure for handling surplus items: the EPCM Consultant prepares the final Project Surplus item List and sends it to the Project Department.  
Next, the Project Department does not keep the list for itself; instead, it forwards that list to every maintenance department.  
The purpose of sending the list to the maintenance groups is explicitly stated—to let them see what surplus material is available and determine if any of it could satisfy future maintenance requirements.  
Therefore, the department that actually receives the surplus list for the purpose of assessing future needs is the maintenance department (or all maintenance departments collectively).  
This aligns with the description that the Project Department distributes the surplus list to all Maintenance Departments so they can assess future requirements and reuse any excess materials.

- Reduce security hazard, enhance safety.
- Make space available for other purpose.
- Recycling for cleaner environment.

Consequently, there accumulates, a large quantity of material which is neither usable for the purpose for which it was originally procured nor of any other operational value. question_text: Who should review draft interim reports and within how many days must they be approved?
answer:
**Who should review draft interim reports and within how many days must they be approved?**  
The Procuring Entity should review draft interim reports, discussing them with the consultants in the field, and must approve them within fifteen days.  

*Rationale:* The manual specifies that the Procuring Entity should not take more than 15 days to review and approve draft interim reports and that they should discuss the drafts with consultants in the field. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 28)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants to know who is responsible for reviewing draft interim reports and how quickly that review must be completed.  
Interim reports are meant to keep the Procuring Entity informed about preliminary results, alternative solutions, and major decisions that need to be made. Because the recommendations in these reports can affect later phases of the assignment, it makes sense that the Procuring Entity would be the party that needs to examine them.  
The Procuring Entity should discuss the draft interim reports with the consultants in the field, indicating that the review is not a solitary activity but involves consultation with the team producing the report.  
Finally, the time limit is specified: the Procuring Entity should not take more than fifteen days to review and approve draft interim reports.  
Putting these points together, the reviewer is the Procuring Entity, they should engage the consultants in the field during the review, and they must finish the approval process within fifteen days.

The assignments, deliverables and reporting should be clearly specified. In particular, for inception and progress reports, there should be a balance between keeping the Procuring Entity well informed and not forcing consultants to spend an excessive amount of time preparing minor reports. The ToR should indicate the format, frequency, and content of reports as well as the number of copies, the language, and the names of the prospective recipients of the reports. For all major reports, an executive summary is recommended as a separate section. Depending on the assignment, the following reports are usually required;

- a) **Inception Report:** This report should be submitted at initial stage of the contract (say about four weeks after the commencement date). Any major inconsistency in the ToR, staffing problems, or deficiency in Procuring Entity's assistance that have become apparent during this period should be included. The inception report is designed to give the Procuring Entity confidence that the assignment can be carried out as planned and as agreed upon in the contract, and should bring to its attention major problems that might affect the direction and progress of the work.
- b) **Progress Reports:** These reports keep the Procuring Entity regularly informed about the progress of the assignment. They may also provide warnings of anticipated problems or serve as a reminder for payment of invoices due. Depending on the assignment, progress reports may be delivered monthly or bimonthly. For feasibility studies and design assignments, delivery of progress reports at two-month intervals is satisfactory. For technical assistance and implementation supervision, for instance, construction, progress reports are best submitted monthly. Progress reports may include a bar chart showing details of progress and any changes in the assignment schedule. Photographs with time-stamping are a quick and easy way of conveying the status of a project, and their use in progress reports should be encouraged. For technical assistance services, progress reports also serve as a means of setting out the work program for the following months. Each team member usually contributes to the preparation of the monthly report.
- c) **Interim Reports:** If the assignment is phased, interim reports are required to inform the Procuring Entity of preliminary results, alternative solutions, and major decisions that need

to be made. Since the recommendations of an interim report may affect later phases of the assignment and even influence the results of the project, the Procuring Entity should discuss the draft interim reports with consultants in the field. The Procuring Entity should not take more than 15 (fifteen) days to review and approve draft interim reports.

question_text: If joint ventures are allowed, has an Implementation Board with participation of all JV partners been provided?

Next, I think about why such a requirement would exist. Joint ventures can sometimes lead to uneven participation or diluted accountability, especially when quality is a major factor in the evaluation. To guard against those risks, any allowance of joint ventures should come with safeguards that make sure all partners stay engaged and deliver their share of the work throughout the contract.  

Looking at the guidance on joint ventures, it says that if they are allowed, adequate safeguards must be put in place to ensure that every JV partner is present and continues to perform services for the entire duration. One concrete safeguard mentioned is the creation of an Implementation Board that brings together all the JV partners, and it also notes that the procuring entity’s project manager may be invited to attend when needed.  

From that, I see that the Implementation Board is not just an optional suggestion; it is presented as a specific measure to fulfill the safeguard obligation. Therefore, if the goal is to meet the safeguard requirement when joint ventures are allowed, providing such a board is the prescribed action.  

Putting the pieces together, the logical conclusion is that yes, an Implementation Board with the participation of all JV partners should be provided as part of the safeguards when joint ventures are permitted.

question_text: According to the Professionalism Principle, what must procuring authorities ensure in the procurement process
answer:
Procuring authorities must ensure the following in the procurement process, in accordance with the Professionalism Principle:

1. **Uphold professionalism, economy, efficiency, effectiveness, and integrity** throughout all procurement activities.  
   *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 17)*  

2. **Avoid wasteful, dilatory, and improper practices** that violate the Code of Integrity for Public Procurement (CIPP) described in Chapter 3 of the manual.  
   *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 17)*  

3. **Adopt a methodology that is reasonable and appropriate to the cost and complexity of the procurement** and that effectively achieves the planned objective of the procurement.  
   *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 17)*  

4. **Bring efficiency, economy, and transparency** to public procurement, ensure fair and equitable treatment of suppliers, and promote competition.  
   *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

5. **Conform to the procedural yardsticks** listed below when conducting public procurement:  

   a. **Subject‑matter description**  
      1. Be objective, functional, generic, and measurable, specifying technical, qualitative, and performance characteristics.  
      2. Not indicate a requirement for a particular trademark, trade name, or brand.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

   b. **Specifications**  
      Clearly spell out quality, type, and quantity in view of the organization’s specific needs; meet basic needs without superfluous or non‑essential features that could cause unwarranted expenditure.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

   c. **Technical specifications basis**  
      Where applicable, base specifications on national technical regulations, recognized national standards, or building codes; if none exist, use relevant international standards. For Government of India‑funded projects abroad, specifications may be based on the host beneficiary government’s standards, provided any deviation is recorded in writing.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

   d. **Quantity control**  
      Avoid purchasing quantities in excess of requirements to prevent inventory carrying costs.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

   e. **Invitation of offers**  
      Invite offers following a fair, transparent, and reasonable procedure.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

   f. **Adequacy of selected offer**  
      Ensure the selected offer adequately meets the requirement in all respects.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

   g. **Price reasonableness**  
      Verify that the price of the selected offer is reasonable and consistent with the required quality.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

   h. **Record of considerations**  
      At each procurement stage, record in precise terms the considerations that influenced the decision.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 18)*  

   i. **Annual Procurement Plan**  
      After budget finalization, prepare and publish an Annual Procurement Plan on the NRL website.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 19)*  

   j. **Compliance with restrictions**  
      Observe any written orders from the Department of Expenditure imposing restrictions (including prior registration or screening) on procurement from specific countries or classes of countries on grounds of defence of India or national security; no procurement may be made in violation of such restrictions.  
      *(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 19)*  

By following these numbered steps and substeps, junior procurement officers can ensure that their procurement activities align with the Professionalism Principle, thereby maintaining compliance, transparency, and effectiveness in public procurement.
cot:
First, I consider what the Professionalism Principle actually demands of those who run public procurements. It is not a vague call for good behavior; it bundles together a set of concrete attributes—professionalism, economy, efficiency, effectiveness, and integrity—that the authority must embody in every step of the process.  

Next, I translate those attributes into specific obligations. To uphold professionalism and integrity, the authority has to steer clear of any wasteful, dilatory, or improper actions that would breach the Code of Integrity for Public Procurement. At the same time, it must adopt a procurement methodology that is sensible given the cost and complexity of the purchase and that actually delivers the intended outcome.  

Then I look at the broader responsibilities that flow from those core duties: the authority should bring efficiency, economy, and transparency to the whole system, treat all suppliers fairly and equitably, and actively promote competition. These are the overarching goals that shape the detailed rules that follow.  

After that, I work through the procedural yardsticks that operationalize the principle. The description of what is being bought must be objective, functional, generic, and measurable, and it must avoid naming any particular brand or trademark. Specifications for quality, type, and quantity need to be spelled out clearly, matching the organization’s real needs without loading in unnecessary features that would drive up cost. When technical standards exist—whether national regulations, recognized national standards, building codes, or, failing those, relevant international standards—the specifications should be based on them; for overseas Indian‑funded projects, the host country’s standards may be used provided any deviation is documented.  

I then note that buying more than what is required should be avoided to keep inventory carrying costs low, and that invitations to submit offers must follow a fair, transparent, and reasonable procedure. The authority must also verify that the chosen offer truly satisfies every requirement and that its price is reasonable in relation to the quality demanded.  

Further, I consider the need for accountability: at each stage of the procurement, the authority has to record precisely what factors influenced its decision. Once the budget is set, an Annual Procurement Plan must be prepared and published on the NRL website. Finally, any written orders from the Department of Expenditure that restrict procurement from certain countries or classes of countries on defence or national‑security grounds must be obeyed, and no purchase may violate those restrictions.  

By moving from the abstract attributes of the principle down to the concrete actions they entail, I see that the procuring authorities must ensure all of the items listed—professionalism, economy, efficiency, effectiveness, integrity; avoidance of wasteful practices; adoption of an appropriate and effective methodology; efficiency, economy, transparency, fair treatment, and promotion of competition; and conformity with each of the procedural yardsticks covering description, specifications, technical basis, quantity control, invitation of offers, adequacy of the selected offer, price reasonableness, record of considerations, annual planning, and compliance with restrictions. This synthesis matches exactly what the answer states.

### ii) Professionalism Principle
As per these synergic attributes, the procuring authorities have a responsibility and accountability to ensure professionalism, economy, efficiency, effectiveness and integrity in the procurement process. They must avoid wasteful, dilatory and improper practices violating the Code of integrity for Public Procurement (CIPP) mentioned in Chapter 3 of this manual. They should, at the same time, ensure that the methodology adopted for procurement should not only be reasonable and appropriate for the cost and complexity but should also effectively achieve the planned objective

of the procurement. As part of this principle, the Government may prescribe professional standards and specify suitable training and certification requirements for officials dealing with procurement matters.

Procuring entity shall have the responsibility and accountability to bring efficiency, economy, and transparency in matters relating to public procurement and for fair and equitable treatment of suppliers and promotion of competition in public procurement.

The procedure to be followed in making public procurement must conform to the following yardsticks:-

- a) *The description of the subject matter of procurement to the extent practicable should -*
  1. *be objective, functional, generic and measurable and specify technical, qualitative and performance characteristics;*
  2. *not indicate a requirement for a particular trade mark, trade name or brand.*
- b) *The specifications in terms of quality, type etc., as also quantity of goods to be procured, should be clearly spelt out keeping in view the specific needs of the procuring organisations. The specifications so worked out should meet the basic needs of the organisation without including superfluous and non-essential features, which may result in unwarranted expenditure.*
- c) *Where applicable, the technical specifications shall, to the extent practicable, be based on the national technical regulations or recognized national standards or building codes, wherever such standards exist, and in their absence, be based on the relevant international standards. In case of Government of India funded projects abroad, the technical specifications may be framed based on requirements and standards of the host beneficiary Government, where such standards exist. Provided that a procuring entity may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, adopt any other technical specification*

- e) *offers should be invited following a fair, transparent and reasonable procedure;*
- f) *the procuring authority should be satisfied that the selected offer adequately meets the requirement in all respects;*
- g) *the procuring authority should satisfy itself that the price of the selected offer is reasonable and consistent with the quality required;*
- h) *at each stage of procurement the concerned procuring authority must place on record, in precise terms, the considerations which weighed with it while taking the procurement decision.*

question_text: Under what circumstances is a contractor entitled to a time extension that would exempt them from liquidated damages for delay?
answer:
**Determining Eligibility for a Time Extension that Exempts the Contractor from Liquidated Damages**

**Purpose:**  
Provide procurement officers with a clear, numbered procedure to assess whether a contractor’s delay qualifies for a time extension, thereby preventing the application of liquidated damages (LD) for that period.

---

### Step 1: Identify the Nature of the Delay  
- **Action:** Review the event that caused the delay (e.g., design change, natural disaster, instruction from the procuring entity).  
- **Tip:** Distinguish between delays attributable to the contractor and those arising from external or contractual sources.  

### Step 2: Verify if the Delay Falls Under an Exempt Category  
Check the delay against the three statutorily recognized grounds for a time extension:  

| Exempt Ground | Description | Typical Evidence |
|---------------|-------------|------------------|
| **Change of Scope** | Modifications to the original works or services that were not contemplated at bid stage. | Variation orders, approved scope change documents. |
| **Force Majeure** | Unforeseeable events beyond the parties’ control (e.g., earthquake, flood, pandemic, war). | Official notices, meteorological reports, government declarations. |
| **Delay Caused by or Attributable to NRL** | Delays initiated by the procuring entity (NRL) or its representatives (e.g., delayed site access, late provision of information). | Correspondence showing NRL’s instruction or delay, minutes of meetings. |

If the delay matches any of these categories, proceed to Step 3; otherwise, the contractor remains liable for LD.

### Step 3: Gather and Document Supporting Evidence  
- **Action:** Collect all relevant records that prove the exempt cause (e.g., variation orders, force‑majeure certificates, NRL‑issued notices).  
- **Action:** Prepare a concise delay analysis showing the start date, expected completion date, and the number of days attributable to the exempt cause.  
- **Common Pitfall:** Submitting vague or incomplete documentation; ensure each day claimed is directly linked to the exempt event.

### Step 4: Notify the Engineer (EIC) and Submit a Formal Time‑Extension Request  
- **Action:** Inform the Engineer‑in‑Charge (EIC) in writing as soon as the exempt delay is identified (contractual notice period usually applies).  
- **Action:** File a formal request for a time extension, attaching the evidence compiled in Step 3 and referencing the relevant contract clause (change of scope, force majeure, or NRL‑caused delay).  
- **Tip:** Use the contract’s prescribed format for extension requests to avoid procedural rejection.

### Step 5: Obtain Approval and Adjust the Contract Schedule  
- **Action:** Await the EIC’s evaluation and formal approval of the extension.  
- **Action:** Upon approval, update the project schedule to reflect the new completion date.  
- **Result:** Liquidated damages are **not** applicable for the period covered by the approved extension; LD would resume only if further delay occurs beyond the extended date.  
- **Common Pitfall:** Assuming the extension is automatic; never delay LD recovery without explicit written approval.

---

**Practical Example**  
A contractor’s work is halted for ten days because a sudden landslide (force majeure) blocks access to the site. The contractor obtains a landslide‑risk certificate from the local authority, notifies the EIC on the second day of the event, and submits a time‑extension request with the certificate and a delay analysis. The EIC approves a ten‑day extension. Consequently, no LD is charged for those ten days; LD would apply only if work remains incomplete after the extended completion date.

By following these steps, procurement officers can consistently determine when a contractor is entitled to a time exemption from liquidated damages, ensuring compliance with contractual provisions and minimizing procedural errors. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 76)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really getting at: it wants to know when a contractor can avoid liquidated damages by securing a time extension. The core idea is that liquidated damages only apply to delays that are the contractor’s responsibility, so any delay that stems from something outside the contractor’s control—or that the procuring entity itself caused—should excuse the contractor from those penalties, provided the proper procedures are followed.

Next, I consider what kinds of delays are typically recognized as excusable in standard contracts. From what I’ve seen, there are three main categories that are almost always accepted: a change in the scope of work that wasn’t anticipated at bid time, a force‑majeure event such as a natural disaster or pandemic that makes performance impossible or impracticable, and any delay that is directly caused by the procuring entity—often labeled as “delay caused by or attributable to NRL” (the entity issuing the contract). These are the grounds that would justify a time extension.

Then I turn to how one would actually prove that a delay falls into one of those categories. It isn’t enough to simply claim the delay was due to a landslide or a design change; the contractor needs concrete evidence. For a scope change, that would be a signed variation order or an approved change notice. For force‑majeure, it might be an official government declaration, a meteorological report, or a certificate from a relevant authority. For procuring‑entity‑caused delay, the contractor would need correspondence, meeting minutes, or instructions showing that the entity delayed access, information, or approvals. Gathering this documentation is crucial because it forms the basis of any extension request.

After the evidence is assembled, the next logical step is to notify the engineer‑in‑charge (or the contract’s designated representative) as soon as the exempt delay is identified. Most contracts stipulate a notice period, so timely communication is essential to avoid procedural rejection. The contractor would then submit a formal time‑extension request, attaching the collected evidence and explicitly citing the relevant contractual clause—whether it’s the change‑of‑scope provision, the force‑majeure clause, or the NRL‑caused delay provision.

Once the request is submitted, the engineer reviews it. If the evidence satisfactorily demonstrates that the delay matches one of the excusable grounds and that the notice requirements were met, the engineer will grant the extension. Upon approval, the project schedule is updated to reflect the new completion date. At that point, the period covered by the extension is removed from the calculation of liquidated damages; LD would only resume if the contractor still fails to finish by the extended date.

Finally, I synthesize this line of reasoning: a contractor is entitled to a time extension that exempts them from liquidated damages precisely when the delay can be traced to a change of scope, a force‑majeure event, or a delay caused by or attributable to the procuring entity, and when the contractor follows the prescribed process—documenting the cause, notifying the engineer, obtaining formal approval, and adjusting the schedule accordingly. Without those steps, the delay remains the contractor’s responsibility and liquidated damages apply.
chunk_content:
### 9.15.7 Liquidated Damages for Delay in Performance and Incentives/ Bonus:-
**Liquidated Damages:** Compensation of loss on account of late delivery (actually incurred as well as notional) where loss is pre-estimated is termed as LD. Recovery of such pre-estimated loss is allowed provided such a term is included in the contract. There is no need to establish actual loss due to late delivery. Price reduction clause (PRC) for late delivery shall convey the same meaning as Liquidated Damages (LD).

The Contractor is liable to pay Liquidated Damages for per day of delay beyond the specified date of completion, an amount equal to 0.5% for every week or part thereof, subject to the total amount of Damages not exceeding 5% (five per cent) of the Contract Price. However, the Contractor is entitled to time extension arising out of delays on account of change of scope and force majeure or delays caused by or attributable to NRL. The Procuring Entity may deduct liquidated damages from payments due to the service provider. Payment of liquidated damages shall not affect the service provider's liabilities.

Normally, tenders shall be invited with reference to a pre-determined period of completion of services. Provision of incentives for completion of service before schedule should be sparingly made after careful assessment of tangible benefits there from and disclosed in the tender documents in clear monetary terms.

Incentives/ Bonus (e.g. one percent of the contract value per month subject to a maximum of five percent of contract value) for early completion and penalties for delay should, therefore, be built into the contract very judiciously. To avail of the incentive clause, it shall be mandatory on the part of the contractor to report the actual date of completion to the concerned Engineer (Engineer herein refers

to EIC). To implement a bonus clause in any tender, prior administrative approval of CFD shall be obtained by indenting/user department.

**9.15.8 Penalty for non-performance:** If the service provider has not corrected a Defect within the time specified in the Procuring Entity's notice, a penalty for Lack of performance will be paid by the service provider. The amount to be paid will be calculated as a percentage of the cost of having the Defect corrected, as assessed by EIC or as described in SCC/GCC.

**9.15.9 Filling up the Financial Bid by the Bidders:** The Bidder should be asked to fill in rates and prices for all items of the Services described in the Activity Schedule. Items for which no rate or price is entered by the Bidder will not be paid for by the Procuring Entity when executed and shall be deemed covered by the other rates and prices in the Activity Schedule. The priced Activity Schedule contains sections on Remuneration for Staff deployed, Reimbursable Expenses and Miscellaneous Expenses. All duties, taxes, and other levies payable by the service provider under the Contract, or for any other cause, as in the month prior to the month of the deadline for submission of bids, should be included/indicated in the total Bid price submitted by the Bidder. Bidding Documents should include a clause that **"if a firm quotes NIL charges/consideration, the bid shall be treated as unresponsive and will not be considered"**. In case of e-tendering, the soft copy BOQ (priced bid format) should be free of ambiguity and user friendly. All necessary information should be provided in the BOQ format to guide the bidder for correct uploading of their quoted price; further, if any formula is used to arrive at the total quoted price from the unit prices entered by the bidder, the formula should be made known to the bidder.

question_text: Before what point must the purchase organisation request tenderers to extend their tenders if an extension is needed?
answer: The purchase organisation must request tenderers to extend their tenders before the expiry of the original tender validity period. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 125)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: it wants the deadline by which the purchasing organization must ask tenderers to prolong their tenders when an extension becomes necessary.  

Next, I recall the rule that governs tender validity extensions. The guidance states that if the organization cannot finalize the contract within the original validity period, it should, preferably, ask all responsive tenderers to extend their tenders **before** that original period runs out.  

From that, I reason that the request cannot be made after the original validity has lapsed, because at that point the tenders would no longer be binding and the extension request would be meaningless. The only logical moment to act is while the original tender is still valid, i.e., prior to its expiry.  

Putting it together, the point in time that triggers the requirement is the expiry of the original tender validity period itself—any request for extension must be submitted before that moment.  

Thus, the purchase organisation must request tenderers to extend their tenders before the expiry of the original tender validity period.
chunk_content:
### 7.5.2 Extension of Tender Validity Period
The entire process of scrutiny and evaluation of tenders, preparation of ranking statement and notification of award must be done expeditiously and within the original tender validity period. The validity period should not be unreasonably long as keeping the tender unconditionally valid for acceptance for a longer period entails the risk of getting higher prices from the tenderers.

If, however, due to some exceptional and unforeseen reasons, the purchase organisation is unable to decide on the placement of the contract within the original validity period, it may preferably request, before expiry of the original validity period, all the responsive tenderers to extend their tenders up to a specified period. While asking for such extension, the tenderers are also to be asked to extend their offers as it is, without any changes therein. They may also be told to extend the validity of the EMD (wherever applicable) for the corresponding additional period (which is to be specified in the request). A tenderer may not agree to such a request and this will not be tantamount to forfeiture of its EMD. But the tenderers, who agree to extend the validity, are to do so without changing any terms, conditions, and so on, of their original tenders.

### 7.5.3 Variation of Quantities at the Time of Award
At the time of awarding the contract, the quantity to be procured must be re-judged based on the current data, since the ground situation may have very well changed. The tendered quantity can be increased or decreased by 25 (twenty-five) per cent for ordering, if so warranted. This may be mentioned in the tender documents. Any larger variation may throw up issues about transparency.

TEC approval should be obtained based on the cash outflow for the entire tendered quantity, including provision for applicable tolerance / enhancements.

In case there is further requirement of quantity after issuance of order, repeat order procedure may be adopted as applicable.

### 7.5.4 Option clause
In case of long running, yearly procurements, to take care of any change in the requirement during the currency of the contract, a plus/minus option clause normally 25 (twenty-five) per cent may be incorporated in the tender document, reserving purchaser's right to increase or decrease the quantity of the required goods up to that limit without any change in the terms and conditions and prices quoted by the tenderers. Higher the option limit more is the uncertainty for the tenderers in formulating their prices and more is the chance of loading on the prices quoted to take care of such uncertainties.

### 7.5.2 Extension of Tender Validity Period
The entire process of scrutiny and evaluation of tenders, preparation of ranking statement and notification of award must be done expeditiously and within the original tender validity period. The validity period should not be unreasonably long as keeping the tender unconditionally valid for acceptance for a longer period entails the risk of getting higher prices from the tenderers.

If, however, due to some exceptional and unforeseen reasons, the purchase organisation is unable to decide on the placement of the contract within the original validity period, it may preferably request, before expiry of the original validity period, all the responsive tenderers to extend their tenders up to a specified period. While asking for such extension, the tenderers are also to be asked to extend their offers as it is, without any changes therein. They may also be told to extend the validity of the EMD (wherever applicable) for the corresponding additional period (which is to be specified in the request). A tenderer may not agree to such a request and this will not be tantamount to forfeiture of its EMD. But the tenderers, who agree to extend the validity, are to do so without changing any terms, conditions, and so on, of their original tenders.

### 7.5.3 Variation of Quantities at the Time of Award
At the time of awarding the contract, the quantity to be procured must be re-judged based on the current data, since the ground situation may have very well changed. The tendered quantity can be increased or decreased by 25 (twenty-five) per cent for ordering, if so warranted. This may be mentioned in the tender documents. Any larger variation may throw up issues about transparency.

TEC approval should be obtained based on the cash outflow for the entire tendered quantity, including provision for applicable tolerance / enhancements.

In case there is further requirement of quantity after issuance of order, repeat order procedure may be adopted as applicable.

### 7.5.4 Option clause
In case of long running, yearly procurements, to take care of any change in the requirement during the currency of the contract, a plus/minus option clause normally 25 (twenty-five) per cent may be incorporated in the tender document, reserving purchaser's right to increase or decrease the quantity of the required goods up to that limit without any change in the terms and conditions and prices quoted by the tenderers. Higher the option limit more is the uncertainty for the tenderers in formulating their prices and more is the chance of loading on the prices quoted to take care of such uncertainties.

question_text: Under which circumstances is a lottery used to select the successful bidder among multiple L1 bidders
answer:
- Vehicle tenders where the detailed estimate incorporates the bidder’s capital, operational expenditure and margin. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 67)  
- Manpower‑oriented tenders with a displayed estimate. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 67)  
- Other tenders with a displayed estimate based on the approved Schedule of Rates (SOR). (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 67)  
- Cases where, after any revised price bid or discount, multiple L1 bidders still have identical prices due to a tie in the original bids. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 67)
cot:
First, I consider why a lottery would be needed at all: it is only resorted to when two or more bidders are tied for the lowest evaluated price (L1) and the tender documents provide no other objective criterion to break that tie.  
Then, I look for situations where the bidding process is structured so that price becomes the sole factor for comparison. This happens when the tender includes a displayed estimate that all bidders must base their offers on, leaving little room for differentiation other than matching that estimate exactly.  
Next, I examine vehicle tenders. The reference explains that the detailed estimate shown in these tenders already incorporates the bidder’s capital outlay, operational expenditure and allowed margin. If several bidders calculate their offers to fit that estimate precisely, their quoted prices will be identical, triggering the lottery rule.  
After that, I turn to manpower‑oriented contracts. Here the estimate is based on prescribed wage rates (basic, statutory and non‑statutory allowances). When bidders quote against this displayed estimate, any that hit the target price will end up tied, again requiring a lottery to select the winner.  
Further, I consider any other tender that uses an approved Schedule of Rates (SOR) as the basis for the displayed estimate. Because the SOR fixes the unit rates, the total price becomes a straightforward calculation; multiple bidders arriving at the same total will be indistinguishable on price alone, so the lottery is prescribed.  
Finally, I reflect on the provision that allows revised price bids or discounts. Even after such revisions, if the original tie persists and the adjusted prices remain equal, the lottery remains the tie‑breaking mechanism.  

Putting these points together, the circumstances in which a lottery is used to select the successful bidder among multiple L1 bidders are exactly those where a displayed estimate—whether it reflects capital and operational costs for vehicles, uniform wage‑based rates for manpower work, or an approved Schedule of Rates for other supplies—leads to identical evaluated prices, or where post‑revision prices still tie because of the original equality.

Selection of successful bidder(s) among multiple L1 bidders shall be determined through lottery in the following circumstances:-

- (i) Vehicle tenders where detailed estimate is displayed considering the bidder's capital and operational expenditure and margin.
- (ii) Manpower oriented tenders with displayed estimates.
- (iii) Other tenders with displayed estimates based on approved SOR.
- (iii) Other than above scenarios, where the prices of multiple L1 bidders remain same even after submission of revised priced bid / discount because of tie in the original prices.

The methodology for conducting lottery shall be specified in the tender documents. Commercial department shall conduct the lottery in presence of representatives from Finance and User department. The concerned bidders shall be invited to witness the lottery.

It may also be decided that in case the L1 agency selected through lottery refuses or fails to execute the job, the job (or balance part of the job) may be subsequently offered to any of the other L1 agencies (not selected for award so far), adopting appropriate selection process by NRL like lottery among the remaining interested agencies. Alternatively, a process for selection of wait listed L1 agency(ies) may be appropriately specified. Such conditions should be specified in the tender documents.

- In case of “refusal”, subsequent award to next eligible agency shall be done within original or extended offer validity.
- In case of “failure”, unexecuted quantities shall be offered to the next eligible agency within maximum one year from the original date of award.

Defaulting supplier/contractor shall be subject to penalties as per procedure.

**9.4.5 Past Experience:** Bid documents normally provide for a qualification criteria considering past experience. Normally past experience in supply of service at a particular station or to Central Government Ministries/ Departments may be considered as restrictive. ### 9.8.1 Cancellation of Contract for Default
Without prejudice to any other remedy for breach of contract, such as removal from the list of registered supplier, by written notice of default sent to the supplier, the contract may be terminated in whole or in part:

- i) If the supplier fails to deliver any or all of the stores within the time period(s) specified in the contract, or any extension thereof granted; and
- ii) If the supplier fails to perform any other obligation under the contract within the period specified in the contract or any extension thereof granted;
- iii) If the contract is terminated in whole or in part, recourse may be taken to any one or more of the following actions:
  - a) Forfeiture of the EMD;
  - b) Upon such terms and in such manner as it deems appropriate, goods similar to those undelivered may be procured and the supplier shall be liable for all available actions against him, as applicable in terms of the contract (including risk purchase); and
  - c) However, the supplier shall continue to fulfil the contract to the extent not terminated.

Before cancelling the contract and taking further action, it may be desirable to obtain legal advice.

### 9.8.2 Termination of Contract for Insolvency
If the supplier becomes bankrupt or becomes otherwise insolvent or undergoes liquidation or loses substantially the technical or financial capability (based on which he was selected for award of contract), at any time, the contract may be terminated, by giving a written notice to the supplier, without compensation to the supplier, provided that such termination will not prejudice or affect any right of action or remedy which has accrued or will accrue thereafter to Procuring Entity.

### 9.8.3 Termination of Contract for Convenience
After placement of the contract, there may be an unforeseen situation compelling Procuring Entity to cancel the contract. In such a case, a suitable notice has to be sent to the supplier for cancellation of the contract, in whole or in part, for its (Procuring Entity's) convenience, inter alia, indicating the date with effect from which the termination will become effective. This is not Procuring Entity's legal right- the contractor has to be persuaded to acquiesce. Depending on the merits of the case, the supplier may have to be suitably compensated on mutually agreed terms for terminating the contract. Suitable provisions to this effect should be incorporated in the tender document as well as in the resultant contract.

## 9.9 Dispute Resolution
Normally, there should not be any scope for dispute between the purchaser and supplier after entering into a mutually agreed valid contract. However, due to various unforeseen reasons, problems may arise during the progress of the contract leading to a disagreement between the purchaser and supplier. Therefore, the conditions governing the contract should contain suitable provisions for settlement of such disputes or differences binding on both parties. The mode of settlement of such disputes/differences should be through arbitration. However, when a dispute/difference arises, both the purchaser and supplier should first try to resolve it amicably by mutual discussion, mediation, and conciliation. If the parties fail to resolve the dispute within 21 (twenty-one) days, then, depending on the position of the case, either the purchaser or supplier should give notice to the other party of its intention to commence arbitration. When the contract is with a domestic supplier, the applicable arbitration procedure shall be as per the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 [Amended 2015 and 2021]. While processing a case for dispute resolution/litigation/arbitration, the procuring entity is to take legal advice, at appropriate stages.

question_text: Provide an example of a schedule‑related failure that leads to a tender being declared unresponsive.
answer: - A tenderer quotes only for the supply of equipment while failing to include installation, commissioning, and operator training as required by the schedule, resulting in the tender being declared unresponsive. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 72)
cot:
First, I consider what a schedule‑related failure might look like in a tender evaluation. The schedule in the bid document spells out the full scope of work that a bidder must commit to—often a combination of supply, installation, commissioning, and any required training or support. If a bidder’s offer does not cover every item listed in that schedule, the bid departs from an essential requirement set out in the procurement documents.  

Looking at a concrete case, the schedule states that the contractor must supply the equipment, install and commission it, and also train the procuring entity’s operators to use the equipment. The bidder in question, however, submits a price only for the supply of the equipment and omits any mention of installation, commissioning, or operator training. Because the bid does not meet the complete requirement prescribed by the schedule, it fails the basic conformity check that is performed during the initial scrutiny of tenders.  

At that stage, any tender that does not satisfy the basic requirements is treated as unresponsive and is set aside from further evaluation. Thus, the act of quoting only for the supply while leaving out the other scheduled activities constitutes a schedule‑related failure that leads directly to the tender being declared unresponsive.
