question_text: How should the procedure for a replacement supply against a rejected lot be conducted
answer:
- Replacement supplies must undergo the exact same pre‑inspection and inspection sequence stipulated in the original contract before they can be accepted by the consignee.  
- Upon rejection, issue a material rejection advice/rejection memo to the firm, purchaser, pre‑inspecting agency, paying authority and any other concerned parties; if a joint inspection is feasible, conduct it with the pre‑inspecting agency and supplier.  
- If the supplier fails to participate in a joint inspection, proceed with the pre‑inspecting agency alone.  
- After the replacement lot passes inspection (or is accepted following rectification), withdraw the earlier rejection advice/memo and notify all previously informed parties of the withdrawal.  

This procedure preserves contractual integrity, mitigates risk of non‑conforming goods, and upholds transparency and value‑for‑money in procurement (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 157).
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is really asking: when a lot delivered to the consignee is found defective and rejected, what steps must be taken if the supplier offers a replacement for that rejected lot? The key is that the replacement should not bypass any contractual safeguards that apply to ordinary deliveries.  

Next, I look at what the contract normally requires for any supply. Typically there is a pre‑inspection stage (if the goods are pre‑inspected) followed by a final inspection at the consignee’s site before acceptance. Since the replacement is essentially a new delivery, it must be subjected to exactly the same sequence of inspections that the original lot would have undergone; otherwise we would be weakening the contractual protection against non‑conforming goods.  

Then I consider what happens at the moment of rejection. The consignee must create a formal record of the rejection so that all parties aware of the transaction are informed and any financial recovery can be pursued. This means issuing a material rejection advice, rejection memo, or debit note to the supplier, the purchasing authority, the pre‑inspection agency, the paying office, and anyone else with an interest in the transaction.  

After the rejection notice is out, it is sensible to verify the defect jointly if possible. A joint inspection with the pre‑inspecting agency and the supplier gives both sides a chance to see the non‑conformity and agree on the facts. If the supplier refuses or is unable to participate, the inspection can still go forward with the pre‑inspecting agency alone; the important point is that the inspection proceeds and the rejection is substantiated.  

Once the replacement lot arrives, it goes through the same pre‑inspection and final inspection steps. If it passes (or is accepted after any necessary rectification), the earlier rejection advice must be formally withdrawn. All parties that received the original rejection notice need to be told that the withdrawal has been made, closing the loop and ensuring that the replacement is now treated as an accepted supply.  

Putting these pieces together, the procedure preserves the contract’s inspection requirements, maintains a clear documentary trail, allows for joint verification when feasible, and ensures that any earlier rejection is rescinded only after the replacement has been validated. This approach protects the buyer from accepting defective goods, upholds transparency, and supports value‑for‑money in the procurement process.

#### ii) **Inspection of Goods on Receipt at Consignee/User's Site**
Post-delivery inspection is carried out on receipt of goods before accepting them. This should be typically done for goods that are available off-the-shelf and are BIS marked. All final goods that may be directly consumed or utilised on delivery (excluding machinery installations, and so on) and for which detailed inspection of the manufacturing process is not required and only a physical inspection regarding their

physical characteristics is required, may be inspected using this method. On receipt of goods at stores, the storekeeper should immediately notify the officer nominated for inspection, requesting to schedule an inspection. The inspecting officer should then fix a date for inspection.

The consignee has the right to reject the goods on receipt during the final inspection on delivery even though the goods have already been inspected and cleared at the pre-dispatch stage by Procuring Entity's inspector. However, such rejection should be strictly within the contractual terms and conditions and no new condition should be adopted while rejecting the goods during final inspection.

Goods accepted by the purchaser after inspections, in terms of the contract, shall in no way dilute the purchaser's right to reject them later, if found deficient in terms of the warranty clause of the contract.

In case of rejection of goods at this stage, the material rejection advice/rejection memo/debit note should be issued. In case of pre-inspected goods, a joint inspection of the rejected lot of goods should be held with the pre-inspecting agency and firm, wherever feasible. In case of failure of the firm to associate with a joint inspection, it should be held with the pre-inspecting agency.

In case of rejection of the pre-inspected supply of goods at the consignee end, the material rejection advice/rejection memo should be sent to all concerned, which is, the firm, purchaser, pre-inspecting agency, paying authority, and so on - without fail where recovery exists. In case of replacement supply against the rejected lot of goods, the process should remain exactly the same in terms of sequence of pre-inspection/inspection as laid down in the contract, prior to acceptance by the consignee. In case of acceptance of the replacement supply/rejected supply after rectification, the earlier issued material rejection advice/ rejection memo should be withdrawn under advice to all concerned.

question_text: What steps should a user department follow to initiate procurement of works in the Aarohan system?
answer: **A:** The user department first verifies that a procurement requirement exists. It then creates a Purchase Requisition (PR) in the Aarohan system, completing all required fields such as name of work, justification, pre‑qualification criteria, scope of work, special requirements, estimated cost, material/equipment responsibilities, completion time, work location, warranty/defect liability, payment terms, budget code (WBS/Cost Centre/GL), supervising authority, and any reference to previous orders. Once the PR is filled out, it is submitted to the Competent Authority for review and release. Only after the Competent Authority releases the PR can the procurement process move forward. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 23)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what “initiate procurement of works” actually means in this context – it starts with the user department confirming that there is a genuine requirement for the work to be done. Without that confirmation, any further action would be premature, so the first mental check is to verify the need and ensure that the work cannot be handled internally with existing resources or ARCs.

Once the requirement is settled, the next logical step is to determine what information must be captured to start the formal process. The Aarohan system expects a Purchase Requisition that includes details such as the work’s name, justification, pre‑qualification criteria, scope, special requirements, estimated cost, responsibilities for materials and equipment, completion schedule, location, warranty terms, payment conditions, the relevant budget code (WBS/Cost Centre/GL), the supervising authority, and any reference to prior orders. Knowing this list helps me understand what data I need to gather before opening the system.

With the requirement verified and the necessary data identified, I move to the Aarohan interface and create a new Purchase Requisition, filling in each of those fields carefully. This step is where the abstract need is translated into a structured request that the system can route forward; I make sure that every mandatory section is completed accurately to avoid later rejections.

After the PR is fully populated, I submit it to the Competent Authority for review. The authority’s role is to examine the requisition, confirm that the justification and all technical and commercial details are sound, and then release it. Only once the PR bears the authority’s release can the procurement workflow advance; otherwise, it remains pending and may be sent back for clarification or revision.

Finally, upon receiving the released PR, the user department can consider the initiation step complete and allow the procurement process to proceed to the next stages such as tendering, evaluation, and contract award. This sequence—verifying need, gathering data, creating and completing the PR in Aarohan, obtaining Competent Authority release, and then moving forward—matches the prescribed steps for initiating procurement of works.

Should Commercial Department feel that any of the PRs received by them could be executed by Company's own resources / skills and available ARCs, they may refer it back to User Department for review (with their reasons) before processing the said PR.

The PR shall contain, inter alia, the following information:

- a) Name of work
- b) Justification of procurement

- c) Pre-Qualification Criteria with definition of “Similar Works”.
- d) Scope of work\* (as a part of Special Terms & Conditions of Contract)

- i) Any special requirements

- s) Reference of last order, if any

Where the jobs involve usage of equipment, which forms major part of the total cost, the company's equipment should be used, subject to availability. The indenting dept. should indicate whether such usage will be on a “free issue” basis or at cost as per procedure.

question_text: What does L1 stand for in the procurement procedure described
answer: L1 stands for the lowest evaluated bid among all qualified bids. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 31)
cot: I need to determine what L1 signifies in the procurement procedure outlined. Scanning the description, I notice that the term L1 appears repeatedly when describing how bids are handled. The very first point under both the divisible and indivisible item procedures states: “Among all qualified bids, the lowest bid will be termed as L1.” This sentence directly assigns the label L1 to the bid that has the lowest evaluated price after all bidders have been qualified. Later steps refer to L1 as the benchmark price that Class‑I local suppliers are asked to match, reinforcing that L1 represents the lowest evaluated bid among the qualified pool. Since the definition is given explicitly and is used consistently throughout the process, the meaning of L1 is simply the lowest evaluated bid among all qualified bids. Thus, L1 stands for the lowest evaluated bid among all qualified bids (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 31).

- a) In procurement of all items/ services/ works which are divisible in nature, the Class I local supplier shall get purchase preference over 'Class II local supplier' as well as 'Non Local Supplier' as per following procedure:

  - ii. In case such lowest eligible Class-I local supplier fails to match the lowest bidder's evaluated price or accepts less than the offered quantity, the next higher Class-I local supplier with the margin of purchase preference shall be invited to match the L1 price for remaining quantity against the respective item(s) of MR and so on, and contract shall be awarded accordingly. In case some quantity is still left uncovered on Class-I local suppliers, then such balance quantity may also be ordered on the L1 bidder.

If 50% quantity of an item works out to a fraction of quantity, the bidder shall be considered for next higher quantity. In case the quantity cannot be split, the order shall be placed with the entire quantity.

question_text: If no further processing is required after a tender cancellation, where should the e-file be kept for future reference
answer: If no further processing is required after a tender cancellation, the e‑file should be kept under the custody of the DO / Commercial for future reference. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 132)
cot:
First I consider what the question is really asking: after a tender has been cancelled and there is nothing more to do with it, where should the electronic file be stored so that it can be referred to later if needed.  
Then I think about the conditions that determine the file’s handling. The process notes that the “Close” button in Aarohan only appears once the cancellation procedure is finished; if the cancellation is done but no further steps are required, the system does not automatically close the file, so a simple note to file can be made just to record the facts.  
Next I look at what the guidance says for the situation where no additional processing is planned. It specifies that the corresponding Aarohan file may still be used for any future refloating, but when there is no such intention, the file should be retained under a specific custodial arrangement.  
Further I reflect on who that custodian is. The instruction points to the DO / Commercial team as the group responsible for keeping the e‑file safe for future reference, ensuring it remains accessible without being actively processed.  
Finally I bring these points together: when a tender cancellation is complete and no further work is needed, the appropriate action is to place the e‑file under the custody of the DO / Commercial for future reference. This matches the required answer.
chunk_content:
Approval for tender cancellation is not required in certain cases, as above. However, as per the process in Aarohan, the file “Close” button does not appear unless the tender cancellation process is completed. Hence an “Other note” for “Tender cancellation” may be initiated stating only a brief statement of facts through a “Note to file” for records.

question_text: According to the SOP, what must be mentioned in the tender when samples are collected from bidders for evaluation
answer: The tender must specify who is responsible for bearing the cost of the sample or its transportation, and it must include a detailed bid‑evaluation process that outlines how weightage will be allocated to the test results of pre‑defined parameters. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 42)
cot:
First, I think about why the SOP would ask for something to be included in the tender when bidders are required to submit samples for evaluation. The purpose is to eliminate any uncertainty that could later lead to disputes or claims of unfair treatment, so the tender must spell out the obligations that arise from the sample‑taking step.  

Next, I consider the specific cases where samples are actually needed—such as for catalysts, chemicals or blend components—where the award decision hinges on measured test results. In those situations it becomes essential to state clearly who will bear the expense of obtaining and shipping the samples; otherwise a bidder could argue that the buyer imposed an unexpected cost.  

Then I turn to the evaluation side of the process. Because the contract will be granted on the basis of those test outcomes, the tender must also contain a thorough description of how the bid evaluation will be carried out. This means explaining how the raw test data will be turned into a score, and in particular indicating what weight each pre‑defined parameter will carry in the overall assessment.  

After that, I see that omitting either of these two elements would leave the procurement open to challenge: missing the cost rule creates financial ambiguity, while missing the evaluation method makes the scoring appear arbitrary and non‑transparent.  

Finally, I combine the two requirements: the tender must explicitly allocate responsibility for the sample or its transportation costs, and it must include a detailed bid‑evaluation process that outlines how weightage is assigned to the test results of the agreed parameters. This matches the answer that the tender must specify who bears the cost and must contain a detailed evaluation process outlining weightage allocation.

question_text: What commitment does the principal make regarding its employees and their family members to prevent corruption
answer: The principal commits that none of its employees—or their family members—will ask for, accept, or be promised any improper gift, payment, or other benefit in connection with the tender or the execution of the contract; they may only accept what they are legally entitled to receive. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 245)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the principal promises to do in order to stop corrupt practices involving its staff and their relatives.  
Looking at the obligations laid out for the principal, the first bullet under its commitments catches my eye: it states that neither an employee nor anyone acting through that employee’s family may seek, be promised, or receive any benefit—whether tangible or intangible—that the employee is not already lawfully allowed to have, especially in relation to the tender or the contract’s execution.  
This tells me the core of the pledge is a blanket prohibition on improper inducements: employees and their family members cannot ask for, accept, or be offered gifts, payments, or any other advantage that would give them an edge beyond what the law permits.  
The only exception carved out is what they are legally entitled to receive, meaning any legitimate remuneration or approved benefit remains permissible.  
Putting these pieces together, the principal’s commitment is exactly that: none of its employees—or their family members—will solicit, accept, or be promised any improper gift, payment, or other benefit connected with the tender or contract performance; they may only retain what they are lawfully owed.
chunk_content:
### Section 1 - Commitments of the Principal
- (1) The Principal commits itself to take all measures necessary to prevent corruption and to observe the following principles:
- a) No employee of the Principal, personally or through family members, will in connection with the tender, or the execution of the contract, demand, take a promise for or accept, for himself/herself or third person, any material or immaterial benefit which he/she is not legally entitled to.
  - b) The Principal will, during the tender process, treat all Bidders with equity and reason. The Principal will, in particular, before and during the tender process, provide to all Bidders the same information and will not provide to any Bidder confidential / additional information through which the Bidder could obtain an advantage in relation to the tender process or the contract execution.
  - c) The Principal will exclude from the process all known prejudiced persons.

- (2) If the Principal obtains information on the conduct of any of its employees which is a criminal offence under the relevant Anti-Corruption Laws of India, or if there be a substantive suspicion in this regard, the Principal will inform its Vigilance Office and in addition can initiate disciplinary actions.

## Section 2 - Commitments of the Bidder / Contractor/Supplier
- (1) The Bidder / Contractor/Supplier commits itself to take all measures necessary to prevent corruption. He commits himself to observe the following principles during his participation in the tender process and during the contract execution.
- a) The Bidder / Contractor/Supplier will not, directly or through any other person or firm, offer, promise or give to any of the Principal's employees involved in the tender process or the execution of the contract or to any third person, any material or immaterial benefit which he/she is not legally entitled to, in order to obtain in exchange, any advantage of any kind whatsoever during the tender process or during the execution of the contract.
  - b) The Bidder / Contractor/Supplier will not enter with other Bidders into any undisclosed agreement or understanding, whether formal or informal. This applies in particular to prices, specifications, certifications, subsidiary contracts, submission or non-submission of bids or any other actions to restrict competitiveness or to introduce cartelisation in the bidding process.
  - c) The Bidder / Contractor/Supplier will not commit any offence under the relevant Anti-Corruption Laws of India; further the Bidder / Contractor/Supplier will not use improperly, for purposes of competition or personal gain, or pass on to others, any information or document provided by the Principal as part of the business relationship, regarding plans, technical proposals and business details, including information contained or transmitted electronically.
  - d) The Bidder / Contractor/Supplier will, when presenting his bid, disclose any and all payments he has made, is committed to, or intends to make to agents, brokers or any other intermediaries in connection with the award of the contract.
- (2) The Bidder / Contractor/Supplier will not instigate third persons to commit offences outlined above or be an accessory to such offences.

question_text: If I have successfully completed the work without any recoverable amounts, will I receive the full security deposit back?
answer: Yes, you will receive the full security deposit back, provided there are no recoverable amounts and the contract scope has not been increased by an amendment. If the defect liability period does not apply, NRL will refund the deposit within 30 days of contract completion; if it does apply, the refund will be made within 60 days after the defect liability period ends, in each case after any necessary adjustments. For one‑time jobs, 80% may be released upfront and the remaining 20% after the contract is closed. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p.44)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: whether completing the work satisfactorily and without any amounts that could be recovered from the deposit entitles the contractor to the full return of that security deposit.  

Next, I think about the conditions that govern the refund. The policy distinguishes two situations—whether a defect liability period is part of the contract or not—and it also notes that any amendment that increases the contract value can affect how much of the deposit is retained.  

Then, I look at the refund mechanics. If there is no defect liability period, the deposit is returned to the contractor’s bank account within thirty days after the work is certified complete, after any permissible adjustments are made. If a defect liability period does apply, the wait is longer: the deposit is refunded within sixty days after the period ends, again after adjustments.  

After that, I examine the impact of a scope change. The rules state that when the work order is amended to increase the total contract value and the defect liability period does not apply, NRL will hold back ten percent of the additional amount as a security deposit; the rest is refundable. When a defect liability period does apply, the contractor must instead deposit an extra ten percent of the increased value, so the original deposit is not touched.  

I also recall the special handling for one‑time jobs: up to eighty percent of the deposit may be released soon after completion, with the remaining twenty percent held until the contract is formally closed.  

Putting it all together, if the work has been finished satisfactorily, there are no recoverable amounts to be deducted, and the contract has not been altered by an amendment that increases its value, then none of the provisions that allow retention apply. Consequently, the contractor is entitled to the full security deposit back, with the timing governed by whether a defect liability period applies (thirty days after completion or sixty days after its end) and, for one‑time jobs, split into an eighty percent upfront release and a twenty percent release upon closure.
chunk_content:
##### 1. Release/refund of security deposit.
(a) The security deposit amount deposited by the contractor against a particular contract or work order (WO) or purchase order (PO) will be retained by NRL till completion of execution of the contract or till end of defect liability period whichever is later as per the terms and conditions of the particular contract. Refund of security deposit amount whether full or part, during any time of execution of the contract and due to any reason will not be admissible.

(b) In the cases **where defect liability period is not applicable** as per contract terms and conditions the security deposit will be refunded to the contractor's bank account as provided by the contractor and registered in the NRL vendor master database, within 30 days from date of completion of contract as certified by the respective Engineer In-Charge (EIC) of NRL and after adjustment of recoveries (if any) as per procedure.

(c) In the cases **where defect liability period is applicable** as per contract terms and conditions the security deposit will be refunded to the contractor's bank account as provided by the contractor and registered in the NRL vendor master database, within 60 days from date of expiry of defect liability period as certified by the respective Engineer In-Charge (EIC) of NRL and after adjustment of recoveries (if any) as per procedure.

(d) **Wherever defect liability period is not applicable**, in case the contractor has deposited the security deposit amount in full as per original PO and successfully executed the work as per contract terms and condition without any recoverable from security deposit amount, however the scope of work / quantity / time period has been extended or increased with increase in total contract value through an amendment over original contract, then security deposit equivalent to 10% of the additional / increased contract (PO) amount will be retained by NRL and the balance amount (if any) of security deposit will be refunded to the contractor period as certified by the respective Engineer In-Charge (EIC) of NRL. This provision will not be applicable for the service / work contracts **where defect liability period is applicable**, and in such cases an additional amount equivalent to 10% of the increased value of contract will be deposited by the contractor immediately after acceptance of amendment of original contract, either in full or in installments.

**Note:** For one time jobs, 80% of SD may be released; balance 20% of the SD to be released after the contract is closed (*Closing may be with/without formal approval, as applicable for individual cases*).

question_text: Who is personally responsible for discharging the duties of the Tender Evaluation Committee?
answer: The nominated officers who make up the Tender Evaluation Committee must personally discharge its duties. They may ask subordinate officers for reports or evaluations, but they remain answerable for those decisions and cannot delegate their deliberations to others. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 132)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know who must personally carry out the duties of the Tender Evaluation Committee.

The Procurement of Goods Manual states that the committee’s duties are to be discharged personally by the nominated officers. That directly ties personal responsibility to those officers.

The manual then clarifies that while these officers may seek assistance from their subordinates in the form of reports or evaluations, they remain answerable for the decisions made, indicating that the ultimate responsibility cannot be shifted away.

Further, it specifies that committee members cannot co‑opt or nominate others to attend deliberations on their behalf, reinforcing that the nominated officers themselves must be present and accountable for the evaluation process.

Putting these points together, the only individuals who bear the personal duty to discharge the Tender Evaluation Committee’s responsibilities are the nominated officers who constitute the committee, even if they rely on subordinate support for information.

This reasoning aligns exactly with the given answer: the nominated officers must personally discharge the duties, may use subordinate reports but remain answerable, and cannot delegate their deliberations.
chunk_content:
Tender Evaluation Committee duties are to be discharged personally by the nominated officers. They may take help of their subordinate officers by way of reports/ evaluations, but they would still be answerable for such decisions. TEC members cannot co-opt or nominate others to attend deliberations on their behalf. TEC deliberations are best held across the table and not through circulation of notes/comments/e-mails etc.

All members of the TEC should resolve their differences through personal discussions instead of making to and fro references in writing. In cases where it is not possible to come to a consensus and differences persist amongst TEC members, the reasons for dissent of a member should be recorded in a balanced manner along with the majority's views on the dissent note. The final recommendations should be that of the majority view. However, such situations should be rare.

### 7.5.13 Independence, Impartiality, Confidentiality and 'No Conflict of Interest' at all Stages of Evaluation of Bids
All technical, commercial and finance officials who have contributed to the techno- commercial or financial evaluation of bids, should deal with the procurement in an independent, impartial manner and should have no conflict of interest with any of the bidder involved in the procurement. They should also maintain confidentiality of the information processed during the evaluation process and not allow it to reach any unauthorised person. All TEC members should sign a declaration at the end of their reports/ noting stating that, "I declare that I have no conflict of interest with any of the bidder in this tender". TEC members may make such a declaration at the end of their reports.

question_text: Besides the supply of goods, what additional works or services (e.g., installation, commissioning, training, technical support, after‑sales service, AMC) may need to be specified in the tender document
answer:
The tender document shall specify, under clause ix) of section 2.2.2, the following additional works or services that may be required to achieve full delivery or completion:

- Installation  
- Commissioning  
- Training  
- Technical support  
- After‑sales service  
- Annual Maintenance Contract (AMC)  
- Any other additional work or related services needed for full delivery/completion  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 42)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: besides the mere provision of the goods, what else must be spelled out in a tender so that the buyer receives a fully functional and supported solution.  
Then, I think about the purpose of a tender document – it must eliminate ambiguity by defining the complete scope of what the supplier is obliged to deliver, not just the physical items but also everything needed to put them into service and keep them running.  
Next, I run through the typical activities that turn delivered equipment into an operational asset and sustain it over its life: the equipment has to be installed at the site, commissioned to verify it works as intended, operators need to be trained, ongoing technical support may be required, after‑sales service ensures any issues are addressed, and a long‑term maintenance arrangement such as an Annual Maintenance Contract keeps the asset in good condition.  
Further, I recall that standard tender templates group these items under a specific clause that captures “other additional work and/or related services required to achieve full delivery/completion”, which explicitly lists installation, commissioning, training, technical support, after‑sales service and AMC, and also allows for any similar services that might be needed.  
Finally, bringing the points together, I conclude that the tender document must specify, under that clause, the additional works or services: installation, commissioning, training, technical support, after‑sales service, Annual Maintenance Contract (AMC), and any other additional work or related services needed to achieve full delivery or completion.

question_text: Why is it not advisable to set a fixed percentage below the estimated cost as an automatic threshold for Abnormally Low Bids?
answer: Setting a fixed percentage below the estimated cost as an automatic threshold for Abnormally Low Bids is not advisable because it overlooks the project‑specific factors that determine whether a low price is genuinely achievable or indicative of insufficient capability. A uniform cutoff cannot account for variations in scope, schedule, risk allocation, or other bid elements that may justify a lower price, nor can it capture bids that are abnormally low yet still above the arbitrary percentage. Instead, the Procuring Entity should seek written clarifications and require bidders to submit detailed price analyses that relate their offered price to the scope, schedule, risk distribution, and any other requirements outlined in the bid documents. Only after evaluating these analyses can the Entity determine whether a bidder has substantially failed to demonstrate the ability to perform the contract at the offered price. This approach ensures a fair, case‑by‑case assessment while safeguarding against unrealistic bids (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 52).
cot:
First, I consider what the goal is when evaluating bids: we want to identify offers that are so low they raise doubts about the bidder’s ability to fulfill the contract, without mistakenly rejecting legitimate competitive prices.  

Then, I think about what makes a bid “abnormally low.” It isn’t just a raw number; it depends on the specific scope of work, the schedule imposed, how risks are allocated, and any special requirements spelled out in the bidding documents. These factors vary from project to project, so a single numeric rule would have to ignore them.  

Next, I examine the consequence of applying a fixed percentage below the estimated cost as an automatic cutoff. Such a rule would treat every project the same, meaning that a bid that is genuinely low because of efficient methods or favorable conditions could be flagged, while another bid that is still above the percentage but nevertheless unrealistic given its unique risk profile could slip through.  

Further, I realize that the proper way to assess abnormality is to look at the bid in context: ask the bidder to explain how the price relates to the scope, timeline, risk distribution, and other bid requirements, and then evaluate whether they can credibly demonstrate capability to deliver at that price. This case‑by‑case inquiry captures the nuances that a blanket percentage misses.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: because a uniform threshold cannot reflect project‑specific realities and may either over‑reject sound bids or under‑detect truly problematic ones, it is not advisable to rely on it. Instead, the procuring entity should seek clarifications and detailed price analyses, judge the bidder’s ability to perform, and make a reasoned, individualized decision. This approach aligns with the need for a fair, context‑sensitive assessment of abnormally low bids.
chunk_content:
## 6.8 Evaluation of Cost
6.8.1 After evaluation of quality has been completed, the Procuring Entity shall notify those consultants whose proposals did not meet the minimum qualifying standard or were considered non-responsive to the RfP and/or ToR (notification through tender portal, with reasons for rejection). In case of QCBS, the Procuring Entity shall simultaneously notify the consultants that have successfully satisfied the qualifying standard or where marks have been awarded, the qualifying marks, and indicate the date and time set for opening the financial proposals. In such a case, the opening date shall preferably be within one weeks after the notification date. The financial proposals shall be opened publicly in the presence of representatives of the technically qualified consultants who choose to attend

6.8.2 For QCBS, the proposal with the lowest offered total price shall be given a financial score of 100 % (one hundred per cent) and other financial proposals given scores that are inversely proportional to their prices. This methodology shall be specified in the RfP document.

6.8.3 For the purpose of comparing proposals, the costs shall be converted to Indian Rupees as stated in the RfP. The dealing officer shall make this conversion by using the BC selling exchange rates for those currencies as per the exchange rate quoted by an official source, for example, the State Bank of India. The RfP shall specify the source of the exchange rate to be used and date of the exchange rate to be taken for comparison of costs. This date shall be the date of opening of technical bids.

6.8.4 For the purpose of evaluation, the total cost shall include all taxes and duties for which the Procuring Entity makes payments to the consultant and other reimbursable expenses, such as travel, translation, report printing, or secretarial expenses as indicated in the RfP document

6.8.5 When using QCBS, the scores of quality and cost scores shall be weighted appropriately and added to determine the most advantageous proposal.

6.8.6 An Abnormally Low Bid is one in which the Bid price, in combination with other elements of the Bid, appears so low that it raises material concerns as to the capability of the Bidder to perform the contract at the offered price. Procuring Entity may in such cases seek written clarifications from the Bidder, including detailed price analyses of its Bid price in relation to scope, schedule, allocation of risks and responsibilities, and any other requirements of the bids document. If, after evaluating the price analyses, procuring entity determines that the Bidder has *substantially failed* to demonstrate its capability to deliver the contract at the offered price, the Procuring Entity may reject the Bid/Proposal. However it would not be advisable to fix a normative percentage below the estimated cost, which would be automatically be considered as an abnormally low bid. Due care should be taken while formulating the specifications at the time of preparation of bid document so as to have a safeguard against the submission of abnormally low bid from the bidder.

As a safeguard, it should be closely monitored by the EIC that final payments in such cases do

not abnormally increases due to extra items. Further, there is no abnormal increase in quantities of the item for which contractors have initially quoted very high rates.

In case of abnormal rates (both low and high), the L1 bidder's confirmation to bridge the gap by providing necessary discount in case of any vitiation of L1 position after execution, should be sought before finalization of the contract.

## 6.9 Selection of the winning consultant
Before a final award is announced, the technical and financial credentials of the selected bidders/ consultant should be cross-checked to the extent feasible.

question_text: What does NRL consider as the threshold for a service provider to be deemed eligible for full marks
answer: NRL deems a service provider eligible for full marks when it achieves an A (Very Good) rating, reflecting outstanding, advanced expertise, top‑level specialists, world‑class capabilities in the assignment’s methodologies, and adherence to established Quality Management procedures. question_text: What evidence must an authorised agent/dealer provide to support their quotation for a manufacturer's product
answer:
- Attach the manufacturer’s authorisation certificate for the product.  
- Include the manufacturer’s confirmation that the required warranty will be extended for the item.  
- Provide certified documentary evidence proving the firm’s status as an authorised agent/dealer of that manufacturer.  

These documents verify that the quotation comes from a responsible party offering a genuine product backed by the manufacturer’s warranty, thereby supporting transparency, value‑for‑money, and risk‑managed procurement. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 97)
cot:
First, I think about why an authorised agent or dealer would need to back up their quotation with any documentation at all. The procuring entity wants to be sure that the quote comes from a responsible party who can actually supply the genuine item and stand behind any warranty obligations, so the evidence must directly address those concerns.

Next, I ask what would convince the buyer that the product is genuine and not a counterfeit or substitute. The most straightforward way is to show that the manufacturer themselves has authorised the sale of that specific item, which points to the need for a manufacturer’s authorisation certificate covering the product in question.

Then I consider the warranty aspect. Even if the product is genuine, the buyer needs assurance that the required warranty will be honoured. That can only come from the manufacturer, so the dealer must obtain the manufacturer’s explicit confirmation that they will extend the promised warranty for the item being quoted.

After that, I reflect on the dealer’s own standing. Simply having a product‑specific authorisation and a warranty pledge does not prove that the dealer is legitimately tied to the manufacturer; they could be presenting forged papers. Therefore, the dealer must also provide certified documentary evidence that demonstrates their status as an authorised agent or dealer of that manufacturer—something like a dealership agreement, authorisation letter, or registration certificate that has been verified.

Putting these three pieces together, the quotation must be accompanied by the manufacturer’s authorisation certificate for the product, the manufacturer’s confirmation that the required warranty will be extended, and certified proof of the dealer’s authorised status. Together they show that the quote originates from a responsible source offering a genuine product backed by the manufacturer’s warranty, satisfying the procuring entity’s need for transparency, value‑for‑money, and risk‑managed procurement.

#### x) Conflict of Interest among Bidders/ Agents
A bidder shall not have conflict of interest with other bidders. Such conflict of interest can lead to anti-competitive practices to the detriment of Procuring Entity's interests. - b) they receive or have received any direct or indirect subsidy/ financial stake from any of them; or
- c) they have the same legal representative/agent for purposes of this bid; or
- d) they have relationship with each other, directly or through common third parties, that puts them in a position to have access to information about or influence on the bid of another Bidder; or

- f) In cases of agents quoting in offshore procurements (GTE), on behalf of their principal manufacturers, one agent cannot represent two manufacturers or quote on their behalf in a particular tender enquiry. One manufacturer can also authorise only one agent/dealer. There can be only one bid from the following:

1. The principal manufacturer directly or through one Indian agent on his behalf; and [in case of receipt of bids from both the Indian agent & the principal, the **principal manufacturer** shall be approached to arrange for withdrawal of one of the bids; in case of non-withdrawal, the bid from the **principal manufacturer** shall be considered]
2. Indian/foreign agent on behalf of only one principal.

- g) a Bidder or any of its affiliates participated as a consultant in the preparation of the design or technical specifications of the contract that is the subject of the Bid;

- h) In case of a holding company having more than one independently manufacturing units, or more than one unit having common business ownership/management, only one unit should quote. This section comprises the list of goods and delivery schedule. If there is no separate TS, then TS, quality assurance and inspections may also be included here. If the tender contains a number of schedules of requirements, it must be clarified, whether evaluation of eligibility/qualifications/financial bids would be on a schedule by schedule basis or on the basis of a total of all schedules put together.

#### xii) **Quotation Received from Dealers/Agents for Items not Manufactured by Them**
When a firm sends a quotation for an item manufactured by a different company, the firm is also required to attach in its quotation that manufacturer's authorisation certificate and also manufacturer's confirmation of extending the required warranty for that product (in addition to the tenderers' confirmation to the required warranty). If the firm is an authorised agent/dealer of that manufacturer, certified documentary evidence to this effect is to be attached along with the quotation. This is necessary to ensure a quotation from a responsible party offering the genuine product, also backed by a warranty obligation from the concerned manufacturer.

question_text: What are the two possible outcomes the Appellate Authority may issue after examining an appeal, before the debarment period ends
answer:
- Verify that, after examining an appeal before the debarment period ends, the Appellate Authority may issue either of the following outcomes:  
  a) Uphold the Competent Authority's decision, with or without any variation or a lesser period of Holiday Listing.  
  b) Annul the Competent Authority's order.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 55)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is asking: it wants the two specific results the Appellate Authority can hand down once it has reviewed an appeal, but only while the debarment period is still running.  

Next, I think about how an appeal is handled under the procurement rules. When an agency files an appeal, the Appellate Authority receives it, may ask the Competent Authority for comments, may even grant a personal hearing, and then, after looking at the case file and the appellant’s submissions, it is empowered to issue a final order before the debarment period expires.  

Now I focus on what that final order can actually look like. The rule spells out that the Appellate Authority may “pass appropriate order” and then explicitly lists the two alternatives it can choose between.  

The first alternative is to uphold the Competent Authority’s original decision. However, upholding does not have to be a blind affirmation; the Authority is allowed to tweak the decision—either leave it unchanged or introduce some variation, such as reducing the length of any Holiday Listing that was imposed.  

The second alternative is the opposite: the Appellate Authority can completely set aside the Competent Authority’s order, effectively annulling it and removing the debarment or Holiday Listing that had been imposed.  

Putting these points together, the only two outcomes the Appellate Authority may issue after examining an appeal, before the debarment period ends, are either to uphold the Competent Authority’s decision (with or without any variation or a lesser period of Holiday Listing) or to annul that decision outright.

question_text: What determines whether a project must implement a system for capturing photographs and videos of construction activities
answer:
- Projects whose value exceeds a specified threshold are required to implement a system for capturing photographs and videos of construction activities.  
- Where practicable, the system may be applied to all projects, irrespective of their value.

First, I need to pinpoint what triggers the obligation to set up a photo‑and‑video capture system for construction work. The core of the question is about the condition that makes the system mandatory rather than optional.  

The guidance ties the requirement to the scale or value of the project: it says that authorities should put such a system in place for projects that exceed a certain threshold value. This suggests that the determining factor is whether the project’s financial size crosses that predefined limit.  

Next, I consider the qualifier that follows: the guidance adds that, where practicable, the system may be applied to all projects, regardless of their value. This indicates that the threshold rule is not absolute; if resources and logistics allow, the same requirement can be extended universally.  

I then check whether any other criteria are mentioned—such as project type, location, or complexity—that could also dictate the need for the system. I do not have the detail on any additional conditions; the only explicit lever is the project value threshold, with a secondary, optional recommendation to broaden its use when feasible.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the primary determinant for mandatory implementation is the project’s value surpassing the specified threshold; secondarily, if it is practical to do so, the requirement can be extended to all projects irrespective of value. This matches the answer that projects above a threshold must implement the system, and where practicable it may be applied to all projects.

question_text: What qualifies as scrap material that can be sold for resale value
answer:
Q: What qualifies as scrap material that can be sold for resale value?  
A: Scrap material that can be sold for resale value consists of process waste, broken or damaged parts, workshop leftovers, and empty containers such as crates, drums or jerry cans that still have market worth. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 165)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know which kinds of materials are considered scrap that can still be sold for some resale value.  
Looking at the broader context of asset disposal, materials are grouped into condemned assets, scrap material, and surplus assets, each with its own criteria.  
The scrap material category is specifically described as items that are no longer useful in their original form but still retain some worth that can be recovered through resale.  
Examples given include process waste, broken or damaged components, workshop leftovers, and various empty containers such as crates, drums, or jerry cans.  
For these items to qualify as sellable scrap, they must still have market value—meaning they can be melted, re‑rolled, recycled, or otherwise reused by a buyer.  
Empty containers, for instance, are only considered scrap after they have been cleaned and are ready to be sent to a drum yard for disposal or resale.  
Putting these points together, the scrap that can be sold for resale value consists of process waste, broken or damaged parts, workshop waste, and empty containers like crates, drums, or jerry cans that still hold resale worth.  
This matches the description of scrap material that retains market value and can be disposed of through sale.

### 10.2.1 Classification of assets which have ceased to be useful:
The assets and materials which have ceased to be useful and may be considered for disposal may be categorized as under:

#### A) Condemned Assets:
- i) Assets / Materials that are not in working condition.
- ii) Assets / Materials that have outlived its normal span of life and beyond economic repair
- iii) Assets / Materials whose shelf life has expired

#### B) Scrap Material:
- i) Process Waste, broken, damage materials, workshop waste etc having resale value.
- ii) Empty containers, crates, drums etc.

#### C) Surplus Assets:
- i) Items that are in working condition but are lying in stores for more than five years (non-moving) shall be deemed as surplus unless there is specific reason (Insurance, Unique Spares etc.) to treat them otherwise.
- ii) Items in working condition but cannot be put into use effectively being outdated due to change in technology / operation.
- iii) Project Surplus

It is very important to categorise the scrapped items under different trade groups based on the use to which the scrap purchaser can put it for commercial use, for example, melting, re-rolling, burning, recycling, and so on. Properly grouped and sorted scrap is likely to attract better value and help in keeping historical data of prices and facilitates fixing of reserve prices.

Following are few examples of categorization of scrap/condemned assets/materials:

- i) Ferrous materials
- ii) Non-Ferrous metallic items (Aluminium, Copper etc.)
- iii) Chemicals and catalysts
- iv) Plastic materials
- v) Drums, Jerry cans and other empty containers

### 10.2.2 Identification And Declaration Of Assets Under Different Classes / Categories
a) Each department shall continuously monitor the assets and material under their custody and accordingly, identify any asset or material that needs to be categorized as Condemned, Scrap or Surplus.

b) Each department shall then, through their HODs, initiate the note for Declaration of the Asset as Condemned, Scrap or Surplus in compliance with the DOA. A survey committee may be constituted by functional head of user dept., if felt necessary.

Sample format for declaration of asset as Condemned, Scrap or Surplus is enclosed as Annexure 25

c) Warehouse department shall continuously monitor the materials under their custody (stored inside godown / under shed / open yard) and accordingly, identify any asset or material that needs to be categorized as Condemned, Scrap or Surplus. Necessary information will be circulated to the respective user departments.

d) After scrutiny of list of materials circulated by Warehouse, respective indenting / user departments shall then, through their HODs, initiate the note for Declaration of the Asset as Condemned, Scrap or Surplus in compliance of DOA.

Then I look for the provision that governs how that deposit is handled when the goods are lifted.  

In the contractual clauses dealing with disposal, there is a specific statement that the security deposit amount shall be adjusted against the invoice raised for uplifting of the quantity delivered in the last consignment or lot of the disposal.  

Reading that sentence, the adjustment means the deposit is subtracted from the invoice total for that final uplift, reducing the amount the buyer needs to pay.  

Putting the pieces together, the answer is clear: yes, the security deposit is adjusted against the invoice for the quantity delivered in the last consignment or lot of the disposal.

question_text: What is required regarding professional liability if the parties wish to limit the consultant’s liability
answer:
**A:** The parties may limit the consultant’s liability only if they ensure three conditions: (1) the limitation does not apply in cases of the consultant’s gross negligence or wilful misconduct; (2) the liability cannot be limited to less than a multiplier of the total contract value, which must be specified in the RFP and special conditions of contract; and (3) the limitation covers only the consultant’s liability to the Procuring Entity, not liability to third parties.  

**Rationale:** These safeguards protect the Procuring Entity while allowing a contractual cap on liability that complies with applicable law. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 45)
cot:
First, I ask myself what the question is really getting at: if the two sides want to put a ceiling on how much the consultant can be held liable for, what safeguards must be built into that ceiling so it isn’t unfair or unenforceable.  

Looking at the broader context of professional services contracts, the baseline rule is that the consultant’s liability is governed by whatever law applies, and the contract normally doesn’t need to touch that unless the parties deliberately choose to cap it. So the moment they decide to introduce a cap, they have to make sure the cap doesn’t undermine the purpose of liability altogether.  

The first thing that comes to mind is that you can’t let a contractor walk away scot‑free for truly reckless behavior. Therefore any limitation must expressly exclude cases of gross negligence or wilful misconduct; otherwise the provision would be void as against public policy.  

Next, I consider how low the cap can be set. If the parties were allowed to shrink the liability to a trivial amount, the procuring entity would be left without meaningful recourse. The reference material makes it clear that the cap must be tied to the size of the engagement itself—specifically, it cannot be less than some multiple of the total contract value, and that multiple has to be spelled out in the request for proposals and the special conditions of the contract.  

Then I think about the scope of who is protected. The contract is between the consultant and the procuring entity, so any limitation on liability should only affect that relationship. Extending the shield to third‑party claims would be inappropriate because those parties aren’t privy to the agreement and could be left without remedy. Hence the limitation must be expressly limited to the consultant’s liability toward the procuring entity, leaving third‑party liability untouched.  

Putting these three points together—no exemption for gross negligence or wilful misconduct, a minimum floor expressed as a multiplier of the contract value that is explicitly stated in the RFP and special conditions, and restriction of the cap to the procuring‑entity relationship—gives the complete set of requirements for a valid limitation of professional liability.  

Synthesizing the above, the answer is that the parties may limit the consultant’s liability only if they ensure those three conditions are met, which balances the procuring entity’s protection with the contractual freedom to cap liability.

question_text: Before substituting pre-dispatch inspection with the manufacturer's in-house inspection report and warranty for imported goods, what factors should the purchaser consider
answer:
Before substituting pre‑dispatch inspection with the manufacturer’s in‑house inspection report and warranty for imported goods, the purchaser should consider the following factors:

1. **Nature and cost of the goods ordered** – assess whether the characteristics and value of the items justify reliance on the supplier’s self‑certification.  
2. **Reputation of the supplier** – evaluate the supplier’s standing in the market to ensure reliability and quality capability.  
3. **Technical and financial competence of the firm** – obtain a report on the supplier’s technical and financial capability, which may be requested from the Indian embassy located in the supplier’s country.  
4. **Independent technical and financial data** – consult trustworthy publications such as Thomas Register, Dun and Bradstreet Register, or similar sources that provide verified information on manufacturing companies in the USA and Europe.  

After reviewing these factors, an appropriate decision on whether to adopt the substitution procedure should be taken.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 158)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the purchaser must weigh before deciding to skip the usual pre‑dispatch inspection and instead trust the maker’s own inspection report and warranty for imported items. The core issue is balancing risk against convenience when the supplier’s self‑certification is offered in place of an independent check.

Looking at the situation, the first thing that comes to mind is the nature and cost of the goods themselves. If the items are low‑value, non‑critical, or have a simple design, the purchaser might feel comfortable relying on the supplier’s word. Conversely, high‑value, complex, or safety‑critical equipment would demand stronger assurance, so the cost and characteristics of the order become a primary filter.

Next, the supplier’s standing in the market naturally follows. A manufacturer with a solid track record, known for consistent quality and adherence to standards, is more likely to produce an inspection report that can be trusted. Reputation therefore acts as a proxy for the reliability of their in‑house checks.

Beyond general reputation, it makes sense to dig deeper into the supplier’s actual technical and financial capacity. Knowing whether the firm has the expertise, equipment, and financial stability to carry out rigorous internal inspections helps gauge whether their self‑certification is credible. This kind of detail can often be obtained through official channels, such as a request to the relevant embassy for a report on the firm’s capabilities.

Even with an embassy report, cross‑checking with independent, widely recognized sources adds another layer of confidence. Publications that compile technical and financial data on manufacturers—think of industry registers or reputable business directories—provide objective information that can confirm or contradict what the supplier claims.

After running through these considerations—goods characteristics, supplier reputation, verified technical‑financial standing, and independent corroboration—the purchaser can synthesize the findings. If the evidence points to low risk and high confidence in the supplier’s own inspection, then waiving the pre‑dispatch check and accepting the manufacturer’s report and warranty becomes a reasonable choice; otherwise, the traditional inspection route should be retained. This reasoning naturally leads to the set of factors the purchaser must evaluate before making the substitution.

#### iii) **Manufacturer's Quality Self-certification**
Reputed manufacturers could be relied upon with respect to certain goods for quality products. These may not be subjected to physical inspection and the materials may be accepted under the firm's quality self-certification. The physical inspection clause stipulating the inspection authority and inspecting officer in such cases should not be included in the contracts entered into. Waiver of pre-dispatch inspection and acceptance of materials under the firm's quality self-certification may be considered where:

- a) The user Departments indicate, in their indent, that physical inspection is not necessary and that the materials can be accepted on the firm's quality self-certification;
- b) The user Department requests for a waiver of inspection to meet urgent requirement and where the firm is agreeable to 100 (hundred) per cent payment against the consignee's receipt and acceptance. In such cases, the user Departments themselves should be responsible for ensuring the quality of goods supplied;

- c) In case of goods to be imported from abroad, pre-dispatch inspection of goods at the supplier's premises involves considerable expenditure to the purchaser. In such a situation, the purchaser may substitute pre-dispatch inspection by its own inspector with manufacturer's in-house inspection report and warranty. However, before adopting this procedure, the nature and cost of the goods ordered, the reputation of the supplier, and so on, should also be kept in view and appropriate decision taken. For checking the reputation and background of the supplier, the purchase organisation may also request the Indian embassy located in that country for a report on the technical and financial competence of the firm. Further, trustworthy publications such as Thomas Register, Dun and Brad Street Register, and so on, are also available in the USA and Europe which provide authentic technical and financial data and details of the manufacturing companies located in those countries. Such publications may also be relied upon for this purpose; and
- d) However, the right of waiver of inspection may be reserved only for specific requirements. Justification for the waiver should be recorded. Also, a suitable clause may be incorporated in the conditions of contract.

#### iv) **Inspection on Installation and Commissioning**
This method is adopted to check the performance and output of equipment or machinery after it is commissioned and operational at site.

### 9.12.3 Types of Inspection Agencies
Normally, inspection modalities or agencies for inspections specified in the contract should not be changed. In rare cases, when this becomes inescapable, it should be done with the approval of the CA, justifying the rare circumstances, ensuring that no undue benefit accrues to the contractor.

#### i) **Internal Inspection Authorities**
Wherever there is technical expertise available in-house, an internal officer of the Indenting Department is nominated for inspection. The consignee should be the final authority for acceptance of goods.

question_text: In what circumstance is an RfP published on an open tender basis without an Expression of Interest (EoI) according to NRL procurement rules
answer: In the procurement of other (non‑consultancy) services, NRL publishes the Request for Proposals (RfP) on an open tender basis without requiring an Expression of Interest (EoI) (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 37). This approach applies specifically when the services being procured fall outside the consultancy category, allowing the RfP to be issued directly to all interested parties.
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: under what situation does NRL issue a Request for Proposals directly as an open tender, bypassing the Expression of Interest stage.  

Looking at the provided material, I notice a parenthetical note that clarifies the procedure for a specific type of procurement. It says that when the procurement concerns services other than consultancy, the process is carried out without an EoI, and consequently the RfP is released on an open tender basis.  

This tells me that the key condition is the nature of the service being acquired—if it falls outside the consultancy category, the usual EoI step is omitted.  

The reasoning behind this omission is that non‑consultancy services are treated as straightforward procurements where inviting all interested parties through an open tender is sufficient, making a preliminary EoI unnecessary.  

Putting these points together, the circumstance in which NRL publishes an RfP on an open tender basis without requiring an Expression of Interest is precisely when the procurement involves other, non‑consultancy services.  

Thus, the answer follows naturally: for non‑consultancy service procurements, NRL skips the EoI and issues the RfP openly to all interested parties.

question_text: What confidentiality responsibilities do TEC members have regarding information processed during the tender evaluation, and to whom must this information not be disclosed?
answer: TEC members must maintain the confidentiality of all information processed during the technical, commercial and financial evaluation of bids and must ensure that such information is not disclosed to any unauthorised person. This obligation is reinforced by the requirement that each member sign a declaration at the end of their reports affirming that they have no personal interest in the companies or agencies participating in the tender process (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 82).

Next, I look at what the guidance says about how they should treat that information – it stresses that they must deal with the procurement independently and impartially, avoid any conflict of interest, and specifically maintain confidentiality of the information processed during the evaluation.  
From that, I infer that the confidentiality duty means they must not let the evaluated data reach anyone who is not authorized to see it; in other words, the information must be kept within the committee and not disclosed to outsiders or any unauthorized person.  
Finally, I note that the requirement is reinforced by asking each member to sign a declaration at the end of their report confirming they have no personal interest in the participating companies, which underscores the need to keep the evaluation details secret and unbiased.  
Putting these points together, the responsibility is to keep all technical, commercial and financial evaluation information confidential and to ensure it is not disclosed to any unauthorised person.

question_text: What conditions must be satisfied regarding the quantity and usage period of materials for which a secured advance is claimed
answer: The quantities of the materials must not be excessive, and the materials must be used within a period of 90 days from the date the advance is granted. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 104)
cot:
First, I consider what a secured advance against material actually means: it is a payment made to the contractor based on the value of materials that have been delivered to the site but have not yet been built into the works. Because the contractor receives money before the materials are consumed, the contract must protect the procuring entity from risk of over‑advance or misuse.

Next, I look for the safeguards that the contract places on this type of advance. The provision limits the amount to a percentage of invoice or BOQ value, but it also attaches two substantive conditions that are independent of the percentage ceiling: the quantities of the materials claimed must not be excessive, and the materials must be put to use within a specified time frame.

Turning to the quantity condition, I reason that “not excessive” is meant to prevent the contractor from inflating the advance by stockpiling far more material than the work actually requires. If the quantities were excessive, the advance could exceed the true value of work to be done, making recovery difficult and exposing the procuring entity to loss. Therefore, the contractor must demonstrate that the claimed quantities are reasonable in relation to the scope of the works.

Then I examine the usage‑period condition. The advance is essentially a loan secured by the materials; to ensure the security remains valid, the materials need to be incorporated into the works promptly. The contract stipulates a maximum period after which the advance must be repaid regardless of consumption, and it ties the eligibility for the advance to the requirement that the materials be used within 90 days of receiving the advance. This time limit guarantees that the materials will not sit idle indefinitely, preserving the lender’s security and facilitating timely recovery.

Finally, I combine these two independent requirements: for a secured advance to be granted, the contractor must show that the material quantities are not excessive relative to the works, and that those materials will be consumed and incorporated into the works within 90 days from the date the advance is made. These are precisely the conditions that must be satisfied.

### 6.5.4 Secured Advance against Material brought to Site
Secured advance on the security of materials (which are not combustible, fragile or perishable in nature) brought to the site but not yet incorporated in the works will be made up to 75 (seventy-five) per cent of invoice value, or the 75 (seventy-five) per cent of the corresponding value of the materials determined on the basis of BOQ rates, whichever is less, subject to the condition that their quantities are not excessive and shall be used within a period of 90 (ninety) days and subject to other stipulations in the contract. The contractor will be required to sign an indenture bond, hypothecating the goods to the procuring entity, and also be responsible for their safe custody. Before the advance is released, the procuring entity may inspect the site to ensure that the Contractor has safeguarded the materials against pilferage and deterioration. It may be ensured that the contractor has not taken any loan/ limit from banks against hypothecation of the materials against which the secured advance is claimed. An undertaking in this regard may also be taken from the contractor.

Generally, as per the provisions of the contracts, the contractors are required to submit proof of cost of materials and the delivery of material at site while claiming such advances. The stock register should be maintained from the commencement of the contract and, unless otherwise prescribed in the contracts, the stock, so considered for advance, should generally be only paid stock (and not brought on credit). Where the materials are supplied from a captive source of the contractor, the reasonableness of the valuation of such materials may be ensured.

The advance will be repaid from each succeeding running bill (periodic/ interim payment) to the extent materials for which advance has been previously paid have been incorporated into the works. In all cases, the repayment of the advance will be affected after expiry of a period of 120 days since payment of advance, whether the material is consumed in the work or not.

Asking for a bid-price inclusive of taxes/ GST would be a violation of the GST Act. Bid format may be suitably modified accordingly. In the transition period, any variation in tax structure/rate due to introduction of GST shall be dealt with under Statutory Variation Clause.

Ministries/ Departments may follow the procedure as mentioned below while dealing with contractor's payment, post GST promulgation:

- a) **Works is treated as a 'Service':** ( GST rate would vary depending on type of work). All works contracts are to be provided with Harmonized System of Nomenclature - HSN Code (actually Service Accounting Code SAC, being a service). The HSN code can be downloaded from the website [www.cbec.gov.in](http://www.cbec.gov.in). Works Contracts in general come under Chapter 99, Section 5, Heading 9954(Construction Services)as 'Composite supply of Works contract as defined in clause 119 of section 2 of CGST Act'. GST rate would be based on the type of contract. In case contract consists of both goods & service, then interpretation regarding nature of contract for determination of GST rate should be done as per clause 8, Chapter III of CGST Act, 2017.

b) The 'on account/ final contract certificate' shall be prepared by the executing department on the basis of quantity of work executed at the contracted rates, duly segregating the GST component as detailed in para (iii) below.
