#### 6. Payment of duty:
6.1 The duty can be paid in the designated banks through TR-6 challans. It is necessary to check the name of the bank and the branch before depositing the duty. Bank endorses the payment particulars in challan which is submitted to the Customs. Facility of e-payment of duty through more than one authorized bank is also available since 2007 at all major Customs locations. Duty has to be paid prior berthing/landing of vessel /aircraft at Port failing which Interest is payable as per Customs norms.

6.2 In order to reduce the transaction costs and expedite Customs clearance the Board has decided to make e-payment of duty mandatory.

#### 7. Amendment of Bill of Entry:
7.1 Whenever mistakes are noticed after submission of documents, amendments to the Bill of Entry is carried out with the approval of Deputy/Assistant Commissioner. The request for amendment may be submitted with the supporting documents. For example, if the amendment of container number is required, a letter from shipping agent is required. On sufficient proof amendment in Bill of Entry may be permitted after the goods have been given out of charge i.e. goods have been cleared.

#### 8. Prior Entry for Bill of Entry:
For faster clearance of the goods, Section 46 of the Customs Act, 1962 allows filing of Bill of Entry prior to arrival of goods. This Bill of Entry is valid if vessel/aircraft carrying the goods arrives within 30 days from the date of presentation of Bill of Entry. The importer must declare that the vessel/aircraft is due within 30 days and present the Bill of Entry for final noting as soon as the IGM is filed.

## 9. Bill of Entry for bond/warehousing:
9.1 A separate form of Bill of Entry is used for clearance of goods for warehousing. All documents, as are required to be attached with a Bill of Entry for home consumption are also required with the Bill of Entry for warehousing which is assessed in the same manner and duty payable is determined. However, since duty is not required to be paid at the time of warehousing, the purpose of assessing the duty at this stage is only to secure the duty in case the goods do not reach the warehouse. The duty is paid at the time of ex-bond clearance of goods for which an Ex-Bond Bill of Entry is filed. The rate of duty applicable to imported goods cleared from a warehouse is the rate in force on the date of filing of Ex-Bond Bill of Entry.

## 10. Export procedure - Shipping Bill:
10.1 For clearance of export goods, the exporter or his agent has to obtain an Importer-Export Code (IEC) number from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade Under the EDI System, IEC number is received by the Customs System from the DGFT online. The exporter is also required to register authorized foreign exchange dealer code (through which export proceeds are expected to be realized) and open a current account in the designated bank for credit of any Drawback incentive. GST number is also to be linked with the IEC number.

10.2 All the exporters intending to export under the export promotion scheme need to get their licences/DEEC book etc. registered at the Customs Station. For such registration, original documents are required.

## 11. Octroi exemption for export goods:
11.1 Since the Shipping Bill is issued by ICEGATE only after the 'Let Export' order is given by Customs, the exporter may make use of export invoice or such other document as required by the Octroi authorities for the purpose of Octroi exemption.

## 12. Waiver of GR form:
12.1 Generally the processing of Shipping Bills requires the production of a GR form that is used to monitor the foreign exchange remittance in respect of the export goods. However, there are few exceptions when the GR form is not required. An example is export of goods valued not more than US \$25,000/- and another is export of gifts valued up to Rs.5,00,000/-.

question_text: How does the treatment of reimbursable items differ between PR estimate and contract value?
answer:
- PR estimate: includes the reimbursable amount, which is shown separately (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 21).  
- Contract value: excludes reimbursement items; the provision for reimbursement is noted separately, with GST also stated separately (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 21).
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know how reimbursable items are handled when preparing a PR estimate versus when stating the final contract value.  

Looking at the description of the PR estimate, I see that the estimate is meant to capture the full financial outgo expected for the work. Because reimbursable items such as PF, ESI, overtime, allowances, safety gear, tolls, travel, accommodation and statutory charges are not to be quoted by the bidder, they still represent a cost that the agency must anticipate. Therefore, the PR estimate incorporates the total amount expected for these reimbursable items, but it presents that amount as a distinct line item so that it can be tracked separately from the bid‑able SOR items.  

Next, I turn to the definition of contract value. The contract value reflects the price that is actually awarded to the contractor for the work they are required to perform under the SOR. Since reimbursable items are not part of the bid price and are to be paid back on submission of evidence, they are excluded from the contract value itself. However, to ensure that the parties are aware of this separate obligation, the contract document notes the provision for reimbursable items as a separate entry, and any applicable GST is also shown apart from the base contract value.  

Comparing the two, the key difference lies in inclusion versus exclusion: the PR estimate builds the reimbursable amount into its total calculation while still highlighting it separately, whereas the contract value strips the reimbursable amount out of the core price and records it only as a separate provision. Both treatments keep the reimbursable component visible, but one treats it as part of the estimated cost and the other treats it as an external adjustment to the awarded price.  

This reasoning leads directly to the conclusion that the PR estimate includes the reimbursable amount (shown separately), while the contract value excludes reimbursement items, with the provision for reimbursement and GST stated separately.
chunk_content:
## 2.10 Estimation for Reimbursement Items
The PR comprise of the SOR of the activities against which the agency has to quote its bid price and perform them as per the terms and conditions of the contract. Normally bidder has to quote for all the items of the SOR.

But in certain contracts, items like PF, ESI, Overtime, Shift/Height Allowance, Safety Items, PPE, Toll Fee, Travel Expenses, Accommodation, Statutory Charges etc. are separately kept in the contracts as “reimbursable items”. These items are kept as ‘SOR items not to be quoted by the bidder’. Contractor has to perform these activities and get reimbursed as per terms & conditions of the contract.

Provision for reimbursement of actual outgo from the contractor is kept, and payment is released on submission of documentary evidence. The rates for reimbursement shall be duly verified for reasonableness by the EIC before certification for payment. This is done to keep such items outside the ‘SOR items to be quoted by bidders’ as a measure to ensure compliance of statutory requirements, quality standards and uniformity.

For estimation of such “reimbursement items” a standard practice should be followed across all departments as far as possible, to ensure meeting the quality norms at uniform rate.

**Treatment of “REIMBURSEMENT ITEMS” in various stages of procurement, shall be as follows:-**

- a) **PR Estimate:** The PR estimate should be inclusive of the reimbursable amount, which is to be shown separately.
- b) **Bidders’ PQC:** The estimated cost for determination of PQC shall be the total estimated cost including ‘reimbursable items’ as well as ‘SOR items to be quoted by bidders’ (excluding GST).
- c) **EMD value limit:** The estimated cost for determination of EMD shall be the total estimated cost including ‘reimbursable items’ as well as ‘SOR items to be quoted by bidders’ (excluding GST).

- d) **TEC Approval:** TEC approval should be based on total financial outgo i.e., including any 'reimbursable items' and including all taxes.
- e) **Contract Value:** The contract value shall be the total awarded value of items, excluding any provision for 'reimbursement items'. Provision for 'reimbursement items' shall be separately mentioned. GST rate shall be separately mentioned.
- f) **Security Deposit / Performance Guarantee:** Security deposit shall be applicable on contract value excluding reimbursement items.
- g) **Job Completion Certificate:** The job completion certificate should be issued for total value of works executed, including any provision for 'reimbursement items'. Executed basic value and executed 'reimbursable items' shall be separately mentioned. (All values excluding GST).
- h) **Contract Variation:** The variation amount and percentage for the purpose of determining approving authority for variation of contract value would be based on the final executed value including any "reimbursement items" but excluding "changes due to inbuilt escalation/variation clause". The base amount shall be the awarded order value based on originally approved TEC. In case of clear original tender provisions for extension/enhancement in AMC/ARC (for 1+1 years, or 2+1 years etc.), the base value shall be the total awarded order value including extension/enhancement. However, all other variations such as extra item, additional qty., increase/decrease in man-days, etc. shall be treated as variation in contract value. Further, authority for approval for final executed contract value should be based on total financial outgo including all taxes as per DOA.
- i) **Liquidated Damages / Price reduction for delay:** LD / PRC shall be applicable on contract value excluding reimbursement items.

question_text: Confirm that, if the MSE bidder matches the L1 evaluated price for a non-divisible item, the order is placed on that MSE bidder.
answer:
- Clause: Purchase preference – non‑divisible item – MSE bidder matching L1 price.  
  - Verification step: Confirm that when the MSE (L3) bidder’s quoted price equals the L1 evaluated price, the procurement order is awarded to the MSE bidder. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 32)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants confirmation that, for a non‑divisible item, when the MSE (Micro and Small Enterprise) bidder’s quoted price is exactly equal to the L1 evaluated price, the procurement order should be awarded to that MSE bidder.  

Next, I isolate the relevant conditions from the purchase‑preference rules for non‑divisible items. The hierarchy is L1 (the lowest evaluated bid, which is not an MSE or a Class‑I local supplier), L2 (a Class‑I local supplier within 20% of L1), and L3 (an MSE bidder within 15% of L1). The rule explicitly states that the MSE bidder is given the preference to match the L1 evaluated price.  

Then, I follow the logical consequence of that preference: if the L3 bidder (the MSE) actually matches the L1 price, the rule says the order shall be placed on him. Only if the MSE does not match does the opportunity shift to the L2 bidder.  

Finally, I verify that no other provision overrides this outcome for a non‑divisible item. The section does not introduce any additional thresholds or exceptions that would cancel the MSE’s right once the price match is achieved, so the conclusion stands firm: when the MSE bidder matches the L1 evaluated price, the order is placed on that MSE bidder.

###### Examples of Purchase Preference:


###### Non divisible item
L1 bidder is non MSE or other than class-I local supplier

L2 bidder is Class-I local supplier (within 20%)

L3 bidder is MSE bidder (within 15%)

MSE bidder shall be given preference to match the L1 evaluated price. If L3 bidder matches the L1 evaluated price, order shall be placed on him, otherwise, option for matching the L1 price shall be given to L2 bidder (Class-I local supplier).

###### Divisible item
L1 bidder is non MSE or other than class-I local supplier

L2 bidder is Class-I local supplier (within 20%)

L3 bidder is MSE bidder (within 15%)

MSE bidder shall be given preference to match the L1 evaluated price. If bidder matches the L1 price, order shall be placed on him for the quantity specified in the bidding document (i.e., 25% of

the quantities against the item(s) of MR). For the balance quantity (i.e. 50% of tendered quantity / value) option for matching the L1 evaluated price shall be given to L2 bidder (Class-I local supplier). Balance quantity (i.e., 25% of the quantities against the item(s) of MR) shall be awarded to natural lowest bidder.

In above case, if there will be 2 or more MSE bidder within 15%, then 25% quantity shall be distributed proportionately / equally among the MSEs who have agreed to match the L1 prices.

- C. In case lowest bidder is a MSE bidder, the entire work shall be awarded to him without resorting to purchase preference to bidders complying with Local Content.
- D. In case lowest bidder is a Class-I local supplier, purchase preference shall be resorted to MSE bidder as per provisions specified in the enquiry document w.r.t. PPP-2012 only.
- d) In case purchase preference is applicable, but negotiation is to be conducted with L1 bidder, negotiation shall be carried out. MSE and/or Class-I local supplier shall be offered to match the negotiated prices (even if, post negotiation, they are higher by more than 20% (for Class-I local supplier)/ 15% (for MSEs) as compared to L1 bidder provided they were within 20% (for Class-I local supplier)/ 15% (for MSEs) of L1 bidder as per original quoted prices) and left out quantity, if any, as per provisions of enquiry document shall be awarded to that bidder.

###### 6. Determination of LC


###### a) LC of goods
- (i) LC of goods shall be computed on the basis of the cost of domestic components in goods, compared to the whole cost of product.
- (ii) The criteria for determination of the local content cost in the goods shall be as follows:
  - a) in the case of direct component (material), based on country of origin;
  - b) in the case of manpower, based on INR component.
- (iii) The calculation of LC of the combination of several kinds of goods shall be based on the ratio of the sum of the multiplication of LC of each of the goods with the acquisition price of each goods to the acquisition price of the combination of goods.

###### b) LC of service
- (i) LC of Service shall be calculated on the basis of the ratio of service cost of domestic component in service to the total cost of service.
- (ii) The total cost of service shall be constituted of the cost spent for rendering of service, covering:
  - a) cost of component (material) which is used;
  - b) manpower and consultant cost; cost of working equipment/ facility; and
  - c) general service cost
- (iii) The criteria for determination of cost of local content in the service shall be as follows:
  - a) in the case of material being used to help the provision of service, based on country of origin;
  - b) in the case of manpower and consultant based on INR component of the services contract;
  - c) in the case of working equipment/facility, based on country of origin; and
  - d) in the case of general service cost, based on the criteria as mentioned in clauses a, b, and c above.
  - e) Indian flag vessels in operation as on date.

question_text: In what currency should Indian agents of foreign suppliers receive their agency commission
answer: - Indian agents of foreign suppliers must receive their agency commission in Indian currency. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 107)
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question really wants to know: which currency should be used when paying the agency commission to an Indian agent who works for a foreign supplier.  

The first thing that comes to mind is the general practice in government procurement—payments for activities that take place inside the country are normally made in the local currency to avoid unnecessary exchange‑rate complications and to keep accounting straightforward.  

Thinking further, I recall that the procurement guidelines distinguish between two kinds of payments: one for the actual imported goods, which can be quoted and settled in foreign currency, and another for any allied work or services that are performed within India, such as installation, commissioning, or agency support, which are to be quoted and paid in Indian rupee.  

Since the agency commission is compensation for a service rendered by an Indian agent operating in India, it naturally falls under the allied work and services category rather than the cost of the imported goods themselves.  

Applying that rule, the commission must therefore be settled in Indian currency, exactly as the manual prescribes for all locally performed services.  

Putting the pieces together, the only consistent answer is that Indian agents of foreign suppliers should receive their agency commission in Indian rupee.

question_text: What contractual information about delivery or completion must be recorded for each tenderer?
answer: - Contractual completion / delivery term of each tenderer shall be recorded. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 71)
cot:
First, I ask myself what the question is really after: it wants to know which contractual detail about delivery or completion has to be written down for every tenderer when the bids are being examined.  
Thinking about why that detail matters, I realize that having a clear delivery or completion schedule lets the evaluation team compare offers on a common time basis and spot any deviations that could affect price or project timing.  
Next, I turn to the rules for preparing the comparative statement, which is the tool used to line up all the tenders side by side. The guidelines list a series of items that must appear in that statement so that the comparison is meaningful and complete.  
Scanning through those items, one clause catches my eye: it says that the contractual completion or delivery term of all parties shall be given in the tabulation.  
Because the statement is constructed tenderer by tenderer, this requirement translates directly into recording the completion or delivery term for each individual tenderer in the comparative sheet.  
Putting the pieces together, I conclude that the contractual completion or delivery term of each tenderer is the precise piece of contractual information that must be recorded.
chunk_content:
### Broad guidelines for preparation of Comparative statement:
- i) To facilitate proper bid analysis, the comparative statement shall be made of all the tenders received on the following basis:
  - a) Price quoted by all the firms shall be given. Where alternative specifications has been offered for the jobs under reference and are acceptable, their prices shall also be indicated along with suitable explanatory note concerning deviations.  
The item wise estimate or Last Paid Unit Price (LPP) shall also be given in this tabulation to make comparison of estimate or LPP with the tendered rates.
  - b) Prices quoted shall be reduced to a common base for a meaningful comparison.
  - c) Where earnest money is required, mention to be made whether it has been furnished or not.
  - d) All deviations either in specifications or in standard terms and conditions shall specifically be highlighted, particularly those having a bearing on price or delivery shall be indicated.
  - e) Contractual completion / delivery term of all parties shall be given.
  - f) Discount / Rebate if any offered to be indicated.
  - g) Foreign exchange required in the case of imports shall be indicated.
  - h) Incidence of GST/ Customs Duty/ Excise Duty/ or other Statutory levies, shall be quantified and clearly shown.
  - i) Packing, Handling, Forwarding and Transportation Charges, insurance as applicable should be specified and the incidence thereof should be shown.
  - j) Payment terms and particulars of advance if any and / or progress payments if any demanded shall be indicated. Where advance payment is involved, the cost implications must be determined / indicated.
  - k) Prices escalation clause, if any to be clearly indicated and the cost implication loaded in the tender evaluation.
  - l) Taking all factors into consideration, comparative cost evaluation statement shall be made to give a realistic, representative and comprehensive cost comparison.
  - m) Applicable Purchase preferences and the policies of the Government with regard to MSE and other guidelines shall be suitably brought out in the evaluation sheet for the guidance of the TEC.
- ii) The comparative statement shall be uploaded in Aarohan system by the dealing officer of the Commercial dept.
- iii) The Commercial Department would prepare a detailed note (TEC note) to the Tender Committee / CA highlighting the main points with the recommendation for the award of the contract. The tender papers enclosed along with the above note should include the comprehensive tabulation drawn as indicated above to arrive at a meaningful comparison for

effective decision-making. There should be no ambiguity in any of the data presented for consideration.

- iv) Explanation should be given for variation between prices quoted in the tender and the evaluated prices. Any positive or negative loading done to render the comparison meaningful should be properly explained. Clarifications sought from the tenderers and the resulting impact on the quotation if any should be specifically mentioned. It should be ensured that all technical details; specification drawings and other aspects contained in the offers have been thoroughly checked for conformity with the tender enquiry before presentation to the Committee.

In short, a factual, informative and technically clear material should be portrayed in the noting to the Committee / CA to facilitate taking decisions for the contracts without further reference to the field units.

question_text: What is the purpose of the bank guarantee required under Annexure 19 for tender participation
answer: The bank guarantee required under Annexure 19 serves as an irrevocable Earnest Money Deposit guarantee. It must be submitted by the tenderer as a condition precedent to participate in the tender, obliging the bank to pay the guaranteed amount immediately on demand by Numaligarh Refinery Ltd, without reservation or protest, and the amount may be forfeited if any contingency specified in the tender document occurs. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 144)
cot:
First, I consider why a tender would ask for a bank guarantee at all – it is usually to prove that the bidder is serious and to protect the owner if the bidder backs out or fails to meet obligations.  

Looking at the guarantee’s wording, it is described as irrevocable and payable immediately on demand, with no reservation or protest, which tells me it is meant to be a swift, enforceable security rather than a lengthy claim process.  

The guarantee is linked to an Earnest Money Deposit amount, indicating that it stands in place of a cash deposit that would otherwise be held by the owner.  

Because it is a condition precedent for participation, the tenderer must provide this guarantee before the bid is even considered, so the guarantee functions as a gate‑keeping mechanism that filters out non‑serious bidders.  

Finally, the note that the guaranteed sum is liable to be forfeited on any contingency mentioned in the tender document shows that the guarantee’s purpose is to allow the owner to recover the EMD automatically if the tenderer defaults or violates tender terms.  

Putting these points together, the bank guarantee under Annexure 19 serves as an irrevocable Earnest Money Deposit guarantee: it must be submitted upfront to enable tender participation, obliges the bank to pay the amount instantly on demand without protest, and lets the owner forfeit the sum if any tender‑specified contingency occurs.

question_text: How is the Shipping Bill generated for my export shipment?
answer: After the Customs Appraiser gives the “Let Export” order on the EDI system, the Shipping Bill is generated online. One copy of the generated Shipping Bill is sent directly to you, and another copy is forwarded to your bank through the RBI. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 226)
cot:
First, I think about what initiates the creation of a Shipping Bill for an export shipment. The question is asking specifically how the bill itself is produced, so I need to locate the point in the process where the document is generated.

Then, I consider the overall flow of export customs procedures. Goods arrive at the dock, are checked against the Shipping Bill and other declarations, and undergo customs examination. Only after the examination is satisfied does customs give clearance for the goods to leave.

Next, I focus on the role of the Customs Appraiser. Once the examination is complete and the officer is satisfied, the Appraiser issues a “Let Export” order on the EDI system. This order is the formal authorization that the shipment may proceed.

Following that, the EDI system is designed to react to the Let Export order. As soon as that order is recorded, the system automatically creates the Shipping Bill online, producing an electronic version of the document.

After the Shipping Bill is generated, the system handles its distribution. One copy is transmitted directly to the exporter—me—so I have the proof of export, while another copy is sent to the exporter’s bank through the Reserve Bank of India, which is needed for payment and drawback processing.

Finally, I check that this sequence matches the description: the Shipping Bill is generated online after the Customs Appraiser’s Let Export order on the EDI system, with one copy going to the exporter and another to the bank via the RBI. This aligns precisely with the given answer, and no extra conclusions are introduced.

## 13. Arrival of export goods at docks:
13.1. The goods brought for the purpose of export are allowed entry to the Dock on the strength of the Shipping Bill so filed through ICEGATE online and other declarations filed by the exporter/CHA.

## 14. Customs examination of export goods:
14.1 After the receipt of the goods in the Docks, the exporter/CHA may contact the Customs Officer designated for the purpose, and present the check list with the endorsement of custodian and other declarations along with all original documents such as, Invoice and Packing list, AR-4, etc. The Customs Officer may verify the quantity of the goods actually received and enter into the system and thereafter mark the Electronic Shipping Bill and also hand over all original documents to the Dock Appraiser who assigns a Customs Officer for examination and indicate the officers' name and the packages to be examined, if any, on the check list and return it to the exporter/CHA. There are various examination norms which may have to be referred w.r.t. export consignments keeping in view the quantum of incentive, value of export goods, the country of destination etc.

## 15. Generation of Shipping Bills:
15.1 After the "Let Export" order is given on the EDI system by the Appraiser, the Shipping Bill is generated online. One copy is transmitted directly to the Exporter and another to the Bank through RBI. Drawback is credited to Exporter's bank account only after filing of EGM.

## 16. Export General Manifest:
16.1 All the shipping lines/agents need to furnish the Export General Manifests, Shipping Bill-wise, to the Customs electronically before departure of the conveyance.

## Classification/Assessment of Projects Imports, Baggage and Postal imports


### 1. Project imports:
1.1 'Project Imports' is an Indian innovation to facilitate setting up of and expansion of industrial projects. Normally, imported goods are classified separately under different tariff headings and assessed to applicable Customs duty, but as a variety of goods are imported for setting up an industrial project their separate classification and valuation for assessment to duty becomes cumbersome. Further, the suppliers of a contracted project, do not value each and every item or parts of machinery which are supplied in stages. Hence, ascertaining values for different items delay assessment leading to demurrage and time and cost overruns for the project. Therefore, to facilitate

smooth and quick assessment by a simplified process of classification and valuation, the goods imported under Project Import Scheme are placed under a single Tariff Heading 9801 in the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. The Central Government has formulated the Project Import Regulations, 1986 prescribing the procedure for effecting imports under this scheme.

1.2 The Project Import Scheme seeks to achieve the objective of simplifying the assessment in respect of import of capital goods and related items required for setting up of a project by classifying all goods under heading 9801 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and prescribing a uniform Customs duty rate for them even though other headings may cover these goods more specifically. Thus, a number of notifications have been issued notifying a large number of projects for assessment under Tariff Heading 9801, which may have to be referred for availing the scheme.

question_text: What manual verification step confirms that a Bill of Entry has been noted/registered against the IGM filed by the carrier
answer: Manual verification step: The Noting Section verifies that the consignment sought to be cleared has been manifested in the particular vessel as recorded in the IGM, thereby confirming the noting/registration of the Bill of Entry against the IGM. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 223)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants the specific manual action that confirms a Bill of Entry has been noted or registered against the IGM filed by the carrier.  
Then, I recall that in the manual process the Bill of Entry must be taken to the Noting Section, where officials perform a check before any further processing.  
Next, I identify what that check entails: the Noting Section compares the details of the consignment the importer wishes to clear with the information recorded in the IGM for the vessel that is supposed to have carried the goods.  
Looking at this further, the purpose of the comparison is to verify that the goods described in the Bill of Entry were actually manifested on that particular vessel; only when this match is found does the section assign a Bill of Entry number and stamp the copies.  
Finally, this verification by the Noting Section is exactly the manual step that confirms the noting/registration of the Bill of Entry against the IGM, because it establishes the link between the declared consignment and the carrier's manifest before the document proceeds to appraisal.
chunk_content:
2.6 The first stage for processing a Bill of Entry is termed as the noting/registration of the Bill of Entry vis-a-vis the IGM filed by the carrier. In the manual format, the importer has to get the Bill of Entry noted in the concerned Noting Section which checks the consignment sought to be cleared having been manifested in the particular vessel and a Bill of Entry number is generated and indicated on all copies. After noting, the Bill of Entry gets sent to the appraising section of the Custom House for assessment functions, payment of duty etc. In the EDI system, the noting aspect is checked by the system itself, which also generates Bill of Entry number.

2.7 After noting/registration the Bill of Entry is forwarded manually or electronically to the concerned Appraising Group in the Custom House dealing with the commodity sought to be cleared. answer: The contractor must obtain the engineer’s approval for each quarry and borrow area before beginning quarrying or borrow‑area excavation activities (see 6.1.5 Approval of Quarries and Borrow Areas and Materials). (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 90)

Next, I focus on the clause that deals with quarries and borrow areas; it makes clear that the engineer’s sign‑off is required for each individual site before the contractor may start extracting material.  
I note that this approval is not a blanket permission; it must be obtained separately for every quarry and borrow area the contractor intends to use, and it encompasses both the location and the material to be taken from it.  
Finally, putting these points together, I conclude that the contractor must obtain the engineer’s approval for each quarry and borrow area prior to commencing any quarrying or borrow‑area excavation activities.

Looking at the agreement, the contractor’s promise is framed as a covenant to “duly carry out and complete the work … for the owner at its specified site to its complete satisfaction.” This tells me right away that the location— the owner’s specified site— and the standard of satisfaction are fundamental conditions.  
Next, I note that the completion must not be arbitrary; it has to align with everything the contract defines as the work. That includes the works themselves, the specifications, the schedule of rates, and the plans that are mentioned, enumerated or referred to in the contract.  
Beyond those explicit documents, the contractor is also bound to follow any directions that come from the owner’s authorized engineer‑in‑charge, who supervises the execution and gives instructions from time to time.  
The contract further requires the contractor to perform all other acts that are either expressly mentioned in the agreement, implied by its provisions, or reasonably necessary to bring the work to completion.  
Finally, all of this must happen within the timing and manner laid out by the contract’s terms and conditions— the agreed‑upon schedule, the prescribed methods, and any stipulations that govern how and when the work is to be done.  
Putting these pieces together, the conditions under which the contractor must complete the work to the owner’s satisfaction are: performing the work at the owner’s specified site, achieving the owner’s complete satisfaction, doing so in strict accordance with the works, specifications, schedule of rates, and plans referenced in the contract, obeying the engineer‑in‑charge’s instructions, carrying out any additional acts implied or reasonably necessary for completion, and observing the times and manner prescribed by the contract’s terms and conditions.

question_text: What could happen if the TRC evaluates proposals without predefined grades?
answer: **A:** Without predefined grades, evaluators may interpret the same criteria differently, leading to inconsistent scores; their personal leniency or strictness could be exaggerated because there are no shared definitions; and large score differences caused by misunderstandings of the terms of reference or improper use of the evaluation criteria would be difficult to justify or reconcile. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 47)
cot:
I need to think about what the TRC is supposed to do when it evaluates technical proposals and why having a predefined grading system matters.  

First, the whole point of a grading system is to give everyone a common reference point—so that when we look at a criterion we all know what a “good,” “average,” or “poor” rating looks like in concrete terms.  

If that system isn’t set up beforehand, each evaluator is left to interpret the criteria on their own. That means two people might read the same requirement and decide it means different things, simply because of their own background or how they’ve understood the terms of reference.  

Because of those differing interpretations, the scores they assign can end up all over the place, even when the proposals are actually similar in quality. The variation isn’t reflecting real differences; it’s just reflecting that we’re not speaking the same language about what the criteria entail.  

Beyond that, every evaluator has a natural tendency to be either generous or strict. Without a shared scale to anchor those tendencies, there’s nothing to pull the scores toward a middle ground, so any personal bias gets magnified and shows up more clearly in the final numbers.  

Finally, when the scores diverge for these reasons—whether it’s because we misunderstood the ToR or we applied the criteria inconsistently—it becomes very hard to explain or justify the outcome. There’s no clear benchmark to point to, so the committee struggles to reconcile the differences or defend the recommendation to the approving authority.  

Putting those pieces together, evaluating proposals without predefined grades would lead to inconsistent scoring due to varied criterion interpretations, exaggerated personal leniency or strictness, and large, hard‑to‑justify score differences stemming from misunderstandings of the terms of reference or improper use of the evaluation criteria.

question_text: Which sections of the Standard Bidding Document (SBD) should be used unaltered to ensure uniformity across procurements?
answer: To ensure uniformity across procurements, the standard provisions in most sections of the Standard Bidding Document (SBD)/SRfPD must be used unaltered. Any modifications required to suit a specific procurement should be made only in the variable sections, such as Special Instructions to Bidders or special conditions of contract. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 91)
cot:
First, I think about what it means to have uniformity across procurements: every bidding process should start from the same baseline so that bidders face consistent rules and expectations.  

Looking at how the Standard Bidding Document is structured, it separates the parts that are meant to stay the same for all procurements from the parts that can be tailored to a particular purchase.  

The reference makes it clear that the “standard provisions in most sections of the SBD/SRfPD are to be used unaltered” if we want that uniformity.  

It also points out that any changes needed to fit a specific procurement should be made only in the “variable sections,” which are exemplified by the Special Instructions to Bidders or the special conditions of contract.  

Putting those pieces together, the sections that must remain unchanged are precisely the standard provisions—the non‑variable parts of the SBD—while the variable sections are the appropriate place for adjustments.  

Thus, to ensure uniformity across procurements, the standard provisions in most sections of the SBD/SRfPD should be used unaltered, with modifications confined to the variable sections such as Special Instructions to Bidders or special conditions of contract.

question_text: Under which circumstances may a procurement be carried out on a single tender basis?
answer:
A procurement may be carried out on a single tender basis only when one of the following circumstances applies:

- The material to be manufactured/fabricated or the services to be obtained are of a specialized or proprietary nature.  
- Under technical or professional advice, works are to be obtained from specialized parties or individuals (e.g., soil investigation, land valuation, arbitration, HR/Finance/IT interventions, technical investigation).  
- The situation warrants immediate or urgent action.  
- Indigenous development of items for import substitution is involved, allowing an invitation of offer from a single party specializing in the field/commodity followed by negotiations.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 65)
cot:
I need to figure out when a procurement can be done with only one tender invited.  
First, I think about what a single tender actually means: it’s an invitation sent to just one firm, so the organization must have a clear reason to limit competition.  
Next, I recall the rules that spell out the exact situations where this is allowed. The policy lays out a specific list under the nomination‑basis tender section, indicating that single‑tender procurements are permissible only in those cases.  
Considering that list, the first condition covers items or services that are truly specialized or proprietary—there’s simply no alternative supplier that can meet the requirement.  
The second condition mentions cases where technical or professional advice directs the work to a particular expert or firm, such as soil investigations, land valuations, arbitration, or specialized HR/Finance/IT and technical studies.  
Third, the policy allows a single tender when the situation demands immediate or urgent action, leaving no time for a normal competitive process.  
Finally, it notes that for indigenous development aimed at import substitution, it’s acceptable to approach a single party that specializes in the relevant field or commodity and then negotiate the offer.  
I verify that these four points exhaust the permitted circumstances; the policy makes clear that no other grounds justify a single‑tender approach.  
Putting it all together, I conclude that a procurement may be carried out on a single tender basis only when one of those four specialized, advisory, urgent, or import‑substitution scenarios applies.

question_text: Who typically makes up the Tender Evaluation Committee and what are their roles?

# Chapter 5: Evaluation of Bids and Award of Work


## 5.1 Evaluation of Bids
**5.1.1** The evaluation of Bids is one of the most significant areas of purchase management and the process must be transparent. All tenders are to be evaluated strictly on the basis of the terms and conditions incorporated in the tender document and those stipulated by the tenderers in their tenders. The Contracting Authority may include quality, price, technical merit, aesthetic and functional characteristics, environmental characteristics, running costs, cost- effectiveness, after-sales service and technical assistance, delivery date and delivery period or period of completion etc. No criteria shall be used for evaluation of tenders that cannot be verified or not stated in the contract, with the exception of provisions of laws in force. No hearsay information or hitherto undeclared condition should be brought in while evaluating the tenders. Similarly, no tender enquiry condition (especially the significant/ essential ones) should be overlooked/ relaxed while evaluating the tenders. The aim should be to ensure that no tenderer gets undue advantage at the cost of other tenderers and/ or at the cost of Procuring Entity. Information relating to evaluation of tenders and the Tender Committee's (TC's) deliberations should be confidential and not be shared with persons not officially connected with the process. The process of tender evaluation proceeds is described in the subsequent paras.

**5.1.2** Evaluation of group tenders:

Methodology needs to be laid down in the tender document for priced bid opening and subsequent evaluation in case of composite tenders floated for several similar jobs grouped together in one tender document with preconditions like awarding one group to one vendor only.

If the job volume is planned to be distributed to two or more contractors, modality for the same should be clearly spelt out in the tender document.

## 5.2 Delegation of Authority (DOA)
**5.2.1** Evaluation is carried out by Tender Evaluation Committee (TEC) generally consisting of three or more members with requisite experience and competence. Members include representative of Commercial Dept., a Financial representative and a representative of the user as per DOA. No member of the tender committee should be reporting directly to any other member of such committee. For different categories of procurement and different threshold values of procurements DOA should be followed to ensure checks & balances in the Tender Evaluation Process. Commercial dealing officer(s) will receive the bids opened along with other documents from the tender opening officials and are responsible for safe-custody of the documents and for processing involved at all steps in finalising the Procurement.

## 5.3 Preparation of Comparative Statement and Briefing Note
**5.3.1** The Procuring Entity should prepare a comparative statement of quotations received in the order in which tenders were opened. In case of Techno-Commercial bid comparative statement will have information about deciding responsiveness and eligibility of bids and evaluation of Technical suitability of offers. In case of Financial bid it would have information about rates quoted (including taxes or otherwise), discount, if any, and any other information having implications on ranking of bids etc. The comparative statement so prepared along with Tender Evaluation Committee (TEC) recommendation note duly signed by the initiating / recommending member(s) are put up before the appropriate authority for approval as per DOA.

question_text: What is the minimum threshold for a price adjustment to be payable
answer: - Price adjustment is payable only when it exceeds 2 % of the base contract price (Po); adjustments ≤ 2 % of Po are not payable. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 208)
cot:
I need to figure out what the smallest price‑adjustment amount is that would actually trigger a payment under the contract.  
First, I scan the provisions for any rule that talks about when an adjustment is *not* payable, because that will tell me the cutoff point.  
I see a statement that says no price adjustment shall be payable if it is less than or equal to two percent of the base contract price Po.  
That means anything that falls at or below that 2 % level is ignored for payment purposes.  
Consequently, for an adjustment to be payable it must exceed that limit; it has to be more than 2 % of Po.  
Since the adjustment is expressed as a proportion of Po, the threshold itself is simply 2 % of Po—anything just above that amount becomes payable, while anything at or below it is not.  
So the minimum threshold for a price adjustment to be payable is just over 2 % of the base contract price Po; adjustments ≤ 2 % of Po are not payable.

question_text: How should arbitration clauses with foreign firms be structured, particularly for large value contracts
answer:

question_text: How should technical and financial proposals be submitted to safeguard the integrity of the procurement process
answer:
**How to Submit Technical and Financial Proposals to Safeguard the Procurement Process**  

**Step 1: Prepare each proposal separately**  
- Complete the technical proposal in accordance with the RfP requirements.  
- Complete the financial proposal in accordance with the RfP requirements.  

**Step 2: Place each proposal in its own sealed envelope**  
- Insert the technical proposal into an envelope, seal it, and label it clearly as “Technical Proposal”.  
- Insert the financial proposal into a second envelope, seal it, and label it clearly as “Financial Proposal”.  

**Step 3: Combine the two sealed envelopes into an outer sealed envelope**  
- Put the sealed technical envelope and the sealed financial envelope together inside a third envelope.  
- Seal the outer envelope and label it (e.g., “Bid Submission – [Project Name]”).  

**Step 4: Submit the outer envelope by the stipulated deadline**  
- Deliver the outer sealed envelope to the designated submission point (e.g., the e‑Procurement portal or the physical bid box) **before** the closing time for receipt of proposals.  
- If the procurement is conducted through e‑Procurement, upload the scanned copies of the three envelopes as a single package in accordance with the portal’s instructions.  

**Step 5: Verify that no late bids are accepted**  
- Confirm that the submission timestamp (or physical receipt log) shows receipt **on or before** the closing time.  
- Any proposal received after the closing time must be rejected outright.  

**Step 6: Understand the opening procedure**  
- After the closing time, the technical envelopes are opened immediately by the Consultancy Evaluation Committee (CEC) or Tender Evaluation Committee (TEC).  
- The financial envelopes remain sealed and are opened publicly **only** for those bidders whose technical proposals have been deemed qualified.  

### Practical Example  
A bidder for a consultancy assignment prepares a 25‑page technical proposal and a 5‑page financial proposal.  
1. The technical proposal is placed in Envelope A, sealed, and marked “Technical Proposal”.  
2. The financial proposal is placed in Envelope B, sealed, and marked “Financial Proposal”.  
3. Both Envelope A and Envelope B are inserted into Envelope C, which is sealed and labeled “Bid Submission – Road‑Design Consultancy”.  
4. Envelope C is uploaded to the e‑Procurement system at 09:45 AM on the deadline day (the closing time is 10:00 AM).  
5. At 10:05 AM, the CEC opens Envelope C, extracts Envelope A and Envelope B, opens Envelope A immediately, and keeps Envelope B sealed until the technical evaluation is complete.  

### Common Pitfalls to Avoid  
- **Mixing proposals**: placing technical and financial documents in the same envelope violates the requirement for separate sealed envelopes.  
- **Missing outer seal**: submitting only the two inner envelopes without an outer sealed envelope exposes the financial proposal to premature viewing.  
- **Late submission**: any delay, even a few minutes, results in automatic disqualification.  
- **Incorrect submission channel**: using email or courier when the RfP mandates e‑Procurement can lead to rejection.  
- **Inadequate labeling**: unclear or missing labels can cause confusion during the opening process and may be treated as a procedural error.  

By following these numbered steps—preparing separate proposals, sealing them individually, combining them in an outer sealed envelope, submitting before the deadline via the prescribed method, and observing the prescribed opening procedure—you safeguard the integrity of the procurement process as required.  

(Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 46)
cot:
First, I think about what could undermine the fairness of a procurement process—mainly the risk that financial details influence the technical evaluation or that late submissions give some bidders an unfair advantage. To prevent that, the two parts of a bid must be kept completely separate until the technical merit has been judged on its own merits.  

That leads me to the idea of sealing each proposal in its own envelope so that the contents cannot be seen or altered before the designated opening time. If the technical and financial documents were placed together, an evaluator might inadvertently glimpse cost information while reviewing the technical response, which would bias the assessment.  

Next, I consider how to handle the two sealed envelopes together without breaking that separation. Placing both inner envelopes inside a third, outer sealed envelope keeps them united for submission while preserving the inner seals. The outer envelope can be labeled clearly so that the receiving office knows it contains a complete bid, yet the inner seals remain intact until the opening stage.  

Now I turn to the timing of submission. To avoid any perception of favoritism, all bidders must deliver their bids at the same moment, and any bid arriving after the stipulated deadline must be rejected outright. This rule eliminates the possibility of a bidder gaining extra time to improve their proposal after seeing others’ submissions.  

Because many organizations now use electronic procurement, the physical envelopes can be represented by scanned copies uploaded as a single package through the e‑procurement portal. The electronic system must enforce the same deadline check and preserve the integrity of the sealed‑envelope concept by treating the uploaded file as a locked unit that can only be opened after the closing time.  

After the deadline passes, the opening procedure itself must protect the financial information. The outer envelope is opened, the inner technical envelope is extracted and opened immediately by the evaluation committee, while the financial envelope stays sealed. Only after the technical evaluation concludes and a bidder is deemed technically qualified does the financial envelope get opened in a public setting. This staged opening guarantees that financial scores are never seen before technical merit is established.  

Finally, I run through a quick mental checklist to catch common mistakes: ensuring each proposal is sealed separately, not forgetting the outer seal, submitting before the cutoff, using the correct submission channel, and labeling everything clearly. If any of those steps are missed, the bid could be disqualified or the process could be compromised.  

Putting all of these considerations together yields the prescribed method: prepare technical and financial proposals separately, seal each in its own envelope, place the two sealed envelopes inside a third sealed envelope, submit the outer package before the deadline via the stipulated (often electronic) channel, verify that no late bids are accepted, and then follow the opening sequence where technical bids are opened first and financial bids remain sealed until technical qualification is confirmed. This approach safeguards the integrity of the procurement process by keeping financial information hidden until the technical evaluation is complete and by enforcing equal, timely submission for all bidders.

question_text: In what way do the documented payment terms promote transparency and value for money in domestic procurement
answer:
The documented payment terms for domestic procurement enhance transparency and safeguard value for money by tying disbursements to verifiable milestones, using traceable electronic payment methods, and requiring a standardized set of documents that are rigorously checked before payment is released.  

- Payments are released only after confirmed milestones such as proof of dispatch, receipt and acceptance at site, or successful installation and commissioning, ensuring funds are spent on delivered, accepted goods (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 108).  
- The preference for FOR destination/delivery at site terms places the risk of safe arrival on the supplier, providing clear visibility of logistics performance and protecting corporate assets (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 108).  
- Electronic payments via NEFT/RTGS or Advice to Bank create an auditable, traceable trail that supports financial oversight and deters fraudulent activity (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 108).  
- A prescribed documentation package—invoice with specifications, packing list, transport documents, e‑waybill, and guarantee/inspection certificates—is systematically verified by receiving and payment sections, establishing a transparent audit trail that confirms quality and compliance prior to payment (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 109).  
- For contracts that include installation/commissioning, staged payment schedules (e.g., 60/30/10 or 90/10) align cash outflow with performance, ensuring payment only for completed, accepted work and preserving budget integrity (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 108).  

These mechanisms collectively reinforce corporate governance, promote financial accountability, and ensure that procurement expenditures deliver the intended value.
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is really asking: it wants to know how the payment terms that are written down for buying goods inside the country help make the process open and ensure that every rupee spent gives the best possible return.  

To answer that, I should look at what those payment terms actually say. They break down the payment into chunks that are released only when certain, checkable events happen—like showing that the goods have been dispatched, that they have arrived and been accepted at the site, or that any installation and commissioning work has been completed successfully.  

Seeing that, the first way transparency and value for money arise is clear: money is not handed over until there is proof that the supplier has actually fulfilled a concrete step of the contract. If the goods never leave the factory, the first installment isn’t paid; if they arrive damaged or aren’t accepted, the later installments are withheld. This creates a direct link between spending and verified performance, which discourages paying for nothing or for sub‑standard work.  

Next, I notice that the terms differ depending on where the responsibility for delivery ends. When the contract specifies FOR destination/delivery at site, the supplier must get the goods all the way to the buyer’s location and have them accepted before receiving most of the payment. That shifts the risk of loss or damage in transit onto the supplier, giving the buyer a clear view of how well the supplier handles logistics and protecting the buyer’s assets. If the terms were FOR dispatching station instead, the buyer would bear that risk earlier, which would obscure who is responsible for any problems that occur during shipment.  

Another layer is how the payments are actually made. The manual says that domestic suppliers are paid through NEFT/RTGS or Advice to Bank, both of which are electronic, traceable methods. Every transaction leaves a digital record that can be audited, making it harder to hide improper payments and giving finance teams a straightforward way to track where money went and when.  

Then there is the paperwork that must accompany each payment request. The supplier has to submit an invoice with full specifications, a packing list, transport documents such as a railway receipt or consignment note, an e‑waybill, and any guarantee or inspection certificates. The receiving department checks the goods against these papers, and the payment section verifies the tax invoice before releasing funds. This multi‑step verification creates a documented trail that shows exactly what was ordered, what was shipped, what arrived, and whether it met quality standards—all before any money changes hands.  

For contracts that also include installation and commissioning, the payment schedule is staged even further: a portion on dispatch, another on receipt and acceptance, and the final slice only after the supplier proves that the equipment works as intended. This aligns cash outflow with the completion of each substantive task, ensuring that the buyer does not pay for work that is unfinished or unsatisfactory.  

Putting all these pieces together, the payment terms promote transparency by making every disbursement contingent on verifiable, observable events and by requiring a standardized, checked set of documents that leave an audit trail. They promote value for money by placing performance risk on the supplier, using traceable electronic payments, and releasing funds only when the buyer has actually received and accepted conforming goods or services. The result is a procurement process where spending is tightly coupled to verified delivery, which safeguards both financial accountability and the achievement of the intended value from each purchase.

## 6.3 Terms of Payment for Domestic Goods
Where the terms of delivery are FOR Dispatching Station, the payment terms, depending on the value and nature of the goods, mode of transportation, and so on, maybe 60 to 100 (sixty to hundred) per cent on proof of dispatch and other related documents and balance on receipt at site and acceptance by the consignee.

Where the terms of delivery is FOR destination/delivery at site, the usual payment term is 100 (hundred) per cent on receipt and acceptance of goods by the consignee and on production of all required documents by the supplier.

Where goods to be supplied also need installation and commissioning by the supplier, the payment terms are generally:

- i) For a contract with terms of delivery as FOR dispatching station -- 60 (sixty) per cent on proof of dispatch along with other specified documents, 30 (thirty) per cent on receipt of the goods at site by the consignee and balance 10 (ten) per cent on successful installation and commissioning and acceptance by the consignee; and
- ii) For a contract with terms of delivery as FOR destination/delivery at site -- 90 (ninety) per cent on receipt and acceptance of goods by the consignee at destination and on production of all required documents by the supplier and balance 10 (ten) per cent on successful installation and commissioning and acceptance by the consignee.

Note: Generally (especially for goods requiring installation and commissioning at site by the supplier), the desirable terms of delivery are FOR destination/delivery at site, so that the supplier remains responsible for safe arrival of the ordered goods at the site. Therefore, unless otherwise decided ex-works or FOR dispatching station terms should be avoided.

### 6.3.1 Modes of Payment for Domestic Goods
Payments to domestic suppliers are made through NEFT/RTGS mode or Advice to Bank.

### 6.3.2 Documents for Payment for Domestic Goods as applicable
- i) Supplier's Invoice indicating, *inter alia* description and specification of the goods, quantity, unit price, total value;
- ii) Packing list;
- iii) Railway receipt/consignment note;
- iv) E-Waybill
- v) Manufacturer's guarantee certificate and inspection certificate;
- vi) Any other document(s) as and if required in terms of the contract.

Above documents will be verified by the department(s) receiving and inspecting the goods. Tax invoice will be verified by the payment section.

## 6.4 Terms of Payment for Imported Goods
**6.4.1** Usual payment terms, unless otherwise directed by CA, are indicated below:

- i) Cases where installation, erection and commissioning (if applicable) are not the **responsibility of the supplier** -- 100 (hundred) per cent net FOB/FAS/CFR/CIF/CIP price is to be paid against invoice, shipping documents,

- inspection certificate (where applicable), manufacturers' test certificate, and so on;
- ii) Cases where installation, erection and commissioning are the responsibility of the supplier -- 80 - 90 (eighty to ninety) per cent net FOB/FAS/CFR/CIF/CIP price will be paid against the invoice, inspection certificate (where applicable), shipping documents, and so on, and balance within 21-30 (twenty-one to thirty) days of successful installation and commissioning at the consignee's premises and acceptance by the consignee; and
- iii) Payment of agency commission, if payable, against FOB/FAS/CFR/CIF/CIP contract - the entire 100 (hundred) per cent agency commission is generally paid (in non-convertible Indian Rupees on the basis of BC selling rate of exchange) after all other payments have been made to the supplier in terms of the contract.

question_text: Is there a value limit for using empanelled contractors, and who sets this limit
answer:
Yes, there is a defined value limit for using empanelled contractors, and this limit is set by NRL.  
The manual notes that empanelment of contractors may be confined to tenders up to a certain threshold value, as decided by NRL, and that NRL has a practice of empanelling contractors for defined value limits (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 32).
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know whether there is a specific monetary ceiling for using contractors who are on an empanelled list, and if such a ceiling exists, which authority establishes it.  

The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals note that the practice of empanelment may be limited to tenders only up to a certain threshold value.  

The threshold value is “as decided by NRL,” indicating that NRL sets the limit.  

NRL routinely empanels contractors for defined value limits and validity periods, reinforcing that the limit is not arbitrary but a formal, established boundary set by NRL.  

Putting these points together, I conclude that yes, there is a defined value limit for using empanelled contractors, and that limit is established by NRL.

The number of consultants in this moderated long-list should not be less than three. In case sufficient consultants cannot be located, then the responses may be called from lesser number of consultants, but not less than three in any case, after taking CA's approval. To smoothen this shortlisting of consultants for projects below Rs.10 Crores, Procuring entities who do frequent procurement of consultancy services, may consider preparation of a Panel of qualified consultants, after evaluation of their credentials, on the lines of registration of vendors in procurement of goods. If the complexity of the project so justifies, a formal EoI may be advertised as in above, even for procurements below Rs.10 crores

**Empanelment of contractors:** Empanelment / registration of contractors may be done for those specific goods and services which are required regularly. Performance of such empanelled contractors should be reviewed periodically. The list of empanelled / registered contractors shall be updated on a regular basis. Empanelment of contractors shall be done in a fair and equitable manner, preferably online after giving due publicity. The practice of empanelment of contractors may be confined to tenders up to certain threshold value, as decided by NRL. NRL has a practice of empanelment of contractors for various nature of jobs (either for direct allocation of jobs based on pre-fixed rates and modality, through tendering or through individual tenders to the empanelled agencies) for defined value limit as well as validity period of empanelment. Modality for such empanelment may be adopted on case to case basis with due approval of CA as per DOA.

#### i) **Letter of Invitation:**
It shall include a copy of the advertisement whereby consultants are invited to submit their EoI.

#### ii) **Instructions to the consultants**
It may include instructions regarding nature of job; submission requirement; requirement of bid processing fees; if any; last date of submission; place of submission; and any related instruction;

#### iii) **Description of Services - Brief Purpose and Scope of Work**
This may include brief purpose/objective statement; Service Outcomes Statement; broad scope of work including Time-frames; inputs to be provided by the Procuring Entity; and expected deliverables of the assignment. This may also include the place of execution of the assignment. The request for EoI shall not include the assignment ToR. The consultants may also be asked to send their comments on the objectives and scope of the work or service projected in the enquiry.

question_text: How are contract rate increases resulting from a price escalation clause treated with respect to contract changes and approvals
answer:
- Contract rate increases arising from a price escalation clause are **not treated as changes to the concluded contract**.  
- Such increases **do not require separate approval** provided they remain within the approved ceiling.  
- Payment certification for these increases can be performed by the **Engineer‑in‑Charge or Administrative‑in‑Charge**.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 107)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the question is really asking: when a contract includes a price escalation clause and the contract rate goes up because of that clause, how should those increases be viewed in terms of contract modifications and the approval process?  

The key is to look at the nature of the price escalation clause itself. It is a provision that was already agreed upon when the contract was signed, so any adjustment it triggers is simply the contract operating as intended, not a new alteration to the agreement.  

Because the adjustment is built into the original terms, it shouldn’t be classified as a “change to the concluded contract.” If it were, every time the index moved we’d need a fresh amendment, which defeats the purpose of having an escalation mechanism in the first place.  

Next, I consider what limits are placed on such adjustments. The clause normally sets a ceiling—either a yearly percentage, an overall cap, or both. As long as the increase stays within that pre‑approved ceiling, there’s no need to seek additional sanction; the parties have already consented to the range of possible variation.  

Finally, I think about who can authorize payment for these increases. Since they are not treated as contractual changes, the routine certification process suffices. The Engineer‑in‑Charge or the Administrative‑in‑Charge, who already oversee day‑to‑day execution and invoicing, can certify the escalated amounts for payment without escalating the matter to higher approval authorities.  

Putting it together: contract rate increases stemming from a price escalation clause are not contract changes, they require no separate approval when within the agreed ceiling, and they can be certified for payment by the Engineer‑in‑Charge or Administrative‑in‑Charge.

question_text: What procedure is required to enable a meaningful price comparison among tenders
answer:
- List the price quoted by each tenderer, including alternative specifications with explanatory notes (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Provide the item‑wise estimate or Last Paid Unit Price (LPP) for comparison with the tendered rates (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Reduce all quoted prices to a common base to enable a meaningful comparison (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Highlight every deviation in specifications or standard terms and conditions, especially those affecting price or delivery (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- State the contractual completion or delivery term offered by each tenderer (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Indicate any discount or rebate offered (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Show the foreign exchange requirement for imported items (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Quantify and clearly show the incidence of GST, Customs Duty, Excise Duty or other statutory levies (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Specify packing, handling, forwarding, transportation charges and insurance, and indicate their cost incidence (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Determine and indicate the cost implications of any advance payment provisions (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Clearly indicate any price escalation clause and load its cost implication into the tender evaluation (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Incorporate applicable purchase preferences and government policies (e.g., MSE) into the evaluation sheet for the Tender Evaluation Committee (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Taking all the above factors into account, prepare a comparative cost evaluation statement that gives a realistic, representative and comprehensive cost comparison (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Upload the comparative statement in the Aarohan system by the dealing officer of the Commercial Department (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Prepare a detailed TEC note to the Tender Committee/CA, highlighting main points and recommendation, and enclose the comprehensive tabulation for decision‑making (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Provide a technical explanation for any variation between tendered prices and evaluated prices, detailing any positive or negative loadings and clarifications sought from tenderers (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).  
- Verify that all technical details, specification drawings and other offer contents conform to the tender enquiry before presentation to the Committee (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 117).
cot:
First, I think about what it means to compare tenders meaningfully – the prices must be comparable on the same footing, so I need to gather every element that influences the final cost each bidder is offering.  

Next, I list the basic price each tenderer has quoted, making sure to note any alternative specifications they have proposed and adding a brief explanation of how those alternatives differ from the baseline requirement.  

Then, I bring in the item‑wise estimate or the last paid unit price for each line item; having this reference point lets me see whether a tendered rate is above, below, or in line with what has been paid before.  

After that, I adjust all quoted prices to a common base – stripping out any location‑specific factors, different currencies, or varying tax treatments – so that the numbers I am looking at truly reflect the same scope of work.  

With the prices normalized, I turn my attention to every deviation: changes in specifications, different delivery schedules, or special terms and conditions. I highlight those that could affect price or timing, because ignoring them would distort the comparison.  

I also record the contractual completion or delivery period each bidder is offering, any discounts or rebates they have mentioned, and the amount of foreign exchange required for imported components.  

Further, I quantify all statutory charges – GST, customs duty, excise duty, or other levies – and show how they add to the base price. I do the same for packing, handling, forwarding, transportation, and insurance, making sure their cost impact is visible.  

If a tender includes advance payment terms, I work out the financial implication of that and note it; similarly, I identify any price‑escalation clause, calculate its expected effect over the contract period, and load that amount into the evaluated price.  

I then incorporate any applicable purchase preferences or government policies – such as those for micro‑ and small‑enterprises – into the evaluation sheet so that the tender committee sees the full picture.  

Taking all of these adjusted elements together, I construct a comparative cost evaluation statement that presents a realistic, representative, and comprehensive view of each offer’s total cost.  

Finally, I make sure this statement is uploaded to the Aarohan system by the commercial department’s dealing officer, prepare a detailed TEC note that summarizes the key findings and recommendation, attach the comprehensive tabulation for the committee’s review, provide a technical explanation for any differences between the tendered and evaluated prices, and verify that every technical detail, drawing, and specification in the offers conforms to the original tender enquiry before the committee makes its decision.

### Broad guidelines for preparation of Comparative statement:
- i) To facilitate proper bid analysis, the comparative statement shall be made of all the

tenders received on the following basis:

- a) Price quoted by all the firms shall be given. Where alternative specifications has been offered for the jobs under reference and are acceptable, their prices shall also be indicated along with suitable explanatory note concerning deviations.  
The item wise estimate / Last Paid Unit Price (LPP) shall also be given in this tabulation to make comparison of estimate / LPP with the tendered rates.
  - b) Prices quoted shall be reduced to a common base for a meaningful comparison.
  - c) All deviations either in specifications or in standard terms and conditions shall specifically be highlighted, particularly those having a bearing on price or delivery shall be indicated.
  - d) Contractual completion / delivery term of all parties shall be given.
  - e) Discount / Rebate if any offered to be indicated.
  - f) Foreign exchange required in the case of imports shall be indicated.
  - g) Incidence of GST/ Customs Duty/ Excise Duty/ or other Statutory levies, shall be quantified and clearly shown.
  - h) Packing, Handling, Forwarding and Transportation Charges, insurance as applicable should be specified and the incidence thereof should be shown.
  - i) Where advance payment is involved, the cost implications must be determined / indicated.
  - j) Prices escalation clause, if any to be clearly indicated and the cost implication loaded in the tender evaluation.
  - k) Taking all factors into consideration, comparative cost evaluation statement shall be made to give a realistic, representative and comprehensive cost comparison.
  - l) Applicable Purchase preferences and the policies of the Government with regard to MSE and other guidelines shall be suitably brought out in the evaluation sheet for the guidance of the TEC.
- ii) The comparative statement shall be uploaded in Aarohan system by the dealing officer of the Commercial dept.
- iii) The Commercial Department would prepare a detailed note (TEC note) to the Tender Committee / CA highlighting the main points with the recommendation for the award of the contract. The tender papers enclosed along with the above note should include the

comprehensive tabulation drawn as indicated above to arrive at a meaningful comparison for effective decision-making. There should be no ambiguity in any of the data presented for consideration.

iv) Technical explanation should be given for variation between prices quoted in the tender and the evaluated prices. Any positive or negative loading done to render the comparison meaningful should be properly explained. Clarifications sought from the tenderers and the resulting impact on the quotation if any should be specifically mentioned. It should be ensured that all technical details; specification drawings and other aspects contained in the offers have been thoroughly checked for conformity with the tender enquiry before presentation to the Committee.

v) In short, a factual, informative and technically cleared material should be portrayed in the noting to the Committee / CA to facilitate taking decisions for the contracts without further reference to the field units.

The comparative statement so prepared should be enclosed along with TEC note for approval of award as per DOA.
