answer: - ☐ Verify that the Nodal Department directly intimated the agency of its Holiday Listing placement when the listing is based on Ministry advice, and that no show cause notice or formal decision by the Competent Authority was required. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 55)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants to know which entity directly informs an agency that it has been placed in the Holiday List when that placement stems from the Ministry’s advice.  

In the Holiday Listing process, a show‑cause notice and a formal decision by the Competent Authority are normally involved, but there is a special case where the advice comes from the Administrative Ministry. In that special case the usual procedural steps are bypassed.  

When the Ministry’s advice triggers the Holiday Listing, the Nodal Department takes over the communication role—it directly informs the agency that it has been placed in the Holiday List by NRL, and it does so without issuing a show‑cause notice or awaiting a Competent Authority decision.  

This means the responsibility for the direct intimation lies squarely with the Nodal Department; no other body (such as the Competent Authority or the Ministry itself) is required to perform that notification under the Ministry‑advice scenario.  

Putting these points together, the answer is clear: the Nodal Department is the entity responsible for directly intimating the agency about its Holiday Listing placement when the listing is based on the Ministry’s advice, and this occurs without the need for a show‑cause notice or a formal Competent Authority decision.

- ii. Consideration of any appeal for review, filed after expiry of the above period, shall be at the sole discretion of the Appellate Authority;
- iii. On receipt of the Appeal from the Agency, the Appellate Authority, if it so desires, may call for comments from the Competent Authority;
- iv. The Appellate Authority, if it so desires, may also give an opportunity for personal hearing to the Appellant Agency;
- v. After examining the facts of the case and documents available on record and considering the submissions of the Appellant Agency, the Appellate Authority may pass appropriate order before the period of debarment is over by which the Appellate Authority may either:
  - a) Uphold the decision of Competent authority with or without any variation / lesser period of Holiday Listing; OR
  - b) Annul the order of the Competent Authority.

- vi. No Appeal is permitted in case an Agency is placed in Holiday List by NRL, based on Ministry's advice.

##### 3.5.4.2(a) Provision for revocation:
A debarment order may be revoked before the expiry of the Order, by the competent authority, if it is of the opinion that the disability already suffered is adequate in the circumstances of the case or for any other reason.

### 9.7.2 Terms of Delivery
Terms of delivery (FOR, FOB, CIF, and CFR, and so on), inter alia, determine the delivery point of the ordered goods from where the purchaser is to receive/collect the goods. It also decides the legally important issue of when the 'titles of the goods' have passed to the purchaser. The delivery period is to be read in conjunction with the terms of delivery, therefore the delivery is taken to have been made at the time when goods reach the delivery point as per the delivery terms. The delivery condition of FOR NRL (Location) may be adopted as far as possible.

### 9.7.3 Extension of Delivery
Suppliers shall be required to adhere to the delivery schedule specified in the purchase order and, if there is delay in supplies, LD shall be levied wherever there is failure by the party. Extension of the delivery date amounts to amendment of the contract. Such an extension can be only done with the consent of both parties (that is, the purchaser and supplier). No extension of the delivery date is to be granted suo motu unless the supplier specifically asks for it.

The confirmation of extension of delivery period (provisional / firm) should inter-alia contain the following:-

- (i) The time for delivery is extended from (CDD) to (extended CDD)
- (ii) Applicability & mention of LD clause beyond the original contract delivery date / the last unconditionally re-fixed delivery date.
- (iii) Requirement of extension of the validity period of the performance guarantee.
- (iv) That the above extension of delivery date will also be subject to the Denial Clause.

On receiving the supplier's communication, the procuring entity shall examine the proposal and, on approval from the CA, may agree to extend the delivery schedule, with or without LD

### 9.7.4 Delay in Supplies for which Supplier is not Responsible
Normally, in the following circumstances, the contractual delivery period needs to be re-fixed to take care of the lost period, without imposing any penalty to the supplier:

- i) Cases where the manufacture of stores is dependent on the approval of the advance sample and delay occurs in approving the sample though submitted by the supplier in time;

- ii) Where extension in the delivery period is granted on account of some omission on the part of the purchaser which affects the due performance of the contract by the supplier; and
- iii) Cases where the purchaser controls the entire production.

question_text: Why is it important to restrict competition to bidders with requisite capabilities in PQB
answer:
- Ensures that only bidders possessing the required technical, financial, and infrastructural capability compete, which is essential for the successful performance of high‑value or complex contracts. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)  
- Prevents better‑qualified bidders from being eliminated due to higher bid prices that reflect their superior capability, thereby preserving fair competition among capable firms. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)  
- Supports transparency and fairness by limiting competition to those who can meet the contract’s demands, reducing the risk of cartelization among shortlisted bidders. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)  
- Aligns the procurement process with the entity’s objective of obtaining value for money while avoiding unnecessary price inflation caused by mismatched capabilities. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)
cot:
First, I think about what the core issue is when a contract is high‑value or technically complex: the success of the work hinges on the supplier having the right expertise, financial strength and equipment, so the procurement must make sure that only firms that actually possess those attributes are allowed to bid.  

Then, I sort out the key conditions that arise if we do not restrict the field. Unqualified bidders tend to submit lower prices because they lack the costly infrastructure and experienced staff that capable firms maintain; if they win, the contract is likely to suffer delays, defects or even failure, which defeats the purpose of the procurement.  

Next, I derive the consequence for the capable bidders themselves. Because their higher capability translates into higher legitimate costs, their bids are naturally higher than those of the under‑qualified competitors. When the latter are allowed to compete, the capable firms can be priced out of the process despite being the only ones able to deliver the work satisfactorily, which undermines fair competition.  

Further, I deepen the analysis by looking at how limiting the field to pre‑qualified bidders addresses these problems. By shortlisting only those who meet the technical, financial and infrastructural criteria, we ensure that every remaining participant can perform the contract, so the competition is genuinely about price and service quality among equals. This also reduces the temptation for collusion, because the group is smaller, known and has already been vetted, making the process more transparent and less prone to cartel‑like behavior.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: restricting competition to bidders with the requisite capabilities safeguards contract performance, prevents capable firms from being eliminated on price alone, preserves a transparent and fair competitive environment, and ultimately delivers value for money by avoiding costly rework or failure while still obtaining a price that reflects the true cost of delivering the work. This aligns directly with the procurement entity’s objective of securing successful, cost‑effective outcomes for high‑value or complex contracts.

### 3.3.6 Pre-qualification Bidding [PQB]
- i) In high value contracts or complex technical requirements where capability of source of supply is crucial (for example in construction of complex bridges), for the successful performance of the

contract, besides considering techno- commercial suitability, it is necessary to ensure that competition is only among bidders with requisite capabilities matching the challenges of the task. In case bidders with inadequate capability are allowed to compete, the better qualified bidders would be eliminated, since their bid price is likely to be higher commensurate with their higher capability and infrastructure. In such situations a separate stage of PQB bidding system may be considered (or single stage multiple envelope bidding - please refer para 3.3.4 above). In PQB stage, competent qualified tenderers are shortlisted prior to the issue of the bid document exclusively to shortlisted bidders in the second stage by using a Pre- qualification Criterion (PQC).

ii) Pre-qualification Bids (PQBs) should meet the norms of transparency, fairness and maintenance of competition. *Since PQB system may strain the transparency principle and there is heightened risk of cartelization among shortlisted bidders, PQB should be done only as an exception under specified circumstances. It should not be a routine/ normal mode of procurement of works and an eligibility criteria clause (post-qualification) as part of single/ two envelope/ cover tendering should suffice in normal/ routine situations. PQB bidding as a separate stage is contra-indicated in the following circumstances:*

- i) Where procurement can be done through limited tender enquiries;
- ii) Where the requirement is technically and commercially simple enough that pre-qualification of the bidder is not crucial for the performance of the contract, for example, routine residential buildings; and
- iii) *Where the procurement is of medium value (say less than Rs 100 crore) or moderately complex in nature and the time, effort and money required from the bidder to participate in a tender is not very high, a clear-cut, (preferably fail-pass) post-qualification criteria can be specified in a three envelope single stage bidding (instead of separate PQB bidding), so that a bidder's risk of having his bid rejected on grounds of qualifications is remote if due diligence is exercised by him.*
- iv) **Two stage PQB** should be done only in appropriately justified situations. Alternatively Single Stage multiple envelop system may be used for prequalification, in which chances of anti-competitive behaviour and time- taken is significantly lesser.

iii) **PRE-QUALIFICATION CRITERIA:** PQC should be unrestrictive enough so as not to leave out even one capable bidder/ contractor. Otherwise, it can lead to higher prices of procurement works/ services. However, on the other hand, these criteria should be restrictive enough so as not to allow even one incapable bidder/ contractor and thus vitiate fair competition for capable bidders/ contractors to the detriment of the Procuring Entity's objectives. A misjudgement in either direction may be detrimental. Certain guidelines-regarding the framing of PQC have been laid down. Due consideration should be given while framing PQC, to its effect on adequacy of competition. PQC should therefore be carefully decided for each procurement. ### 4.9.2 Sealing and Marking of Tenders
The tender document is to indicate the total number of tender sets (e.g., in duplicate or in triplicate etc) required to be submitted. In case bids are asked in a number of copies, the tenderer is to seal the original and each copy of the tender in separate envelopes, duly marking the same as "original", "duplicate" and so on and also marking these as mentioned above. In case of two envelope bidding system, the techno- commercial bid and financial bid should be sealed by the tenderer in separate inner covers duly marking these as 'Techno-commercial Bid' and 'Financial Bid' and marked with the address of the purchase office and the tender reference number on the envelopes. Further, the sentence "NOT TO BE OPENED" before (due date & time of tender opening) are also to be put on these envelopes and these sealed inner covers are to be put in a bigger outer cover which should also be sealed and duly super scribed in a similar manner. If the outer envelope is not sealed and marked properly as above, the Procuring Entity will not assume any responsibility for its misplacement, premature opening, late opening etc. These details regarding the submission of bids should also form a part of the ITB and AITB in the tender documents; all the above instructions are to be suitably incorporated in the tender documents.

### 4.9.3 Withdrawal, Substitution and Modification of Tenders
The tenderer, after submitting the tender, is permitted to withdraw, substitute or modify the tenders in writing without forfeiture of Bid Security/ EMD, provided these are received duly sealed and marked like the original tender, up to the date and time of receipt of the tender. Any such request received after the prescribed date and time of receipt of tenders will not be considered. No bid may be withdrawn in the interval between the deadline for submission of bids and expiration of the period of bid validity. Withdrawal of a bid during this period will result in forfeiture of the bidder's bid security (EMD) and other sanctions.

From there, I reason about what the customs procedure prescribes in this situation: because the goods conform to the registered contract, the Bill of Entry can be cleared without further scrutiny, but duty still needs to be paid, so the entry is assessed provisionally and then passed to the importer or his agent for duty settlement.  

I then think about the administrative follow‑up: the Project Import Group must keep a record that the goods have been cleared, so it notes the description and value of the cleared items in the Project Contract Register and in the project‑specific file it maintains.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: if the description, value and quantity are in order during verification, the Bill of Entry receives a provisional assessment, is handed over to the importer for duty payment, and the Project Import Group records the description and value in its register and file. ## 2. Registration of contracts:
2.1 In terms of Regulation 4 of the Project Import Regulations, 1986 (PIR) the basic requirement for availing the benefit of assessment under Tariff Heading No. 9801 is that the importer should have entered into one or more contracts with the suppliers of the goods for setting up a project. Such contracts should be registered prior to clearance in the Custom House through which the goods are expected to be imported. The importer shall apply for such registration in writing to the proper officer of Customs. To expedite registration, the importers are advised to submit the following documents along with the application for registration:

- (ii) Industrial Licence and letter of intent, SSI Certificate granted by the appropriate authority with a copy thereof.
- (iii) Original Import licence, if any, with a list of items showing the dimensions, specifications, quantity, quality, value of each item duly attested by the Licensing Authority and a copy thereof.
- (iv) Recommendatory letter for duty concession from the concerned Sponsoring Authority, showing the description, quantity, specification, quality, dimension of each item and indicating whether the recommendatory letter is for initial set-up or substantial expansion, giving the installed capacity and proposed addition thereto. ESSENTIALITY CERTIFICATE.
- (v) Process flow chart, plant layout, drawings showing the arrangement of imported machines along with an attested copy of the Project Report submitted to the Sponsoring authorities, Financial Institution, etc.
- (vi) Write up, drawings, catalogues and literature of the items under import.
- (vii) Two attested copies of foreign collaboration agreement, technical agreement, know-how, basic/detailed engineering agreement, equipment supply agreement, service agreement, or any other agreement with foreign collaborators/suppliers/ persons including the details of payment actually made or to be made.

2.2 After satisfying that goods are eligible for project imports benefit and importer has submitted all the required documents, the contract is registered by the Custom House and as a token of registration the provisional duty bond is accepted by the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs, Project Import Group. The details of the contracts are entered in the register kept for the purpose and a Project Contract Registration Number is assigned and communicated to the importer. The importer is required to refer to this number in all subsequent correspondence.

## 3. Clearance of goods after registration:
3.1 On every Bill of Entry filed for clearance of goods under the Project Import Scheme, the

importer/CHA is required to indicate the Project Contract Registration Number allotted to it. ### 6.7.6 Payment of Final Bill
When a final bill (bill summary; GST/tax invoice may be collected prior to final payment certification) of the contractor is submitted, the following requirements shall be compiled by the engineer-in-charge in addition to the requirements applicable to the running account bills:

- i) A Deviation Statement shall be prepared by the Engineer-in-charge showing the quantity and cost of each item of work executed as compared to the estimated quantities and amount of the contract giving reasons for excesses and savings, extra/substituted items, as applicable.
- ii) A time extension statement with reasons and details, if applicable
- iii) A completion certificate (**Annexure 11**) in the prescribed form stating that the work has been completed in all respects strictly according to the specifications given in the tender documents.
- iv) A final statement of recoveries / deductions / penalties / clearance of hold amount, if any (**Annexure 12 and Annexure 13**) along with a certificate that no other amount is recoverable from the contractor on any account.
- v) A certificate from the contractor shall be obtained on the final bill that he has no further claims than those given in the final bill and that he accepts the payment in full and final settlement of all his claims.

If the contractor has any claim still persisting at the time of preparation of final bill, it should be ensured that the contractor attaches a statement of claims to the final bill giving particulars of such claims, grounds on which it is based and the amount claimed duly supported with copies of notices sent to the Engineer-in- Charge.

- vi) A material appropriation statement (**Annexure 26**) shall be given by the Engineer-in-charge indicating the details of issue voucher reference numbers, quantity issued, quantify utilised in the work and the amount chargeable to the contractor for non-return / excess consumption of materials in accordance with the terms of the contract. The quantity of theoretical consumption as indicated by the Engineer-in-Charge in the material appropriation statement shall be accepted as final.
- vii) An undertaking from the contractor that he has discharged all his obligation under various laws and he would indemnify the owner if there is any demand against the Company on his account. A labour liability certificate (in case labour is involved)
- viii) Any special certificates, if required, from any statutory authorities
- ix) A contractor performance evaluation statement as per performance evaluation policy in vogue.

The Payments against final bills should be authorised only after the certification of Engineer-in-charge of contract execution (and User department, wherever applicable) for completeness of the job as per scope of work as well as regarding clearance of the work site.

Following additional test checks shall be exercised by Finance Department (payment section)

in respect of final bills:

- i) That the certificates and statements required to be submitted by the Engineer-in-charge along with the final bill have been submitted.
- ii) The material appropriation statement shall be checked to see whether the allowance allowed are in line with the provisions of contract only. No other checking in this regard need to be made.
- iii) It shall be seen that the work has been completed by the contractor within the stipulated period or within such extended time as may be given by the Engineer-in-charge.
- iv) If extension of time has been granted to the contractor, Finance Department shall see that order amendment or approval copy is made available.

After the bills have been checked, adjustment entries required, if any, shall be passed by Finance officials and final payment shall be authorized by finance officials.

All the payments related to WOs shall be made as per contract conditions.

question_text: How should emergency purchase prices or distress sale prices be treated in TEC proceedings according to point (vii)?

When recording emergency purchase or distress‑sale prices in TEC proceedings, you must clearly note that these figures are not reliable benchmarks for future procurements. The TEC record should include a statement such as:  

*“These prices are not valid LPP for comparison in future procurement.”*  

This disclaimer ensures that anomalous prices from emergencies or distress sales are not mistakenly used as a basis for judging reasonableness in later tenders. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 126)

First, I need to grasp what the question is asking: it wants to know how emergency purchase prices or distress‑sale prices should be handled when they appear in TEC proceedings, specifically according to point (vii).  

Next, I recall what point (vii) prescribes: it warns that prices obtained in emergencies or from distress sales are not reliable guides for future procurement and that the TEC record must make it clear that such prices cannot be used as a valid last purchase price (LPP) for later comparisons.  

From that, I see the practical implication: whenever such a price is entered into the TEC notes, I must attach a disclaimer that flags its limited usefulness. This disclaimer should explicitly state that the price is not a valid LPP for comparison in future procurement.  

Adding this note serves a deeper purpose—it prevents the anomalous price from being mistakenly taken as a benchmark when assessing the reasonableness of rates in later tenders, thereby protecting the integrity of the price‑reasonableness judgment process.  

Finally, synthesizing these steps, the correct treatment is to record the emergency or distress‑sale price alongside a clear statement such as: “These prices are not valid LPP for comparison in future procurement.” This ensures the price is documented but not misused as a reference for future procurements.

question_text: How should auditors verify that the technical specifications for procurement consider the environmental‑friendly material requirement mentioned in clause ix)
answer:
1. Verify that the technical specifications explicitly require the use of environmental‑friendly materials as a selection factor. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 41)  
2. Verify that the specifications include considerations of efficiency, optimum fuel/power consumption, reduced noise and emission levels, and low maintenance cost. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 41)  
3. Verify that life‑cycle cost analysis and net present value (NPV) weighting with an annuity discount percentage are prescribed for equipment procurement. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 41)  
4. Verify that compulsory buy‑back provisions are included for equipment containing hazardous materials, where feasible. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 41)  
5. Verify that, for appliances covered by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) labelling scheme, the technical specifications mandate the applicable BEE star‑rating thresholds (e.g., 5‑star for split ACs with >1000 h annual use, 3‑star for limited‑use ACs, 4‑star for frost‑free refrigerators, 5‑star for ceiling fans and water heaters) or, where BEE ratings are not yet available, require the minimum energy‑efficiency level derived from the scheme. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 41)  
6. Verify that, when BEE labelling is not applicable, the specifications allow the use of other Type III Eco‑labels conforming to ISO 14020 or recognised voluntary environmental standards to express sustainability criteria. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 41)
cot:
First, I ask myself what the auditor actually needs to confirm: that the technical specifications really embed the environmental‑friendly material directive from clause ix) and not just pay lip service to it. That means looking for an explicit statement that such materials must be used or given preference in the procurement.

question_text: What three conditions must be met to justify hiring an individual consultant?
answer:
The three conditions that must be met to justify hiring an individual consultant are:  

1. The assignment does not require a team of personnel.  
2. No additional outside professional support is needed.  
3. The individual’s experience and qualifications are the paramount requirement.  

These criteria ensure that a single consultant can adequately fulfill the task without external assistance and that the consultant’s specific expertise is the key factor in the selection decision (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 57).
cot:
First, I ask myself what makes it sensible to bring in just one consultant rather than a group or a firm. The answer lies in the nature of the task itself: if the work can be completed by a single person, there is no need to assemble a team, so the first condition that comes to mind is that the assignment must not require a team of personnel.  

Next, I think about what would happen if that lone consultant needed help from other specialists. If outside professional support were necessary, the individual would not be able to carry out the assignment on their own, defeating the purpose of hiring a solo consultant. Therefore, the second condition must be that no additional outside professional support is required.  

Then I turn to why we would choose this particular individual over anyone else. The selection process for individual consultants hinges on the person’s own background—what they know, what they have done, and how well they fit the specific demands of the job. If something else, like cost or availability, were the main driver, the consultant’s expertise would not be the paramount factor. Hence, the third condition is that the individual’s experience and qualifications are the paramount requirement.  

I check that these three points together cover all the reasons for opting for an individual consultant: they ensure the work is suitably scoped for one person, that the person can work independently, and that the decision is based on the consultant’s unique suitability.  

Putting it all together, the three conditions that justify hiring an individual consultant are: the assignment does not require a team, no additional outside professional support is needed, and the consultant’s experience and qualifications are the paramount requirement.

## 7.2 Selection of Individual consultants/ service providers
7.2.1 Individual consultants/ service providers are normally employed on assignments for which

- i) Teams of personnel is not required;
- ii) No additional outside professional support is required, and
- iii) The experience and qualifications of the individual are the paramount requirement.

7.2.2 The procedures for selecting individual consultants/ service providers are similar to, but much simpler than, those for selecting teams of consultants/ service providers from a firm. Process of selection of Individual consultants/ service providers entails:

- i) Preparing a Consultancy and other services package including the ToR, time frame, number of person-months, budget, Tendering / EoI Short-listing criteria and getting it approved by the CA;
- ii) **Notification:** Notification in such case should be given on Central Public Procurement

Portal (CPMP) at [www.eprocure.gov.in](http://www.eprocure.gov.in) and on Government E- Market (GeM). An organisation having its own website should also publish all its advertised tender enquiries on the website. The notification for invitation of tenders should give the complete web address from where the bidding documents can be downloaded.

- iii) **Method of Selection:** They shall be selected through comparison of qualifications of the candidates who have expressed interest in the assignment or have been approached directly by the Procuring Entity. Candidates who are already employed with the Procuring Entity shall meet all relevant qualifications and shall be fully capable of carrying out the assignment. Capability is judged on the basis of academic background, experience, and, as appropriate, knowledge of the local conditions, such as local language, culture, administrative system, and government organisation.
- iv) **Direct Negotiation:** Individual consultants/ service providers may be selected on a direct negotiation basis with due justification in exceptional cases such as: (a) tasks that are a continuation of previous work that the consultant/ service provider has carried out and for which the consultant/ service provider was selected competitively; (b) emergency situations resulting from natural disasters; and (c) when the individual is the only consultant/ service provider qualified for the assignment. Individual consultants/ service providers may be (among others) independent consultants/ service providers; consultants/ service providers recruited from firms; or consultants/ service providers recruited from academic, government, or international agencies.
- v) **Staff or Associates of Consultancy/ service provider Firms:** If the candidate is permanent staff or associates of a Consultancy firm the conflict of interest provisions described in these guidelines shall apply to the parent firm.

## 7.3 Selection of Specialized Agencies/ Institutions
7.3.1 From time to time, there may be a need to recruit a specialized agency or institution to undertake a specific task for which it is particularly well suited. Such agencies may be Government/ Semi-Government Agencies, Universities or Professional Institutions.

7.3.2 In some cases, the agency or institution has access to special expertise or special backup and support facilities that make it worthwhile considering recruitment on an SSS basis. In such cases, there must be full justification that the use of SSS is in the best interests of Procuring Entity.

7.3.3 In cases, of Government and semi-Government Agency SSS would be an appropriate method of recruitment.

7.3.4 Individual consultants/ service providers recruited from agencies and institutions may be selected in the same way as any other independent consultants/ service providers.

question_text: In the Schedule of Requirements, what additional components may be included if a separate Technical Specification is not provided
answer: If a separate Technical Specification is not provided, the Schedule of Requirements shall also incorporate the Technical Specification, quality assurance provisions, and inspection requirements. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 97)
cot:
First, I need to understand exactly what the question is asking: it wants to know what extra elements might be added to the Schedule of Requirements when there is no standalone Technical Specification document.  

Next, I turn to the description of the Schedule of Requirements itself. The reference explains that this section normally contains the list of goods and the delivery schedule, but it also includes a conditional note about what happens if a separate Technical Specification is not provided.  

Reading that conditional note, it says that in the absence of a separate TS, the Technical Specification, together with quality assurance and inspection provisions, may also be included in the Schedule of Requirements.  

From this, I can see that the three items mentioned—Technical Specification, quality assurance, and inspection requirements—are precisely the additional components that can be incorporated into the Schedule of Requirements under that condition.  

Finally, I synthesize the information: if a separate Technical Specification is not supplied, the Schedule of Requirements should also encompass the Technical Specification, quality assurance provisions, and inspection requirements, which matches the given answer.

#### x) Conflict of Interest among Bidders/ Agents
A bidder shall not have conflict of interest with other bidders. Such conflict of interest can lead to anti-competitive practices to the detriment of Procuring Entity's interests. The bidder found to have a conflict of interest shall be disqualified. A bidder may be considered to have a conflict of interest with one or more parties in this bidding process, if:

- a) they have controlling partner(s) in common; or
- b) they receive or have received any direct or indirect subsidy/ financial stake from any of them; or
- c) they have the same legal representative/agent for purposes of this bid; or
- d) they have relationship with each other, directly or through common third parties, that puts them in a position to have access to information about or influence on the bid of another Bidder; or
- e) Bidder participates in more than one bid in this bidding process. Participation by a Bidder in more than one Bid will result in the disqualification of all bids in

which the parties are involved. However, this does not limit the inclusion of the components/ sub-assembly/ Assemblies from one bidding manufacturer in more than one bid.

- f) In cases of agents quoting in offshore procurements (GTE), on behalf of their principal manufacturers, one agent cannot represent two manufacturers or quote on their behalf in a particular tender enquiry. One manufacturer can also authorise only one agent/dealer. There can be only one bid from the following:

1. The principal manufacturer directly or through one Indian agent on his behalf; and [in case of receipt of bids from both the Indian agent & the principal, the **principal manufacturer** shall be approached to arrange for withdrawal of one of the bids; in case of non-withdrawal, the bid from the **principal manufacturer** shall be considered]
2. Indian/foreign agent on behalf of only one principal.

- g) a Bidder or any of its affiliates participated as a consultant in the preparation of the design or technical specifications of the contract that is the subject of the Bid;

- h) In case of a holding company having more than one independently manufacturing units, or more than one unit having common business ownership/management, only one unit should quote. Similar restrictions would apply to closely related sister companies. Bidders must proactively declare such sister/ common business/ management units in same/ similar line of business.

#### xi) **Schedule of Requirements**
This section comprises the list of goods and delivery schedule. If there is no separate TS, then TS, quality assurance and inspections may also be included here. If the tender contains a number of schedules of requirements, it must be clarified, whether evaluation of eligibility/qualifications/financial bids would be on a schedule by schedule basis or on the basis of a total of all schedules put together.

#### xii) **Quotation Received from Dealers/Agents for Items not Manufactured by Them**
When a firm sends a quotation for an item manufactured by a different company, the firm is also required to attach in its quotation that manufacturer's authorisation certificate and also manufacturer's confirmation of extending the required warranty for that product (in addition to the tenderers' confirmation to the required warranty). If the firm is an authorised agent/dealer of that manufacturer, certified documentary evidence to this effect is to be attached along with the quotation. This is necessary to ensure a quotation from a responsible party offering the genuine product, also backed by a warranty obligation from the concerned manufacturer.

question_text: Do I need to get a certificate from a Chartered Engineer for each piece of machinery I import
answer: Yes, you will need to obtain a certificate from a registered Chartered Engineer for each piece of machinery you import. This certificate, which confirms the installation of the imported items, must be included with your reconciliation statement when you finalize the assessment of your shipment. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 228)
cot: I begin by wondering what the rules actually demand when I bring machinery into the country. The provision that governs the finalization of an import assessment tells me that, alongside the reconciliation statement, I must submit a certificate from a registered Chartered Engineer. That certificate’s purpose is to verify that the imported machinery has been installed. The wording is specific: it calls for a certificate certifying the installation of “each of the imported items of machinery.” This phrasing makes it clear that the requirement applies to every individual machine, not just a blanket certificate for the whole shipment. So, if I am importing several pieces of equipment, I need to obtain a separate engineer’s certificate for each one and attach all of those certificates to my reconciliation statement when I file it within the allowed period after the last consignment clears. Putting those steps together leads me to conclude that yes, I must get a certificate from a Chartered Engineer for each piece of machinery I import.

question_text: Why did the Board decide to make e‑payment of duty mandatory?
answer: The Board decided to make e‑payment of duty mandatory in order to **reduce transaction costs and speed up Customs clearance**. By requiring electronic payments, importers avoid the delays and extra expenses associated with manual challan processing, and they can take advantage of the e‑payment facility that has been available through multiple authorized banks since 2007 at all major Customs locations. This change helps ensure that duty is settled before vessel or aircraft arrival, preventing interest charges and keeping the clearance process moving smoothly. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 225)
cot:
First, I think about what the Board is trying to achieve with this policy change. The decision to make something mandatory usually stems from a desire to solve a recurring problem or to improve an existing process, so I look for what pain points the current duty‑payment system creates.

Next, I consider how duty is normally paid. The reference mentions that importers can deposit duty through TR‑6 challans at designated banks, which requires them to physically go to a bank, verify the branch, and then submit the endorsed challan to Customs. That process inevitably involves time spent traveling, waiting in line, and handling paper documents, all of which add to the transaction cost and slow down the overall clearance timeline.

Then, I note that an alternative has been available for some time. Since 2007, importers have been able to pay duty electronically through more than one authorized bank at all major Customs locations. This e‑payment option removes the need for paper challans and bank visits, allowing the payment to be completed quickly and with fewer administrative steps.

After that, I connect the timing of payment to clearance requirements. Duty must be settled before a vessel or aircraft berths or lands; otherwise, interest accrues under Customs norms. If the manual challan process causes delays, importers risk missing the pre‑arrival deadline and incurring extra charges, which further hampers the flow of goods through the port.

Finally, I synthesize these observations: by mandating e‑payment, the Board eliminates the costly, time‑consuming manual challan route, ensures that duty is paid swiftly and reliably before arrival, and thereby reduces transaction costs while expediting Customs clearance. This directly matches the stated reason for the decision.

#### 6. Payment of duty:
6.1 The duty can be paid in the designated banks through TR-6 challans. It is necessary to check the name of the bank and the branch before depositing the duty. Bank endorses the payment particulars in challan which is submitted to the Customs. Facility of e-payment of duty through more than one authorized bank is also available since 2007 at all major Customs locations. Duty has to be paid prior berthing/landing of vessel /aircraft at Port failing which Interest is payable as per Customs norms.

6.2 In order to reduce the transaction costs and expedite Customs clearance the Board has decided to make e-payment of duty mandatory.

#### 7. Amendment of Bill of Entry:
7.1 Whenever mistakes are noticed after submission of documents, amendments to the Bill of Entry is carried out with the approval of Deputy/Assistant Commissioner. The request for amendment may be submitted with the supporting documents. For example, if the amendment of container number is required, a letter from shipping agent is required. On sufficient proof amendment in Bill of Entry may be permitted after the goods have been given out of charge i.e. goods have been cleared.

#### 8. Prior Entry for Bill of Entry:
For faster clearance of the goods, Section 46 of the Customs Act, 1962 allows filing of Bill of Entry prior to arrival of goods. This Bill of Entry is valid if vessel/aircraft carrying the goods arrives within 30 days from the date of presentation of Bill of Entry. The importer must declare that the vessel/aircraft is due within 30 days and present the Bill of Entry for final noting as soon as the IGM is filed.

## 9. Bill of Entry for bond/warehousing:
9.1 A separate form of Bill of Entry is used for clearance of goods for warehousing. All documents, as are required to be attached with a Bill of Entry for home consumption are also required with the Bill of Entry for warehousing which is assessed in the same manner and duty payable is determined. However, since duty is not required to be paid at the time of warehousing, the purpose of assessing the duty at this stage is only to secure the duty in case the goods do not reach the warehouse. The duty is paid at the time of ex-bond clearance of goods for which an Ex-Bond Bill of Entry is filed. The rate of duty applicable to imported goods cleared from a warehouse is the rate in force on the date of filing of Ex-Bond Bill of Entry.

## 10. Export procedure - Shipping Bill:
10.1 For clearance of export goods, the exporter or his agent has to obtain an Importer-Export Code (IEC) number from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade Under the EDI System, IEC number is received by the Customs System from the DGFT online. The exporter is also required to register authorized foreign exchange dealer code (through which export proceeds are expected to be realized) and open a current account in the designated bank for credit of any Drawback incentive. GST number is also to be linked with the IEC number.

10.2 All the exporters intending to export under the export promotion scheme need to get their licences/DEEC book etc. registered at the Customs Station. For such registration, original documents are required.

## 11. Octroi exemption for export goods:
11.1 Since the Shipping Bill is issued by ICEGATE only after the 'Let Export' order is given by Customs, the exporter may make use of export invoice or such other document as required by the Octroi authorities for the purpose of Octroi exemption.

## 12. Waiver of GR form:
12.1 Generally the processing of Shipping Bills requires the production of a GR form that is used to monitor the foreign exchange remittance in respect of the export goods. However, there are few exceptions when the GR form is not required. An example is export of goods valued not more than US \$25,000/- and another is export of gifts valued up to Rs.5,00,000/-.

question_text: What is the effect of a lawsuit filed against the bank within six months after the guarantee’s expiry date
answer: If a lawsuit is filed against the bank within six months after the guarantee’s expiry date, the guarantee’s rights are forfeited and the bank is relieved and discharged from all liabilities under the guarantee. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 142)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know the consequence when a lawsuit is brought against the bank after the guarantee has already expired, but the suit is filed within six months of that expiry date.  

Next, I look at the guarantee’s terms to see how it treats the period after expiry. The document states that the guarantee remains in force until a certain date, but it also includes a proviso that the guarantor’s liability continues only if a claim is not made within six months after the guarantee’s expiry.  

Then, I focus on the exact wording of that proviso: unless a suit or action to enforce a claim is filed against the bank within six months from the expiry date, the beneficiary’s rights under the guarantee are forfeited and the bank is relieved and discharged from all liabilities thereunder.  

From this, I deduce that filing a lawsuit within that six‑month window actually activates the forfeiture clause—the condition that would otherwise release the bank is not met because the suit has been timely filed, so the guarantee’s rights are lost and the bank is no longer liable.  

Finally, I synthesize the reasoning: a lawsuit filed against the bank within six months after the guarantee’s expiry triggers the forfeiture provision, meaning the guarantee’s rights are nullified and the bank is discharged from any further obligation under the guarantee. This matches the given answer.

4. When General Conditions of Contract (GCC) are present, do not alter the GCC; introduce any needed changes exclusively through Special Conditions of Contract. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 92)  
5. Define clear and fair technical and financial eligibility criteria for bidders, prescribing appropriate parameters that reflect the procurement’s specific circumstances. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 92)  
6. Adopt open online tendering as the default method and keep the experience criteria broad‑based to allow participation of bidders with relevant similar experience. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 92)  
7. For large‑value tenders, conduct a pre‑bid conference and state its place and time in the tender document or publicise it via the procuring entity’s website or newspaper. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 92)

First, I notice that the root of interpretation problems and overruns lies in vague or incomplete tender documents—when clauses are open to more than one reading or when essential contractual elements are missing, parties can disagree on scope, timing or cost, which then translates into delays and budget excesses.  
So the first thing to address is the clarity and completeness of the document itself: it must be written in plain, unambiguous language and it has to contain every provision that will govern the contract, from technical specifications and drawings to commercial terms such as inspection procedures, payment schedules, the obligations of both the procuring entity and the supplier, time‑frames or milestones, tax implications, compliance requirements and a dispute‑resolution mechanism.  
Next, I think about how to achieve that level of detail without reinventing the wheel each time. The most efficient way is to start from the model tender documents issued by the Department of Expenditure, which already embody best‑practice wording and structure, and then tailor only those parts that are specific to the procurement at hand—this ensures consistency while still allowing necessary customization.  
When the model includes General Conditions of Contract, I recognize that altering those core conditions can create confusion and undermine the standardized framework; therefore any needed changes should be introduced exclusively through Special Conditions of Contract, leaving the GCC untouched.  
Beyond the contractual text, I consider who will be able to respond to the tender. To keep the evaluation objective and avoid disputes over bidder suitability, the eligibility criteria—both technical and financial—must be set clearly, fairly and in line with the particular demands of the project, using appropriate parameters that reflect the needed quality, time and cost balance.  
I also reflect on the mechanics of the tendering process itself. Making open online tendering the default method promotes transparency and widens the pool of potential participants, while keeping the experience criteria broad enough lets firms with relevant similar experience compete without unnecessary barriers.  
Finally, for high‑value procurements where the stakes are higher, I see value in holding a pre‑bid conference. By stating the place and time of that conference in the tender document—or publicizing it through the entity’s website or newspapers—prospective bidders can seek clarification up front, which further reduces the chance of later misunderstandings that could lead to time or cost overruns.  

Putting these thoughts together, the actions needed to avoid differing interpretations and potential overruns are: draft the tender with clear, unambiguous language and include all necessary provisions; base it on the DoE model tender documents, customizing only where required; preserve any General Conditions of Contract and place variations in Special Conditions of Contract; define clear, fair technical and financial eligibility criteria suited to the procurement; adopt open online tendering as the default and keep experience criteria broad‑based; and for large‑value tenders, conduct a pre‑bid conference and communicate its details in the document or via public notice.

question_text: Why must eligibility criteria be measurable and based on verifiable documents according to the guidance?
answer:
- To enable objective, consistent assessment of bidders against predefined standards. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)  
- To allow verification through supporting documents, ensuring that claims can be cross‑checked and validated. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)  
- To facilitate scoring or pass‑fail decisions by providing clear, quantifiable metrics that can be summed and compared to the minimum qualifying threshold. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)  
- To maintain transparency and fairness in the short‑listing process, reducing subjectivity and potential disputes. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)
cot:
First, I consider what the eligibility criteria are actually used for: they form the basis for deciding which bidders move forward to the next stage, so whatever we put in them must be something we can trust to differentiate firms accurately.  

If the criteria are vague or based on impressions, two reviewers could reach different conclusions about the same bidder, which would undermine the whole short‑listing process. Therefore the criteria need to be expressed in a way that yields the same result regardless of who is evaluating them—i.e., they must be measurable.  

Measurability alone isn’t enough unless we have something concrete to measure against. A claim such as “we have extensive experience” is meaningless unless it can be backed up by evidence that anyone can check. That pushes the design toward requiring supporting documents—turnover statements, profit logs, certificates, etc.—that can be verified independently.  

When the criteria are both measurable and tied to verifiable documents, we can turn each bidder’s information into a score or a simple pass‑fail decision. Scores can be added up using the pre‑declared weightings, and a minimum threshold can be applied uniformly; alternatively, a pass‑fail rule can be checked against each documented requirement.  

Because the evaluation now rests on clear, observable data rather than subjective judgment, the process becomes transparent: bidders see exactly what is required, reviewers can show how they arrived at their decision, and any disagreement can be traced back to a specific document or numeric value. This transparency inherently reduces the chance of bias and limits potential disputes.  

Putting these strands together, the guidance insists on measurable, document‑based eligibility criteria so that we can assess bidders objectively, verify their claims through reliable evidence, produce comparable scores or pass‑fail outcomes, and keep the short‑listing open, fair, and free from unnecessary contention.

question_text: What initial actions must the indenting department take when raising a purchase requisition for an online order
answer:
To initiate an online purchase requisition, the indenting department must:

- Raise a purchase requisition (PR) in the system.  
- Submit the estimated price of the item together with the basis for that estimate (e.g., price paid for similar items on the last purchase order or current market price).  
- Nominate an officer of grade A or above to serve on the purchase committee.  
- Forward the completed proposal to the Commercial Department through the Functional Head of the indenting department.  

These actions embed early cost validation, clear accountability, and procedural oversight, thereby reinforcing transparency, value‑for‑money, and risk‑aligned procurement that supports corporate financial objectives. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 70)
cot:
First, I consider what triggers the procurement process for an online order – it begins with the indenting department formally recording the need in the system, so raising a purchase requisition is the essential first move.  
Next, I think about what information the requisition must carry to be useful downstream; without a realistic cost estimate and a clear basis for that estimate (such as recent purchase prices or prevailing market rates), the later evaluation would lack a benchmark, so the department must attach the estimated price together with the reasoning behind it.  
Then, I reflect on who will actually assess the offers from various websites; the procedure calls for a small purchase committee, and to ensure authority and expertise, the indenting department must nominate an officer at grade A or above to sit on that committee.  
After the requisition is prepared with the estimate and the nominee, it cannot sit idle; it needs to be forwarded for review and approval, which means sending the completed proposal to the Commercial Department, but it must travel through the indenting department’s Functional Head to maintain proper routing and accountability.  
Looking at these actions together, I see how they embed early cost validation, clear responsibility, and procedural oversight – each step adds a layer of checks that promote transparency, value‑for‑money, and risk‑aware purchasing, aligning the procurement with broader financial objectives.  
Thus, the initial actions the indenting department must take when raising a purchase requisition for an online order are exactly: raise the PR in the system, submit the estimated price with its basis, nominate a grade A or above officer for the purchase committee, and forward the proposal to Commercial via the Functional Head.

question_text: In the drawback‑based re‑import scenario, what specific amount of duty must be paid upon re‑importation?
answer: In a drawback‑based re‑import scenario, the duty payable upon re‑importation equals the amount of customs duty that was previously relieved through the duty drawback (or rebate) claimed on the exported goods – i.e., the duties equivalent to the export incentive availed must be paid. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 237)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what a drawback‑based re‑import situation entails: the goods were originally exported after a duty drawback (or rebate) had been claimed, meaning a portion of the customs duty that would have been due on those goods was relieved at the time of export.  

Next, I recall the general rule that customs duty is imposed on the act of importation itself, and no automatic distinction is made for goods that have previously had duty paid or relieved; therefore, unless a specific exemption applies, the goods would attract duty again upon re‑import.  

Then I look at the relief provisions for re‑imported goods. The key point is that when goods return after having been exported under a drawback claim, the exemption is not blanket; instead, the duty that had been waived through the drawback must be recovered to prevent a double benefit. In other words, the amount of duty that was originally relieved via the drawback becomes payable again when the goods are brought back.  

Building on that, I reason that the duty to be paid upon re‑import is precisely equivalent to the drawback amount that had been availed on the original export. This ensures that the exporter does not retain the drawback benefit while also enjoying a duty‑free re‑import.  

Finally, synthesizing the above, the specific duty payable in a drawback‑based re‑import scenario is the customs duty that was previously relieved through the duty drawback (or rebate) claimed on the exported goods – i.e., the duties equivalent to the export incentive availed must be paid upon re‑importation.
chunk_content:
### 2. Re-importation of indigenously manufactured/imported goods:
2.1 Under Section 12 of the Custom Act, 1962 import duties of Customs are leviable on all import goods, and no distinction is made whether the goods being imported had discharged duties earlier are being re-imported after exportation for particular purposes. Similarly, even if goods are indigenously manufactured which had been exported earlier under various export incentive schemes or duty drawback claim or even without any export incentive claim, when these are re-imported they attract the Customs duty leviable on like import goods (as the duty is on the act of importation) unless an exemption notification is issued.

2.2 To avoid incidence of double duty on re-imported goods such when sent abroad for repairs, certain relief from duty has been provided. Similarly, where the goods are indigenously manufactured, they should bear the GST, which may not have been discharged at the time of exportation. Further, the exporters should not retain any benefits obtained as an export incentive if the goods are re-imported.

2.3 The salient elements of the duty exemption governing the re-imported goods are as follows:

(i) On re-import of indigenously manufactured goods under duty Drawback/rebate claims, export under bond or under other claim of export incentives, essentially the duties equivalent to the export incentives etc. availed have to be paid, on reimportation. Thus, if the goods were exported on payment of GST, without claiming any rebate, and without claiming any export incentives such as Drawback or benefits of the duty exemption schemes, EPCG/DEPB schemes, and where the indigenously manufactured goods are being returned then no Customs duties are leviable. Further, where the indigenously manufactured goods are exported for repair and returned without claiming any benefits, duty is to be paid on a value comprising fair cost of repairs including cost of materials used in repairs, insurance and freight charges both ways. Basically the benefit is available if the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs is satisfied that the goods are the same which were exported earlier and certain other conditions as laid down in the said

notification are fulfilled.

(ii) Goods manufactured in India or parts thereof that are re-imported for repairs or reconditioning or reprocessing/refining/remaking etc. are exempt from duty subject to the condition that the re-importation takes place within a specified period; the goods are re-exported within six months of re-importation; the Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Customs is satisfied as regards the identity of the goods; and certain other conditions ensuring re-export including execution of bonds are fulfilled.

(iii) Re-imported private personal property, which was imported earlier but exported out for any alteration, renovation, repair free of charge etc. is exempt from duty subject to the condition that the goods are repaired on free of charge basis in accordance with the terms of warranty given by the manufacturers and in accordance with the established trade practice and Drawback or other incentives have not been availed. However, certain Custom duties equivalent to the cost of alterations/renovations/additions/repairs, if any, are payable.

question_text: How does NRL assist the buyer if heavy lifting equipment is needed at Numaligarh
answer:
- NRL provides heavy‑lifting equipment (e.g., crane, hydra) to the buyer at Numaligarh when needed, subject to equipment availability, at NRL’s prevailing rental rate, with the buyer required to deposit the rental charges in advance.  
- This prepaid‑rental support enables timely material handling, limits the buyer’s capital outlay, and reduces schedule risk, thereby reinforcing transparent, value‑for‑money procurement aligned with corporate objectives.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 170)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is asking: it wants to know how NRL supports the buyer when heavy‑lifting gear such as a crane or hydra is required at the Numaligarh site.  

The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals specify that while moving the goods is normally the buyer’s responsibility, there is a specific provision that says if the buyer needs heavy‑lifting equipment at Numaligarh, NRL will make that equipment available, provided it is on hand, and will charge the prevailing rental rate, with the buyer required to pay that rental in advance.  

From that clause I can pull out the key conditions that must be met for NRL’s help to kick in: the equipment must be available in NRL’s fleet, the rate applied is NRL’s current rental price, and the buyer has to deposit the rental amount before the equipment is released.  

With those conditions in mind, the assistance works like this: NRL supplies the crane or hydra on a rental basis, so the buyer does not have to purchase or mobilize their own heavy‑lifting assets. Because the rental is paid upfront, the buyer’s cash outflow is predictable and limited to the hire cost, avoiding a large capital expenditure. The equipment being on site and ready to use means the buyer can start lifting and moving the materials as soon as the delivery order is issued, which keeps the schedule tight and reduces the risk of delays that could arise from arranging third‑party lifts on short notice.  

Thinking further about the broader procurement picture, this arrangement aligns with the goal of transparent, value‑for‑money purchasing. By having NRL provide the lift equipment at a known rental rate and requiring advance payment, the process stays within the documented terms of the auction/tender, eliminates hidden costs, and supports the corporate objective of obtaining goods efficiently without unnecessary financial burden on the buyer.  

Putting it all together, NRL’s role is to make heavy‑lifting equipment available to the buyer at Numaligarh when needed, subject to availability, at NRL’s prevailing rental charge, with the buyer paying that rental in advance; this enables timely material handling, limits the buyer’s capital outlay, and reduces schedule risk, thereby reinforcing a transparent and cost‑effective procurement process.

### iii) Government e-Marketplace (GeM)
To ensure better transparency and higher efficiency an online Government e- Marketplace (GeM- an e-commerce marketplace) has been developed for common use goods and services. In GeM product or services are offered by a number of eligible sellers and all the eligible buyers can view/ compare all the product/ services and select the product/ services offered by any one of the seller. In general, because online marketplaces aggregate product/ services from a wide array of providers, selection is usually wider, availability is higher, and prices are more competitive than in vendor-specific online retail stores. The procurement process on GeM is online and electronic -

end to end from placement of supply order to payment to suppliers. The registration of suppliers on GeM is online and automatic based on ID authentication etc. The procuring authorities have to assess the reasonability of rates. Buyer's transactions are processed by the GeM portal and then product/ services are delivered and fulfilled directly by the participating sellers. Tools of reverse bidding and e-auction are also available which can be utilised for the procurement of bulk quantities. The Procurement of Goods and Services by Ministries or Departments are mandatory for Goods or Services available on GeM. Ministries/ Departments are expected to work with GeM in making available on the GeM platform as many products/ services by making available such Goods and Services which are regularly procured by them.

Currently functionality for floating tenders for works contracts is not available in GeM. When the functionality for works contracts is made available by GeM, tendering for works contracts through GeM will be adopted suitably.

## 1.8 The Law of Agency - applicable to Procurement of Works
In addition to Laws which are applicable to Public Procurement of Works mentioned above, the Law of Agency (Section 182 to section 238, of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) implies that Contractor would be an Agent of the Procuring Entity, to execute the works on its behalf. Hence, there exists a Principal/ Employer and Agent relationship between Procuring Entity and such Contractor. As per this law, the employer is vicariously legally and financially liable for actions of its Agents. For example, a violation of certain labour laws in deputing staff for Procuring Entity's contract by the agents may render the Procuring Entity legally and financially liable for such violations, under certain circumstances. The Procuring Entities need to be aware of such eventualities. Standard Bidding Documents should take care of this aspect.

### 9.14.1 Goods Receipt and Inspection Report
If the received material successfully passes the quantity and quality checks, accounting of material received shall be on the basis of the Goods Receipt and Inspection Report (GRInsR) (Annexure 17) prepared after inspection and acceptance of the material which will be signed by the concerned officers. This includes cases where payment is made to the supplier on proof of dispatch, for which inspection at the suppliers' premises is conducted by an authorised officer of Procuring Entity prior to dispatch by suppliers. This excludes cases of imported materials where accounting will be done on completion of certain further formalities as per regulations and practices. While preliminary receipt is only an acknowledgement of quantity received, GRInsR is an acknowledgement of receipt of the correct quantity as well as quality of goods. GRInsR is a voucher which forms the basis for the supplier to claim payment as per the contract. It also is a voucher for account of the received material in the inventory accounts. Along with the GRInsR, material is handed over to the warehouse where it is to be stored.

In case of rejected quantity the supplier should be intimated for repair/replacement at the earliest. question_text: In the case where bids are received from both an Indian agent and the principal manufacturer for the same item, what step should an auditor verify has been taken to resolve the duplication
answer: The auditor should verify that, upon receipt of bids from both the Indian agent and the principal manufacturer for the same item, the procuring entity approached the principal manufacturer to arrange for withdrawal of one of the duplicate bids; and that, if withdrawal was not effected, the bid from the principal manufacturer was retained while the agent’s bid was set aside. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 97)
cot:
First, I note that the situation involves two bids for the identical item—one coming from an Indian agent and the other directly from the principal manufacturer.  
Seeing this, I recall the conflict‑of‑interest provision that permits only a single bid from either the principal itself or through one authorized Indian agent; having both would create a prohibited duplication.  
Given that rule, the next logical step is to determine how the duplication should be eliminated: the procuring entity must act to have one of the bids withdrawn so that only a single, compliant offer remains.  
Looking at the specific guidance for this case, it specifies that the principal manufacturer should be approached to arrange the withdrawal of one bid; if the principal does not withdraw, its bid is the one that stands while the agent’s bid is set aside.  
Therefore, to satisfy the auditor’s responsibility, I need to verify that the procuring entity indeed contacted the principal manufacturer to seek withdrawal of the duplicate bid and, when withdrawal was not obtained, that the principal’s bid was retained and the agent’s bid was disregarded.  
By confirming that these actions were taken, the auditor can be confident that the duplication was resolved in accordance with the required procedure.

#### x) Conflict of Interest among Bidders/ Agents
A bidder shall not have conflict of interest with other bidders. Such conflict of interest can lead to anti-competitive practices to the detriment of Procuring Entity's interests. The bidder found to have a conflict of interest shall be disqualified. A bidder may be considered to have a conflict of interest with one or more parties in this bidding process, if:

- a) they have controlling partner(s) in common; or
- b) they receive or have received any direct or indirect subsidy/ financial stake from any of them; or
- c) they have the same legal representative/agent for purposes of this bid; or
- d) they have relationship with each other, directly or through common third parties, that puts them in a position to have access to information about or influence on the bid of another Bidder; or
- e) Bidder participates in more than one bid in this bidding process. Participation by a Bidder in more than one Bid will result in the disqualification of all bids in

which the parties are involved. However, this does not limit the inclusion of the components/ sub-assembly/ Assemblies from one bidding manufacturer in more than one bid.

- f) In cases of agents quoting in offshore procurements (GTE), on behalf of their principal manufacturers, one agent cannot represent two manufacturers or quote on their behalf in a particular tender enquiry. One manufacturer can also authorise only one agent/dealer. There can be only one bid from the following:

1. The principal manufacturer directly or through one Indian agent on his behalf; and [in case of receipt of bids from both the Indian agent & the principal, the **principal manufacturer** shall be approached to arrange for withdrawal of one of the bids; in case of non-withdrawal, the bid from the **principal manufacturer** shall be considered]
2. Indian/foreign agent on behalf of only one principal.

- g) a Bidder or any of its affiliates participated as a consultant in the preparation of the design or technical specifications of the contract that is the subject of the Bid;

- h) In case of a holding company having more than one independently manufacturing units, or more than one unit having common business ownership/management, only one unit should quote. Similar restrictions would apply to closely related sister companies. Bidders must proactively declare such sister/ common business/ management units in same/ similar line of business.

#### xi) **Schedule of Requirements**
This section comprises the list of goods and delivery schedule. If there is no separate TS, then TS, quality assurance and inspections may also be included here. If the tender contains a number of schedules of requirements, it must be clarified, whether evaluation of eligibility/qualifications/financial bids would be on a schedule by schedule basis or on the basis of a total of all schedules put together.

#### xii) **Quotation Received from Dealers/Agents for Items not Manufactured by Them**
When a firm sends a quotation for an item manufactured by a different company, the firm is also required to attach in its quotation that manufacturer's authorisation certificate and also manufacturer's confirmation of extending the required warranty for that product (in addition to the tenderers' confirmation to the required warranty). If the firm is an authorised agent/dealer of that manufacturer, certified documentary evidence to this effect is to be attached along with the quotation. This is necessary to ensure a quotation from a responsible party offering the genuine product, also backed by a warranty obligation from the concerned manufacturer.

question_text: Under what conditions may expenditure be incurred for the benefit of a particular person or section of the people according to the financial propriety standards
answer:
- Expenditure that benefits a particular person or section of the people may be incurred only when:  
  - a claim for the amount could be enforced in a Court of Law; or  
  - the expenditure is made in pursuance of a recognized policy or custom.  

This limitation protects public funds from private diversion unless justified by legal entitlement or sanctioned practice, thereby reinforcing transparency, value‑for‑money, and alignment with strategic procurement goals. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 24)
cot: First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants the circumstances under which public money can be spent to advantage a specific person or group without violating financial propriety. Then I think about the overarching spirit of the canons: they demand that officials treat public funds with the same care as their own, avoid excess, and prevent self‑advantage. Next I focus on the canon that directly deals with benefiting a particular person or section. It states that such expenditure is prohibited unless certain conditions are met. Examining those conditions, I see two alternatives: either the amount could be recovered through a legal claim, meaning there is an enforceable right to the payment, or the spending follows an established policy or custom that has been accepted as normal practice. I weigh these alternatives and realize they are the only exceptions spelled out; any other reason would be a private diversion of public funds. Finally, I synthesize the point: expenditure for a particular beneficiary is permissible only when a court‑enforceable claim exists or when it is done in line with a recognized policy or custom.

## 1.8 Standards (Canons) of Financial Propriety
Public Procurement like any other expenditure in Government must conform to the Standards (also called Canons) of Financial Propriety.

**Standards of financial propriety:** *Every officer incurring or authorizing expenditure from public moneys should be guided by high standards of financial propriety. Every officer should also enforce financial order and strict economy and see that all relevant financial rules and regulations are observed, by his own office and by subordinate disbursing officers. Among the principles on which emphasis is generally laid are the following:-*

- i) *Every officer is expected to exercise the same vigilance in respect of expenditure incurred from public moneys as a person of ordinary prudence would exercise in respect of expenditure of his own money.*
- ii) *The expenditure should not be prima facie more than the occasion demands.*
- iii) *No authority should exercise its powers of sanctioning expenditure to pass an order which will be directly or indirectly to its own advantage.*

- iv) *Expenditure from public moneys should not be incurred for the benefit of a particular person or a section of the people, unless -*
  - a) *a claim for the amount could be enforced in a Court of Law, orb) the expenditure is in pursuance of a recognized policy or custom.*
- v) *The amount of allowances granted to meet expenditure of a particular type should be so regulated that the allowances are not on the whole a source of profit to the recipients.*
- vi) *While discharging the duties of financial concurrence of any public expenditure, such authorities subsequent to such decision, shall not be involved in any future audit responsibilities which may create conflict of interest.*
