answer:
- The PRC must specify the date of receipt of goods, milestone achievement, or service delivery as indicated in the certificate. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must bear the consignee’s digital signature or e‑sign. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must be generated online on the GeM portal. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must be a Provisional Receipt Certificate (PRC). (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must be issued on a “said to contain basis”. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)  
- It must be issued within 48 hours of the seller’s entry of delivery, milestone achievement, or service delivery. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 85)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: it wants to know the mandatory elements that must appear in a Provisional Receipt Certificate (PRC) when the consignee creates it on the GeM portal.  
Then, I recall that upon delivery the consignee should receive the goods/services and issue an online Provisional Receipt Certificate, with his/her digital signature or e‑sign, mentioning the date of receipt, and that this is done on a “said to contain basis” within 48 hours of the seller’s entry.  
Next, I isolate each distinct requirement: the certificate must be provisional, it must be generated online on the GeM portal, it must bear the consignee’s digital or e‑signature, it must state the date of receipt of goods, milestone achievement, or service delivery, it must be based on a said to contain assessment, and it must be issued within the 48‑hour window after the seller’s logged delivery.  
Further, I note that none of these points are optional or implied elsewhere; the Procurement of Goods Manual repeatedly stresses that the consignee has to mandatorily acknowledge receipt through generation of the PRC, and that the timing, the digital signature, the said to contain basis, and the provisional nature are all explicit conditions for a valid PRC.  
Finally, I bring the pieces together and conclude that a PRC generated by the consignee on GeM must include the date of receipt, the consignee’s digital signature or e‑sign, be created online on the GeM portal, be a Provisional Receipt Certificate, be issued on a said to contain basis, and be issued within 48 hours of the seller’s entry of delivery, milestone achievement, or service delivery.

question_text: If no natural person meets the ownership thresholds, who is deemed the beneficial owner under the Order
answer: - If no natural person meets the ownership thresholds, the beneficial owner is the natural person who holds the position of senior managing official. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 20)
cot:
I start by asking what the question is really after: it wants to know who is treated as the beneficial owner when nobody satisfies the ownership‑based tests laid out in the Order.  

I then think about how the Order defines beneficial owner. It breaks the definition down by entity type—companies or LLPs, partnerships, unincorporated associations, and trusts—each tying the role to a natural person who holds a certain share of capital, profits or property, or who exercises control through other means.  

Looking at those definitions, I see the specific thresholds: for a company or LLP it’s a controlling ownership interest; for a partnership or an unincorporated association it’s more than fifteen percent of capital or profits; for a trust it’s a fifteen percent or more interest plus anyone with ultimate effective control.

That fallback says that, in the absence of a qualifying natural person under the ownership tests, the beneficial owner is the natural person who holds the position of senior managing official of the entity.  

Putting it all together, when no one meets the ownership thresholds, the Order deems the senior managing official to be the beneficial owner.

question_text: What is the implication of allowing tender cancellation without approval when no bids are received?
answer: Allowing tender cancellation without approval when no bids are received eliminates the need for endorsement from Functional Heads (Commercial and User Department), the Chief Financial Director, or the superior committee that would otherwise approve the tender. This streamlines the decision‑making process, reduces administrative delay, and conserves resources while still requiring a corrigendum to be published on the e‑tendering portal (CPP or GeM) to maintain transparency and auditability. By enabling swift cancellation, the organization avoids unnecessary expenditure on bid evaluation, supports corporate goals of value for money, and strengthens risk‑management controls over procurement activities. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 131)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants to know what happens when the rules let a tender be cancelled without needing any approval if no bids come in.  
Looking at the policy, I see that approval for cancellation is waived specifically when no bid is received by the deadline, including any extensions.  
Normally, cancelling a tender would require a note from the Commercial Dealing Officer to be sent up for endorsement—first to the Functional Heads of Commercial and the User Department, then possibly to the Chief Financial Director, and finally to the senior committee that would have approved the award.  
Because the rule removes that approval step in the no‑bid scenario, the organization no longer has to route the cancellation request through those layers; the decision can be made directly by the officer handling the tender.  
Eliminating those routing steps means the decision is made faster, cutting down administrative delay and saving the time and effort that would have been spent preparing approval notes and waiting for sign‑offs.  
Even though approval isn’t needed, the process still mandates that a corrigendum be posted on the e‑tendering portal (CPP or GeM) to announce the cancellation, so transparency and an audit trail are preserved.  
By avoiding the usual evaluation work that would follow a bid opening, the agency also sidesteps unnecessary costs associated with reviewing non‑existent proposals, which aligns with the goal of obtaining value for money.  
Finally, being able to cancel swiftly when there is no interest reduces the risk of proceeding with a flawed or unattractive procurement, thereby strengthening overall risk‑management controls in the purchasing function.  
Putting these points together, the implication is that allowing tender cancellation without approval when no bids are received streamlines decision‑making, cuts delays and resource use, still requires a public corrigendum for transparency, saves evaluation expenses, supports value‑for‑money objectives, and enhances risk‑management oversight.

question_text: In the Revised Offer in Negotiations format, what are the two alternatives presented to the bidder regarding the rates quoted in the original tender?
answer:
The Revised Offer in Negotiations format presents the bidder with two mutually exclusive alternatives concerning the rates originally quoted in the tender:

1. **Maintain the original rates** – the bidder declares that it is not prepared to reduce the rates already quoted in the original tender, and those rates will remain valid up to a specified date.  
2. **Offer reduced rates** – the bidder states that it will reduce its rates as detailed in an enclosed schedule of items.

These alternatives are explicitly laid out in the Revised Offer in Negotiations template, allowing the bidder to choose either to keep the tender‑price unchanged or to propose a revised, lower price schedule (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 125).

First, I consider what the Revised Offer in Negotiations is meant to achieve: it gives the bidder a chance to respond to the procuring entity’s concern that the original tender rates are too high, while still keeping the negotiation process formal.

Then, I notice a contrasting clause right after that, where the bidder states that it will reduce its rates as detailed in an attached schedule of items, and acknowledges that the original bidding document’s provisions remain binding.  

I realize these two statements are presented as alternatives—each begins with “Or” and offers a mutually exclusive choice: either keep the original quotation unchanged or submit a new, lower quotation.  

Finally, I synthesize that the Revised Offer in Negotiations format therefore offers the bidder exactly two options concerning the original rates: maintain them as‑is, or propose a reduced rate schedule. This matches the answer that the two alternatives are to keep the original rates or to offer reduced rates.

question_text: What is the maximum period allowed to offer unexecuted quantities to another agency after a failure by the selected L1 agency
answer: - Unexecuted quantities may be offered to another eligible agency within a maximum of one year from the original date of award following a failure by the selected L1 agency. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 68)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants the longest time allowed to re‑offer the part of the work that was not carried out when the initially chosen L1 bidder cannot fulfill the contract.  

Next, I look at the distinction the procurement rules make between a simple refusal and an actual failure to perform. For a refusal, the next eligible agency can be approached only while the original offer is still valid, whether that validity is the original period or any agreed extension.  

When the situation is a failure, the rules are stricter because the work has already been started and then stopped. In that case the unexecuted portion must be offered to another eligible L1 bidder, but the timing is linked to the date when the original award was made.  

I recall that the policy specifies a ceiling for this re‑offering period: it may not exceed one year measured from the original award date. This limit ensures that the re‑tendering does not drag on indefinitely while still giving the agency a reasonable window to find a replacement.  

Putting these points together, the maximum period allowed to offer the unexecuted quantities to another agency after a failure by the selected L1 agency is one year from the original date of award.

question_text: What should TRC members do when evaluating a proposal?
answer:
**A:** TRC members must independently score each proposal using only the submitted document, then jointly review and discuss individual scores to finalize them, calculate the average score per criterion to rank proposals, identify the top‑ranked proposal for award, prepare a technical evaluation report that records the scores and explains the decisions, obtain competent‑authority approval while keeping the report confidential, retain all evaluation records, and forward only technically qualified consultants to the financial‑bid stage.  
**Rationale:** These steps are prescribed in sections 6.7.3‑6.7.8 of the procurement manual to ensure an independent, transparent, and confidential evaluation process. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 51)
cot:
First, I need to grasp the core requirement: TRC members must evaluate a proposal without influencing it, relying only on what was submitted.  
That means each member should work alone, read the proposal as it stands, and assign scores to each criterion based solely on the submitted document.  
After the individual scoring, the next logical step is to bring those separate judgments together—members should meet, compare their scores, discuss any discrepancies, and agree on a final set of scores for each criterion.  
Once the scores are finalized, the group can derive a composite picture by averaging the scores for each criterion across all members; this average provides a fair, consolidated rating that can be used to rank the proposals.  
With the averaged scores in hand, the TRC can then order the proposals from highest to lowest and pinpoint the one that stands out as the best candidate for award.  
Having identified the top proposal, the TRC must record the whole process: a technical evaluation report that lists the scores per criterion and sub‑criterion, explains why the scores were given, and justifies the selection.  
Before the report can be used, it needs the competent authority’s sign‑off, and once approved it must remain confidential, with all related paperwork retained until the project is finished and audited.  
Finally, only those consultants who satisfied the technical thresholds established in the evaluation are allowed to move forward to the financial‑bid stage, ensuring that the subsequent cost comparison is limited to technically qualified firms.  

This sequence captures exactly what TRC members should do when evaluating a proposal.

A: The minimum response required is two bids. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 55)

I remember that the standard requirement for a limited tender is to receive at least three bids, just like an open tender.  
However, there is an explicit exception that applies when the limited tender is sent out to only two parties.  
In that specific case, the rule states that the minimum acceptable response drops to the number of parties invited, which is two.  
Since the question describes exactly that situation—a limited tender issued to just two parties—the exception applies directly.  
Therefore, the minimum response that would be considered acceptable in this scenario is two bids.

question_text: According to the control and regulatory provisions, what must all goods brought into the country or meant for export do before clearance
answer:
- Pass through authorized Customs points (ports, airports, Inland Container Depots, or Land Customs Stations) as notified by the Board.  
- Be reported to Customs upon arrival or prior to export.  
- Fulfil all prescribed legal and procedural requirements under the Customs Act, 1962 and allied laws, including payment of any leviable duties.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 219)
cot: I need to determine what the control and regulatory rules require of goods before they can be cleared. The provisions explain that the Board is empowered to designate specific places—such as customs ports, airports, inland container depots, and land customs stations—as the only locations where imported goods may be unloaded or export goods loaded. This tells me that any shipment must first reach one of those authorized points; otherwise it cannot even begin the customs process. The same section goes on to state that once the goods arrive at such a point they must be reported to Customs, and the importers or exporters have to fulfil all the legal and procedural obligations set out in the Customs Act, 1962 and allied laws, which includes paying any duty that is levied. Bringing these three ideas together leads to the conclusion that, before clearance, goods must pass through an authorized customs point, be reported to Customs, and satisfy the prescribed legal and procedural requirements, including the payment of any leviable duties.
chunk_content:
#### 1. Statutory provisions for levy of Customs duty:
Customs duty in India is defined under the Customs Act, 1962 and enables the government to levy duty on exports and imports etc. All matters related to customs duty fall under the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).

Customs duties are computed on a specific or ad valorem basis. In other words, it is calculated on the value of goods. Such value is determined as per the rules laid down in the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.

1.1 Entry No. 83 of List 1 to Schedule VII of the Constitution empowers the Union Government to legislate and collect duties on imports and exports. Accordingly, the Customs Act, 1962, effective from 1-2-1963 provides vide its Section 12 for the levy of duties on goods imported into or exported from India. The items and the rates of duties leviable thereon are specified in two Schedules to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

1.2 Levy of duties on ad-valorem (i.e. with reference to value) basis is the predominant mode of levy. For this purpose the value of the imported goods is required to be determined as per provisions of Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with the Customs Valuation (Determination of Prices Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.:-

#### 2. Control and regulatory provisions:
2.1 In terms of the Customs Act, 1962 the Board is given the powers to appoint Customs ports, airports and Inland Container Depots (ICD) where alone the imported goods can be brought in for unloading or export goods loaded. Similar powers have been given to the Board to notify places as Land Customs Stations (LCS) for clearance of goods imported or exported by land or by inland water. Thus, various airports, ports, ICDs and LCSs have been notified across the country and also routes have been specified for carrying out trade with neighboring countries like Nepal.

2.2 Essentially all goods brought into the country or meant for export must pass through authorized points, be reported to Customs, and the importers/exporters must fulfil the prescribed legal and procedural requirements laid down under Customs Act, 1962 and allied laws including payment of the duties leviable, if any.

#### 3. Role of custodians:
3.1 In regard to all imported goods unloaded in a Customs area, the Commissioner of Customs is required to appoint a custodian under whose custody the imported goods shall remain till these are cleared for home consumption, or are warehoused or transhipped as provided in the law. With the growth of containerized traffic the facility of Customs clearances in the interiors of the country has also been provided by opening various ICDs, which are actually dry ports and here too the goods remain with the appointed custodian till these are cleared by the Customs. In addition to custodians appointed by the Commissioner of Customs, the Customs Act, 1962 recognizes other custodians as provided under any other law.

question_text: Under what condition can the bank guarantee be extended beyond its initial validity
answer: The bank guarantee can be extended beyond its initial validity if the contract for which the guarantee was issued is not completed or fully performed. In that case, the bank agrees to keep the guarantee in force until the contract is fulfilled. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 251)
cot:
I start by asking what the guarantee’s normal lifespan looks like and what might cause it to last longer. The document tells me that the guarantee is issued for a set period and will remain in force up to a certain date in the first instance. That gives me the baseline: there is an initial validity that the bank agrees to honor unless something changes. 

Next I search for any language that talks about changing that end date. I notice a clause that says the guarantee will stay in force “until …” but then adds a conditional statement: if the contract for which the guarantee was given is not completed or fully performed, the surety (the bank) agrees to further extend the guarantee until the contract is fulfilled. 

This conditional is the only place where the guarantee’s duration is explicitly tied to an event beyond the original expiry date. It makes sense that the bank would only agree to keep the guarantee alive when the underlying obligation—the supplier’s performance under the contract—has not yet been satisfied. If the contract were already complete, there would be no need for the guarantee to persist. 

Putting those pieces together, I see that the guarantee can be extended beyond its initial validity precisely when the contract it supports remains unfinished or unperformed. In that situation the bank commits to keeping the guarantee active until the contract is finally completed. 

Therefore, the condition for extension is the incomplete or non‑full performance of the contract for which the guarantee was issued. This matches the answer that the guarantee can be extended if the contract is not completed or fully performed, with the bank agreeing to keep it in force until the contract is fulfilled.

question_text: What should be included in the institutional arrangements made by the procuring entity concerning EMDs and performance securities
answer:
- Establish a suitable mechanism for the safe custody of EMDs and performance securities. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)  
- Implement a monitoring system for EMDs, performance securities, and other instruments. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)  
- Define institutional arrangements to take all necessary actions on time for extension, encashment, or refund of EMDs and performance securities as required. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)  
- Conduct a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments that are due to expire within the next three months. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)  
- Review the progress of the corresponding contracts during the monthly monitoring activity. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)  
- Seek extensions of bank guarantees and other instruments immediately when warranted and implement them within the existing validity period. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)  
- Never hand over a bank guarantee to the contractor for the purpose of extending its validity. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)  
- Consider computerising the monitoring system to provide automatic alerts about impending validity lapses. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)  
- For the release of bank guarantees, require the executing agency to forward a proposal accompanied by its recommendations in accordance with the contract conditions. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)
cot:
First, I consider what the procuring entity must do with earnest money deposits and performance securities: they need to be kept safe, tracked over time, and acted upon promptly when they expire or are due for release.  
Then, I think about the practical steps that would achieve those goals—establishing a secure storage method, putting in place a system that watches the instruments, and assigning clear responsibilities for any required actions such as extending, encashing, or refunding them.  
Next, I work out the details of that system: a regular check‑up schedule makes sense, so a monthly review of all bank guarantees that will lapse in the coming three months would catch expiring items early, and during that same review it is logical to also look at how the related contracts are progressing to decide whether an extension is warranted.  
After that, I refine the response to those findings: if a guarantee is close to expiring and the contract still needs it, the extension should be requested right away and completed before the current validity ends, and the guarantee should never be given to the contractor just to extend its life because that defeats the purpose of control.  
I then consider how to make the monitoring more reliable—automating the process with computerised alerts would help guarantee that no expiry date is missed without constant manual effort.  
Finally, I address the release of guarantees: the entity should not return a security on its own initiative; instead, the executing agency must submit a formal proposal, backed by its recommendations, that follows the contract terms before any bank guarantee is released.  
Putting these considerations together, the institutional arrangements the procuring entity should make are exactly a safe‑custody mechanism, a monitoring system, defined timely actions for extension/encashment/refund, monthly reviews of expiring guarantees and contract progress, immediate extension when needed, never handing over a guarantee to the contractor for extension, possible computerisation with automatic alerts, and a requirement that the executing agency forward a release proposal with recommendations per contract conditions.

## 4.13 Sources and Verification of Bank Guarantees
Bank Guarantee for Bid Security (EMD) or Performance Guarantee (Security Deposit) should be irrevocable and operative Bank Guarantee (BG) as per format enclosed in the Bid Document and should be issued by a Scheduled Commercial (i.e. Indian or Foreign Banks included in the Second Schedule of Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 excluding Co-operative banks or Regional Rural Banks). In case of foreign bidders or in case of GTE, if Bank Guarantee is from a foreign bank branch situated outside India, the Bank Guarantee must be issued through any of the Scheduled Commercial Bank. In case BG is issued directly by a bank outside India, it should be executed on Letter Head of the Bank and should be advised and made payable through their Indian Branch/Corresponding Bank in India. The Issuing Bank should also state the name and designation of the next Higher Authority of the Officials who have issued the Bank Guarantee.

Bank guarantees submitted by the tenderers/ contractors as EMD/ performance securities need to be immediately verified from the issuing bank before acceptance. There may not be any need to get the Bank Guarantee vetted from legal/ finance authority if it is in the specified format. Guidelines for verification of BGs submitted by the bidders/ contractors against EMD/ performance security/ advance payments and for various other purposes are as follows:

- i) BG shall be as per the prescribed formats
- ii) The BG contains the name, designation and code number of the Bank officer(s) signing the guarantee(s);
- iii) The address and other details (including telephone no.) of the controlling officer of the bank are obtained from the branch of the bank issuing the BG (this should be included in all BGs);

The confirmation from the issuing branch of the bank is obtained in writing through registered post/ speed post/ courier /direct e-mail/ SFMS. The bank should be advised to confirm the issuance of the BGs specifically quoting the letter of Procurement Entity on the printed official letterhead of the bank indicating address and other details (including telephone nos.) of the bank and the name, designation and code number of the officer(s) confirming the issuance of the BG;

As far as possible organizations should follow e-verification of bank guarantees as per the procedure prescribed by Reserve Bank of India. Bank guarantee should be routed through SFMS platform.

Bank guarantees, either received in physical form or electronic form, should be verified for its genuineness following prescribed method for the same and the Organisations should do due diligence on genuineness of the Bank Guarantees before acceptance of the same.

## 4.14 Safe Custody and Monitoring of Securities
A suitable mechanism for safe custody and monitoring of EMDs and performance securities and other instruments should be evolved and implemented by procuring entity. Institutional arrangements shall be made for taking all necessary actions on time for extension or encashment or refund of EMDs and performance securities, as the case may be. Monitoring should also include a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments expiring in next three months, along with a review of the progress of the corresponding contracts. Extension of bank guarantees and other instruments, where warranted, should be sought immediately and implemented within their validity period. Bank Guarantee should never be handed over to the contractor for propose of extension of validity. Such a system of monitoring of securities and other instruments may be considered to be computerised with automatic alerts about lapse of validity etc. For release of BGs, the proposal shall be forwarded by the executing agency with its recommendations in accordance with the contract conditions.

question_text: If the buyer finds deficiencies in the original tender notice, what must they do before issuing a new one?
answer: If the buyer spots problems with the original tender notice, they must first get the cancellation approved, note the reasons in writing and let all bidders know about the decision. Before putting out a new notice, they need to go back and check that the original enquiry included all the required elements—standard conditions, suitable qualification criteria, technical and commercial terms, adequate publicity and enough time for bidders to respond. Any missing or deficient items should be corrected, and only after those fixes are made can a fresh tender be issued. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 130)
cot: When the buyer spots a deficiency in the original tender notice, the first thing that comes to mind is that the current process cannot continue as is; it must be stopped and a cancellation approved. I would need to secure that approval, record the reasons for the cancellation in writing, and promptly inform every bidder who took part so that everyone is aware of the decision to withdraw the notice. Only after that formal clearance is in place does it make sense to look back at how the notice was originally put together. I would examine whether the enquiry included all the required elements—standard conditions, suitable qualification criteria, the necessary technical and commercial terms, adequate publicity, and enough time for bidders to prepare their responses. If any of those items are missing or insufficient, they have to be corrected before a new notice can be drafted. Once the shortcomings are fixed and the enquiry meets all the formal requirements, the buyer can then go ahead and issue a fresh tender. This sequence ensures that the cancellation is properly authorized, the rationale is transparent, and the revised notice addresses the original deficiencies, allowing a fair and compliant re‑tendering process.

question_text: When there is no other estimated cost, what serves as the basis for judging the reasonableness of rates
answer: When no other estimated cost is available, the reasonableness of rates is judged by comparing the proposed price with the Last Purchase Price (LPP) – the price paid in the most recent successful contract for the same item. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 126)
cot:
I need to figure out what can be used to judge whether a rate is reasonable when there isn’t any other estimated cost to fall back on.  
First, the core of the problem is that a reasonableness judgment still has to be made, so we must find some observable price that can serve as a benchmark.  
Since the usual fallback—an internal estimate or a market‑based cost—is missing, the next logical step is to look at what the organization has actually paid for the same item in the recent past.  
The most recent successful purchase gives a concrete, verified figure that reflects the same specifications, taxes, delivery terms and other charges that would apply to the new contract.  
That figure is what the procurement guidance calls the Last Purchase Price, or LPP, and it becomes the reference point against which the proposed rate is compared.  
Therefore, when no other estimated cost is available, the basis for judging the reasonableness of rates is a comparison with the Last Purchase Price – the price paid in the latest successful contract for the same item.

question_text: What criteria does the TRC use to decide if a proposal is unsuitable
answer:
A proposal is deemed unsuitable by the TRC if it lacks earnest money (bid security), is unsigned or incomplete, does not fully and properly respond to the Terms of Reference, has a validity period shorter than that prescribed in the RfP, or fails to comply with important aspects described in the RfP.  

These conditions show the proposal is non‑responsive, so the TRC rejects it before moving on to the technical evaluation. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 50)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the TRC looks for when it labels a proposal unsuitable, so I start by thinking about the overall purpose of their initial review.  
The TRC reads every proposal first without giving scores; this pass is meant to catch any glaring problems like missing pieces, deviations from the terms of reference, or unclear sections that would need extra attention later.  
The specific red flags that cause a proposal to be tossed out right away include: if there’s no earnest money or bid security attached, if the document isn’t signed or is missing required sections, if it doesn’t fully and properly answer the terms of reference, or if its validity period falls short of what the request for proposals prescribes.  
Beyond those specific items, there’s a broader rule that the proposal must comply with the important aspects spelled out in the RfP; failing to meet any of those also marks it as unsuitable.  
All of these shortcomings make the proposal non‑responsive, which means the TRC doesn’t even move on to scoring the technical quality—it rejects the proposal at this responsiveness check.  
Putting it together, the criteria the TRC uses to deem a proposal unsuitable are exactly the lack of bid security, an unsigned or incomplete submission, an inadequate response to the terms of reference, a validity period shorter than required, and any failure to comply with the important aspects of the RfP. These conditions signal non‑responsiveness and lead to immediate rejection before technical evaluation.
chunk_content: Each member of the TRC should first read all proposals, without scoring them. This first review helps determine whether the proposals are free of significant omissions or deviations from the ToR or other key requirements of the RfP; it also allows TRC members to assess the overall clarity of the proposals and identify elements that will require special attention in the evaluation. Proposals without earnest money (bid security), unsigned and incomplete (i.e. when the required bid formats have not been submitted), not responding to the ToR fully and properly and those with lesser validity than that prescribed in the RfP will be summarily rejected as being non-responsive, before taking up the appraisal of the technical proposal for evaluation of quality. TRC shall evaluate each proposal on the basis of its responsiveness to the ToR. A proposal shall be considered unsuitable and shall be rejected at this stage if it fails to comply with important aspects as described in the RfP.

question_text: What is considered the consideration for the forfeiture of earnest money in case of default on revised rates
answer: - Eligibility as a valid tenderer is the consideration for the forfeiture of earnest money if the bidder defaults on the revised rate agreement. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 125)
cot:
First, I need to unpack what the question is asking: it wants to know what serves as the consideration—i.e., the value exchanged—when a bidder loses their earnest money for failing to honor a revised rate agreement.  

Next, I recall that in a negotiated tender process the bidder submits a revised offer after discussions, and that offer contains a specific clause about the consequences of not abiding by the agreed‑upon rates.  

Looking at that clause, it says that if the bidder defaults on the revised rate, they will forfeit the earnest money they deposited with the original tender, and it goes on to state that their eligibility to remain a valid tenderer is what is deemed to be the consideration for that forfeiture.  

This means the bidder receives something in return for risking the earnest money: the continued recognition as a legitimate tenderer whose offer can still be accepted under the revised terms.  

Putting it together, the consideration exchanged for the potential loss of earnest money is precisely the bidder’s retained status as a valid tenderer under the revised offer.  

Therefore, the answer is that eligibility as a valid tenderer is the consideration for the forfeiture of earnest money in case of default on the revised rates.

question_text: What records should be collected and kept as proof of publicity for tenders published on the website
answer:
- Collect and retain records of all tenders published on the procuring entity's website as proof of publicity. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 94)  
- Document the complete details of the dates on which each advertisement actually appeared on the website. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 94)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is asking: it wants to know which specific records must be gathered and preserved to demonstrate that a tender was properly publicized when it was posted on the procuring entity’s website.  

Next, I consider what would constitute valid proof of publicity in an online context. Simply stating that a tender was uploaded isn’t enough; there has to be tangible evidence showing that the notice was actually visible on the site at a certain time.  

Thinking about how such evidence is typically handled, the most straightforward approach is to keep a copy of the webpage or a screenshot that captures the tender notice as it appeared, along with any system logs that record the posting event. These items together serve as a record that the tender was indeed published.  

Then I reflect on what additional detail would strengthen that proof. If the record only shows that the notice existed at some point, it doesn’t confirm the exact timing of its appearance. Therefore, noting the precise dates on which each advertisement was displayed on the website becomes essential, as it ties the publicity to a specific timeframe and allows verification against procurement timelines.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the required proof consists of retaining the actual records of each tender notice posted on the website and meticulously documenting the dates on which those notices appeared. This directly satisfies the need for demonstrable publicity of tenders published online.

question_text: Which legal entities are eligible to participate in tenders as per the eligibility criteria
answer:
- Private legal entities (e.g., privately incorporated companies)  
- Government‑owned legal entities (e.g., state‑owned enterprises)  
- Joint ventures or limited liability partnerships, when the tender expressly permits them, with all partners jointly and severally liable  
- Must hold valid registration with the Employees Provident Fund Organization under the EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, where applicable  
- Excludes firms that have been engaged by the procuring entity for consultancy services on the same project (unless continuing the same consultancy work) and firms deemed non‑performing by the Procuring Entity  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 55)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know which kinds of legal entities are allowed to take part in a tender according to the eligibility rules set out in the procurement manual.  

The eligibility criteria make it clear that the bidder must be a legal entity, and they specifically distinguish between private‑owned and government‑owned forms. So right away I can note that both privately incorporated companies and state‑owned enterprises satisfy the basic entity requirement.  

Next, the manual adds a condition about statutory registration: wherever the Employees Provident Fund and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952 applies, the bidder must hold a valid registration with the EPF Organization. This is not a separate category of entity but a prerequisite that any private or government‑owned bidder must meet if the act is relevant to their operations.  

Then there is a provision for collaborative structures. The rules state that when a tender expressly allows Joint Ventures or Limited Liability Partnerships, all partners in such arrangements are jointly and severally liable for the work. This means that JVs and LLPs are eligible, but only when the tender document itself permits them; they are not automatically eligible for every tender.  

After that, the manual lists two important exclusions. First, a firm that has been hired by the procuring entity to provide consultancy services for the same project cannot later bid for goods or works on that project, unless the bidding is merely a continuation of the very consultancy work they were already doing. Second, any firm that the procuring entity has officially determined to be non‑performing is barred from bidding during the period of that determination.  

Putting these pieces together, the eligible participants are: private legal entities, government‑owned legal entities, and, when the tender specifically allows them, joint ventures or LLPs with joint and several liability—provided they hold the required EPF registration where applicable—and they are not excluded by the consultancy or non‑performance rules. This matches the list of eligible entities given in the answer.

### 4.4.1 (B) Minimum Response in Open/Limited Tenders:
1. **"Minimum Response"** shall be considered as under, and no separate approval note to be processed for un-priced bid opening:
  - i. Where the enquiry is issued on open tender basis, the minimum response shall be 03 (three) bids.
  - ii. Where the enquiry is issued on limited tender basis, the minimum response shall be 03 (three) bids. Wherever limited tender is issued to two parties only, minimum response shall be two.
2. Respective purchase officer shall suitably extend the bid due date in either of the following two situations:
  - i) Where Minimum response is not obtained, Purchase officer can give first extension of up to one week but subsequent extensions shall require Commercial HOD's consent. Indentor and HOD of user dept. is to be notified about such extensions.
  - ii) Where Minimum response is obtained but one or more of the vendors have requested for extension by the due date. In such a cases, user dept HOD's prior consent shall be obtained.
3. Normally two extensions shall be given to any enquiry. In case, even after two bid due date extension(s), minimum response is not obtained, whatever bids are received, may be opened. In the case of no response, refloating may be done only in consultation with user department.
4. Where extension is required for any reason(s) beyond two extensions, Commercial HOD's prior consent shall be obtained. Reason for such extensions should be recorded.

## 4.5 Eligibility and Qualifications of Bidders


### 4.5.1 Eligibility of Bidders
- i) All eligible bidders meeting the eligibility criteria as defined in ITB can participate in the

tender. The bidder should be a private or government-owned legal entity.

- ii) Bidder should have valid registration with Employees Provident Fund organization under 'EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952', wherever applicable.
- iii) Tenders where Joint Ventures / LLPs (limited liability partnerships) are allowed, all the partners shall be jointly and severally liable (as applicable) for the successful completion of the work.
- iv) A firm that has been engaged by the procuring entity to provide consultancy services for the preparation or implementation of a project, and any of its affiliates (associates, subsidiary, JV partner), shall not be eligible for subsequently providing goods or works (other than a continuation of the firm's earlier consultancy services) for the same project.

question_text: To which type of procurement is the manual applicable as stated in Section 1.3.1
answer:
The manual is applicable to the procurement of **Works**, which encompasses three categories as defined in Sections 1.3.1 and 1.3.2:

- **Original Works** – new constructions, site preparation, additions and alterations to existing structures, and special repairs to newly purchased or previously abandoned buildings or structures that involve remodelling or replacement.  
- **Minor Works** – works that add capital value to existing assets without creating new assets.  
- **Repair Works** – undertakings to maintain buildings and fixtures that do not add to asset value; these are further divided into **Annual repairs** (routine, yearly operation and maintenance) and **Special repairs** (major repairs performed as required).  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 11)
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question is really after: it wants to know which kind of procurement the manual covers, as explicitly stated in section 1.3.1.  
My first step is to locate that section in the material and see what it says about applicability. I notice the heading “1.3.1 Works” and the bold sentence that follows, which tells me the manual is meant for the procurement of ‘Works’ as defined in the procurement glossary.  
Next, I consider what “Works” actually entails in this context. The very next subsection, 1.3.2, dives into the classification of works, breaking it down into three main groups: Original Works, Minor Works, and Repair Works. It also explains that Repair Works can be split further into annual and special repairs.  
Seeing this, I realize that the manual’s scope isn’t just a vague reference to works; it is specifically tied to those three categories and their sub‑types.  
Putting it together, I conclude that the manual applies to procurement of Works, encompassing Original Works, Minor Works, and Repair Works (with annual and special repairs as the two repair sub‑categories). This matches the answer given.

## 1.2 Amendments and Revision of this Manual
The Commercial Function shall be the nodal agency for this Manual. For any revision relating to this manual, necessary action will be initiated by Commercial Department, and approval of Committee of Functional Directors shall be obtained for adoption of the same. Revision of certain clause (if specifically mentioned, like Para 3.2.5, 4.9.1A, 6.5.2 (v), 6.10.2 (i), 7.6 (G) in the manual for works) may require approval from the Board of Directors.

Any revision of the current Govt. policies such as MSE order 2012, PP-LC (MII) policy etc. released by the Govt./MoPNG from time to time, or introduction of new policy by the Govt./MoPNG and applicable for NRL may be implemented suitably through internal circular issued by functional head of Commercial Department. No separate approval from higher authority is required in case the guidelines are adopted without any customization for NRL.

Such revisions/introductions shall be issued in the form of circulars as and when applicable, and treated as part of this manual. However, comprehensive review and revision of the procurement manuals should be made periodically, but not later than 03 years.

## 1.3 Applicability of this Manual
1.3.1 **Works:** This manual is applicable to procurement of ‘Works’ as defined in “Procurement Glossary”

1.3.2 **Classification of Works:** The civil works are classified into three categories: (a) Original Works (b) Minor Works and (c) Repairs Works. "Original works" means all new constructions, site preparation, additions and alterations to existing works. It also includes special repairs to newly purchased or previously abandoned buildings or structures, including remodelling or replacement. "Minor works" mean works which add capital value to existing assets but do not create new assets. "Repair works" means works undertaken to maintain building and fixtures. Expenditure on Repair Work does not add to the value of the asset and only restores the functionality of the asset. Repair Work can be further categorized as (i) Annual repairs covering routine and yearly operation and maintenance work on buildings and services (ii) Special repairs, which are undertaken as and when required, covering major repairs to existing buildings or services. Some types of the Special repairs may qualify to be categorised as 'Original Work' as mentioned earlier.

The Interpretation or any conflicts between various documents shall be governed by the following order of precedence:-

- 1) Manual for procurement of Goods, Works or Consultancy & Other Services, as applicable.
- 2) Special Conditions of Contract (SCC) and other terms and conditions of the tender.
- 3) General Purchase Conditions (GPC) / General Conditions of Contracts (GCC).

## 1.4 Basic Aims of Procurement - Five R's of Procurement
In every procurement, public or private, the basic aim is to achieve just the right balance between costs and requirements concerning five parameters called the five R's of procurement. The entire process of procurement (from the time that need for an item, facility or services is identified till the need is satisfied) is designed to achieve following basic aims. Although couched in jargon of procurement of Goods, it's equally applicable to procurement of Works. The term 'Right' is used here in the sense of being optimal:

- i) Right quality;
- ii) Right quantity;
- iii) Right price;
- iv) Right time and place; and
- v) Right source.

*(For more details on basic aims of procurement, please refer to Chapter 1 of the Manual for Procurement of Goods)*

question_text: What is the consequence if documents remain unauthenticated till the given timeline for tenders above Rs.5 Crore?
answer: If the documents submitted by the L1 (successful) bidder for a tender valued at Rs.5 Crore or more are not authenticated within the stipulated time, NRL will first issue a final reminder to the issuing authority. Should authentication still not be obtained, the bidder’s bid will be rejected and the tender will be cancelled and refloated, with no further approval required for this action (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 136).
cot:
I start by focusing on the core of the question: what happens when the required documents are not authenticated within the set deadline for tenders that exceed Rs. 5 Crore.

First, I note that the NRL and Government of India procurement manuals treat tenders of this value differently from smaller ones; for contracts of Rs. 5 Crore or more, the L1 (successful) bidder’s credential documents must be verified directly with the issuing authority.

Next, I consider what the procedure says when that verification does not happen in time. The manuals state that if the documents remain unauthenticated till the given timeline, NRL reserves the right to reject the bid.

Then I trace the actual steps NRL follows before reaching that rejection. It first issues a final reminder to the issuing authority, giving them one more chance to provide the authentication.

If the reminder does not yield a response, the bidder’s submission is deemed insufficient and the L1 bidder’s bid is rejected.

After the rejection, the tender cannot proceed with that bidder, so the tender is cancelled and re‑floated; importantly, the cancellation and re‑float can be done without needing any further approvals.

Putting these pieces together, the consequence of missing the authentication deadline is that NRL will send a final reminder, and if authentication still fails, the bidder’s bid will be rejected, the tender will be cancelled and re‑issued, and no additional approval is required for that action.

question_text: Why is it important for senior management to understand the definition of a bidder when overseeing procurement
answer:
Understanding who qualifies as a bidder is essential for senior management to safeguard procurement integrity and drive corporate objectives.  

- It clarifies eligibility, ensuring that only eligible persons, firms, companies, or consortia may participate, which blocks unauthorized entries.  
- It supports compliance by enabling verification that invitations, evaluations, and award decisions follow the procuring entity’s rules, thereby reducing legal and financial exposure.  
- It enhances transparency, as clear bidder criteria promote fair competition and help secure value‑for‑money outcomes.  
- It informs risk management, allowing leaders to assess potential conflicts of interest and oversee bid‑security requirements effectively.  
- It aligns procurement with strategic objectives, guiding the organization toward suppliers that meet established standards and local‑content policies.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 10)
cot:
First, I consider what senior management actually needs to guard when they oversee a procurement process: they must be sure that only the right parties are allowed to compete, because any slip‑up here can undermine the whole effort.  

Looking at the definition of a bidder, it tells me that a bidder is any eligible person, firm, company—or even a consortium—that is taking part in the procurement initiated by the procuring entity. The key words are “eligible” and “participating in a procurement process.”  

If management does not grasp who qualifies as eligible, they cannot effectively screen out those who should not be invited. Allowing an ineligible bidder to slip in would open the door to non‑compliant offers, potential fraud, or challenges later on, which directly threatens procurement integrity.  

With a clear picture of the bidder definition, management can check that the invitation to bid, the evaluation criteria, and the final award decision all respect the eligibility rules set out by the organization. This verification step is what keeps the process compliant with internal policies and external regulations, thereby limiting legal and financial exposure.  

Beyond compliance, knowing exactly who can be a bidder promotes transparency. When the criteria for eligibility are explicit and understood, all potential suppliers see a level playing field, which encourages fair competition and helps the organization secure the best value for its money.  

This transparency also feeds into risk management. By being able to verify that each bidder meets the eligibility standards, senior leaders can more easily spot conflicts of interest, assess the adequacy of bid‑security instruments, and ensure that any consortium structures are properly accounted for.  

Finally, when the bidder definition is linked to broader strategic goals—such as local‑content preferences or supplier‑development initiatives—management can steer procurement toward partners that truly support the organization’s long‑term objectives, turning a routine oversight task into a lever for corporate strategy.  

Putting these pieces together, it becomes clear that understanding who counts as a bidder is not just a technical detail; it is the foundation for safeguarding integrity, ensuring compliance, fostering transparency, managing risk, and aligning procurement with the organization’s strategic aims.

question_text: In the absence of an explicit statement about alternative offers, what is the default position according to the SOP?
answer: The tender document must expressly state that alternative offers, makes, or models will be considered; in the absence of such an explicit statement, alternative offers are not permitted. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 121)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: when the standard operating procedure does not say anything about allowing alternative offers, what position does it take by default?  

Next, I recall the part of the SOP that deals with technical evaluation, where it explains how the tender document should treat alternative offers, makes, or models. It points out that the document must make a clear statement about whether such alternatives will be considered.  

Then I notice the specific qualifier that follows: if there is no express statement to that effect, the alternatives are not to be allowed. This wording makes it clear that silence on the matter is interpreted as a prohibition rather than a permission.  

I check that this interpretation fits with the overall principle that the evaluation must be based only on what is explicitly included in the tender document, and any condition not stated should not form the basis of the assessment.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the default position, in the absence of an explicit provision, is that alternative offers, makes, or models are not permitted; the tender document must expressly state that they will be considered for them to be allowed. This matches the given answer.

question_text: What actions must the Procuring Entity undertake concerning land acquisition and statutory clearances before contract award, as described in 6.1.3
answer: The Procuring Entity must initiate land acquisition well in advance of contract award and aim to complete it entirely, or at least substantially, before the award is made (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 89). Concurrently, it must obtain all requisite statutory approvals, permissions, clearances, and certificates from the relevant local bodies and authorities—including district authorities, municipal corporations, panchayati raj institutions, town planning boards, electricity boards/fire departments, state and central pollution control boards, state and central environmental authorities, and forest and wildlife authorities—to ensure that no impediment remains to the progress of the work (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 89). Furthermore, the Entity is required to fulfill all or most of these conditions precedent prior to issuing the Letter of Award, as any delay in doing so may trigger delay claims from the contractor and lead to time and cost overruns (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 89). By aligning the timing of land acquisition with the securing of statutory clearances, the Procuring Entity satisfies the precondition requirements set out in the NRL manual and mitigates the risk of contractual disputes. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 89)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the Procuring Entity is responsible for before a contract is awarded, focusing on land acquisition and the necessary clearances.  
The core idea is that certain conditions precedent must be satisfied—particularly those related to securing the land and obtaining all required permissions—before the contract can move forward.  
The Procuring Entity should start the land acquisition process well in advance, with the goal of having it either fully finished or at least substantially completed by the time the contract is awarded.  
At the same time, the Entity must actively pursue all statutory approvals, permissions, clearances, and certificates from the relevant local and central authorities—such as district bodies, municipal corporations, panchayati raj institutions, town planning boards, electricity or fire departments, pollution control boards, environmental agencies, and forest or wildlife offices—to ensure nothing will impede the work once it begins.  
Because any delay in meeting these conditions can lead to delay claims from the contractor and cause time and cost overruns, the Entity is expected to fulfill most, if not all, of these prerequisites before issuing the Letter of Award.  
By aligning the timing of land acquisition with the acquisition of statutory clearances, the Procuring Entity satisfies the precondition requirements, thereby minimizing the risk of contractual disputes and keeping the project on schedule.

question_text: To which Customs officer should I send my refund application
answer: You should send your refund application (in duplicate) to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 229)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know where to send a refund application for customs duties.  

Next, I recall that refunds of excess duty or interest are covered under the customs law, and the procedure for making such a claim is specified in the regulations.  

Looking at the details about refunds, I see that any person seeking a refund must submit an application in duplicate, using the prescribed form.  

The regulations further state that this duplicate application should be directed to the officer who has jurisdiction over the matter—specifically, the Deputy or Assistant Commissioner of Customs responsible for that area.  

Putting these points together, the logical destination for the refund application is the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs, and it must be submitted in duplicate as required.  

Therefore, the answer is that the refund application (in duplicate) should be sent to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs.

#### 1. Introduction:
1.1 A number of ports, airports, Inland Container Depots (ICD), Container Freight Stations (CFS) having Customs clearance facilities have been developed in the country to reduce congestion at the gateway ports/airports and to allow importers and exporters to take Customs clearance of imported and export goods at their door steps. The objectives of bringing the Customs facility to door step of importing community and decongesting the gateway ports/ airports requires the movement of imported cargo or export cargo between a port/airport and other ports/airports, ICDs/CFSs in India or a port / airport abroad.

1.2 As per the Customs Act, 1962 duty becomes payable immediately after imported goods are landed at a port or airport. To avoid payment of duty at the port of landing in cases where goods are to be carried to another port / airport or ICD/CFS or to a port / airport abroad, the Customs Act, 1962 provides a facility of transshipment of cargo without payment of duty. The goods can be transhipped from one port / airport to another port / airport / ICD / CFS either by vessel, air, rail or road or by combination of more than one such mode of transport.

## 2. Transshipment of imported containerized cargo from gateway port to another port/ ICD / CFS in India:
2.1 The transshipment procedure of imported cargo is governed by Section 54 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Goods Imported (Conditions of Transshipment) Regulations, 1995 as well as relevant Board's circulars and instructions.

2.2 Transshipment Permit is the permission granted by the Customs, at the port / airport of unloading of imported goods, to shipping agents for carriage of goods to another port / airport / ICD / CFS in India. The shipping agent submits an application along-with transshipment forms (5 copies), sub-manifest and a copy of IGM to the Customs. The Customs scrutinizes the details furnished by the shipping agents in the application for transshipment. In case, the documents are in order and there is no alert notice against the shipping agent, permission for transshipment is granted. For further insight into this aspect if situation demands for such an arrangement, relevant provisions of rules and procedures as relevant may be reviewed before opting the transshipment option.

## Customs Refunds


### 1. Introduction:
1.1 On import or export of goods, at times duty may be paid in excess of what was actually leviable. Such excess payment may be due to lack of information on the part of importer/exporter or non-submission of documents required for claim of lower value or rate of duty. Sometimes, such excess payment of duty may be due to shortage/short landing, pilferage of goods or even incorrect assessment of duty by Customs. In such cases, refund of excess amount of duty paid can be claimed by the importer or exporter. If any excess interest has been paid by the importer/exporter on the amount of duty paid in excess, its refund can also be claimed.

### 2. Legal provisions:
2.1 Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962 deals with the refund of duty and interest. As provided therein, refund of duty and interest can be claimed either by a person who has paid the duty in pursuance to an order of assessment or a person who has borne the duty.

2.2 Any person claiming refund of any duty or interest has to make an application in duplicate in the form as prescribed in the Customs Refund Application (Form) Regulations, 1995, to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs.

question_text: Under what circumstances might a fresh publication of the tender be required after an amendment
answer:
Fresh publication of a tender after an amendment is warranted when the change is substantive or when bidders lack sufficient time to prepare revised bids.  

- The amendment significantly alters the technical, commercial, or contractual requirements of the original tender.  
- The remaining period before the original bid‑submission deadline is too short for tenderers to respond adequately, necessitating an extension of the submission date and associated timelines (tender validity, EMD/bid security, etc.).  

In these situations, the procurement process must re‑issue the tender notice using the same procedure as the original publication to ensure transparency, fair competition, and continued alignment with corporate value‑for‑money objectives. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 102)
cot:
First, I think about why a tender that has already been issued might need to be revisited after an amendment. The central concern is whether the change affects the bidders’ ability to prepare a competitive and compliant bid on equal footing with others.  

Then, I identify the two situations that would make such a revisit necessary. One is when the amendment alters the technical, commercial or contractual requirements in a significant way, so that the original scope no longer reflects what is actually being sought. The other is when the time left before the original bid‑submission deadline is too short for tenderers to absorb the change, prepare a revised bid and still meet the deadline.  

Next, I reason through each situation. If the amendment is substantive, bidders would have to redesign their solutions, adjust pricing or reconsider compliance, which would put those who acted on the original documents at a disadvantage unless the tender is re‑issued with the updated requirements. If the amendment leaves little time, even a minor change could be unfair because bidders simply cannot produce a proper revised bid in the remaining period; merely extending the deadline does not correct the fact that the original notice still outlines an outdated schedule and possibly outdated requirements.  

Further, I consider what the procurement process must do to restore fairness. In both cases the appropriate remedy is to issue a fresh tender notice that incorporates the amended requirements and the new submission timeline, using the same publication procedure that was used for the original tender. This resets the clock, updates all related timelines (tender validity, EMD/bid security, etc.), and gives every potential bidder an equal opportunity to respond to the fully revised solicitation.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: a fresh publication of the tender after an amendment is required when the amendment either substantively changes the scope of the procurement or when the remaining time for bidders to respond is insufficient, because in either scenario re‑issuing the tender notice ensures transparency, equal treatment and the integrity of the competitive process.

question_text: Does the guarantee allow the beneficiary to postpone exercising any powers or rights without affecting the guarantee
answer:
Step‑by‑Step Operational Checklist for Verifying Postponement Rights under the Bank Guarantee for Security Deposit  

1. Locate Clause 2 of the guarantee format.  
2. Read the clause: “You will have the full liberty without reference to us and without affecting this guarantee postpone for any time or from time to time the exercise of any of the powers and rights conferred on you under the contract …”  
3. Confirm that the wording grants the beneficiary full liberty to postpone.  
4. Verify that the clause explicitly states that such postponement does **not** affect the guarantee.  
5. Note that the postponement may be for any duration and may be exercised repeatedly.  
6. Record that the beneficiary may also forbear from enforcing any powers or rights without impacting the guarantee.  
7. Conclude that, per the guarantee, the beneficiary is allowed to postpone exercising any powers or rights without affecting the guarantee.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 142)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: whether the beneficiary can delay using any of its rights under the guarantee without causing the guarantee to lapse or be affected. To answer that, I need to see if the guarantee itself contains a provision that expressly permits such postponement and states that it does not affect the guarantee’s validity.  

Next, I recall the relevant provision in the guarantee format. Clause 2 of the guarantee format deals with the beneficiary’s liberty to act. It states that the beneficiary will have the full liberty, without reference to the guarantor and without affecting this guarantee, to postpone for any time or from time to time the exercise of any powers and rights conferred under the contract, and also to forbear from enforcing those powers or rights.  

From this wording I confirm that the guarantee explicitly grants the beneficiary the freedom to postpone. The phrase “without affecting this guarantee” directly answers the concern about impact. Moreover, the clause allows postponement for any duration and permits it to be exercised repeatedly, as indicated by “for any time or from time to time”.  

I also note that the same clause mentions the beneficiary may forbear from enforcing any powers or rights, which is another form of postponement, and again stresses that this does not affect the guarantee.  

Putting these observations together, I conclude that the guarantee does indeed allow the beneficiary to postpone exercising any powers or rights without affecting the guarantee, and the operational steps to verify this are to locate clause 2, read its wording, confirm the grant of liberty, verify the non‑affecting statement, note the unlimited and repeatable nature of the postponement, recognize the forbearance option, and then affirm the conclusion.

question_text: When is direct negotiation justified because the individual is the only qualified consultant
answer:
**A:** Direct negotiation is justified when the individual is the only consultant or service provider qualified for the assignment.  
**Rationale:** This situation is listed as an exceptional case for using direct negotiation in section 7.2.2(iv) of the procurement manual, which permits direct negotiation — with proper justification — when the individual is the sole qualified provider for the task (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 58).
cot:
I’m trying to figure out under what circumstances direct negotiation can be used when the individual consultant is the only one who qualifies for the assignment.  
First, I note that the standard approach for hiring individual consultants is to compare qualifications through a competitive process, because that ensures fairness and transparency.  
However, the guidelines also recognize that there are situations where a full competition would be impractical or unnecessary, and they carve out a few exceptional cases for direct negotiation.  
Looking at those exceptions, one is when the work is a straightforward continuation of something the consultant has already done successfully under a competitive selection.  
Another is when an emergency—like a natural disaster—requires immediate action and there isn’t time for a lengthy procurement cycle.  
The third exception is specifically about the consultant’s uniqueness: if after searching the market it turns out that only this particular individual possesses the required experience, qualifications, or specialized knowledge, then there is effectively no alternative to consider.  
In that scenario, forcing a competitive process would be meaningless because no other candidate could meet the requirements, and it would only add delay and cost.  
Therefore, the justification for direct negotiation hinges on the condition that the individual is the sole qualified provider for the task.  
Putting it all together, the answer is that direct negotiation is justified precisely when the individual is the only consultant or service provider qualified for the assignment.

## 7.2 Selection of Individual consultants/ service providers
7.2.1 Individual consultants/ service providers are normally employed on assignments for which

- i) Teams of personnel is not required;
- ii) No additional outside professional support is required, and
- iii) The experience and qualifications of the individual are the paramount requirement.

7.2.2 The procedures for selecting individual consultants/ service providers are similar to, but much simpler than, those for selecting teams of consultants/ service providers from a firm. Process of selection of Individual consultants/ service providers entails:

- i) Preparing a Consultancy and other services package including the ToR, time frame, number of person-months, budget, Tendering / EoI Short-listing criteria and getting it approved by the CA;
- ii) **Notification:** Notification in such case should be given on Central Public Procurement

Portal (CPMP) at [www.eprocure.gov.in](http://www.eprocure.gov.in) and on Government E- Market (GeM). An organisation having its own website should also publish all its advertised tender enquiries on the website. The notification for invitation of tenders should give the complete web address from where the bidding documents can be downloaded.

- iii) **Method of Selection:** They shall be selected through comparison of qualifications of the candidates who have expressed interest in the assignment or have been approached directly by the Procuring Entity. Candidates who are already employed with the Procuring Entity shall meet all relevant qualifications and shall be fully capable of carrying out the assignment. Capability is judged on the basis of academic background, experience, and, as appropriate, knowledge of the local conditions, such as local language, culture, administrative system, and government organisation.
- iv) **Direct Negotiation:** Individual consultants/ service providers may be selected on a direct negotiation basis with due justification in exceptional cases such as: (a) tasks that are a continuation of previous work that the consultant/ service provider has carried out and for which the consultant/ service provider was selected competitively; (b) emergency situations resulting from natural disasters; and (c) when the individual is the only consultant/ service provider qualified for the assignment. Individual consultants/ service providers may be (among others) independent consultants/ service providers; consultants/ service providers recruited from firms; or consultants/ service providers recruited from academic, government, or international agencies.
- v) **Staff or Associates of Consultancy/ service provider Firms:** If the candidate is permanent staff or associates of a Consultancy firm the conflict of interest provisions described in these guidelines shall apply to the parent firm.

## 7.3 Selection of Specialized Agencies/ Institutions

7.3.2 In some cases, the agency or institution has access to special expertise or special backup and support facilities that make it worthwhile considering recruitment on an SSS basis. In such cases, there must be full justification that the use of SSS is in the best interests of Procuring Entity.

question_text: What is the purpose of the first (additional) envelope in a 1S3E bidding process?
answer: - The first (additional) envelope contains the post‑qualification documents (EMD and eligibility papers) and is opened first to evaluate bidders against a fail‑pass qualification criterion; only those who pass this post‑qualification proceed to have their techno‑commercial and financial envelopes assessed. (Procurement of Works Manual, p.31)
cot:
First, I consider what distinguishes a 1S3E process from the more familiar two‑envelope approach: it adds a third envelope that is opened before the usual techno‑commercial and financial packets.  
Next, I think about why an additional opening step would be useful—there must be a way to filter out unsuitable bidders early, without exposing their price or detailed technical proposals.  
That leads me to ask what kind of information can support a simple pass‑or‑fail test; it would need to be limited to eligibility credentials, earnest money deposits, and similar basic documents that do not reveal pricing or performance specifics.  
So the extra envelope must hold precisely those post‑qualification items: the EMD and eligibility paperwork, which can be checked against a predefined fail‑pass criterion.  
When the bid opening date arrives, only this first envelope is unsealed; evaluators apply the qualification test, and bidders who satisfy it are deemed responsive and move forward, while those who do not are eliminated and their remaining envelopes stay closed.  
Finally, this sequence shows that the purpose of the first (additional) envelope in a 1S3E system is to contain the post‑qualification documents and to be opened first so that only qualified bidders proceed to have their techno‑commercial and financial bids evaluated.
