## 3.1 Types of Contracts
There are different basis for linking payments to the performance of services (called types of contracts). Bids are called and evaluated based on the type of contract. The choice of the type of contract should be based on Value-for-Money (VfM) with due regard to the nature of assignment. Adoption of an inappropriate type of contract could lead to a situation of lack of competition, contractual disputes and non-performance/failure of the contract.

Each type of contract is described briefly in subsequent paras, and criteria are suggested for their adoption. Mostly used types of contracts are:

- i) Lump sum (Firm Fixed Price) contract;
- ii) Time based (Retainer-ship) contracts;
- iii) Percentage (Success Fee) contract;
- iv) Indefinite delivery contract.

*However, in case of Procurement/ Outsourcing of other (non-consulting) Services depending on the nature of services, can be either Lump-sum contracts, Time-based (Retainer-ship) contracts, or unit (item/ service) rate (say Taxi Service on per Km basis) based contract (as in case of Goods and Works) - or a mix of these. In certain uncertain but regularly needed services, indefinite delivery contracts, based on time or unit (item/ service) rates may be appropriate. Other types of contracts are not usual in procurement of other services.*

## 3.2 Lump Sum (Firm Fixed Price) Contract
3.2.1 The lump sum (firm fixed price) contract is the preferred form of contract and under normal circumstances; the Procuring Entity shall use this form of contract. Consultant's proposal is deemed to include all prices - no arithmetical correction or price adjustments are allowed during evaluation. Lump sum consultancy contracts are easy to administer because there is fixed price for a fixed scope and payments are linked to clearly specified outputs/ milestones/ deliverables such as reports, documents, drawings, bills of quantities, software programs and so on. In view of Risks mentioned below this type of contracts are widely used for simple planning and feasibility studies, environmental studies, detailed design of standard or common structures, preparation of data processing systems, and so forth.

Lump sum service contracts should be used mainly for assignments in which the quality, scope and the timing of the required output of the consultants/ service providers are clearly defined. The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables and certificate for its acceptability may be recorded. Payment should be made only against certificate of acceptance of deliverables.

While the payments are not linked to time, the assignment should be monitored per month to ensure that the output per month is in line with planned and estimated time-line.

## 3.3 Time-Based Contract
3.3.1 In Time-based contracts payments are based on agreed hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly rates for staff (who in consultancy contracts are normally named, but not so in other services) and on reimbursable items using actual expenses and/or agreed unit prices. This type of contract is appropriate when Lump sum contract is not feasible due to difficulties in defining the scope and the length of services, either because the inputs required for attaining the objectives of the assignment is difficult to assess or because the services are tied up to activities by others for which the completion period may vary.

This type of contract is widely used for complex studies, supervision of construction, advisory services, and most training assignments etc.

The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables. Payments should be released only against certification by EIC.

Contracts need to be closely monitored and administered by the EIC to ensure that the progress of assignment is commensurate with the time spent and that the resources for which payment is claimed have actually efficiently and productively been deployed on the assignment during the period.

question_text: Within how many days from the date of the Sale Order/Acceptance Letter must the successful buyer deposit the offered price including taxes and duties in advance
answer: The successful buyer must deposit the offered price including taxes and duties in advance within 15 days from the date of the Sale Order/Acceptance Letter. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 172)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: it wants the exact number of days a successful buyer has to pay the full offered price—taxes and duties included—after receiving the Sale Order or Acceptance Letter.  

Next, I scan the procedural rules for any mention of payment deadlines tied to that specific document. The section that deals with what happens if a buyer fails to pay stands out, because it contrasts two time frames: one for sending a reminder and another for the offer to lapse.  

Within that section, I see a clause that explicitly ties the deposit of the offered price, taxes and duties included, to the date of the “Sale Order / Acceptance Letter.” It says that if the buyer does not make that advance deposit within a certain number of days, a reminder is issued; only after a longer period does the offer become invalid.  

The first time frame mentioned is 15 days from the date of the Sale Order/Acceptance Letter—this is the point at which the buyer is expected to have deposited the amount to avoid a reminder. The second, longer period of 30 days is the ultimate cutoff before the offer is cancelled.  

Since the question asks for the deadline by which the buyer must deposit the amount in advance, the relevant benchmark is the earlier limit, i.e., the 15‑day window, because fulfilling the obligation within that period satisfies the requirement and prevents the reminder process from being triggered.  

Putting it together, the successful buyer must deposit the offered price, including all taxes and duties, in advance within 15 days from the date of the Sale Order/Acceptance Letter. This matches the answer that the deposit is due within 15 days.

question_text: Can a force majeure claim be made after the fact (ex‑post facto) according to the clause
answer: - Force majeure notices must be given promptly; ex‑post facto claims are not permitted (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 91).
cot:
I need to figure out whether the contract lets a party invoke force majeure after the event has already happened. First, I’ll parse what the question is really asking: it’s about the timing of a force majeure notice—can it be given retrospectively, or must it be contemporaneous with the occurrence? 

Next, I’ll look for the specific language that governs force majeure in the clause. The provision says that when a force majeure event occurs, the affected party must give notice of the event as soon as possible. It also explicitly states that the force majeure cannot be claimed ex‑post facto. 

From the “as soon as possible” requirement, I infer that the notice must be tied closely to the moment the event arises; delaying notice defeats the purpose of the clause, which is to suspend obligations only while the event is actually preventing performance. 

The explicit ban on ex‑post facto claims reinforces that interpretation: even if a party later realizes that an event qualified as force majeure, they cannot retroactively invoke it to excuse past non‑performance. The clause is designed to give the other party timely information so they can assess impacts, mitigate losses, or arrange alternatives. 

Putting those points together, the logic is clear: the contract demands prompt notice and disallows any claim made after the fact, meaning a force majeure assertion must be made contemporaneously with the event, not later. 

Therefore, the answer is that a force majeure claim cannot be made ex‑post facto; notices must be given promptly, and retrospective claims are not permitted.

### 6.4.1 Time At Large
When the Procuring Entity does not explicitly express and reserve its rights and remedies under the contract for delays in execution, it legally forfeits his right to such remedies. Under such circumstances Time is said to become at large and the contractor gets freed from his obligation to complete within the specified time. To avoid such a situation, before the expiry of originally stipulated date of completion, the Procuring Entity should extend the currency of the contract/agreement and set a new time limit for completion and make the extended time as essence of the contract, stipulating that this is being done without prejudice to his right to recover damages and other remedies as per the contract.

### 6.4.2 Force Majeure (FM) Clause
A Force Majeure (FM) means extraordinary events or circumstance beyond human control such as an event described as an act of God (like a natural calamity) or events such as a war, strike, riots, rebellion or sabotage, lockouts, crimes, hostility, acts of public enemy, civil commotion, fires, explosions, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, quarantine restrictions and freight embargoes (but not including negligence or wrong-doing, predictable/seasonal rain and any other events specifically excluded in the clause). An FM clause in the contract frees both parties from contractual liability or obligation when prevented by such events from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. An FM clause does not excuse a party's non-performance entirely, but only suspends it for the duration of the FM. The firm has to give notice of FM as soon as possible and it cannot be claimed ex-post facto. There may be a FM situation affecting the purchase organisation only. question_text: Why are large score differences caused by poor understanding of the Terms of Reference difficult to reconcile
answer:
- Evaluators may differ widely in how they define, understand, or interpret the same criterion and the Terms of Reference, reflecting their subjective experience. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 47)  
- Lack of common definitions allows individual generosity or severity in judgment to magnify score disparities, hindering alignment. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 47)  
- Large score gaps caused by inadequate ToR comprehension or improper use of evaluation criteria become difficult to reconcile and explain. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 47)
cot:
First, I think about what makes it hard to bring scores back into alignment when they diverge widely. The core issue lies in how evaluators interpret the Terms of Reference and the evaluation criteria—if everyone has a different mental picture of what a requirement means, their scores will naturally spread out.  

Next, I consider the conditions that allow those differing interpretations to turn into big gaps. When there is no shared, predefined definition for each criterion, each evaluator’s personal tendency to be generous or severe gets unchecked. One person’s lenient reading can award high marks while another’s strict reading gives low marks, and without a common benchmark those tendencies amplify rather than cancel out.  

Then, I follow the logic of what happens once those amplified differences appear. Because the scoring was done without a preset grading scale, the TRC members had to judge responsiveness on the fly, guided only by their own experience. This makes it difficult to trace back why a particular score was given; the rationale rests on subjective judgment that isn’t anchored in a common framework.  

After that, I deepen the analysis by noting that the lack of a predefined grading system also prevents transparency and consistency. Approving authorities cannot easily see whether a score reflects a genuine assessment of the proposal or merely an individual’s idiosyncratic view, so any attempt to justify or adjust the scores feels arbitrary.  

Finally, putting these pieces together, I see why large score differences caused by poor understanding of the Terms of Reference are hard to reconcile: evaluators differ widely in how they define, understand, or interpret the same criterion and the ToR, their individual generosity or severity magnifies score disparities when common definitions are missing, and the resulting gaps become difficult to explain or justify because they stem from subjective judgments without a shared reference point.

question_text: How are revisions to current government policies or new policies from Govt./MoPNG implemented for NRL
answer:
**A:** Revisions or new government policies are put into effect by issuing an internal circular from the functional head of the Commercial Department. This circular is treated as part of the procurement manual and does not require additional higher‑level approval as long as the policy is adopted without customization for NRL.  

**Rationale:** The manual specifies that any Govt./MoPNG policy change or new policy applicable to NRL may be implemented through such a circular, which becomes part of the manual and needs no separate approval when no customization is made. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p.10)
cot:
I start by clarifying what the question is really asking: it wants to know the procedural route NRL follows when a government policy is updated or a new policy is issued by Govt./MoPNG and needs to be applied internally.  

First, I identify who owns the process within NRL. The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals designate the Commercial Function as the nodal agency for this procurement manual, so any action that ties back to the manual would naturally flow through the Commercial Department.  

Next, I distinguish between two types of changes: revisions to the manual itself, which require approval from the Committee of Functional Directors (and sometimes the Board), and changes that originate outside NRL, namely government policies. The manuals treat the latter separately, indicating that they do not follow the same formal approval path as manual amendments.  

Then I focus on the specific provision for government‑originated policies. The manuals state that any revision of an existing Govt./MoPNG order or the introduction of a new policy that is applicable to NRL can be put into effect simply by issuing an internal circular from the functional head of the Commercial Department.  

I consider the implications of that circular. The circular is treated as part of the manual, meaning it gains the same standing as the manual’s clauses. Importantly, it also notes that no separate higher‑level approval is needed as long as the policy is adopted without any customization for NRL.  

Putting those pieces together, I see that the implementation mechanism is exactly an internal circular issued by the Commercial Department’s functional head, which becomes part of the procurement manual and bypasses additional approvals when the policy is taken verbatim.  

This reasoning leads directly to the answer: revisions or new government policies are implemented via an internal circular from the Commercial Department’s functional head, treated as part of the manual, and requiring no extra approval if no customization is made.

question_text: Who approves any special conditions attached to a Purchase Requisition
answer: The Head of Department (HOD) of the department that is requesting the purchase — the indenting department — approves any special conditions that are attached to a Purchase Requisition. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 45)
cot:

Next, I recall how a Purchase Requisition is structured. The requisition includes an item description that can carry special terms and conditions, and there is a separate field labeled “Any special requirements (SCC)” that captures those conditions.  

Then, I note the rule that governs those special requirements: the Procurement of Goods Manual states that special conditions (SCC) shall be approved by the Head of Department of the indenting department—the department that originates the requisition.  

From that, I infer that the “indenting department” is precisely the user department (Operations, Maintenance, HR, etc.) that creates the PR, and its head is the authority responsible for signing off on the special conditions attached to it.  

Finally, I synthesize the pieces: the approval authority for special conditions on a Purchase Requisition is the Head of the department that is requesting the purchase, i.e., the HOD of the indenting department. This matches the answer that the HOD of the indenting department approves any special conditions attached to a Purchase Requisition.

question_text: If NRL arranges transport, where should the special instructions be included
answer: When NRL arranges the transport, any special instructions regarding the mode of transport, loading, avoiding transshipment or providing escorts are built into the transportation contract itself. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 154)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know where special instructions should be placed when NRL is responsible for arranging the transport of goods.  

Next, I consider the scenario described—when the procuring entity (NRL) itself handles transportation rather than leaving it to the supplier. In that case, the usual practice of telling the supplier how to ship the items shifts to an internal arrangement that NRL must manage.  

Looking at the guidance for transporting high‑value or critical equipment, it states that special instructions concerning the mode of transport, loading, avoiding transshipment, or providing escorts must be conveyed to the supplier. Importantly, it adds a qualifier: if the transport is arranged by the procuring entity, those same instructions can be built directly into the transportation contract.  

Since NRL is the procuring entity arranging the transport, the qualifier applies, meaning the special instructions are not sent separately to the supplier but are incorporated into the contract that governs the transportation service NRL has secured.  

Therefore, the logical conclusion is that when NRL arranges the transport, any required special instructions regarding mode of transport, loading, avoidance of transshipment, or provision of escorts are included within the transportation contract itself.

question_text: Which modes of transport can be used for transshipping cargo between ports, airports, ICDs, or CFSs
answer:
To transship cargo between ports, airports, ICDs, or CFSs, the permissible modes of transport are:

- Vessel  
- Air  
- Rail  
- Road  
- Any combination of more than one of the above modes  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 229)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the question is really asking: it wants to know which transportation methods are permitted when moving cargo between ports, airports, inland container depots, or container freight stations for the purpose of transshipment.  

Next, I consider the regulatory backdrop that governs such movements. The customs framework allows cargo to be moved without paying duty if it is being transshipped, and the rule that enables this also spells out how the cargo may be carried.  

Looking at that rule, it explicitly names the allowable carriers: goods can be moved by vessel, by aircraft, by rail, or by road. These are the basic, stand‑alone modes that the regulation mentions.  

Beyond the single‑mode options, the same provision also notes that more than one of these methods can be used together. In other words, a combination—such as rail followed by road, or air followed by vessel—is also acceptable as long as each leg falls within the listed categories.  

Putting these points together, the permissible ways to transship cargo between the specified facilities are therefore vessel, air, rail, road, or any combination of two or more of those modes. This matches the answer that lists exactly those options.

#### 1. Introduction:
1.1 A number of ports, airports, Inland Container Depots (ICD), Container Freight Stations (CFS) having Customs clearance facilities have been developed in the country to reduce congestion at the gateway ports/airports and to allow importers and exporters to take Customs clearance of imported and export goods at their door steps. The objectives of bringing the Customs facility to door step of importing community and decongesting the gateway ports/ airports requires the movement of imported cargo or export cargo between a port/airport and other ports/airports, ICDs/CFSs in India or a port / airport abroad.

1.2 As per the Customs Act, 1962 duty becomes payable immediately after imported goods are landed at a port or airport. To avoid payment of duty at the port of landing in cases where goods are to be carried to another port / airport or ICD/CFS or to a port / airport abroad, the Customs Act, 1962 provides a facility of transshipment of cargo without payment of duty. The goods can be transhipped from one port / airport to another port / airport / ICD / CFS either by vessel, air, rail or road or by combination of more than one such mode of transport.

## 2. Transshipment of imported containerized cargo from gateway port to another port/ ICD / CFS in India:
2.1 The transshipment procedure of imported cargo is governed by Section 54 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Goods Imported (Conditions of Transshipment) Regulations, 1995 as well as relevant Board's circulars and instructions.

2.2 Transshipment Permit is the permission granted by the Customs, at the port / airport of unloading of imported goods, to shipping agents for carriage of goods to another port / airport / ICD / CFS in India. The shipping agent submits an application along-with transshipment forms (5 copies), sub-manifest and a copy of IGM to the Customs. The Customs scrutinizes the details furnished by the shipping agents in the application for transshipment. In case, the documents are in order and there is no alert notice against the shipping agent, permission for transshipment is granted. For further insight into this aspect if situation demands for such an arrangement, relevant provisions of rules and procedures as relevant may be reviewed before opting the transshipment option.

## Customs Refunds


### 1. Introduction:
1.1 On import or export of goods, at times duty may be paid in excess of what was actually leviable. Such excess payment may be due to lack of information on the part of importer/exporter or non-submission of documents required for claim of lower value or rate of duty. Sometimes, such excess payment of duty may be due to shortage/short landing, pilferage of goods or even incorrect assessment of duty by Customs. In such cases, refund of excess amount of duty paid can be claimed by the importer or exporter. If any excess interest has been paid by the importer/exporter on the amount of duty paid in excess, its refund can also be claimed.

### 2. Legal provisions:
2.1 Section 27 of the Customs Act, 1962 deals with the refund of duty and interest. As provided therein, refund of duty and interest can be claimed either by a person who has paid the duty in pursuance to an order of assessment or a person who has borne the duty.

2.2 Any person claiming refund of any duty or interest has to make an application in duplicate in the form as prescribed in the Customs Refund Application (Form) Regulations, 1995, to the jurisdictional Deputy/Assistant Commissioner of Customs.

question_text: Is it possible to get a refund of the security deposit while the contract work is still in progress?
answer:
Q: Is it possible to get a refund of the security deposit while the contract work is still in progress?  
A: No. The security deposit is retained by NRL until the contract execution is completed (or until the defect liability period ends, whichever is later). Refund of the security deposit—whether full or partial—is not admissible during any time of execution of the contract for any reason. Refund can only be made after completion of the work (or after the defect liability period) as specified in the manual. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 66)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: whether a contractor can receive any portion of the security deposit back while the work under the contract is still being carried out.  

Next, I look at the rules governing the security deposit. The policy makes it clear that the deposit is held by NRL until the contract work is finished, or until the defect liability period ends—whichever comes later. It also explicitly states that a refund, whether full or partial, is not permissible at any point during the execution of the contract, regardless of the reason.  

From that, I see that the only moments when the deposit can be released are after the work is completed (and any defect liability period has elapsed) or, in special cases like one‑time jobs, after the contract is closed. There is no provision for an interim payout while the work is still ongoing.  

Putting those points together, the answer follows naturally: while the contract work is still in progress, the security deposit remains withheld and cannot be refunded.  

Therefore, the correct response is that a refund of the security deposit during ongoing contract work is not possible.

question_text: In what manner do reverse bidding and e-auction tools on GeM support the procurement of bulk quantities?
answer: The reverse bidding and e-auction tools on GeM can be utilised for the procurement of bulk quantities. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 13)
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question is really after: it wants to know how the reverse bidding and e-auction features on GeM actually help when a buyer needs to purchase large volumes of a product or service.  

First, I picture GeM as an online marketplace that brings together many eligible sellers for common‑use goods and services, so the platform already offers a wide selection and competitive pricing by virtue of aggregation.  

Next, I focus on the reverse bidding tool. In a reverse bid, the buyer posts a requirement and sellers compete by lowering their prices; this competition drives the cost down, which is especially advantageous when the order size is large because even a small percentage saving translates into significant absolute savings.  

Then I turn to the e‑auction tool. An e‑auction runs in real time, allowing multiple sellers to bid against each other until the best price emerges. The transparency and speed of this process make it well suited for bulk purchases, where the buyer can quickly secure a favorable rate for a large quantity without lengthy negotiations.  

What’s worth noting here is that the reference material explicitly states that these tools are available and can be utilised for the procurement of bulk quantities. Putting the pieces together, the manner in which reverse bidding and e‑auction support bulk procurement is precisely by enabling competitive, price‑discovering mechanisms that can be applied to large‑volume orders on the GeM platform.  

Therefore, the reverse bidding and e-auction tools on GeM can be utilised for the procurement of bulk quantities.

## 1.8 The Law of Agency - applicable to Procurement of Works
In addition to Laws which are applicable to Public Procurement of Works mentioned above, the Law of Agency (Section 182 to section 238, of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) implies that Contractor would be an Agent of the Procuring Entity, to execute the works on its behalf. Hence, there exists a Principal/ Employer and Agent relationship between Procuring Entity and such Contractor. As per this law, the employer is vicariously legally and financially liable for actions of its Agents. For example, a violation of certain labour laws in deputing staff for Procuring Entity's contract by the agents may render the Procuring Entity legally and financially liable for such violations, under certain circumstances. The Procuring Entities need to be aware of such eventualities. Standard Bidding Documents should take care of this aspect.

question_text: Under what circumstances can a Bank Guarantee be accepted as an alternative to electronic EMD payment
answer: ** A Bank Guarantee may be used instead of the electronic EMD payment when the EMD amount exceeds Rs. 5 lakhs. In such cases the guarantee must be issued by any Scheduled Bank in the prescribed format and routed through the SFMS platform. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 63)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is really asking: it wants to know when a Bank Guarantee can stand in for the usual electronic EMD payment.  

Looking at the procurement rules, the standard practice is to collect EMD electronically through an online payment gateway, and this is the default method for most cases.  

However, the rules also carve out an exception: electronic EMD is mandatory only when the amount does not exceed a certain ceiling, which is set at Rs. 5 lakhs.  

When the required EMD goes above that ceiling, the electronic route is no longer the prescribed default, and an alternative mode of submission is permitted.  

The alternative explicitly allowed is a Bank Guarantee issued by any Scheduled Bank, formatted as prescribed, and it must be routed through the SFMS platform to ensure traceability and security.  

All other conditions governing bid security—such as its validity period, refund procedures, and forfeiture triggers—remain unchanged; they simply apply to the guarantee in the same way they would to an electronic deposit.  

Putting these points together, the circumstance under which a Bank Guarantee can replace electronic EMD payment is precisely when the EMD amount exceeds Rs. 5 lakhs, with the guarantee meeting the scheduled‑bank, prescribed‑format, and SFMS‑routing requirements.

question_text: What does a turnkey contract typically cover when procuring goods?
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question is really after: it wants to know the typical scope of a turnkey contract when we’re buying goods.  
A turnkey agreement isn’t just about handing over equipment; it’s framed as a full‑service package that the contractor assumes.  
The contractor’s role begins with manufacturing and supplying the machinery—or a set of machines that work together, even if some aren’t made by the supplier themselves.  
Next, the contractor must also assemble, install, and erect that equipment at the site, then commission the plant so it delivers the performance and output levels the buyer specified.  
Beyond those core tasks, any incidental works or services needed to support the installation fall under the contractor’s remit, and the contractor is responsible for designing the plant based on the buyer’s performance requirements and quoting accordingly.  
Finally, the contractor provides all the goods, machinery, and equipment necessary for the plant to operate as intended, while the purchasing organization only supplies the inputs and facilities outlined in the tender documents.  
Putting those pieces together, I conclude that a turnkey contract in goods procurement covers everything from design and manufacture through supply, assembly, installation, commissioning, and any supporting services—delivering a ready‑to‑operate facility to the buyer.
chunk_content: In the context of procurement of goods, a turnkey contract may include the manufacture, supply, assembly, installation/ commissioning of equipment (or a group of plant and machines working in tandem - even though some of the machines may not be manufactured by the supplier himself) and some incidental works or services. Generally, in the tender enquiry documents for a turn key contract, the purchase organization specifies the performance and output required from the plant proposed to be set up and broadly outlines the various parameters it visualizes for the desired plant. The inputs and other facilities, which the purchase organization will provide to the contractor, are also indicated in the tender enquiry document. The contractor is to design the plant and quote accordingly. The responsibility of the contractor will include supplying the required goods, machinery, equipment etc. needed for the plant; assembling, installing and erecting the same at site as needed; commissioning the plant to meet the required output etc., as specified in the tender enquiry documents.

### 2.2.1 Conflict of Interest in case of consultants
- i) The consultant is required to provide professional, objective, and impartial advice, at all times holding the Procuring Entity's interests paramount, strictly avoiding conflicts with other assignments or his/its own corporate interests, and acting without any consideration for future work.

- iii) Without limitation on the generality of the foregoing, and unless stated otherwise in the data sheet for the RfP document, the consultant (i.e., private entities) shall not be hired under the circumstances set forth below:

Fairness and transparency in the selection process require that the consultants or their affiliates competing for a specific assignment do not derive an unfair competitive advantage from having provided consultancy services related to the assignment in question. question_text: How does the NRL manual advise on the use of incentives for early completion in terms of frequency and assessment
answer: The NRL manual advises that incentives for early completion should be granted sparingly, only after a careful assessment of the tangible benefits they are expected to yield, and must be disclosed in the tender documents in explicit monetary terms. It further recommends that such incentive clauses be incorporated into the contract judiciously, noting that a typical structure might award up to one percent of the contract value per month for early completion, subject to an overall ceiling of five percent of the contract price (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 92).
cot: I start by recalling what the NRL manual says about giving bonuses for finishing work ahead of schedule. The NRL manual advises that such incentives should be used sparingly and only after a careful assessment of the tangible benefits they are expected to bring, and that they must be written into the tender documents in clear monetary terms. This makes me think that the advice is to treat the bonus as an exception rather than a routine provision, and to verify that early completion actually yields measurable value before offering it. Next, the NRL manual provides an illustrative structure: a bonus of roughly one percent of the contract value for each month the work is completed early, subject to an overall cap of five percent of the contract price. From this example I infer both the permissible frequency—up to a monthly award—and the upper limit that keeps the incentive proportionate to the contract size. Combining the need for sparing, benefit‑based assessment, clear monetary disclosure, and the typical monthly‑based ceiling leads me to the conclusion that the NRL manual advises granting early‑completion incentives only after a careful benefit assessment, disclosing them explicitly in monetary terms, and structuring them so that they can be awarded at up to one percent per month but not exceeding five percent of the total contract value.

### 6.4.3 Delays in Execution
- i) A work may be completed ahead of schedule or delayed due to unforeseen fortuitous circumstances, extra effort or developments beyond the control of the procuring entity or the tenderer and it is sometimes difficult to apportion credit or responsibility. The contractor may experience delay or disruption due to his own actions or inaction, those of his sub-contractor or other contractors, those of the procuring entity or the engineer, or other causes. Such delays expose the non- performing party to various sanctions under the contract. These sanctions include extension of time, damages or default termination of the contract. While examining the

request of the contractor for extension of time, the engineer shall consider all circumstances and categorise the delays as follows:

- a) **Excusable delays** - Force Majeure (FM), that is, acts of God, abnormal weather, floods, and so on, applies;
  - b) **Compensable delays** - or Compensation Events, which put full burden of responsibility on the Procuring Entity as covered in the GCC; and
  - c) **Inexcusable delay (contractor's own faults)**, which puts the full burden of responsibility on the contractor.
  - d) **Concurrent delays** - when two or more events responsible for delay overlap each other. The **delays** may be attributable to the Procuring Entity or the contractor or none, and fall in above categories. The eligibility for extension of time (EOT) should be determined by plotting each contributing concurrent delay on the critical path. The Procuring Entity should see that the concurrent delays do not result in unnecessary extra extension of time.
- ii) Once the delay is categorised, it should then be determined not only whether the contractor is eligible for time extension and/ or monetary relief but also whether sanctions, such as Liquidated Damage (LD) or default termination, can be imposed on the contractor.

### 6.4.4 Liquidated Damages and Incentives/Bonus
Normally, tenders shall be invited with reference to a pre-determined period of completion of works. Provision of incentives for completion of work before schedule should be sparingly made after careful assessment of tangible benefits there from and disclosed in the tender documents in clear monetary terms.

Incentives/Bonus (e.g. one percent of the contract value per month subject to a maximum of five percent of contract value) for early completion and penalties for delay should, therefore, be built into the contract very judiciously. To avail of the incentive clause, it shall be mandatory on the part of the contractor to report the actual date of completion to the concerned Engineer (Engineer herein refers to EIC). To implement a bonus clause in any tender, prior administrative approval of CFD shall be obtained by indenting/user department.

In case of delay in completion of the contract, liquidated damages should be levied. The penalties proposed for identified lapses of omission or commission must be disclosed in the tender documents in clear monetary terms.

**Liquidated Damages:** Compensation of loss on account of late delivery (actually incurred as well as notional) where loss is pre-estimated is termed as LD. Recovery of such pre-estimated loss is allowed provided such a term is included in the contract. There is no need to establish actual loss due to late delivery. Price reduction clause (PRC) for late delivery shall convey the same meaning as Liquidated Damages (LD).

The Contractor is liable to pay Liquidated Damages for per day of delay beyond the specified date of completion, an amount equal to 0.5% for every week or part thereof, subject to the total amount of Damages not exceeding 5% (five per cent) of the Contract Price. However, the Contractor is entitled to time extension arising out of delays on account of change of scope and force majeure or delays caused by or attributable to NRL.

question_text: What is the purpose of the margin of purchase preference in the bidding process?
answer: The margin of purchase preference is the price band that lets a Class‑I local supplier compete for the contract even when they aren’t the absolute lowest bidder. If a local supplier’s quoted price falls within this margin, they can be invited to match the lowest evaluated price (L1). When they successfully match L1, they are awarded the contract—or the portion of it reserved for local preference—giving them a fair chance to win work while still keeping the buyer’s price competitive. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 31)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the margin of purchase preference actually represents in the bidding rules. It is not a fixed discount or a penalty; rather, it is a permissible price range that a Class‑I local supplier’s bid may fall into and still be considered for the preference mechanism.  

Next, I see that the bidding process first determines the lowest evaluated price, L1, among all qualified offers. If L1 happens to come from a Class‑I local supplier, the contract is awarded outright and the margin is irrelevant. The margin only comes into play when L1 is not a local supplier, meaning the buyer would otherwise have to accept a higher‑priced, non‑local offer.  

At that point, the rules look for the lowest‑priced Class‑I local supplier whose quoted price lies within the margin of purchase preference. Being inside this band signals that the supplier’s price is close enough to L1 that, if they are willing to match L1 exactly, the buyer does not suffer a significant price increase while still fulfilling the policy goal of supporting local content.  

The supplier is then invited to match the L1 price for a portion (or all, depending on divisibility) of the requirement. If they accept and match L1, they win the contract—or the allocated share—because their price, after matching, is effectively the same as the lowest bid but they satisfy the local‑content preference.  

If the first local supplier cannot or will not match L1, the process moves to the next higher Class‑I local supplier that still falls within the margin, repeating the invitation to match L1. This cascading approach ensures that every eligible local supplier gets a fair chance, as long as their price stays within the allowed band.  

Finally, if no local supplier within the margin can match L1, the buyer falls back to the original L1 bidder, preserving price competitiveness. Thus, the margin of purchase preference serves as the price band that lets a Class‑I local supplier compete for the contract even when they are not the absolute lowest bidder, allowing them to match L1 and secure the award while keeping the buyer’s overall cost reasonable.

question_text: When may an inspection report for spare parts be issued relative to the main equipment?
answer:
**Procedure for Issuing an Inspection Report for Spare Parts**

1. **Confirm acceptance of the main equipment** – Ensure that the inspection report for the main plant or equipment has been completed and that the equipment has been accepted before any action is taken on the spares.  
2. **Prepare the inspection report for the spares** – After the main equipment is accepted, issue a separate inspection report for the spare parts, detailing the inspection performed, samples examined, requirements per the relevant specification or contract, and observations. Each copy must bear the inspector’s name, stamp, and designation.  
3. **Do not issue the spares report prior to main‑equipment acceptance** – Under no circumstances should an inspection report for spare parts be issued before the main equipment has been accepted.  

*Cross‑reference: Clause 9.12.4(ii) – Inspection of plant and equipment with spares.*  
(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 160)
cot:
I start by asking what the question really wants to know: under what circumstances can an inspection report for spare parts be released when those spares are ordered together with the main equipment.  

Scanning the guidance, I see a clear statement that when plant and equipment are ordered with spares, the inspection report for the spares should not be issued before the main equipment has been accepted. That tells me the timing hinges on the acceptance status of the main plant.  

So the first thing I need to confirm is that the main equipment has undergone its inspection, passed all tests, and been formally accepted. Only after that condition is met can I even think about preparing a report for the spares.  

Once the main equipment acceptance is verified, I move on to actually issuing the spare‑parts report. I make sure it is a separate document that details what was inspected, which samples were examined, the relevant specification or contract requirements, and any observations, and that each copy carries the inspector’s name, stamp and designation.  

I also keep in mind that the report must not be released early; issuing it before the main equipment acceptance would violate the rule, so I hold off until the acceptance step is complete.  

Putting these pieces together, I conclude that an inspection report for spare parts may be issued only after the main equipment has been accepted, and never before that point.

Hence the bidder from such country would not be qualified for award of the tender irrespective of the Order (Public Procurement No. 1) dated 23rd July 2020. In such a case, there is no need to scrap the tender.
  3. Example 3: The facts are as in Example 1, but the bidder from a country which shares a land border with India, though technically qualified, is not eligible for award due to the application of price preference as per other orders/ rules. In such a case, there is no need to scrap the tender.
  4. Example 4: Three bids are received in a tender. One of them is a bidder from a country sharing a land border with India. The bidder from such a country does not meet the technical requirements and hence is not qualified. There is no need to scrap the tender.

## 1.8 Standards (Canons) of Financial Propriety
Public Procurement like any other expenditure in Government must conform to the Standards (also called Canons) of Financial Propriety.

**Standards of financial propriety:** *Every officer incurring or authorizing expenditure from public moneys should be guided by high standards of financial propriety. Every officer should also enforce financial order and strict economy and see that all relevant financial rules and regulations are observed, by his own office and by subordinate disbursing officers. Among the principles on which emphasis is generally laid are the following:-*

- i) *Every officer is expected to exercise the same vigilance in respect of expenditure incurred from public moneys as a person of ordinary prudence would exercise in respect of expenditure of his own money.*
- ii) *The expenditure should not be prima facie more than the occasion demands.*
- iii) *No authority should exercise its powers of sanctioning expenditure to pass an order which will be directly or indirectly to its own advantage.*

- iv) *Expenditure from public moneys should not be incurred for the benefit of a particular person or a section of the people, unless -*
  - a) *a claim for the amount could be enforced in a Court of Law, orb) the expenditure is in pursuance of a recognized policy or custom.*
- v) *The amount of allowances granted to meet expenditure of a particular type should be so regulated that the allowances are not on the whole a source of profit to the recipients.*
- vi) *While discharging the duties of financial concurrence of any public expenditure, such authorities subsequent to such decision, shall not be involved in any future audit responsibilities which may create conflict of interest.*

question_text: According to the Transparency Principle, what limitation is placed on procuring authorities concerning actions not pre‑declared in published documents
answer: Procuring authorities must limit their activities to only those actions that have been explicitly pre‑declared in the relevant published documents; any action that has not been so declared is prohibited. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 17)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is asking: it wants to know what the Transparency Principle says about what procuring authorities may or may not do when an action has not been set out beforehand in their published documents.  

Next, I think about what the Transparency Principle entails beyond just being a buzzword. The NRL and Government of India procurement manuals stress that authorities must be transparent, fair, equal, and open, ensuring that information is shared symmetrically and that processes are predictable and free from hidden agendas.  

Then, I focus on the specific wording that ties the principle to pre‑declaration. The principle enjoins upon the Procuring Authorities to do only that which it had professed to do as pre‑declared in the relevant published documents and not to do anything that had not been so declared. This makes it clear that the principle is not just about openness in general but about a strict boundary: authorities are limited to the actions they have already announced.  

From that, I infer the concrete limitation: if an action has not been pre‑declared in the relevant published documents, the authority is not permitted to carry it out. In other words, any undeclared action is prohibited, and the authority must confine its activities to the set of actions it has already made public.  

Finally, I combine these points to state the limitation plainly: procuring authorities must restrict themselves to only those actions that have been explicitly pre‑declared in the published documents; any action lacking such a declaration is not allowed. This matches the answer that the principle bars authorities from undertaking undeclared actions.
chunk_content:
All procuring authorities are responsible and accountable to ensure transparency, fairness, equality, competition and appeal rights. This involves simultaneous,

symmetric and unrestricted dissemination of information to all likely bidders, sufficient for them to know and understand the availability of bidding opportunities and actual means, processes and time-limits prescribed for completion of registration of bidders, bidding, evaluation, grievance redressal, award and management of contracts. It implies that such officers must ensure that there is consistency (absence of subjectivity), predictability (absence of arbitrariness), clarity, openness (absence of secretiveness), equal opportunities (absence of discrimination) in processes. In essence Transparency Principle also enjoins upon the Procuring Authorities' *to do only that which it had professed to do as pre-declared in the relevant published documents and not to do anything that had not been so declared*'. As part of this principle, all procuring entities should ensure that offers should be invited following a fair and transparent procedure and also ensure publication of all relevant information on the Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP).

question_text: What is the purpose of preparing a well-thought-through cost estimate?
answer: **A:** The purpose is to enable realistic budgetary resources to be earmarked for the assignment. A thorough cost estimate identifies the required manpower, logistics, physical inputs and miscellaneous costs, which allows the organization to allocate appropriate funds. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 29)
cot: I’m trying to figure out why we bother putting together a careful cost estimate in the first place. The core issue is that, before any work can start, the organization needs to know how much money it should set aside so that the assignment can be carried out without running into funding shortfalls or wasting excess cash. To answer that, I have to first understand what drives the cost of the assignment – essentially, what resources will be consumed. That means looking at the people who will work on it, the travel and logistics they’ll need, the physical equipment or materials required, and any ancillary items like support services, contingencies, taxes or profit margins. Once I’ve identified those resource categories, the next step is to quantify them: estimate the staff‑months or hours, apply appropriate remuneration rates, forecast the number of trips and associated travel costs, assess the quantity and unit price of equipment, and add in percentages for things like contingencies and taxes. By doing this, I arrive at a total figure that reflects a realistic picture of what the work will actually cost, taking into account inflation and other variables during the assignment period. With that credible total in hand, the decision‑makers have a solid basis to earmark budgetary resources – they can allocate just enough funds to cover the expected expenses, avoiding both under‑funding that could jeopardize the project and over‑funding that would tie up money unnecessarily. In short, the purpose of preparing a well‑thought‑through cost estimate is to enable realistic budgetary resources to be earmarked, ensuring the organization can allocate appropriate funds based on a detailed assessment of manpower, logistics, physical inputs and miscellaneous costs.
chunk_content:
## 4.2 Estimating Costs, Setting the Budget, and Seeking Approval
4.2.1 Preparation of a well-thought-through cost estimate is essential if realistic budgetary resources are to be earmarked.

- i) **Categories:** Costs shall be divided into two broad categories: (a) fee or remuneration (according to the type of contract used); and (b) reimbursable costs. Depending on the nature of the assignment, cost estimates may be prepared either in local currency or with a combination of local plus foreign currencies. Cost estimate should provide for forecast of inflation during the period of assignment.
- ii) **Estimated Resources:** The cost estimate shall be based on the assessment of the resources needed to carry out the assignment:
  - a) Manpower/Staff cost (taking account of time, skill & experience)
  - b) Logistical support (City, National and International Travels/ Trips and durations), and
  - c) Physical inputs (for example, vehicles, laboratory equipment, tools & tackles)
  - d) Miscellaneous (Support services, contingencies and Profit element, taxes and duties)
- iii) **Rates:** Costs are normally estimated using unit rates (staff remuneration rates, reimbursable expenses) and quantities (exceptionally some items may be estimated on the lump-sum basis or percentage basis - Contingencies and support services). Rates of payment should be identified (including applicable taxes if any) in local and foreign currency for Staff Time, Logistics Costs and Costs of various physical inputs/ support services.
- iv) **Staff Costs:** The estimate of staff cost is based on an estimate of the personnel time (staff-months or staff-hours) required for carrying out the assignment taking into account the time required by each expert, his or her billing rate, and the related direct cost component.

In general, staff remuneration rates include basic salary, social charges, overheads, fees or profit and allowances.

- v) **Logistic Costs:** Number of trips required should be estimated as required to carry out various activities. Travel costs may be included for city travel, National and International travel and stay.
- vi) **Physical Inputs Costs:** Assessment of such costs would depend on the technical requirements of equipment.
- vii) **Miscellaneous costs:** Support services may be taken as a percentage of staff costs. Contingencies and Profit elements are usually taken as a percentage of the total cost of the Consultancy. To this would be added the taxes and duties likely to be incurred by the consultants.

4.2.2 Although assignments vary in size, length and nature, it is possible to make a cost estimate by breaking down the assignment's activities into the following cost categories:

- i) Professional and support staff;
- ii) Travel, Hotel, and transport;
- iii) Mobilisation and demobilisation;
- iv) Office rent, Furniture/ Equipment, supplies, Utilities, IT equipment and communication;
- v) Assignment related surveys, training programmes;
- vi) Translation, report printing;
- vii) Contingencies: miscellaneous, insurance, shipping; and
- viii) Indirect local taxes and duties in connection with carrying out the services.

If, in particular cases, estimates cannot be made meaningfully, full reason should be recorded.

question_text: In what language should reports be written according to the ToR
answer: Reports should be written in the language specified in the Terms of Reference (ToR). The ToR explicitly states the language that must be used for all reports, along with format, frequency, content, number of copies, and recipients. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 28)
cot:
The question is asking what language the reports must be written in according to the Terms of Reference.  
First, I think about what the ToR normally covers when it comes to reporting requirements.  
It usually spells out practical details like how often reports are due, what they should contain, how many copies are needed, and who receives them.  
Scanning the description of the ToR, I see that it explicitly mentions that the ToR should indicate the format, frequency, and content of reports **as well as the number of copies, the language, and the names of the prospective recipients**.  
That tells me that the language to be used for the reports is not left to guesswork; it is one of the items the ToR is required to specify.  
Therefore, the reports must be written in whatever language the ToR states for that particular assignment.  
Putting it together, the answer is that reports should be written in the language specified in the Terms of Reference.
chunk_content:
The assignments, deliverables and reporting should be clearly specified. In particular, for inception and progress reports, there should be a balance between keeping the Procuring Entity well informed and not forcing consultants to spend an excessive amount of time preparing minor reports. The ToR should indicate the format, frequency, and content of reports as well as the number of copies, the language, and the names of the prospective recipients of the reports. For all major reports, an executive summary is recommended as a separate section. Depending on the assignment, the following reports are usually required;

- a) **Inception Report:** This report should be submitted at initial stage of the contract (say about four weeks after the commencement date). Any major inconsistency in the ToR, staffing problems, or deficiency in Procuring Entity's assistance that have become apparent during this period should be included. The inception report is designed to give the Procuring Entity confidence that the assignment can be carried out as planned and as agreed upon in the contract, and should bring to its attention major problems that might affect the direction and progress of the work.
- b) **Progress Reports:** These reports keep the Procuring Entity regularly informed about the progress of the assignment. They may also provide warnings of anticipated problems or serve as a reminder for payment of invoices due. Depending on the assignment, progress reports may be delivered monthly or bimonthly. For feasibility studies and design assignments, delivery of progress reports at two-month intervals is satisfactory. For technical assistance and implementation supervision, for instance, construction, progress reports are best submitted monthly. Progress reports may include a bar chart showing details of progress and any changes in the assignment schedule. Photographs with time-stamping are a quick and easy way of conveying the status of a project, and their use in progress reports should be encouraged. For technical assistance services, progress reports also serve as a means of setting out the work program for the following months. Each team member usually contributes to the preparation of the monthly report.
- c) **Interim Reports:** If the assignment is phased, interim reports are required to inform the Procuring Entity of preliminary results, alternative solutions, and major decisions that need

to be made. Since the recommendations of an interim report may affect later phases of the assignment and even influence the results of the project, the Procuring Entity should discuss the draft interim reports with consultants in the field. The Procuring Entity should not take more than 15 (fifteen) days to review and approve draft interim reports.

question_text: Which authority receives the parcel mail after it is handed over by the Postmaster
answer: The Customs authority receives the parcel mail after it is handed over by the Postmaster. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 235)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what happens right after the Postmaster’s action in the parcel‑mail flow. The question asks which authority takes over the parcel mail once the Postmaster has handed it over, so I focus on the hand‑off step described in the procedure.

Looking at the steps outlined, the Postmaster’s role includes handing over the parcels together with a set of documents—parcel bills, senders’ declarations, customs declarations, and any other required paperwork—to another entity. This hand‑off is explicitly stated as the point where the Postmaster transfers responsibility.

The recipient of those parcels and documents is identified as the Customs office; the Customs Appraiser then scrutinizes the parcel bills, decides which parcels need detention, assesses duty, and eventually returns the processed bills to the Postmaster. This shows that Customs is the authority that actually receives and works with the parcel mail after the Postmaster’s hand‑off.

Since the Customs takes charge of examining, assessing, and duty‑calculating the parcels, it follows logically that the Customs authority is the one that receives the parcel mail from the Postmaster. No other authority is mentioned as intervening at that stage, and the subsequent actions (detention, assessment, duty calculation) are all performed by Customs.

Putting these observations together, the authority that receives the parcel mail after the Postmaster hands it over is the Customs authority.
chunk_content:
6.1 Rules Regarding Postal Parcels and Letter Packets from Foreign Ports in/out of India prescribe procedure for landing and clearing at notified ports/airports/ LCSs of parcels and packets forwarded by foreign mails or passenger vessels or airliners. The procedure broadly is as under:

(a) The boxes or bags containing the parcels shall be labeled as "Postal Parcel", "Parcel Post", "Parcel Mail", "Letter Mail" and will be allowed to pass at specified the Foreign Parcel Department of the Foreign Post Offices and Sub Foreign Post Offices.

(b) On receipt of the parcel mail, the Postmaster hands over to the Customs the following documents:

- (i) A memo showing the total number of parcels received from each country of origin;
- (ii) Parcel Bills in sheet form (in triplicate) and the senders' declarations (if available) and any other relevant documents that may be required for the examination, assessment etc. by the Customs Department;
- (iii) The relative Customs Declarations and dispatch notes (if any); and
- (iv) Any other information required in connection with the preparation of the Parcel Bills which the Post Office is able to furnish.

(c) On receipt of the documents, the Customs Appraiser shall scrutinize the particulars given in the Parcel Bill and identify the parcels to be detained for examination either for want of necessary particulars or defective description or suspected misdeclaration or under-valuation of contents. The remaining parcels are to be assessed by showing the rates of duty on the declarations or Parcel Bill, as the case may be. For this purpose, the Appraisers are generally guided by the particulars given in the Parcel Bill or Customs declarations and dispatch notes (if any). When any invoice, document or information is required to ascertain the real value, quantity or description of the contents of a parcel, the addressee may be called upon by way of a notice to produce or furnish such invoice, document and information.

(d) Whenever necessary, the values from the declarations are entered into the Parcel Bill and after conversion into Indian Currency at the ruling rates of exchange, the amount of duty is calculated and entered. The relevant copies of Parcel Bills with the declarations so completed are then returned to the Postmaster.

(e) Duty is calculated at the rate and valuation in force on the date that the postal authorities present a list of such goods to the Customs. In case the parcels are brought through a vessel and postal authorities present list of goods before arrival of the vessel, the rate of duty and tariff value shall be the date on which Inward Entry is granted to the vessel.

(f) All parcels marked for detention are to be detained by the Postmaster. Rest of the parcels will go forward for delivery to the addressee on payment of the duty marked on each parcel.

(g) The detained parcels are submitted together with the Parcel Bill to the Customs. After examining them and filling in details of contents of value in the Parcel Bills, Customs Appraiser notes down the rate and amount of duty against each item. The remark "Examined" is then entered against the entry in the Parcel Bill relating to each parcel examined by the Customs Appraiser and the Postmaster's copies will be returned by the Customs.

(h) In the case of receipt of letter mail bags, the Postmaster gets the bags opened and scrutinized under the supervision of the Customs with a view to identify all packets containing dutiable articles. Such packets are to be detained and presented in due course to the Customs Appraiser with letter mail bill and assessment memos for assessment. After examining them and filling the details of contents of value in the bill, the Customs Appraiser will note the rate and amount of duty against each item. He will likewise fill in these details on the assessment memos to be forwarded along with each packet.

question_text: When should a lump sum (firm fixed price) contract be used according to the manual
answer:
A lump sum (firm fixed price) contract should be used when the assignment’s quality, scope, and timing of the required output are clearly defined.  

This is the preferred contract type under normal circumstances because it offers a fixed price for a fixed scope, making administration straightforward—payments are linked to specific outputs, milestones, or deliverables such as reports, drawings, or software programs. It is well‑suited for simple planning and feasibility studies, environmental studies, detailed design of standard or common structures, and preparation of data processing systems, and it requires monthly monitoring to ensure progress aligns with the planned timeline. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 20)
cot:
I need to figure out the circumstances under which a lump‑sum, firm‑fixed‑price contract is the appropriate choice.  
The contract type is defined by a single, all‑inclusive price that covers a predetermined scope of work, and payment is triggered only when specific, agreed‑upon deliverables are accepted.  
Because the price does not change with time or effort, the arrangement only makes sense when the buyer can describe exactly what they expect to receive—both in terms of what the output will look like (quality) and when it will be ready (timing).  
If the scope or the required outputs are vague, the fixed price would either leave the provider exposed to unforeseen work or force the buyer to pay for work that isn’t clearly defined, which defeats the purpose of the lump‑sum approach.  
The reference material notes that this contract is widely used for straightforward assignments such as feasibility studies, environmental assessments, standard‑detail designs, and basic data‑processing systems—precisely the kinds of tasks where the deliverables (reports, drawings, software) can be spelled out in advance and measured against milestones.  
It also mentions that even though payments aren’t tied to hours, the work should still be monitored monthly to confirm that progress stays aligned with the planned schedule, reinforcing the idea that timing must be known up front.  
Putting these points together, the logical condition for selecting a lump‑sum contract is that the assignment’s quality, scope, and timing of the required output are clearly defined from the outset.  
That matches the answer: a lump‑sum (firm fixed price) contract should be used when the assignment’s quality, scope, and timing of the required output are clearly defined.

## 3.1 Types of Contracts
There are different basis for linking payments to the performance of services (called types of contracts). Bids are called and evaluated based on the type of contract. The choice of the type of contract should be based on Value-for-Money (VfM) with due regard to the nature of assignment. Adoption of an inappropriate type of contract could lead to a situation of lack of competition, contractual disputes and non-performance/failure of the contract.

Each type of contract is described briefly in subsequent paras, and criteria are suggested for their adoption. Mostly used types of contracts are:

- i) Lump sum (Firm Fixed Price) contract;
- ii) Time based (Retainer-ship) contracts;
- iii) Percentage (Success Fee) contract;
- iv) Indefinite delivery contract.

*However, in case of Procurement/ Outsourcing of other (non-consulting) Services depending on the nature of services, can be either Lump-sum contracts, Time-based (Retainer-ship) contracts, or unit (item/ service) rate (say Taxi Service on per Km basis) based contract (as in case of Goods and Works) - or a mix of these. In certain uncertain but regularly needed services, indefinite delivery contracts, based on time or unit (item/ service) rates may be appropriate. Other types of contracts are not usual in procurement of other services.*

## 3.2 Lump Sum (Firm Fixed Price) Contract
3.2.1 The lump sum (firm fixed price) contract is the preferred form of contract and under normal circumstances; the Procuring Entity shall use this form of contract. Consultant's proposal is deemed to include all prices - no arithmetical correction or price adjustments are allowed during evaluation. Lump sum consultancy contracts are easy to administer because there is fixed price for a fixed scope and payments are linked to clearly specified outputs/ milestones/ deliverables such as reports, documents, drawings, bills of quantities, software programs and so on. In view of Risks mentioned below this type of contracts are widely used for simple planning and feasibility studies, environmental studies, detailed design of standard or common structures, preparation of data processing systems, and so forth.

Lump sum service contracts should be used mainly for assignments in which the quality, scope and the timing of the required output of the consultants/ service providers are clearly defined. The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables and certificate for its acceptability may be recorded. Payment should be made only against certificate of acceptance of deliverables.

While the payments are not linked to time, the assignment should be monitored per month to ensure that the output per month is in line with planned and estimated time-line.

## 3.3 Time-Based Contract
3.3.1 In Time-based contracts payments are based on agreed hourly, daily, weekly, or monthly rates for staff (who in consultancy contracts are normally named, but not so in other services) and on reimbursable items using actual expenses and/or agreed unit prices. This type of contract is appropriate when Lump sum contract is not feasible due to difficulties in defining the scope and the length of services, either because the inputs required for attaining the objectives of the assignment is difficult to assess or because the services are tied up to activities by others for which the completion period may vary.

This type of contract is widely used for complex studies, supervision of construction, advisory services, and most training assignments etc.

The contract should include provision for evaluation of quality and scope of deliverables. Payments should be released only against certification by EIC.

Contracts need to be closely monitored and administered by the EIC to ensure that the progress of assignment is commensurate with the time spent and that the resources for which payment is claimed have actually efficiently and productively been deployed on the assignment during the period.

question_text: How are incentives or bonuses structured for early completion of supplies
answer: Incentives or bonuses for completing supplies ahead of schedule are usually expressed as a set percentage of the contract value for each month you finish early. For example, the bonus might be 1 % of the contract value per month, with the total bonus capped at a maximum of 5 % of the contract value. The exact rate and any upper limit are clearly stated in the tender documents in plain monetary terms, and before a bonus clause can be included in a tender, it must receive prior administrative approval from the CFD (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 149).
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: how a contract might reward a supplier for finishing the supply ahead of the scheduled date.  
Then, I consider that such a reward is usually tied to the amount of time saved, so it makes sense to express it as a rate applied to the contract value for each unit of time the delivery is early.  
Next, I recall that the rate is often set as a fixed percentage of the contract value per month (or week) of early completion, and to protect the buyer from excessive payouts a ceiling is placed on the total bonus that can be earned.  
Further, I note that the exact percentage and any upper limit must be spelled out in plain monetary terms inside the tender documents so that bidders can see precisely what they stand to gain.  
Finally, I remember that before a bonus clause of this sort can be inserted into a tender, it has to receive prior administrative approval from the responsible authority—typically the CFD—to ensure it complies with procurement policy, as noted in the Procurement of Goods Manual (p. 149).  

Putting these points together, the incentive or bonus for early completion is structured as a set percentage of the contract value for each month finished early (for example, 1 % per month), with the total bonus capped at a maximum percentage of the contract value (such as 5 %), the rate and limit clearly stated in the tender documents in plain monetary terms, and the clause requiring prior administrative approval from the CFD.

### 9.7.5 Force Majeure Clause
A Force Majeure (FM) means extraordinary events or circumstance beyond human control such as an event described as an act of God (like a natural calamity) or events such as a war, strike, riots, rebellion or sabotage, lockouts, crimes, hostility, acts of public enemy, civil commotion, fires, explosions, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, quarantine restrictions and freight embargoes (but not including negligence or wrong-doing, predictable/seasonal rain and any other events specifically excluded in the clause). An FM clause in the contract frees both parties from contractual liability or obligation when prevented by such events from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. An FM clause does not excuse a party's non-performance entirely, but only suspends it for the duration of the FM. The firm has to give notice of FM as soon as possible and it cannot be claimed ex-post facto. There may be a FM situation affecting the purchase organisation only. In such a situation, the purchase organisation is to communicate with the supplier along similar lines as above for further necessary action. If the performance in whole or in part or any obligation under this contract is prevented or delayed by any reason of FM for a period exceeding 90 (ninety) days, either party may at its option terminate the contract without any financial repercussion on either side.

Any delays in or failure of the performance of either party hereto shall not constitute default hereunder or give rise to any claims for damages, if any, to the extent such delays or failure of performance is caused by force majeure.

### 9.7.6 Denial Clause
Since delay in delivery is a default by the seller. In such a case, the buyer should protect himself against extra expenditure during the extended period by stipulating a denial clause (over and above levy of LD) in the letter informing the supplier of extension of the delivery period. In the denial clause, any increase in statutory duties and/or upward rise in prices due to the PVC clause and/or any adverse fluctuation in foreign exchange are to be borne by the seller during the extended delivery period, while the purchaser reserves his right to get any benefit of a downward revisions in statutory duties, PVC and foreign exchange rate. Thus, PVC, other variations and foreign exchange clauses operate only during the original delivery period.

### 9.7.7 Liquidated Damages and Incentives/ Bonus
Compensation of loss on account of late delivery (actually incurred as well as notional) where loss is pre-estimated is termed as LD. Recovery of such pre-estimated loss is allowed provided such a term is included in the contract. There is no need to establish actual loss due to late delivery. Price reduction clause (PRC) for late delivery shall convey the same meaning as Liquidated Damages (LD).

Normally, tenders shall be invited with reference to a pre-determined period of completion of supplies. Provision of incentives for completion of supplies before schedule should be sparingly made after careful assessment of tangible benefits there from and disclosed in the tender documents in clear

monetary terms.

Incentives/ Bonus (e.g. one percent of the contract value per month subject to a maximum of five percent of contract value) for early completion and penalties for delay should, therefore, be built into the contract very judiciously. To implement a bonus clause in any tender, prior administrative approval of CFD shall be obtained by indenting/user department.

question_text: What instrument may be used to furnish the initial or total security deposit instead of cash
answer: - Bank Guarantee from any Scheduled Bank (in the prescribed form) (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 43)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: it wants to know what can be used in place of cash to meet either the initial or the total security‑deposit requirement.  
Then I think about the contractual provisions for the deposit – the contractor has to put up a certain percentage of the contract value, but the rules give flexibility on how that amount is supplied.  
The Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual states that besides paying the amount in cash, the contractor may, at his option, furnish the deposit through a bank guarantee.  
I note the specific conditions attached to that option: the guarantee must be issued by any scheduled bank and must follow the prescribed format.  
Putting these points together, the instrument that can replace cash for furnishing the initial or total security deposit is a bank guarantee from a scheduled bank, issued in the prescribed form.
