#### v) **SECURITY DEPOSIT:**
(i) A sum of Ten percent (10%)\* of the accepted value of the tender shall be deposited by the the CONTRACTOR as Security Deposit with the OWNER (NRL). This may be deposited initially at two and half percent (2.5%) of the value of CONTRACT (referred as Initial Security Deposit) within Twenty one (21) days of receipt by him of the Work Order / LOA and the balance Seven and half percent (7.5%) will be recovered in installments through deductions at the rate of Ten percent (10%) of the value of each running account bill till total Security Deposit amount is collected, after which no further deductions from Bills will be made on this account, subject to Clause (iii) below.

(ii) Alternatively, the contractor may, at his option, deposit the full amount of Ten percent (10%) of the accepted value of the Tender towards the Security Deposit within Twenty one (21) days of receipt by him of the Work Order / LOA. contractor can furnish the Initial or Total Security Deposit amount through a Bank Guarantee from any Scheduled Bank in the prescribed form.

(iii) However if the value of WORK as per actual execution exceeds the accepted value of Tender i.e., value given in the Purchase Order, further recoveries towards Security Deposit shall be effected at Ten percent (10%) of the value in excess of the accepted value of the Tender from running Bills and final Bill. Similarly if the value as per actual execution is less than the accepted value of Tender, recovery towards Security Deposit, effected in the running Bills, in excess of Ten percent (10%) of the value of WORK as per actual execution shall be refunded to the contractor along with final Bill.

(iv) **CONVERSION OF EMD TO SECURITY DEPOSIT:** The earnest money deposit (EMD) of the contractor whose tender may be accepted, if paid in forms other than Bank Guarantee, can be converted to and adjusted with security deposit for due performance of the contract if the contractor so desires.

In case of non-submission of Initial Security Deposit (ISD) within the specified time of 21 days (or till first bill is due for payment) after placement of order/LOA, an equivalent amount shall be deducted from his first bill (or balance ISD from subsequent bills if the value of first bill is less than the ISD) and kept as ISD.

In the event of extension (provisional or firm) of Time of the contract , if granted, the contractor shall be required to suitably extend the period of Bank Guarantee if submitted, towards security Deposit/retention money suitably.

This Retention amount or Bank Guarantee furnished against security deposit shall be released only on expiry of the period of liability and also based on the certification of the Engineer-in-charge that no defect/damage has been reported / observed during the stipulated period of liability for the contract.

All compensation or other sums of money payable by the contractor to the owner under terms of this contract may be deducted from or paid by the encashment of a sufficient part of his security deposit or from any sums which may be due or may become due to the contractor by the owner on any account whatsoever and in the event of his security deposit being reduced by reasons of any such deductions of said, the aforesaid contractor shall within ten days thereafter make good in cash or Bank drafts as aforesaid any sum or sums which may have

been deducted from his security deposit, or any part thereof. No interest shall be payable by the owner for sum deposited as security deposit.

For a contract value upto Rupees 5 (five) lakh, submission of Security Deposit may be exempted.

question_text: What activities are included in monitoring the progress of an assignment as outlined in the manual
answer:
The activities involved in monitoring the progress of an assignment are: issuing the notice to proceed; reviewing the inception phase; deciding on possible scope modifications and issuing contract variations; monitoring progress and confirming that key experts are employed, including review of reports and draft/final reports; handling billing, payment and expenditure tracking versus progress; resolving problems faced by consultants or service providers and managing disputes or arbitration; terminating services before contract end if needed; releasing final payment and any guarantees and closing the contract; conducting a post‑contract evaluation; and carrying out any other responsibilities assigned in the GCC, SCC, etc. (<Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 60>)

These steps are outlined to ensure the assignment stays aligned with the procuring entity’s objectives, maintains quality, and allows for timely corrective actions.
cot:
First, I think about what it means to monitor the progress of an assignment: it involves overseeing that the work starts correctly, stays on track, meets quality and scope requirements, handles finances, deals with issues, and is properly closed out.  
Next, I consider the typical phases of a contract‑based assignment—starting with authorization, moving through planning and execution, then finishing with settlement and review—and note that monitoring must touch each of these phases.  
Then I recall that the guidance begins the monitoring process with issuing a notice to proceed, which formally authorizes the consultant to begin work.  
After that, the next logical checkpoint is reviewing the inception phase to confirm that the initial work plan and field‑work arrangements align with the procuring entity’s objectives.  
Following the inception check, the guidance points out that scope may need adjusting, so deciding on possible modifications and issuing contract variations becomes part of the monitoring role.  
During ongoing execution, monitoring includes verifying that key experts are actually engaged, reviewing progress reports, and checking draft and final reports to ensure the assignment is being carried out as specified.  
Financial oversight is also built into monitoring: tracking billing, processing payments, and comparing expenditures against the work completed to date.  
When problems arise—whether technical, managerial, or contractual—the monitor must step in to resolve them, manage disputes, and, if necessary, pursue arbitration.  
If performance remains unsatisfactory despite these efforts, the guidance allows for terminating the services before the contract’s scheduled end.  
Once the work is completed satisfactorily, the monitor oversees the release of final payment, any applicable guarantees, and the formal closure of the contract.  
Finally, a post‑contract evaluation is conducted to capture lessons learned, and any additional duties prescribed in the general or special conditions of the contract are carried out.  
Putting these elements together yields the complete set of activities that constitute monitoring the progress of an assignment: issuing the notice to proceed; reviewing the inception phase; deciding on possible scope modifications and issuing contract variations; monitoring progress and confirming key experts are employed, including review of reports and draft/final reports; handling billing, payment and expenditure tracking versus progress; resolving problems faced by consultants or service providers and managing disputes or arbitration; terminating services before contract end if needed; releasing final payment and any guarantees and closing the contract; conducting a post‑contract evaluation; and performing any other responsibilities assigned in the GCC, SCC, etc.

question_text: What market condition must be satisfied for a repeat order to be approved
answer: - The market must not have shown any reduction in rates for the same material or service since the original order was placed (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 71). This condition safeguards value for money and supports cost‑control objectives.
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants the specific market condition that must be met before a repeat order can be given the go‑ahead.  
Turning my attention to the guidelines for repeat orders, I see a list of requirements that must all be satisfied. Among them, one clause stands out because it directly references the market – it says that the rates for the same material or job must not have fallen since the original order was issued.  
This makes sense as a market‑focused rule: if prices have dropped, buying again at the old, higher price would mean paying more than necessary, which would undermine the goal of getting the best value.  
Thinking further, the purpose of imposing this condition is to protect the organization from overpaying and to keep costs under control; it ensures that the repeat order continues to reflect a competitive price rather than an outdated, inflated one.  
Putting these pieces together, the market condition that must hold for a repeat order to be approved is simply that there has been no reduction in the rates for the relevant material or service since the original order was placed, thereby safeguarding value for money and supporting cost‑control objectives.

## 4.11 Repeat Orders
Where the same material has been purchased or work contracted before, repeat order may be placed, provided the following conditions are satisfied and so recorded:

question_text: What common elements are considered in both the eligibility criteria and the evaluation of EoI?
answer: Both the eligibility criteria and the evaluation of the Expression of Interest (EoI) consider the bidder’s past experience of performance in a similar context, technical capabilities, and financial strength as common elements for assessing suitability. These factors are explicitly listed in the eligibility criteria (past experience of the firm with similar requirements, technical capabilities, and financial strength of the bidder) and are reiterated in the evaluation section, which states that bidders should be evaluated based on past experience, financial strength, and technical capabilities, among others. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 34)
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question is really after: it wants to know what factors show up in both the eligibility requirements for an Expression of Interest and the way those expressions are later judged.  

First, I turn to the part that spells out the eligibility criteria. It says the invitation should lay down clear, measurable criteria, and then gives an example table. In that table I see three broad headings—past experience of the firm with similar requirements, technical capabilities, and financial strength of the bidder—each of which can be broken down further (like turnover and net profit for financial strength). Those are the building blocks the agency uses to decide who can even submit an EoI.  

Next, I look at the section that describes how the EoIs are evaluated once they come in. It tells me that bidders are scored for short‑listing based on their past experience of performance in a similar context, their financial strength, and their technical capabilities, among other possible factors. The wording mirrors the eligibility headings almost exactly, noting that these three areas are central to the scoring process.  

Now I compare the two lists side by side in my mind. The eligibility side mentions past experience, technical capabilities, and financial strength. The evaluation side mentions past experience, financial strength, and technical capabilities. The match is clear: each of those three appears in both places, while other items like quality accreditations or specific sub‑criteria show up only in the eligibility table.  

Seeing that overlap, I conclude that the common elements considered in both the eligibility criteria and the evaluation of an EoI are the bidder’s past experience in a similar context, their technical capabilities, and their financial strength. Those are the factors that the agency uses first to filter who can apply and then to rank who gets short‑listed.

iv) **Eligibility criteria:** The invitation to EoI should clearly lay down the eligibility criteria, which should be applied for short listing. Supporting documents required need to be clearly mentioned. An example of EoI eligibility criteria is shown in Table 1. However, appropriate eligibility criteria have to be designed, keeping in mind the specific objectives of the EoI. Criteria used should be measurable and based on documents that are verifiable. Definitions and explanatory notes shall be provided for each criteria that are simple and unambiguous. It may also be advisable to cross-check and verify these documents, when in doubt.

**Table 1: An example of EoI eligibility criteria**

| Criteria                                              | Sub-criteria                               | Weightage* | Break-up of Weightages |
|-------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|------------|------------------------|
| Past experience of the firm with similar requirements |                                            | A*         |                        |
| Technical capabilities                                |                                            | D*         |                        |
| Financial strength of the bidder                      |                                            | B*         |                        |
|                                                       | Turnover figures of the last three years   |            | B1*                    |
|                                                       | Net profit figures of the last three years |            | B2*                    |
| Quality accreditations, licensing requirements        |                                            | C*         |                        |

\*Weightages (out of 100) should be pre-decided and declared in EoI documents by the CA based on assessment of the required profiles of the potential bidders. The marking/ grading scheme for allotting marks (out of 100) for various parameters should also be laid down.

v) **Evaluation of EoI:** The bidders should be evaluated for short listing, inter-alia, based on their past experience of performance in a similar context, financial strength and technical capabilities, among others. Each bidder should be assigned scores based on the sum of marks obtained for each parameter multiplied by the weightages assigned to that parameter. All bidders who secure the minimum required marks [normally 60 (sixty) per cent] should be shortlisted. The minimum qualifying marks should be specified in the EoI document. Alternatively, instead of weighted evaluation, the EoI document may specify a 'fail-pass criteria' with the minimum qualifying requirement for each of the criteria, such as minimum years of experience, minimum number of Works executed and minimum financial turnover. Under such circumstances, all bidders who meet the minimum requirement, as specified, should be shortlisted. The short list should normally comprise at least four firms.

question_text: How does the GeM platform facilitate transparency and efficiency in procurement
answer:
- GeM offers an online marketplace where eligible sellers list goods/services and all eligible buyers can view, compare, and select from any supplier, increasing transparency (Procurement of Works Manual, p.13).  
- By aggregating offerings from a wide range of providers, GeM provides wider selection, higher availability, and more competitive prices than vendor‑specific stores (Procurement of Works Manual, p.13).  
- The procurement process on GeM is fully electronic and end‑to‑end, covering order placement, supplier registration, rate reasonableness assessment, payment, and fulfillment, which streamlines operations and reduces processing time (Procurement of Works Manual, p.13‑14).  
- Supplier registration is online and automatic via ID authentication, accelerating vendor onboarding (Procurement of Works Manual, p.13).  
- Buyer transactions are processed through the GeM portal, with delivery and fulfillment managed directly by participating sellers, ensuring traceable and auditable records (Procurement of Works Manual, p.14).  
- Reverse bidding and e‑auction tools available on GeM enable transparent price discovery for bulk quantities, enhancing cost efficiency (Procurement of Works Manual, p.14).  
- Procurement of goods and services available on GeM is mandatory for ministries and departments, standardising the process across government entities (Procurement of Works Manual, p.14).
cot:
First, I think about what makes a procurement process transparent: if every eligible buyer can see what’s on offer and compare it side‑by‑side with other sellers, there’s little room for hidden preferences or opaque negotiations. That’s exactly what GeM provides—an online marketplace where suppliers list their goods and services and all government buyers can view, compare and choose from any of them.  

Seeing that the platform gathers products from many different providers, I realize that the sheer breadth of catalogues naturally gives buyers a wider selection, higher availability of items, and, because multiple sellers compete for the same buyer, prices tend to be more competitive than they would be in a single‑vendor store. This competitive environment is a direct source of both transparency (prices are visible) and efficiency (better value is obtained quickly).  

Next, I consider how the actual buying steps are handled. On GeM the whole cycle—from placing a supply order, through supplier registration, checking the reasonableness of rates, making payment, to final fulfillment—is carried out electronically and end‑to‑end. Removing paper‑based hand‑offs and manual data entry cuts processing time and reduces errors, which boosts efficiency while leaving a digital trace that can be audited, reinforcing transparency.  

A key enabler of that smooth flow is the way suppliers join the system. Registration on GeM is done online and is automatic once the supplier’s identity is verified, so vendors can start selling almost immediately without lengthy bureaucratic clearance. This speeds up onboarding and keeps the marketplace populated with active sellers.  

When a buyer completes a purchase, the transaction is processed through the GeM portal itself, and the ordered items are shipped and fulfilled directly by the participating seller. Because the portal records every step—order, payment, dispatch—there’s a clear, auditable trail that anyone with authority can follow, which further secures transparency and prevents bottlenecks in the fulfillment stage.  

For larger volume purchases, GeM offers tools like reverse bidding and e‑auction. These mechanisms let buyers invite suppliers to compete openly on price, with the bidding process visible to all parties. The result is a transparent price discovery mechanism that drives down costs for bulk orders, adding another layer of efficiency.  

Finally, I note that the government has made it mandatory for ministries and departments to procure any goods or services that are available on GeM. This rule ensures that the transparent, efficient process is applied uniformly across all government entities, eliminating ad‑hoc purchasing practices and consolidating the benefits of the platform throughout the public sector.  

Putting these points together, it’s clear that GeM’s combination of open visibility, supplier aggregation, end‑to‑end electronic handling, rapid registration, traceable transactions, competitive bidding tools, and mandatory use creates a procurement environment that is both markedly more transparent and significantly more efficient.

### iii) Government e-Marketplace (GeM)
To ensure better transparency and higher efficiency an online Government e- Marketplace (GeM- an e-commerce marketplace) has been developed for common use goods and services. In GeM product or services are offered by a number of eligible sellers and all the eligible buyers can view/ compare all the product/ services and select the product/ services offered by any one of the seller. In general, because online marketplaces aggregate product/ services from a wide array of providers, selection is usually wider, availability is higher, and prices are more competitive than in vendor-specific online retail stores. The procurement process on GeM is online and electronic -

The registration of suppliers on GeM is online and automatic based on ID authentication etc. The procuring authorities have to assess the reasonability of rates. Buyer's transactions are processed by the GeM portal and then product/ services are delivered and fulfilled directly by the participating sellers. Tools of reverse bidding and e-auction are also available which can be utilised for the procurement of bulk quantities. The Procurement of Goods and Services by Ministries or Departments are mandatory for Goods or Services available on GeM. Ministries/ Departments are expected to work with GeM in making available on the GeM platform as many products/ services by making available such Goods and Services which are regularly procured by them.

Currently functionality for floating tenders for works contracts is not available in GeM. When the functionality for works contracts is made available by GeM, tendering for works contracts through GeM will be adopted suitably.

## 1.8 The Law of Agency - applicable to Procurement of Works
In addition to Laws which are applicable to Public Procurement of Works mentioned above, the Law of Agency (Section 182 to section 238, of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) implies that Contractor would be an Agent of the Procuring Entity, to execute the works on its behalf. Hence, there exists a Principal/ Employer and Agent relationship between Procuring Entity and such Contractor. As per this law, the employer is vicariously legally and financially liable for actions of its Agents. For example, a violation of certain labour laws in deputing staff for Procuring Entity's contract by the agents may render the Procuring Entity legally and financially liable for such violations, under certain circumstances. The Procuring Entities need to be aware of such eventualities. Standard Bidding Documents should take care of this aspect.

question_text: Through which communication methods can written confirmation of a bank guarantee’s issuance be obtained from the issuing branch
answer:
1. Obtain written confirmation of the bank guarantee’s issuance by requesting it through registered post.  
2. Obtain written confirmation of the bank guarantee’s issuance by requesting it through speed post.  
3. Obtain written confirmation of the bank guarantee’s issuance by requesting it through courier.  
4. Obtain written confirmation of the bank guarantee’s issuance by requesting it via direct e‑mail.  
5. Obtain written confirmation of the bank guarantee’s issuance by requesting it through the SFMS platform.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 67)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants the ways in which a written confirmation that a bank guarantee has been issued can be obtained from the branch that issued it.  
The core requirement is that the confirmation must be in writing, so I should look for any mention of how the issuing branch can send such a confirmation back to the requesting party.  
The Procurement of Works Manual discusses verification of bank guarantees and specifically notes that the confirmation from the issuing branch is obtained in writing through several channels.  
The channels are listed as registered post, speed post, courier, direct e‑mail, and the SFMS platform.  
Each of these represents a distinct method for delivering a written confirmation: registered post and speed post are postal services that provide a traceable receipt, courier offers a similar service with often faster delivery, direct e‑mail provides an electronic written record, and SFMS is the secure financial messaging system used for bank‑to‑bank communication.  
Since the question asks for all possible communication methods that satisfy the requirement, I consider each of these items as a valid answer.  
I verify that none of the other details—such as the format of the guarantee or the need for officer names—introduce additional methods, so the list remains complete.  
Putting it together, the written confirmation of a bank guarantee’s issuance can be obtained by requesting it via registered post, speed post, courier, direct e‑mail, or through the SFMS platform.

## 4.13 Sources and Verification of Bank Guarantees
Bank Guarantee for Bid Security (EMD) or Performance Guarantee (Security Deposit) should be irrevocable and operative Bank Guarantee (BG) as per format enclosed in the Bid Document and should be issued by a Scheduled Commercial (i.e. Indian or Foreign Banks included in the Second Schedule of Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 excluding Co-operative banks or Regional Rural Banks). In case of foreign bidders or in case of GTE, if Bank Guarantee is from a foreign bank branch situated outside India, the Bank Guarantee must be issued through any of the Scheduled Commercial Bank. In case BG is issued directly by a bank outside India, it should be executed on Letter Head of the Bank and should be advised and made payable through their Indian Branch/Corresponding Bank in India. The Issuing Bank should also state the name and designation of the next Higher Authority of the Officials who have issued the Bank Guarantee.

Bank guarantees submitted by the tenderers/ contractors as EMD/ performance securities need to be immediately verified from the issuing bank before acceptance. There may not be any need to get the Bank Guarantee vetted from legal/ finance authority if it is in the specified format. Guidelines for verification of BGs submitted by the bidders/ contractors against EMD/ performance security/ advance payments and for various other purposes are as follows:

- i) BG shall be as per the prescribed formats
- ii) The BG contains the name, designation and code number of the Bank officer(s) signing the guarantee(s);
- iii) The address and other details (including telephone no.) of the controlling officer of the bank are obtained from the branch of the bank issuing the BG (this should be included in all BGs);

The confirmation from the issuing branch of the bank is obtained in writing through registered post/ speed post/ courier /direct e-mail/ SFMS. The bank should be advised to confirm the issuance of the BGs specifically quoting the letter of Procurement Entity on the printed official letterhead of the bank indicating address and other details (including telephone nos.) of the bank and the name, designation and code number of the officer(s) confirming the issuance of the BG;

As far as possible organizations should follow e-verification of bank guarantees as per the procedure prescribed by Reserve Bank of India. Bank guarantee should be routed through SFMS platform.

Bank guarantees, either received in physical form or electronic form, should be verified for its genuineness following prescribed method for the same and the Organisations should do due diligence on genuineness of the Bank Guarantees before acceptance of the same.

## 4.14 Safe Custody and Monitoring of Securities
A suitable mechanism for safe custody and monitoring of EMDs and performance securities and other instruments should be evolved and implemented by procuring entity. Institutional arrangements shall be made for taking all necessary actions on time for extension or encashment or refund of EMDs and performance securities, as the case may be. Monitoring should also include a monthly review of all bank guarantees and other instruments expiring in next three months, along with a review of the progress of the corresponding contracts. Extension of bank guarantees and other instruments, where warranted, should be sought immediately and implemented within their validity period. Bank Guarantee should never be handed over to the contractor for propose of extension of validity. Such a system of monitoring of securities and other instruments may be considered to be computerised with automatic alerts about lapse of validity etc. For release of BGs, the proposal shall be forwarded by the executing agency with its recommendations in accordance with the contract conditions.

question_text: According to the guidance, why should the ToR avoid being overly detailed and inflexible
answer:
- Allows competing consultants to propose their own methodology and staffing approaches. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 27)  
- Encourages bidders to comment on the ToR in their proposals, reducing ambiguities during bid preparation and contract negotiation. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 27)  
- Maintains flexibility to minimize the risk of unnecessary extra work, delays, and additional expenses for the Procuring Entity. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 27)
cot:
First, I think about the purpose of a Terms of Reference: it should spell out what the assignment is meant to achieve—its objectives, scope, deliverables, and the responsibilities of both the procuring entity and the consultant.  
Then, I notice that if the ToR becomes too detailed, it starts to dictate not just what needs to be done but also how it should be done, locking in specific methods, staffing patterns, or procedural steps.  
Next, I consider the consultants’ perspective: they compete on their expertise and ability to devise the most suitable approach for a given context; a rigid ToR strips them of that room to innovate and to tailor their team and methodology to the project’s unique demands.  
Further, I see that when the ToR leaves little wiggle room, bidders are less inclined to comment or suggest improvements during the proposal stage, which means any ambiguities or mismatches stay hidden until later, causing friction in bid preparation and contract negotiation.  
After that, I connect those hidden issues to concrete risks for the procuring entity: proposals that are based on an inflexible ToR may lead to work that is either over‑specified or under‑specified, resulting in unnecessary extra effort, schedule slips, and added costs once the contract is underway.  
Finally, I synthesize these points: keeping the ToR comprehensive yet not overly prescriptive preserves flexibility, lets consultants propose their own methodology and staffing, invites useful feedback from bidders, and ultimately reduces the likelihood of wasteful delays and expenses for the procuring entity.

question_text: What must the importer do with the Bill of Entry after the shed examination is completed
answer: - After shed examination, the importer (acting through the CHA) shall obtain two signed copies of the Bill of Entry and two signed copies of the order of clearance from the Shed Appraiser; one copy of the order is retained by the Shed Appraiser attached to the Customs copy of the Bill of Entry. First, I think about why the shed examination matters: it is the point where the goods are checked against the description in the Bill of Entry and an examination report is produced.  
What’s worth noting here is that once the Shed Appraiser finishes the check, he records his findings in the EDI system, which then triggers the creation of the official documents needed for clearance.  
Looking at this further, the system prints the Bill of Entry together with an order of clearance in triplicate, and each copy carries the examination report, the order number and the Appraiser’s name.  
Combining the above analysis, the next logical step is that these printed copies must be signed by the Shed Appraiser before they can be released; the signature validates the examination outcome and the clearance order.  
Seeing how the distribution works, the signed copies are split: two copies of the Bill of Entry and two copies of the order are handed over to the importer (or his CHA), while one copy of the order remains with the Shed Appraiser, attached to the Customs copy of the Bill of Entry for record‑keeping.  
Synthesizing this reasoning, after the shed examination is completed the importer must obtain those two signed Bills of Entry and the two signed orders of clearance from the Shed Appraiser, leaving the retained order copy with the Appraiser as prescribed.

#### 4. Examination of goods:
4.1 All imported goods are required to be examined for verification of correctness of description given in the Bill of Entry. However, ordinarily only a part of the consignment is selected on random selection basis and examined. Also, the goods may be examined prior to assessment in case the importer does not have complete information with him at the time of import and requests for examination of the goods before assessing the duty liability or, if the Customs Appraiser/Assistant Commissioner feels the goods are required to be examined before assessment. This is called First Check Appraisement. The importer has to request for First Check Appraisement at the time of filing the Bill of Entry or at data entry stage giving the reason for the same. The Customs Appraiser records on original copy of the Bill of Entry the examination order and returns the Bill of Entry to the importer/CHA for being taken to the import shed for examination of the goods. Thereafter, Shed Appraiser/Dock Examiner examines the goods as per examination order and records his findings. In case appraising group has called for samples, he forwards sealed samples accordingly. The importer is required to bring back the said Bill of Entry to the assessing officer for assessing the Bill of Entry, which is countersigned by Assistant/Deputy Commissioner if the value is more than Rs.1 lakh.

4.2 The imported goods can also be examined subsequent to assessment and payment of duty. This is called Second Check Appraisement. Most of the consignments are cleared on Second Check Appraisement basis. In this case whole of the consignment is not examined and only those packages which are selected on random basis are examined.

4.3 Under the EDI system, the Bill of Entry, after assessment by the appraising group or first appraisement, as the case may be, needs to be presented at the counter for registration for examination in the import shed. A declaration for correctness of entries and genuineness of the original documents needs to be made at this stage. After registration, the Bill of Entry is passed on to the shed Appraiser for examination of the goods. Along with the Bill of Entry, the CHA is required to present all the necessary supporting documents. After examination of the goods, the Shed Appraiser enters the report in EDI system and transfers first appraisement Bill of Entry to the appraising group and gives 'out of charge' in case of already assessed Bills of Entry. Thereupon, the system prints Bill of Entry and order of clearance (in triplicate). All these copies carry the examination report, order of clearance number and name of Shed Appraiser. Two copies each of Bill of Entry and the order are to be returned to the CHA/importer, after the Appraiser signs them. One copy of the order is attached to the Customs copy of Bill of Entry and retained by the Shed Appraiser.

#### 5. Execution of bonds:
5.1 Wherever necessary, for availing duty free assessment or concessional assessment under different schemes and notifications, execution of end use bonds with Bank Guarantee or other surety is required to be furnished. These have to be executed in prescribed forms before the assessing Appraiser. For instance, when the import of goods are made under Export Promotion schemes, the importer is required to execute bonds with the Customs authorities for fulfilment of conditions of respective notifications. If the importer fails to fulfil the conditions, he has to pay the duty leviable on

those goods. The amount of bond of bond and bank guarantee is in terms of the instructions issued by the Board from time to time as well the conditions of the relevant Notification etc.

question_text: What kind of study might the buyer carry out to compare buying, leasing, or hiring options
answer: The buyer can carry out a techno‑economic evaluation—often a life‑cycle cost analysis if feasible—to compare the costs and benefits of buying, leasing, or hiring the item. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 37)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the buyer is trying to do: they want a systematic way to weigh the alternatives of buying, leasing, or hiring a particular item so they can choose the most advantageous option.  

Looking at the procurement guidance, the decision on how to satisfy a need—whether through owning, leasing, hiring, or outsourcing—is not left to intuition; it calls for a structured assessment that looks at the various ways the requirement can be met.  

The guidance specifies that this assessment should be a techno‑economic evaluation, which essentially means examining both the technical suitability and the economic implications of each alternative.  

When such an evaluation is performed, the most common and robust economic tool mentioned is a life‑cycle cost analysis, which tallies all costs—acquisition, operation, maintenance, and disposal—over the item’s useful life, provided that data and feasibility allow it.  

By conducting this techno‑economic evaluation, and specifically a life‑cycle cost analysis when possible, the buyer can directly compare the total costs and benefits of buying versus leasing versus hiring, thereby arriving at an informed procurement decision.  

Thus, the appropriate study the buyer should carry out is a techno‑economic evaluation—often a life‑cycle cost analysis if feasible—to compare the costs and benefits of the buying, leasing, or hiring options.

**2.1.1** Procurements should be initiated only based on an indent from the user Department. The authority in the user Department initiating the indent for procurement shall first determine the need (including anticipated requirement) for the subject matter of the procurement. Description and Specification of Need assessment is of fundamental importance in ensuring value for money, transparency, competition and level playing field in procurement. The user Department shall maintain all documents relating to the determination and technical/financial/budgetary approvals of the need for procurement. During need assessments, the following matters are decided to comply with the 'Procurement Guidelines':

- i) **The expression/description of the need** keeping in view the Value for Money (VfM) and to ensure wide competition. Therefore to the extent practicable it should be:
  - a) Unambiguous, complete, using common terminology prevalent in relevant trade;
  - b) In accordance with the guidelines prescribed if any in this regard;
  - c) Except in case of proprietary purchase from a selected single source, reference to brand names, catalogue numbers or other details that limit any materials or items to specific manufacturer(s) should be avoided as far as possible. Where unavoidable, such item descriptions should always be followed by the words "or substantially equivalent".
- ii) **Method of satisfying it** (owning/leasing/hiring/outourcing and so on) may be determined as per policies declared in this regard or based on a techno-economic evaluation (using life cycle cost, if feasible) of various alternative methods of satisfaction of the need and compatibility and inter-operability with existing infrastructure or systems.
- iii) The quantity of the subject matter of procurement, commensurate with economy:
  - a) Care should be taken not to make unnecessary procurements much in advance of actual requirements, if such procurement is likely to be unprofitable to the company, coupled with unwarranted inventory-carrying cost. Where sales, consumption or usage limits of requirements have been laid down by the Competent Authority (CA), the officer signing the indent should also certify that the prescribed scales or limits are not exceeded. The authority preparing the indent shall neither package nor divide its procurement or take any other action so as to limit competition among potential bidders or to avoid its obligations under 'Procurement Guidelines'. Provided that in the interest of efficiency, economy, timely completion or supply, wider competition or access to MSEs, a indenting or procuring authority may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, divide its procurement into appropriate packages, or club requirements of other users for procurement. Some requirements e.g. IT Systems may have elements of Goods, Works and Services. It could be either sliced into Goods, Works and Services elements or combined into a package. Such decisions for slicing or packaging should be based on technical and VfM considerations. It is also necessary to round off the calculated quantity to the nearest wagon load/truck load/package to economise on transportation; and
  - b) Units of quantity are a very important parameter. Some items may be manufactured in metric tons but may be used in units of numbers or units of lengths (for example, steel

sheets/structural). For the sake of transparency, it is important to buy an item in units of manufacture. For example, it is better to buy steel/structural in units of weight since it has a tolerance in weight per unit of length; this usually works to the disadvantage of the buyer if it is bought in units of length. The buying and issuing units of an item may be different - but should be standardised.

question_text: If I don’t have my own testing facilities, who has to pay for the outside lab tests
answer: If you don’t have your own testing facilities, you—as the supplier—are responsible for paying the fees for any outside laboratory tests that are required. The procurement rules state that when samples must be sent to an external lab because you lack the necessary testing arrangements, the cost of those tests is to be deposited by you. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 159)
cot:
First, I need to figure out who bears the cost when a laboratory test has to be done outside the supplier’s own facilities. The question is essentially asking about cost allocation in that specific situation.

I think about the two main parties involved: the supplier, who provides the goods, and the procuring entity, which receives and inspects them. The answer will depend on which party is considered responsible for arranging and paying for the test.

Next, I recall the rules that govern external testing. They say that when a supplier does not have the necessary testing arrangements in‑house, the samples must be sent to an approved outside laboratory. In those cases, the responsibility for depositing the testing fees is placed on the supplier.

I also consider the general principle that routine testing before dispatch is normally the supplier’s expense, while testing after receipt falls to the procuring agency. However, the exception for lacking internal facilities overrides the usual split: the supplier still pays because the test is being done in lieu of their own capability.

Putting those points together, if I am the supplier and I lack my own testing facilities, any external lab test that becomes necessary is my financial obligation. I would have to cover the test charges, sample dispatch, transportation, and related costs as stipulated in the liability statement for external testing.

Therefore, the conclusion is clear: the supplier—i.e., you—must pay for the outside laboratory tests when you do not have your own testing facilities.

question_text: How is Local Content calculated for a product supplied to NRL
answer:
Local Content is worked out by comparing the value that comes from India with the total value of the item you are supplying.  

1. Start with the total value of the item (do not include any domestic indirect taxes).  
2. Subtract the value of any imported content in that item – this includes the cost of the imported parts plus all customs duties paid on them.  
3. Divide the result from step 2 by the total value of the item (the figure you used in step 1).  
4. Multiply by 100 to express the outcome as a percentage.  

In short:  

**Local Content % = [(Total value – Imported value including duties) ÷ Total value] × 100**  

This percentage tells NRL how much of the product’s value is added in India. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 11)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is asking: it wants the method for figuring out the local‑content percentage of a product that will be supplied to NRL.  

The core idea behind local content is to measure how much of the item’s value actually originates in India, so I start by recalling that local content is defined as the Indian‑value‑added portion expressed as a share of the item’s total value.  

Next, I pin down the two quantities I must work with. The total value of the item is the price paid for the good, but I have to leave out any net domestic indirect taxes because those are not part of the product’s intrinsic value.  

Then I consider what has to be subtracted from that total: the imported content. This includes not only the purchase price of the foreign‑sourced parts or materials but also all customs duties that were paid on those imports, since duties represent a cost that is not Indian value added.  

With those two figures in hand, I calculate the Indian value added by taking the total value (tax‑exclusive) and subtracting the imported value (including duties).  

To turn this difference into a proportion, I divide the Indian value added by the original total value (the same figure I used in the first step). This yields a fraction that represents the share of the item’s worth that comes from India.  

Finally, I convert that fraction into a percentage by multiplying by one hundred, which gives the local‑content figure that NRL will use to assess compliance with its procurement preferences.  

Putting it all together, the calculation runs: Local Content % = [(Total value – Imported value including duties) ÷ Total value] × 100. This percentage tells NRL how much of the product’s value is actually added in India.

question_text: What must be specified in the tender if the Company supplies materials to be deducted from contractor bills
answer: If the Company supplies materials that are to be deducted from the contractor’s bills, the tender must specify the issue rate of those materials and prescribe the method of accounting for them, including the allowable percentage of wastage. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 51)
cot:
First, I ask myself what the tender needs to capture when the company provides materials that will later be taken off the contractor’s bill.  
The core issue is clarity: the contractor must know exactly what value will be deducted and how that value is calculated.  

Whenever materials are issued on a chargeable basis, the company recovers the landed cost plus overhead and GST from the contractor’s running account bills.  
When the arrangement is flipped so that the company supplies the materials specifically to be deducted from the contractor’s bills, the same principle of transparency applies—there has to be a clear, agreed‑upon rate at which those materials are valued.  

In such a case, the issue rate of the materials must be mentioned in the tender.  
That gives me the first required element: a specified issue rate.  

But a rate alone isn’t enough; the parties also need to know how the quantity of material used will be turned into a monetary amount.  
Accordingly, the method of accounting for the materials—including any allowable percentage of wastage—must also be prescribed.  
This covers how measurements are taken, what deductions for waste are permitted, and how the final deductible sum is arrived at.  

Putting those two pieces together, the tender must lay out both the issue rate and the accounting method (with its wastage allowance) so that there is no ambiguity when the company’s materials are later deducted from the contractor’s bills.  

Therefore, the tender must specify the issue rate of the materials to be supplied by the company and prescribe the method of accounting for them, including the allowable percentage of wastage.

question_text: When should the procuring entity engage external laboratories for testing goods
answer: Engage external laboratories for testing goods when the procuring entity lacks the necessary technical expertise or when the supplier does not have in‑house facilities to perform required type, acceptance, or special tests. External testing is also appropriate when confirmatory testing is deemed desirable before accepting goods to reduce risk and ensure value for money. In such cases, laboratories should be nationally accredited or reliable, with preference given to the National Test House, and sampling must be conducted by a qualified inspection agent. Test reports must include measured values, and records retained for three years. Cost responsibility follows the principle that routine pre‑dispatch testing is borne by the supplier, while post‑receipt testing is borne by the procuring entity; however, if the material fails the test, the testing costs revert to the seller. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 159)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: under what circumstances should a procuring entity look outside its own organization to have goods tested by an external laboratory. The core idea is to guarantee that the goods meet the required specifications when the entity cannot reliably do the testing itself.

Next, I think about the situations that would make internal testing impractical or impossible. If the procuring entity lacks the technical expertise or the necessary equipment to perform a particular type, acceptance, or special test, it makes sense to seek outside help. Likewise, if the supplier does not have in‑house facilities to carry out the required tests, the entity cannot rely on the supplier’s own testing and must turn to an external lab. Sometimes, even when both parties could test, the entity may want an additional confirmatory test before accepting the goods to reduce risk and ensure value for money.

From there, I move on to how such external testing should be organized. The laboratory chosen should be nationally accredited or otherwise proven reliable, with a preference for the National Test House when available, to ensure the results are credible and accepted. Sampling must be done by an inspection agent who is qualified to conduct random sampling in line with quality‑assurance requirements, so that the specimens sent to the lab are representative of the lot. The test report needs to show the actual measured values, not just a pass/fail verdict, and the lab must keep the samples and all related records for at least three years for possible future reference or appeal.

Then I consider the financial side of external testing. Routine tests that are carried out before the goods are dispatched are normally the supplier’s responsibility, while tests performed after the goods have been received by the consignee fall to the procuring entity. However, the guidelines make it clear that if the material fails the test, the cost of that testing reverts to the seller, regardless of who initially bore the expense. This creates a strong incentive for the supplier to ensure their goods are compliant before submission.

Finally, I bring all these points together: external laboratories should be engaged whenever the procuring entity lacks the expertise or facilities to perform needed tests, when the supplier cannot do the testing in‑house, or when a confirmatory test is deemed advisable before acceptance. The lab must be accredited, sampling must be done by a qualified agent, reports must contain detailed values and be retained for three years, and costs follow the rule that pre‑dispatch testing is on the supplier, post‑receipt testing on the procuring entity—except that a failed test shifts the cost back to the seller. This reasoning leads directly to the answer provided.

#### ii) **External Inspecting Authorities**
In case Procuring Entity does not have technical expertise or for other relevant reasons, inspection may also be entrusted to a third-party inspection authority. The procuring entity, however, retains the right to reject the consignment, even if it is cleared by third party inspection authorities.

Sometimes, it becomes necessary to conduct a type test, acceptance test or special test at external laboratories, when facilities for these tests are not available in-house with the supplier or carrying out of confirmatory tests is considered desirable before accepting the goods. The Procuring Entity should draw up a list of approved laboratories for this purpose, to which the samples drawn from the lots offered by the supplier can be sent for tests. The list should also contain approved laboratories, which can be used as referral/appellate laboratories for retest, when samples tested at one laboratory are decided to be re-tested. The following guidelines should apply to such cases:

- a) External testing may invariably be done by national accredited or reliable laboratories, preference being given to National Test House (NTH). For testing the

samples drawn from the lots offered by the supplier, an inspection agent qualified to conduct random sampling in accordance with Quality Assurance requirements should do the selection of samples;

- b) Test reports must contain the values obtained in the tests besides fail/pass results. The laboratory must preserve the sample and test records for a period of three years;
- c) The Department should lay down a liability statement for costs expended on tests, dispatch of samples, transportation costs, test charges, and so on., in respect of samples tested at outside laboratories as may be applicable; and
- d) In cases where the samples are to be tested at the supplier's cost because of non-availability of his own testing arrangements, the responsibility of depositing the testing fees would rest with the supplier.
- e) Normally unless otherwise intended in the contract, charges of routine testing prior to dispatch of materials are to be borne by the supplier and charges of testing of materials after receipt by consignee are to be borne by the procuring agency. Contract should be clear about responsibility of cost of materials expended in tests and charges of special tests e.g. type test or tests at external labs. **Even where procuring entity is responsible for testing charges, if the material fails in the test, the charges would become the responsibility of the seller.**

#### iii) **Joint Inspection on Complaint**
In case a written complaint is received from the supplier disputing the rejection of goods by the Procuring Entity's inspecting officer, it should be jointly investigated by a team consisting of an authorised representative of the Procuring Entity, a senior representative of the inspecting agency who is conversant with the goods and an authorised representative of the supplier.

question_text: Who has the authority to approve any material variation to the terms and conditions of a signed contract?
answer: The competent authority must approve any material variation to the terms and conditions of a signed contract (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 85).
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants to know who holds the power to give approval when a material change is proposed to the terms and conditions of a contract that has already been signed.

Next, I recall the relevant contract provisions. The applicable rule makes it clear that once a contract is in place, its terms and conditions cannot be altered in a material way unless two conditions are met: there must be a valid reason for the change, and the change must have the approval of the competent authority.

From this statement I can deduce that the only entity explicitly named as having the authority to sanction such a variation is the competent authority itself; the provision does not assign this role to any other department or individual, such as the legal team, finance, or administration, which are mentioned only in relation to drafting advice or preliminary vetting.

I then verify that no other part of the manual contradicts this conclusion. The sections about legal, P&A, and finance clearance pertain to the preparation and issuance of the contract, not to post‑sign‑off modifications, and the clause about material variation stands alone as the governing rule for changes after execution.

Putting these points together, the logical answer is that the competent authority is the body that must approve any material variation to the terms and conditions of a signed contract.

Scanning that clause, the period mentioned is eight to ten weeks.  
Putting those pieces together, the Monitor’s deadline for submitting the written report after being notified is therefore eight to ten weeks, and the report is directed to the Chairperson of the Board.  
Thus, the Monitor must submit the written report to the Chairperson of the Board within 8 to 10 weeks after being notified.

question_text: What does the manual say about deviations from the Scope of Work that could cause disputes
answer:
**A:** Disputes may arise when the consultant or service provider deviates from the agreed Scope of Work or work plan, or when the Procuring Entity makes out‑of‑course requests for deviations. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 63)  

**Rationale:** Such deviations create a mismatch between what was contracted and what is actually performed, leading to disagreements that should be dealt with promptly and amicably.
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the manual says about disputes that stem from changes to the agreed work.  
Scanning the section on disputes, I see a sentence that links disagreements directly to alterations in the Scope of Work or work plan.  
It specifies two possible sources: the consultant or service provider straying from what was contracted, and the Procuring Entity making unexpected requests for changes.  
Both situations create a mismatch between what was originally agreed upon and what is actually being done, which naturally leads to contention between the parties.  
Therefore, the manual indicates that disputes may arise when either side deviates from the Scope of Work—either through the provider’s own deviations or through out‑of‑course change requests from the Procuring Entity.

## 8.13 Disputes and Conflicts
8.13.1 Disputes between the consultant/ service provider and the client may arise for a number of reasons. This could relate to technical and administrative matters such as interpretation of contract, payment for services or substitution of key experts - all of which should be dealt with promptly and amicably between the contracting parties in terms of contract provisions. These may be the result of delays prompted by weaknesses on the part of the consultant/ service provider or the Procuring Entity; by a lack of funds; by delays in getting key approvals, data, or information; or by causes beyond anyone's control such as natural disasters. These may be the result of deviations from the Scope of Work or work plan by the consultant/ service provider or out-of-course requests for deviations by the Procuring Entity.

8.13.2 All reasonable efforts should be made to avoid disputes in the first place; both parties should attempt to deal with problems as they arise, on a mutually constructive basis. (This may include the repatriation of consultant/ service provider staff if necessary or a change in the personnel of the Procuring Entity's CMC/EIC) If this is not possible, GCC sets clear procedures for dealing with disputes. This entails provision of a notification of dispute by one party to the other, and provision for a mutual resolution at higher levels of authority within the consultant/ service provider and the Procuring Entity. Finally, if the dispute cannot be amicably settled between the consultant/ service provider and the Procuring Entity, then provision is made for arbitration under the Arbitration Clause. The award decreed by arbitration tribunal is binding.

For further details please refer section 6.10.1 and 6.10.2 of the “Manual for Procurement of Works”

## 8.14 Force Majeure
8.14.1 A Force Majeure (FM) means extraordinary events or circumstance beyond human control such as an event described as an act of God (like a natural calamity) or events such as a war, strike, riots, rebellion or sabotage, lockouts, crimes, hostility, acts of public enemy, civil commotion, fires, explosions, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, quarantine restrictions and freight embargoes (but not including negligence or wrong-doing, predictable/seasonal rain and any other events specifically excluded in the clause). An FM clause in the contract frees both parties from contractual liability or obligation when prevented by such events from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. An FM clause does not excuse a party's non-performance entirely, but only suspends it for the duration of the FM. The firm has to give notice of FM as soon as possible and it cannot be claimed ex-post facto. There may be a FM situation affecting the purchase organisation only. In such a situation, the purchase organisation is to communicate with the supplier along similar lines as above for further necessary action. If the performance in whole or in part or any obligation under this contract is

prevented or delayed by any reason of FM for a period exceeding 90 (ninety) days, either party may at its option terminate the contract without any financial repercussion on either side.

8.14.2 Any delays in or failure of the performance of either party hereto shall not constitute default hereunder or give rise to any claims for damages, if any, to the extent such delays or failure of performance is caused by force majeure.

question_text: What responsibility falls on the user department when they request a waiver of inspection to meet an urgent requirement and the firm agrees to 100% payment against consignee's receipt and acceptance
answer: The user department is responsible for ensuring the quality of goods supplied when it requests a waiver of inspection to meet an urgent requirement and the firm agrees to 100 % payment against consignee’s receipt and acceptance (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 158).
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: when a user department asks to skip the usual pre‑dispatch inspection because the need is urgent and the supplier agrees to be paid in full only after the consignee has received and accepted the goods, who ends up making sure the goods are actually of the right quality?  

Next, I identify the two key conditions that are present – the user department’s explicit request for a waiver of inspection to meet an urgent requirement, and the firm’s willingness to accept 100 % payment against the consignee’s receipt and acceptance.  

Then, I consider what waiving inspection means in practice: without an independent check at the supplier’s site, there is no external verification that the items conform to specifications, so the usual safeguard is removed.  

Looking at the situation, the only party that can step in to fill that gap is the one who asked for the waiver, because they are the ones who have decided that the normal inspection step is unnecessary and are therefore taking on the risk associated with that decision.  

Following that line of thought, it follows that the user department must assume responsibility for confirming the quality of the goods themselves – whether through reliance on the supplier’s self‑certification, any available documentation, or their own verification after receipt – before they can accept the shipment.  

Finally, I synthesize the reasoning: when a user department seeks an inspection waiver for an urgent need and the supplier agrees to full payment upon consignee receipt, the duty to ensure the supplied goods meet the required quality standards falls squarely on that user department.

#### iii) **Manufacturer's Quality Self-certification**
Reputed manufacturers could be relied upon with respect to certain goods for quality products. These may not be subjected to physical inspection and the materials may be accepted under the firm's quality self-certification. The physical inspection clause stipulating the inspection authority and inspecting officer in such cases should not be included in the contracts entered into. Waiver of pre-dispatch inspection and acceptance of materials under the firm's quality self-certification may be considered where:

- a) The user Departments indicate, in their indent, that physical inspection is not necessary and that the materials can be accepted on the firm's quality self-certification;
- b) The user Department requests for a waiver of inspection to meet urgent requirement and where the firm is agreeable to 100 (hundred) per cent payment against the consignee's receipt and acceptance. In such cases, the user Departments themselves should be responsible for ensuring the quality of goods supplied;

- c) In case of goods to be imported from abroad, pre-dispatch inspection of goods at the supplier's premises involves considerable expenditure to the purchaser. In such a situation, the purchaser may substitute pre-dispatch inspection by its own inspector with manufacturer's in-house inspection report and warranty. However, before adopting this procedure, the nature and cost of the goods ordered, the reputation of the supplier, and so on, should also be kept in view and appropriate decision taken. For checking the reputation and background of the supplier, the purchase organisation may also request the Indian embassy located in that country for a report on the technical and financial competence of the firm. Further, trustworthy publications such as Thomas Register, Dun and Brad Street Register, and so on, are also available in the USA and Europe which provide authentic technical and financial data and details of the manufacturing companies located in those countries. Such publications may also be relied upon for this purpose; and
- d) However, the right of waiver of inspection may be reserved only for specific requirements. Justification for the waiver should be recorded. Also, a suitable clause may be incorporated in the conditions of contract.

#### iv) **Inspection on Installation and Commissioning**
This method is adopted to check the performance and output of equipment or machinery after it is commissioned and operational at site.

### 9.12.3 Types of Inspection Agencies
Normally, inspection modalities or agencies for inspections specified in the contract should not be changed. In rare cases, when this becomes inescapable, it should be done with the approval of the CA, justifying the rare circumstances, ensuring that no undue benefit accrues to the contractor.

#### i) **Internal Inspection Authorities**
Wherever there is technical expertise available in-house, an internal officer of the Indenting Department is nominated for inspection. The consignee should be the final authority for acceptance of goods.

question_text: How does the GeM platform enable buyers to view and compare products or services from multiple sellers
answer: **A:** On the GeM platform, eligible sellers list their products or services, and all eligible buyers can see every offering from those sellers. Buyers are able to view the full range of items, compare them side‑by‑side, and then choose the product or service from any seller that best meets their needs. This aggregation of multiple sellers in one online marketplace makes it easier for buyers to assess options and select the most suitable choice. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 13)
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is really asking: it wants to know the mechanism by which the GeM platform lets buyers see and evaluate offerings from different sellers side by side.  

Looking at the description of GeM, it is portrayed as an online government e‑marketplace that brings together many eligible sellers of common‑use goods and services in one digital space. The core idea is that the platform does not belong to any single vendor; instead, it acts as a hub where multiple sellers can list what they have to offer.  

Because the platform is online and accessible to all eligible buyers, once a seller uploads a product or service, that listing becomes visible to every buyer who is authorized to use GeM. There is no restriction that limits a buyer to only one seller’s catalog; the system is designed to show the full inventory of all participating sellers.  

The next logical step is to consider how the platform facilitates comparison. Since all listings reside in the same interface, buyers can open multiple items simultaneously, view their specifications, prices, and other attributes, and place them next to each other for a direct side‑by‑side evaluation. The electronic nature of the marketplace means this can be done instantly without needing to visit separate websites or physical stores.  

Furthermore, the aggregation of many sellers in one place naturally widens the selection, improves availability, and tends to make prices more competitive, which reinforces the usefulness of the view‑and‑compare function. Buyers are not just seeing a single source; they are seeing a spectrum of options that they can weigh against each other.  

Putting these pieces together, the GeM platform enables buyers to view and compare products or services from multiple sellers by acting as an online common‑use marketplace where all eligible sellers list their offerings, the platform makes every listing visible to all eligible buyers, and the unified digital interface allows buyers to examine and juxtapose those listings easily before choosing the one that best fits their needs.

### iii) Government e-Marketplace (GeM)
To ensure better transparency and higher efficiency an online Government e- Marketplace (GeM- an e-commerce marketplace) has been developed for common use goods and services. In GeM product or services are offered by a number of eligible sellers and all the eligible buyers can view/ compare all the product/ services and select the product/ services offered by any one of the seller. In general, because online marketplaces aggregate product/ services from a wide array of providers, selection is usually wider, availability is higher, and prices are more competitive than in vendor-specific online retail stores. The procurement process on GeM is online and electronic -

end to end from placement of supply order to payment to suppliers. The registration of suppliers on GeM is online and automatic based on ID authentication etc. The procuring authorities have to assess the reasonability of rates. Buyer's transactions are processed by the GeM portal and then product/ services are delivered and fulfilled directly by the participating sellers. Tools of reverse bidding and e-auction are also available which can be utilised for the procurement of bulk quantities. The Procurement of Goods and Services by Ministries or Departments are mandatory for Goods or Services available on GeM. Ministries/ Departments are expected to work with GeM in making available on the GeM platform as many products/ services by making available such Goods and Services which are regularly procured by them.

Currently functionality for floating tenders for works contracts is not available in GeM. When the functionality for works contracts is made available by GeM, tendering for works contracts through GeM will be adopted suitably.

## 1.8 The Law of Agency - applicable to Procurement of Works
In addition to Laws which are applicable to Public Procurement of Works mentioned above, the Law of Agency (Section 182 to section 238, of the Indian Contract Act, 1872) implies that Contractor would be an Agent of the Procuring Entity, to execute the works on its behalf. Hence, there exists a Principal/ Employer and Agent relationship between Procuring Entity and such Contractor. As per this law, the employer is vicariously legally and financially liable for actions of its Agents. For example, a violation of certain labour laws in deputing staff for Procuring Entity's contract by the agents may render the Procuring Entity legally and financially liable for such violations, under certain circumstances. The Procuring Entities need to be aware of such eventualities. Standard Bidding Documents should take care of this aspect.

question_text: Why might a new volume be opened for contract management, and what should it contain?
answer: A new volume may be opened for contract management to preserve the integrity of procurement records by limiting frequent exposure of the sensitive procurement file. This volume should contain copies of the successful bid, the Tender Committee Report, the contract, and all correspondence and documents relating to contract management and its closure (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 135).
cot:
First, I think about what the procurement file is meant to hold: it starts with the indent and accumulates every document related to planning, bidding, evaluation, award and the final contract. This creates a single, comprehensive record that tracks the whole process.  

Looking at how this file is used, I notice that contract management often requires repeated reference to the agreement, the winning bid, the evaluation report and related correspondence. If we keep pulling those items out of the main procurement file each time, the file gets handled frequently, which increases the risk of wear, loss or inadvertent exposure of sensitive information contained in other parts of the record.  

To protect the integrity of the main procurement file, it makes sense to isolate the materials that are needed regularly for contract administration. By placing them in a separate volume, we limit how often the original file has to be opened, thereby preserving its security and completeness.  

Now I consider what should go into this new contract‑management volume. Since its purpose is to provide ready reference for the ongoing administration and eventual closure of the contract, it should contain the core contractual documents: a copy of the successful bid, the Tender Committee Report that justified the award, and the contract itself.  

In addition, any correspondence or documents that arise during the execution of the contract—such as change orders, performance reports, notices, and finally the closure paperwork—should also be filed there so that the entire contract lifecycle is accessible in one place.  

Putting these points together, the reason for opening a new volume is to shield the sensitive procurement record from excessive handling, and the volume should hold the successful bid, the Tender Committee Report, the contract, and all contract‑management correspondence and closure documents. This matches the explanation that a new volume preserves integrity by limiting exposure of the main file while keeping the essential contract‑related materials readily available.

### 7.6.4 Framing of Contract
The following general principles should be observed while entering into contracts:

- i) Any agreement shall be issued strictly as per approval of TEC. The terms of contract must be precise, definite and without any ambiguities. The terms should not involve an uncertain or indefinite liability, except in the case of a cost plus contract or where there is PVC in the contract. In other words, no contract involving an uncertain or indefinite

liability or any condition of an unusual character should be entered into without the previous consent of the CA

- ii) All contracts shall contain a provision for
  - a) Recovery of liquidated damages (LD) for delay in performance of the contract on the part of the contractor;
  - b) A warranty clause/defect liability clause should be incorporated in contracts for plant and machinery, requiring the contractor to, without charge, replace, repair or rectify defective goods/ works/services;
- iii) All contracts for supply of goods should reserve the right of the procuring entity to reject goods which do not conform to the specifications;
- iv) Payment of all applicable taxes by the contractor or supplier; and
- v) When a contract is likely to endure for a period of more than two years, it should, wherever feasible, include a provision for an unconditional power of revocation or cancellation by the procuring entity at any time on the expiry of six months' notice to that effect, subject to inclusion of such provision in the tender/RfP document.
- vi) Standard forms of contracts should be invariably adopted, except in following cases:
  - a) Departmental procurement, Spot procurement, Online procurement.
  - b) In cases where standard forms of contracts are not used or where modifications in standard forms are considered necessary in respect of individual contracts, legal and financial advice should be taken in drafting the clauses in the contract and approval of CAs is to be obtained; and

### 7.6.5 Procurement Records
The Procurement file should start with the Indent and related documents. All subsequent documents relating to procurement planning; Copy of Bid Document and documents relating to its formulation, publishing and issue/ uploading; Bid Opening; Bids received; Correspondence and documents (including Technical Evaluation and TEC report) relating to pre-qualification, evaluation, Award of Contract; and finally the Contract copy, should be kept on the file. In case of bulky Bids received, all bids received may be kept in a separate volume, with a copy of accepted bids later being put on the main volume. To maintain integrity of the records relating to Procurement, these files should be kept secure and for contract management a new volume of file may be opened to obviate frequent exposure of sensitive procurement file. In contract management volume, copies of successful bid, Tender Committee Report, Contract may also be kept for ready reference, besides correspondence and documents relating to Contract Management and its closure. In case the documents are preserved in electronic mode adequate information security & access control mechanism should be maintained.
