### 4.4.1 (B) Minimum Response in Open/Limited Tenders:
1. **"Minimum Response"** shall be considered as under, and no separate approval note to be processed for un-priced bid opening:
  - i. Where the enquiry is issued on open tender basis, the minimum response shall be 03 (three) bids.
  - ii. Where the enquiry is issued on limited tender basis, the minimum response shall be 03 (three) bids. Wherever limited tender is issued to two parties only, minimum response shall be two.
2. Respective purchase officer shall suitably extend the bid due date in either of the following two situations:
  - i) Where Minimum response is not obtained, Purchase officer can give first extension of up to one week but subsequent extensions shall require Commercial HOD's consent. Indentor and HOD of user dept. is to be notified about such extensions.
  - ii) Where Minimum response is obtained but one or more of the vendors have requested for extension by the due date. In such a cases, user dept HOD's prior consent shall be obtained.
3. Normally two extensions shall be given to any enquiry. In case, even after two bid due date extension(s), minimum response is not obtained, whatever bids are received, may be opened. In the case of no response, refloating may be done only in consultation with user department.
4. Where extension is required for any reason(s) beyond two extensions, Commercial HOD's prior consent shall be obtained. Reason for such extensions should be recorded.

## 4.5 Eligibility and Qualifications of Bidders


### 4.5.1 Eligibility of Bidders
- i) All eligible bidders meeting the eligibility criteria as defined in ITB can participate in the

tender. The bidder should be a private or government-owned legal entity.

- ii) Bidder should have valid registration with Employees Provident Fund organization under 'EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952', wherever applicable.
- iii) Tenders where Joint Ventures / LLPs (limited liability partnerships) are allowed, all the partners shall be jointly and severally liable (as applicable) for the successful completion of the work.
- iv) A firm that has been engaged by the procuring entity to provide consultancy services for the preparation or implementation of a project, and any of its affiliates (associates, subsidiary, JV partner), shall not be eligible for subsequently providing goods or works (other than a continuation of the firm's earlier consultancy services) for the same project.
- v) A firm determined non-performing by the Procuring Entity shall not be eligible to bid during the period so determined.

### 4.5.2 Qualification of Bidders
Qualification of bidders is done on Pre-qualification Bidding basis (refer Para 3.3.6, PQB) or on post-qualification basis (refer Para 3.3.4, single stage multiple envelope system). In both cases Qualification criteria needs to be laid down in the Bid Document (refer para 3.3.6 iii). If the report only gave a binary outcome, there would be no way to verify how close the result was to the acceptance limits or to investigate any discrepancies later. Therefore, the report needs to show the actual numbers that were measured during the test.

Putting these points together, the test report must include the actual values obtained in the tests, not merely a pass/fail conclusion, and the laboratory must keep the sample and the complete test records for three years. This satisfies both parts of the question.

#### ii) **External Inspecting Authorities**
In case Procuring Entity does not have technical expertise or for other relevant reasons, inspection may also be entrusted to a third-party inspection authority. The procuring entity, however, retains the right to reject the consignment, even if it is cleared by third party inspection authorities.

Sometimes, it becomes necessary to conduct a type test, acceptance test or special test at external laboratories, when facilities for these tests are not available in-house with the supplier or carrying out of confirmatory tests is considered desirable before accepting the goods. The Procuring Entity should draw up a list of approved laboratories for this purpose, to which the samples drawn from the lots offered by the supplier can be sent for tests. The list should also contain approved laboratories, which can be used as referral/appellate laboratories for retest, when samples tested at one laboratory are decided to be re-tested. The following guidelines should apply to such cases:

- a) External testing may invariably be done by national accredited or reliable laboratories, preference being given to National Test House (NTH). For testing the

samples drawn from the lots offered by the supplier, an inspection agent qualified to conduct random sampling in accordance with Quality Assurance requirements should do the selection of samples;

- b) Test reports must contain the values obtained in the tests besides fail/pass results. The laboratory must preserve the sample and test records for a period of three years;
- c) The Department should lay down a liability statement for costs expended on tests, dispatch of samples, transportation costs, test charges, and so on., in respect of samples tested at outside laboratories as may be applicable; and
- d) In cases where the samples are to be tested at the supplier's cost because of non-availability of his own testing arrangements, the responsibility of depositing the testing fees would rest with the supplier.
- e) Normally unless otherwise intended in the contract, charges of routine testing prior to dispatch of materials are to be borne by the supplier and charges of testing of materials after receipt by consignee are to be borne by the procuring agency. Contract should be clear about responsibility of cost of materials expended in tests and charges of special tests e.g. type test or tests at external labs. **Even where procuring entity is responsible for testing charges, if the material fails in the test, the charges would become the responsibility of the seller.**

#### iii) **Joint Inspection on Complaint**
In case a written complaint is received from the supplier disputing the rejection of goods by the Procuring Entity's inspecting officer, it should be jointly investigated by a team consisting of an authorised representative of the Procuring Entity, a senior representative of the inspecting agency who is conversant with the goods and an authorised representative of the supplier.

question_text: In a scenario where procurement is conducted on a nomination basis or from a single/limited source, what does the guideline say about the acceptability of negotiations
answer: When the procurement is done on a nomination basis or comes from a single or limited source, the guideline treats negotiations as an allowable exception rather than the rule. In these circumstances, negotiations may be entered into **only** with the lowest acceptable bidder (L1) who is techno‑commercially responsive for the bulk quantity. The decision to negotiate—and the choice of negotiating partner—must be made by the procuring department or the TEC, and convincing reasons for the negotiation must be recorded by the authority recommending it. The CA is expected to exercise due diligence before accepting a tender, ordering negotiations, or calling for a re‑tender. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 128)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: under what conditions does the guideline allow negotiations when the procurement is done on a nomination basis or comes from a single or limited source?  

I remember that the overall stance in the guideline is that negotiations should be the exception, not the rule, and they are only permissible in clearly defined, exceptional situations.  

When I scan those exceptional situations, I see that nomination‑based procurement and procurement from a single or limited source are explicitly listed as cases where negotiations may be considered.  

That tells me that, in those specific scenarios, negotiations are not outright prohibited; they are allowed but only if certain safeguards are observed.  

The safeguards spell out that negotiations can be held solely with the lowest acceptable bidder (L1) who is techno‑commercially capable of supplying the required bulk quantity, and they must not be extended to any other tenderers, whether they did not bid or were rejected for non‑responsiveness.  

Further, the guideline clarifies who has the authority to decide on negotiations: the procuring department or the Technical Evaluation Committee must make the call, and the authority recommending the negotiation has to record convincing reasons for doing so.  

Finally, the Chief Accountant (or the equivalent CA) is expected to exercise due diligence before accepting a tender, ordering negotiations, or calling for a re‑tender, ensuring that all procedural checks are satisfied.  

Putting these points together leads to the conclusion that, when procurement is nomination‑based or from a single/limited source, negotiations are permissible as an exception, limited to the L1 techno‑commercially responsive bidder, with the decision made by the procuring department or TEC, justified by recorded reasons, and subject to CA due diligence.

question_text: What must the Finance department do after an asset is identified as condemned, scrap, or surplus
answer:
1. Retire the identified condemned, scrap, or surplus asset from the Fixed Asset Register.  
2. Classify the retired asset as “Assets held for Sale.”  
3. Complete the write‑off of the asset in the financial records.  
4. After the write‑off, formally intimate the Warehouse department to proceed with the disposal action.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 167)
cot:
First, I consider what it means for an asset to be labeled condemned, scrap or surplus – it is no longer useful for the organization’s operations and therefore should not remain on the list of active, usable assets.  

Looking at the Fixed Asset Register, its purpose is to track assets that are still in service and contributing to the business, so the next logical step is to remove the identified item from that register.  

Once the asset is taken off the register, it needs a new classification that reflects its intended fate; the appropriate designation is “Assets held for Sale,” indicating that the item is now earmarked for disposal rather than continued use.  

With the asset re‑classified, the financial impact must be recognized: the remaining book value is written off, clearing the asset from the balance sheet and recording any loss or gain associated with its retirement.  

After the write‑off is completed, the Finance department informs the Warehouse team that the asset has been financially retired and is ready for the physical disposal process, allowing Warehouse to proceed with handling, storage, or sale according to the established procedures.  

This sequence—removing from the register, re‑classifying, writing off, and then notifying Warehouse—covers exactly what the Finance department must do after an asset is identified as condemned, scrap, or surplus.

## 4.8 Drawals against Rate Contract (RC)/Framework Contract (FC)
4.8.1 RC is essentially a price agreement with the vendors/contractors at a specified price and terms and conditions during the period covered by the RC. No quantity is mentioned nor is any minimum commitment guaranteed in the RC. RC is most frequently used in procurement of goods, but can as well be used *mutatis mutandis* in works, services and consultancy - where it is commonly known as a Framework Contract (FC). *For appropriate items (please see para 4.8.3 below), drawals against an existing RC exploits the power of collaboration/ clubbing of numerous small and frequent requirements and thus provides best VfM along with a simple and quick procedure.* However, entering into a new RC may have the same procedural complexity, prolonged timeframe and systemic cost as in OTE, which may not be viable for low volumes. In view of Government e Marketplace coming into operation, Rate Contract is not required to be executed for common use items like computers, printers, photocopiers, paper and stationary, other office items like furniture, bottled water etc., which are being placed on GeM and will now be applicable only for specialized and engineering items which are not available on GeM, and are identified as common use items and are needed on recurring basis. For any exceptions to the above, the reason for going for RC should be justified and recorded.

## 4.9 Direct Procurement without Quotation
4.9.1 Direct procurement of goods without formal quotations is normally done for the smallest value procurements. It should be used for off-the-shelf goods of simple and standard specifications and when the required goods are of required specification or needed within required delivery period etc.

- (i) Procurements do not exceed the threshold (for each requirement) for each case as prescribed in DOA;
- (ii) The requirement is urgent but was not covered in the procurement plan; and
- (iii) The requirement is for off-the-shelf goods of simple and standard specifications. Examples of procurement are day-to-day needs of the office and field units, and so on.

### 4.9.2 Terms and Conditions
- i) Such powers can be given to various user sections for operational needs.
- ii) Normally an imprest amount (with facilities for cash/cheque payments) sufficient for two months' estimated procurements can be sanctioned for such officers to handle such procurements. The imprest amount can be recouped on monthly basis by submission of expense vouchers.
- iii) In a summary form, records of bills should be kept
- iv) In larger cities, the presence of reputed Shopping Malls may also be included in the market survey. Reputed internet shopping portals may also be explored.

HODs should carry out periodic review of such direct procurements without quotation to ensure that the demand is not split into small quantities for the sole purpose of avoiding the necessity of getting an approval from the higher authority required for sanctioning the purchase of the original demand or for avoiding LTE or OTE mode of procurement. question_text: What does it mean for an asset to have outlived its normal span of life and be beyond economic repair
answer: An asset that has outlived its normal span of life and is beyond economic repair is one that has reached the end of its expected useful life and fixing it would cost more than the asset is worth, so it is classified as a condemned asset. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 165)
cot:
First, I think about what “outlived its normal span of life” implies: the asset has been in service longer than the period it was originally expected to remain functional, so its design life has been exceeded.  
Next, I consider “beyond economic repair”: even if the asset could be fixed, the cost of those repairs would outweigh the asset’s remaining value or the benefit of keeping it in use, making repair impractical from a cost‑benefit standpoint.  
Putting those two ideas together, the asset is no longer able to perform its intended function effectively, and restoring it would not be justified economically.  
At this point, the asset is essentially useless for ongoing operations; it cannot be relied upon to deliver the expected performance without incurring disproportionate expense.  
Looking at how such items are treated in practice, they are grouped with other materials that are deemed unfit for continued use and are earmarked for disposal rather than further investment.  
Finally, this leads to the conclusion that an asset that has outlived its normal span of life and is beyond economic repair is one that has reached the end of its expected useful life and whose repair would cost more than the asset is worth, and therefore it is classified as a condemned asset.

### 10.2.1 Classification of assets which have ceased to be useful:
The assets and materials which have ceased to be useful and may be considered for disposal may be categorized as under:

#### A) Condemned Assets:
- i) Assets / Materials that are not in working condition.
- ii) Assets / Materials that have outlived its normal span of life and beyond economic repair
- iii) Assets / Materials whose shelf life has expired

#### B) Scrap Material:
- i) Process Waste, broken, damage materials, workshop waste etc having resale value.
- ii) Empty containers, crates, drums etc.

#### C) Surplus Assets:
- i) Items that are in working condition but are lying in stores for more than five years (non-moving) shall be deemed as surplus unless there is specific reason (Insurance, Unique Spares etc.) to treat them otherwise.
- ii) Items in working condition but cannot be put into use effectively being outdated due to change in technology / operation.
- iii) Project Surplus

It is very important to categorise the scrapped items under different trade groups based on the use to which the scrap purchaser can put it for commercial use, for example, melting, re-rolling, burning, recycling, and so on. Properly grouped and sorted scrap is likely to attract better value and help in keeping historical data of prices and facilitates fixing of reserve prices.

Following are few examples of categorization of scrap/condemned assets/materials:

- i) Ferrous materials
- ii) Non-Ferrous metallic items (Aluminium, Copper etc.)
- iii) Chemicals and catalysts
- iv) Plastic materials
- v) Drums, Jerry cans and other empty containers

question_text: According to the guidelines, what two dates must the time lag for price variation be specified for?
answer: The time lag for price variation must be specified for both the **base date** and the **date of supply** (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 111).
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants the two specific dates for which the guidelines require the time lag for price variation to be spelled out.  

Next, I recall how the guidelines define that time lag – it’s the interval between when the raw materials are bought and when the finished goods are submitted for inspection.  

Reading on, the guideline makes it clear that this interval isn’t just a standalone figure; it is tied to two particular points in the contract timeline. It says the time lag applies both for the base date and for the date of supply.  

Because it applies at both ends, the guideline goes on to state that this time lag must be specified for each of those points – in other words, you have to state the lag relative to the base date and also relative to the date of supply.  

Putting those pieces together, the two dates that must be called out are the base date and the date of supply.

question_text: Which columns in the priced bid opening table capture the financial details of a bid?
answer:
- Total Quoted Price (Excl. GST)  
- Rate of GST  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 199)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is asking: it wants to know which columns in the priced‑bid opening table contain the financial information submitted by each bidder. Financial information in a procurement context normally consists of the amount the bidder is offering to pay and any applicable taxes or duties that will be added to that amount.

Next, I scan the table header to see what data fields are presented. The columns are: serial number, bidder names, technical/commercial acceptance, total quoted price (excluding GST), rate of GST, and the bidders’ representatives’ signatures. I note that the first two columns identify who is bidding and whether their offer is acceptable from a technical or commercial standpoint—these are administrative or evaluative fields, not monetary values. The signature column is merely a record of attendance, again non‑financial.

Then I focus on the remaining two columns: “Total Quoted Price (Excl. GST)” and “Rate of GST”. The first directly states the monetary amount the bidder is proposing for the goods or services, stripped of tax. The second specifies the percentage of GST that will be applied to that base price. Together, these two fields allow one to calculate the total payable amount (base price plus GST), which is the complete financial picture of the bid.

I verify that no other column holds a numeric or tax‑related figure; the serial number is just a counter, the acceptance column is a qualitative judgment, and the signature column is procedural. Therefore, the only columns that capture the financial details of a bid are the ones that convey the price and the tax rate.

Putting this together, the financial details are captured by the “Total Quoted Price (Excl. GST)” column and the “Rate of GST” column.

question_text: Is the contractor entitled to any compensation when the contract is ended due to insolvency
answer: No, the contractor is not entitled to any compensation when the contract is terminated for insolvency; the termination is carried out without compensation to the contractor (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 115).
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: whether a contractor has any right to receive payment or other compensation when the contract is brought to an end because the contractor becomes insolvent.  

Next, I consider how contracts typically handle termination. There are usually distinct grounds for ending an agreement—such as breach by the contractor, insolvency of the contractor, or convenience of the procuring entity—and each ground comes with its own set of consequences.  

Turning my attention to the insolvency scenario, I recall that the provision governing termination for insolvency specifies that the procuring entity may end the contract by giving a written notice to the contractor. Importantly, the wording states that this termination is carried out “without compensation to the contractor.”  

I then note that the clause does mention that the procuring entity’s existing rights of action or remedies are preserved, but it does not create any corresponding obligation to pay the contractor for work already done or for any losses arising from the termination itself.  

Putting these points together, the logical conclusion is that when a contract is terminated on the basis of the contractor’s insolvency, the contractor is not entitled to any compensation; the termination is expressly without compensation.

### 6.11.2 Cancellation of Contract for Default
Without prejudice to any other remedy for breach of contract, by written notice of default sent to the Contractor, the contract may be terminated in whole or in part, if the contractor:

- i) has seriously or repeatedly breached the contract, including
  - a) failure to complete the work within the time period(s) specified in the contract, or any extension thereof granted;
  - b) failure to obey instructions in relation to his progress or defective work, material or plant;
  - c) breach of the prohibition against sub-contracting
  - d) Failure to supply sufficient and suitable constructional plant, temporary works, labour and material as proposed in the work programme;
  - e) Substantial suspension of work for more than the specified days without authority from the engineer and failure to proceed with the work within the specified days of receipt of notice from the engineer
  - f) Failure to comply with the requirements regarding JVs
- ii) committed fraud
- iii) If the contractor fails to perform any other obligation under the contract within the period specified in the contract or any extension thereof granted.
- iv) If the contract is terminated in whole or in part, recourse may be taken to any one or more of the following actions:
  - a) Forfeiture of the security deposit;
  - b) Upon such terms and in such manner as it deems appropriate, taking over the site and to complete the works himself or with another contractor (risk Purchase) and use the contractor's materials, equipment, temporary works as he/ they think proper; and
  - c) However, the contractor shall continue to fulfil the contract to the extent not terminated.

Before cancelling the contract and taking further action, it may be desirable to obtain legal advice.

### 6.11.3 Termination of Contract for Insolvency
If the contractor becomes bankrupt or becomes otherwise insolvent or undergoes liquidation or loses

substantially the technical or financial capability (based on which he was selected for award of contract), at any time, the contract may be terminated, by giving a written notice to the contractor, without compensation to the contractor, provided that such termination will not prejudice or affect any right of action or remedy which has accrued or will accrue thereafter to Procuring Entity.

### 6.11.4 Termination of Contract for Procuring Entity's Failure or Convenience
After placement of the contract, there may be an unforeseen situation compelling Procuring Entity to cancel the contract. In such a case, a suitable notice has to be sent to the contractor for cancellation of the contract, in whole or in part, for its (Procuring Entity's) convenience, inter alia, indicating the date with effect from which the termination will become effective. This is not Procuring Entity's legal right- the contractor has to be persuaded to acquiesce. Depending on the merits of the case, the contractor may have to be suitably compensated on mutually agreed terms for terminating the contract. Suitable provisions to this effect should be incorporated in the tender document as well as in the resultant contract. If termination occurs because of Procuring Entity's convenience or a fundamental breach on his part, the engineer will certify the value of works executed, value of any materials lying at site, reasonable cost of removal of equipment, repatriation of project staff, cost of protecting and securing the works and deducting from it: (i) pending advances; (ii) other recoveries; and (iii) taxes as due.

question_text: On which value is the security deposit calculated?
answer:
- Identify the contract value, excluding any reimbursement items. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 65)  
- Use the accepted value of the tender (as stated in the Purchase Order) as the base for calculating the security deposit. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 65)  
- Calculate ten percent (10 %) of that accepted tender value to obtain the required security deposit amount. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 65)  
- If the actual executed work value differs from the accepted tender value, adjust recoveries or refunds at ten percent (10 %) of the excess or shortfall accordingly. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 66)  
- For contracts up to five lakh rupees (excluding reimbursement items), security deposit submission may be exempted. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 66)
cot:
First, I ask myself what the question is really after: it wants to know the basis on which the security deposit amount is figured out. The provisions contain repeated references to a percentage of something called the “accepted value of the tender” and also mentions of contract value, so I need to isolate which figure serves as the foundation.

Then, I note that the security deposit is explicitly set at ten percent of the accepted value of the tender, and the Procurement of Works Manual clarifies that this percentage applies to the contract value after any reimbursement items are stripped away. This tells me that the calculation starts with the tender amount that has been agreed upon, excluding reimbursements.

Next, I consider how the deposit is actually collected. Whether paid up front or recovered in installments from running bills, the recovery rate is ten percent of each bill until the full ten percent of the tender value is reached. This reinforces that the running bill amounts are being measured against the same tender‑based figure, confirming that the tender value is the constant reference point.

Further, I examine the adjustment clause. If the work actually executed ends up being more or less than the tender value, any extra or missing amount is dealt with by applying the same ten percent rate to the difference. This shows that the ten percent factor is always tied to the tender‑based value, and adjustments are made relative to it rather than to some other metric.

Finally, I see the exemption rule: for contracts whose value—again, the contract value excluding reimbursement items—does not exceed five lakh rupees, the security deposit may be waived. This exemption is framed in terms of the same contract value, confirming that the threshold and the calculation share the same base.

Putting these observations together, the security deposit is calculated on the accepted value of the tender, which is the contract value after removing any reimbursement items, using a ten percent rate, with adjustments for variations in actual execution and a possible waiver for small contracts.

question_text: By how much can the quantity ordered be increased or decreased at the time of award?
answer: At the time of award, the quantity ordered can be increased or decreased by up to 25 percent (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 125).
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: it wants the permissible range for changing the ordered quantity when the contract is actually awarded.

Next, the procurement guidance explains that, after evaluating tenders, the purchaser should re‑judge the quantity based on the latest situation and that the tendered amount can be altered if warranted.

Then, the exact figure that governs how large that alteration may be is that the quantity may be increased or decreased by twenty‑five percent for ordering, and any larger change could raise transparency issues.

After that, there are caveats that modify this limit. A larger variation would require additional justification, implying that the twenty‑five percent figure is the maximum allowed without further approvals.

Finally, I synthesize these points: the rule permits a quantity change at award, and the ceiling for that change is twenty‑five percent either upward or downward. Hence, the quantity ordered can be increased or decreased by up to 25 percent at the time of award.
chunk_content:
### 7.5.2 Extension of Tender Validity Period
The entire process of scrutiny and evaluation of tenders, preparation of ranking statement and notification of award must be done expeditiously and within the original tender validity period. The validity period should not be unreasonably long as keeping the tender unconditionally valid for acceptance for a longer period entails the risk of getting higher prices from the tenderers.

If, however, due to some exceptional and unforeseen reasons, the purchase organisation is unable to decide on the placement of the contract within the original validity period, it may preferably request, before expiry of the original validity period, all the responsive tenderers to extend their tenders up to a specified period. While asking for such extension, the tenderers are also to be asked to extend their offers as it is, without any changes therein. They may also be told to extend the validity of the EMD (wherever applicable) for the corresponding additional period (which is to be specified in the request). A tenderer may not agree to such a request and this will not be tantamount to forfeiture of its EMD. But the tenderers, who agree to extend the validity, are to do so without changing any terms, conditions, and so on, of their original tenders.

### 7.5.3 Variation of Quantities at the Time of Award
At the time of awarding the contract, the quantity to be procured must be re-judged based on the current data, since the ground situation may have very well changed. The tendered quantity can be increased or decreased by 25 (twenty-five) per cent for ordering, if so warranted. This may be mentioned in the tender documents. Any larger variation may throw up issues about transparency.

TEC approval should be obtained based on the cash outflow for the entire tendered quantity, including provision for applicable tolerance / enhancements.

In case there is further requirement of quantity after issuance of order, repeat order procedure may be adopted as applicable.

### 7.5.4 Option clause
In case of long running, yearly procurements, to take care of any change in the requirement during the currency of the contract, a plus/minus option clause normally 25 (twenty-five) per cent may be incorporated in the tender document, reserving purchaser's right to increase or decrease the quantity of the required goods up to that limit without any change in the terms and conditions and prices quoted by the tenderers. Higher the option limit more is the uncertainty for the tenderers in formulating their prices and more is the chance of loading on the prices quoted to take care of such uncertainties.

question_text: According to the standards of financial propriety, what vigilance should officers exercise regarding expenditure from public moneys
answer: - Officers must exercise the same vigilance over expenditure from public moneys as a person of ordinary prudence would exercise over their own money. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 12)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the standards of financial propriety prescribe for officers who handle public money. The question is asking specifically about the vigilance they should exercise, so I look for the rule that directly addresses the attitude or care an officer must show when spending public funds.

Scanning the principles, the first one under the Standards of Financial Propriety catches my eye: it says that every officer incurring or authorizing expenditure from public moneys should be guided by the same vigilance a person of ordinary prudence would exercise over his own money. This seems to be the exact prescription for the kind of care required.

I pause to unpack what “ordinary prudence” means in this context. It implies the level of caution, scrutiny, and restraint that a reasonable person would apply when managing their personal finances—checking prices, avoiding unnecessary expenses, ensuring the spend is justified, and not allowing waste or extravagance.

Linking that back to public expenditure, the principle is essentially saying that officers should treat public money as if it were their own, applying the same personal discipline and careful judgment. This creates a built‑in safeguard against misuse, because the officer’s own sense of financial responsibility becomes the benchmark.

I check whether any other principle might also speak to vigilance, but the others focus on avoiding self‑advantage, limiting expenditure to what the occasion demands, preventing undue benefit to individuals, regulating allowances, and avoiding conflicts of interest in audit. While important, they do not directly define the vigilance standard itself; they elaborate on related safeguards.

Thus, the core answer emerges directly from that first canon: officers must exercise the same vigilance over public money as a person of ordinary prudence would exercise over their own money. This matches the statement I need to reach, confirming that the reasoning is sound and complete.
chunk_content:
## 1.5 Fundamental Principles of Public Procurement
Over and above the basic aims of procurement, the obligations of procuring authorities can be grouped into following five fundamental principles of public procurement, which all procuring authorities must abide by and be accountable for:

- i) Transparency principle;
- ii) Professionalism principle;
- iii) Broader obligations principle;

*(For more details on principles of procurement, please refer to Chapter 1 of the Manual for Procurement of Goods 1).*

## 1.6 Standards (Canons) of Financial Propriety
Public Procurement like any other expenditure in Government must conform to the Standards (also called Canons) of Financial Propriety.

*"Standards of financial propriety: Every officer incurring or authorizing expenditure from public moneys should be guided by high standards of financial propriety. Every officer should also enforce financial order and strict economy and see that all relevant financial rules and regulations are observed, by his own office and by subordinate disbursing officers. Among the principles on which emphasis is generally laid are the following:-*

- i) *Every officer is expected to exercise the same vigilance in respect of expenditure incurred from public moneys as a person of ordinary prudence would exercise in respect of expenditure of his own money.*
- ii) *The expenditure should not be prima facie more than the occasion demands.*
- iii) *No authority should exercise its powers of sanctioning expenditure to pass an order which will be directly or indirectly to its own advantage.*
- iv) *Expenditure from public moneys should not be incurred for the benefit of a particular person or a section of the people, unless -*
  - i) *a claim for the amount could be enforced in a Court of Law, or*
  - ii) *The expenditure is in pursuance of a recognized policy or custom.*
- v) *The amount of allowances granted to meet expenditure of a particular type should be so regulated that the allowances are not on the whole a source of profit to the recipients.*
- vi) *While discharging the duties of financial concurrence of any public expenditure, such authorities subsequent to such decision, shall not be involved in any future audit responsibilities which may create conflict of interest.*

## 1.7 Public Procurement Infrastructure at the Centre


### i) Procurement Policy Division
Procurement Policy Division (PPD) in Department of Expenditure; Ministry of Finance has been created to encourage uniformity and harmonisation in public procurement processes by setting guidelines, dissemination of best practices, providing guidance, oversight and capacity building and issuing of procurement manuals. However, Centralisation of procurement or involvement in procurement processes is not the intended purpose of creation of PPD.

### ii) Central Public Procurement Portal
Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP) has been designed, developed and hosted by National Informatics Centre (NIC, Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology) in association with Dept. of Expenditure to ensure transparency in the public procurement process. The primary objective of the Central Public Procurement portal is to provide a single point access to the information on procurements made across various Ministries and the Departments. The CPPP has e-publishing and e-procurement modules. It is mandatory for all Ministries/ Departments of the Central Government, Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and Autonomous and Statutory Bodies to publish on the CPPP all their tender enquiries and information about the resulting contracts.

question_text: How should the base date be specified in a price variation clause?
answer: **A:** The base date should be given as the exact month and year to which the contract price is linked, allowing price variations to be calculated by reference to the indices prevailing in that month and year. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 105)
cot:
First, I need to understand what a price variation clause is meant to do: it adjusts the contract price when the costs of key inputs like labour, materials or fuel change over the life of the project. The adjustment is made by comparing current cost levels with a reference point that was agreed upon when the contract was signed.  

Next, I consider what that reference point must look like for the calculation to work. The clause will use published indices—such as those from government agencies, chambers of commerce or commodity exchanges—to measure how prices have moved. To turn an index value into a monetary adjustment, the contract has to know what index value corresponded to the original price. Therefore the reference point must be tied to a specific time period for which the index is known.  

Then I think about the granularity of that time period. Indices are typically released monthly (or sometimes quarterly), and they are reported as a value for a given month and year. If the contract only specified a year, the exact month‑level index would be ambiguous, leading to disagreement over which figure to use. Specifying both month and year removes that ambiguity and gives a single, unambiguous index value to serve as the base.  

After that, I verify that this specification satisfies the purpose of the clause. With a clear month‑year base date, the party calculating the variation can take the index for that month‑year, compare it to the index for the month in which the adjustment is being made, apply the agreed weightings and formula, and arrive at a fair adjustment for labour, material and POL costs. This also makes it easier to compare bids, because every tenderer will be using the same base date when they quote their prices.  

Finally, I pull the reasoning together: the base date in a price variation clause must be stated as the precise month and year to which the contract price is linked. Doing so provides the exact index level needed as the starting point for all subsequent variation calculations, ensuring the adjustments are objective, reproducible and aligned with the indices that will be used throughout the contract. This matches the requirement that the base date be given as the exact month and year to which the price is linked, allowing variations to be calculated by reference to the indices prevailing in that month and year.

This will deal with rise and fall of the prices in construction materials/ labour and other key inputs. However, this shall not be applicable in the contracts where period of completion is 12 (twelve) months or less. The provision of price variation clauses enables contractors to factor this reduced risk and quote more competitive prices.

The amount payable to the contractor shall be adjusted in respect of the rise or fall in the cost of labour, Petroleum, Oils and Lubricants (POL) and materials to the work for which appropriate formulae shall be prescribed in the contract and shall form part of the tender document.

To the extent that full compensation for any rise or fall in costs to the contractor is not covered by the provisions of the contract, the unit rates and prices included in the contract shall be deemed to include amounts to cover the contingencies of such uncovered portion of rise or fall of costs.

The formulae may be based on weightages of the material/ labour/ POL and cost indices/ base prices. Indices shall be appropriate for their purpose and shall relate to the contractor's proposed source of supply of inputs on the basis of which his contract price shall have been computed.

If any statutory regulations or bye-laws come into force after submission of the bids, which cause additional or reduced cost to the contractor in the execution of the contract, such statutory additional or reduced cost (except which are covered in cost indices) shall be added or deducted from the contract price.

Short-term contracts where the delivery period does not extend beyond 12 (twelve) months should normally be concluded with a firm price fixed by inviting tenders accordingly. However, even for shorter deliveries, the price adjustment [or Price Variation Clause (PVC)] may be stipulated for items with inputs (raw material, man power, etc.), prone to short-term price volatility - especially for critical or high value works - otherwise there is a possibility of the contract failing or the purchaser having to pay a higher price if prices fall.

Where it is decided to conclude the contract with a variable price, an appropriate clause incorporating, inter-alia, a suitable price variation formula should also be provided in the tender documents, to calculate the price variation between the base level and scheduled delivery date. It is best to proactively provide our own PVC in the tender document to discourage different bidders quoting different formulae and different base dates, which may lead to problems on bringing their prices on a common comparable footing.

The variations are to be calculated periodically by using indices published by Governments/ chambers of commerce/London Metal Exchange / any other neutral and fair source of indices. Suitable weights are to be assigned to the applicable elements, that is, fixed overheads and profits, material and labour in the price variation formula. If the production of goods needs more than one raw material, the input cost of material may be further sub-divided for different categories of material, for which cost indices are published.

The following are important elements of PVC:

- a) The price agreed upon should specify the base date, that is, the month and year to which the price is linked to enable variations being calculated with reference to the price indices prevailing in that month and year;
- b) The price variation formula must also stipulate a minimum percentage of variation of the contract price, only above which the price variation will be admissible (for example, where the resultant increase is lower than, say, two per cent of the

contract price, no price adjustment will be made in favour of the supplier);

question_text: What is mandatory for audited annual reports or financial statements issued after July 2019?
answer: - Audited annual reports or financial statements issued after July 2019 must be accompanied by a UDIN number; reports without a UDIN are not considered for evaluation. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 37)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: it wants to know what must be present for audited annual reports or financial statements that are dated after July 2019.  
The Procurement of Works Manual specifies that, beginning in July 2019, every audited annual report or financial statement needs to be accompanied by a UDIN number.  
It further states that any financial report issued after July 2019 that does not have a UDIN will not be considered for evaluation.  
Putting those points together, the mandatory element for such reports is the UDIN number; without it, the report is rejected.  
Therefore, the answer is that audited annual reports or financial statements issued after July 2019 must be accompanied by a UDIN number, and reports lacking a UDIN are not accepted.

question_text: What type of goods are typically subject to post‑delivery inspection on receipt at the consignee’s site?
answer: Off‑the‑shelf, BIS‑marked final goods that are intended for immediate consumption or use (excluding machinery installations) and require only a physical inspection of their physical characteristics—without a detailed manufacturing‑process inspection—are typically subject to post‑delivery inspection on receipt at the consignee’s site. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 157)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: which kinds of items normally get checked after they arrive at the buyer’s place before they are accepted.  

Then I recall the description of post‑delivery inspection: it takes place on receipt, before acceptance, and is meant for goods that are ready‑to‑use off the shelf and carry a BIS mark.  

Next, I note that this is limited to final goods that will be consumed or used right away, and it explicitly excludes things like machinery installations that would need a more elaborate examination.  

Further, I understand that only a simple physical check of the item’s outward characteristics is required; there is no need to re‑examine the whole manufacturing process.  

Putting these points together, the goods that satisfy all these conditions are off‑the‑shelf, BIS‑marked final products intended for immediate use (excluding machinery installations) that need only a physical inspection of their physical traits.  

Therefore, those are the types of goods that are typically subject to post‑delivery inspection on receipt at the consignee’s site.
chunk_content:
#### ii) **Inspection of Goods on Receipt at Consignee/User's Site**
Post-delivery inspection is carried out on receipt of goods before accepting them. This should be typically done for goods that are available off-the-shelf and are BIS marked. All final goods that may be directly consumed or utilised on delivery (excluding machinery installations, and so on) and for which detailed inspection of the manufacturing process is not required and only a physical inspection regarding their

physical characteristics is required, may be inspected using this method. On receipt of goods at stores, the storekeeper should immediately notify the officer nominated for inspection, requesting to schedule an inspection. The inspecting officer should then fix a date for inspection.

The consignee has the right to reject the goods on receipt during the final inspection on delivery even though the goods have already been inspected and cleared at the pre-dispatch stage by Procuring Entity's inspector. However, such rejection should be strictly within the contractual terms and conditions and no new condition should be adopted while rejecting the goods during final inspection.

Goods accepted by the purchaser after inspections, in terms of the contract, shall in no way dilute the purchaser's right to reject them later, if found deficient in terms of the warranty clause of the contract.

In case of rejection of goods at this stage, the material rejection advice/rejection memo/debit note should be issued. In case of pre-inspected goods, a joint inspection of the rejected lot of goods should be held with the pre-inspecting agency and firm, wherever feasible. In case of failure of the firm to associate with a joint inspection, it should be held with the pre-inspecting agency.

In case of rejection of the pre-inspected supply of goods at the consignee end, the material rejection advice/rejection memo should be sent to all concerned, which is, the firm, purchaser, pre-inspecting agency, paying authority, and so on - without fail where recovery exists. In case of replacement supply against the rejected lot of goods, the process should remain exactly the same in terms of sequence of pre-inspection/inspection as laid down in the contract, prior to acceptance by the consignee. In case of acceptance of the replacement supply/rejected supply after rectification, the earlier issued material rejection advice/ rejection memo should be withdrawn under advice to all concerned.

question_text: Which Incoterms term indicates that the seller pays for carriage to the named place of destination
answer: The Incoterm that indicates the seller pays for carriage to the named place of destination is **CPT – Carriage Paid To** (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 115).
cot:
First, I need to identify what the question is asking for: an Incoterm where the seller assumes the cost of transporting the goods to a specific destination point.  

Next, I think about how Incoterms are organized in terms of who bears the freight charges. The Ex‑Group places all costs on the buyer from the point of departure, so none of those terms fit. The Free Group explicitly states that the seller does not pay freight, which also rules out those options.  

That leaves the C Group, where the seller is responsible for paying the freight. Within this group there are several specific terms. CPT stands for Carriage Paid To, which directly indicates that the seller pays for carriage to a named place of destination. CIP includes insurance in addition to carriage, while CFR and CIF are restricted to sea or inland waterway transport only.  

Since the question does not mention any mode restriction and only concerns carriage to a named place, CPT is the term that precisely matches the description.  

Finally, I verify that this aligns with the answer provided: the seller pays for carriage to the named place of destination under CPT – Carriage Paid To.

The risk to goods (damage, loss, shortage, and so on) is the responsibility of the person who holds the 'title of goods' at that point of time. This may be different from actual physical possession of such goods. Normally, unless otherwise defined, the title of goods passes from the supplier to the purchaser in accordance with the terms of delivery (FOR, CFR, among others). The terms of delivery, therefore, specify when the ownership and title of goods pass from the seller to buyer, along with the associated risks. Incoterms as described by the International Chamber of Commerce are an internationally accepted interpretation of the terms of delivery. These terms of delivery allocate responsibilities to the buyer and seller, with respect to: - i) Control and care of the goods while in transit; - ii) Carrier selection, transfers and related issues; - iii) Costs of freight, insurance, taxes, duties and forwarding fees; and - iv) Documentation, problem resolution and other related issues. In use since 1936, Incoterms have been revised in 2010. Out of the 11 Incoterms options, seven apply to all modes of transportation whereas four apply only to water transportation.

question_text: Besides service payments, what other sums may the contractor be required to pay the owner according to the contract
answer:
- Payments for controlled items of consumable materials.  
- Payments for loss or damage to the owner's equipment, materials, construction plant and machinery.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 140)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know, apart from the service payments the contractor makes for things like power and water, what additional amounts the contract might obligate the contractor to pay the owner.  

I recall that the contract distinguishes between payments for services rendered by the owner and other kinds of sums that can become due. The service payments are explicitly mentioned as covering utilities such as power supply and water supply.  

The contract lists further obligations in a clause that speaks of “such other sums as may become payable to the OWNER.” This phrase signals that there are categories of payment beyond the service fees.  

Within that same clause, two distinct categories are specified: one relates to the controlled items of consumable materials, and the other concerns loss or damage to the owner’s equipment, materials, construction plant, and machinery.  

These two categories naturally fit the pattern of “other sums” because they are not tied to the provision of services like power or water; instead they arise from the use or handling of materials and from potential harm to the owner’s assets.  

Putting it together, besides the service payments, the contractor may be required to pay the owner for the controlled consumable materials used in the works and for any loss or damage inflicted on the owner’s equipment, materials, plant, or machinery.  

This matches the answer given: payments for controlled items of consumable materials and payments for loss or damage to the owner's equipment, materials, construction plant and machinery.
