question_text: What information will the buyer give me in the tender documents for a turnkey project?
answer: The buyer’s tender documents will tell you the performance and output the plant must achieve, outline the main parameters they have in mind for the plant, and list the inputs and other facilities they will provide. This information lets you design the plant and prepare your quote accordingly. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 141)
cot:
I start by thinking about what a turnkey arrangement really means: the buyer wants a fully operational plant handed over ready to run, so they need to tell the contractor exactly what that plant must do.  
The first piece of information, therefore, is the required performance and output – the throughput, quality standards, or any other measurable result the plant has to achieve once it’s commissioned.  
Next, the buyer has to convey how they imagine the plant working; this means spelling out the main parameters they have in mind, such as design capacity, operating pressure, temperature ranges, efficiency targets, or any specific configuration details that will guide the contractor’s design.  
Then, because the contractor won’t be providing everything from scratch, the buyer must list what they themselves will supply – things like utilities, site preparation, existing buildings, or ancillary services – so the contractor knows which inputs and facilities are already available and which need to be sourced or built.  
Armed with the performance target, the key parameters, and the clear outline of buyer‑provided inputs and facilities, the contractor can now develop a plant design that meets the spec and put together a realistic quote.  
Running through these points, I see that they exactly match what the answer states: the tender documents give the performance and output, outline the main parameters, and list the inputs and facilities the buyer will provide, enabling the contractor to design the plant and prepare a quote.
chunk_content: In the context of procurement of goods, a turnkey contract may include the manufacture, supply, assembly, installation/ commissioning of equipment (or a group of plant and machines working in tandem - even though some of the machines may not be manufactured by the supplier himself) and some incidental works or services. Generally, in the tender enquiry documents for a turn key contract, the purchase organization specifies the performance and output required from the plant proposed to be set up and broadly outlines the various parameters it visualizes for the desired plant. The inputs and other facilities, which the purchase organization will provide to the contractor, are also indicated in the tender enquiry document. The contractor is to design the plant and quote accordingly. The responsibility of the contractor will include supplying the required goods, machinery, equipment etc. needed for the plant; assembling, installing and erecting the same at site as needed; commissioning the plant to meet the required output etc., as specified in the tender enquiry documents.

question_text: Is the physical examination of export documents, gifts, samples, and export goods limited to a maximum of 10% of total courier consignments or based on specific intelligence?
answer:
- Clause 4.1(b): Physical examination of export documents, gifts, samples, and export goods.  
  - Verification: Ensure that the physical examination is limited to a maximum of 10 % of total courier consignments or based on specific intelligence; any consignment selected for examination must be examined 100 % (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 233).
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants to know whether the physical examination of export documents, gifts, samples, and export goods is capped at 10 % of all courier consignments or can be triggered by specific intelligence.  

Next, I focus on the part of the reference that deals with courier consignments, because the question explicitly mentions courier shipments.  

Within that section, I look for the paragraph that talks about physical examination of export‑related items—documents, gifts, samples, and the goods themselves.  

I find a statement that says the physical examination of those export items is limited to a maximum of 10 % of the total courier consignments, unless there is specific intelligence, in which case the examination can be based on that intelligence; any consignment chosen for examination must be examined fully (100 %).  

Putting those pieces together, the rule directly answers the question: the examination is indeed limited to a maximum of 10 % of total courier consignments or can be conducted on the basis of specific intelligence, with selected consignments examined completely.  

Thus, the correct reference is the clause covering physical examination of export documents, gifts, samples, and export goods under the courier examination norms.
chunk_content:
#### 4. Examination norms for goods imported or exported by courier:
4.1 The following examination norms are provided for import and export of courier consignments:

(a) 100% screening of import/ export consignments (documents and all types of cargo) is required to be done through X-ray or other NII techniques. Wherever possible the facility of X-ray machines available with Customs could be used; otherwise the airlines or AAI's screening facility may be

resorted to for such • screening. Further, wherever feasible such screening by multi-agencies could be combined to reduce the time taken and avoid duplicity.

(b) Physical examination of export documents, gifts, samples and export goods limited up to a maximum of 10% of the total courier consignments or specific intelligence. The consignments so selected will be examined 100%.

(c) Physical examination of import documents, gifts, samples and dutiable goods limited up to a maximum of 10% of the total courier consignments. The consignments so selected will be examined 100%.

(d) Selection of consignments physical examination would be based on the various parameters such as nature of goods, value, weight, status of importer etc.

(e) Commissioner of Customs in respective port can exercise the discretion of random examination of goods, on specific parameter such as country of import/export, nature of goods as presently provided in the EDI system.

(f) Any consignment can be examined by the Customs (even upto 100% examination), if there is any specific intelligence or there is doubt during X-ray in respect of the said consignment.

(g) Under the automated process the consignments would be identified for examination on the basis of 'risk analysis'.

## 5. Import and Export through Post


### 1. Introduction:
1.1 The facility for import and export of goods by Post Parcels is provided by the Postal Department at its Foreign Post Offices and sub-Foreign Post Offices. Customs facilities for examination, assessment, clearance etc. are available at these Post Offices. Limited facility for export clearances is also available at

Export Extension Counters opened by the Postal Department where parcels for # export are accepted and cleared by the Customs.

### 2. Legal Provisions:
2.1 Goods imported through post are classified under Chapter Heading 9804 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and rate of duty applicable thereon is charged on all the goods imported by post. Importantly, Heading 9804 specifically applies to goods permitted for import through post which are exempted from prohibition under Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992.

2.2 Goods imported or exported by post are governed by Sections 82, 83 and 84 of the Customs Act, 1962 whereas the procedure for clearance of goods through post is prescribed in Rules regarding Postal Parcels and Letter Packets from Foreign Ports In/Out of India of 1953.

2.3 In respect of import and exports through post, any label or declaration accompanying the packet or parcel containing details like description, quantity and value of the goods is treated as entry for import or export of the goods and no separate manifest for such goods is required to be filed.

2.4 The relevant date for rate of duty and tariff value, if any, applicable in respect of imports through post is the date on which the postal authorities present to the Proper Officer of Customs the list containing details of the goods for assessment. Thus, presentation of said list is equivalent to filing of

Bill of Entry so far as assessment of goods imported by post is concerned.

2.5 If the post parcels come through a vessel and the said list presented by the postal authorities is presented before arrival of the vessel, the rate of duty and tariff value applicable shall be as on the date of arrival of the vessel i.e. Entry Inward of the vessel.

2.6 In respect of export goods, the relevant date for rate of duty and tariff value, if any, applicable, is the date on which the exporter delivers the goods to postal authorities for exportation.

question_text: What is the stated purpose of the Courier Imports and Exports (Electronic Declaration and Processing) Regulations, 2010?
answer: - Verify that the Courier Imports and Exports (Electronic Declaration and Processing) Regulations, 2010 are applied to facilitate quick Customs clearance of courier‑imported or courier‑exported goods after any required duties have been discharged, thereby enabling timely delivery to the consignees. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 222)
cot:
First, I focus on what the question is really asking: it wants the explicit purpose attributed to the Courier Imports and Exports (Electronic Declaration and Processing) Regulations, 2010.
Then, I recall the description of how courier‑borne goods are handled, noting that this regulation is grouped with the earlier Clearance Regulations and immediately followed by a statement about what those rules achieve.
The Procurement of Goods Manual states that these regulations “facilitate such goods in terms of quick Customs clearance, after discharge of duties, if any, for delivery to the consignees,” which directly links the regulation to a speed‑up of the clearance process once any duties are settled.
Seeing that the purpose is tied to both the speed of clearance and the subsequent delivery, I also note the mention of dedicated courier terminals staffed by customs officers, which reinforces the idea that the regulation is meant to streamline the flow of courier cargo.
Putting these pieces together, I conclude that the stated purpose of the Courier Imports and Exports (Electronic Declaration and Processing) Regulations, 2010 is to enable quick customs clearance of courier‑imported or courier‑exported goods after any required duties have been paid, thereby ensuring that the goods can be delivered promptly to the consignees.
chunk_content:
#### 8. Import/Export by post/courier:
8.1 Customs is charged with coordination with Postal authorities for giving Customs clearances after appropriate checks on selective basis of various goods coming as post parcels etc. Customs also ensure that these postal mail/packets/parcels enter into the country in accordance with the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962. Unless the goods brought by post are within the value limits prescribed for free gift or free samples these have to be assessed to duties by Customs and the same indicated to

Postal authorities. The duties are collected before the Postal authorities deliver the goods to addressees.

8.2 Imports/exports through couriers are governed by the Courier Imports and Exports (Clearance) Regulations, 1998 and the Courier Imports and Exports (Electronic Declaration and Processing) Regulations, 2010. These Regulations facilitate such goods in terms of quick Customs clearance, after discharge of duties, if any, for delivery to the consignees. At few places dedicated Courier terminals manned by Customs officers (akin to Air Cargo Complexes) are established to handle courier cargo.

### Detailed Procedure for clearance of Imported and Exported goods:
1. The imported goods before clearance for home consumption or for warehousing are required to comply with prescribed Customs clearance formalities. This includes presentation of a Bill of Entry containing details such as description of goods, value, quantity, and exemption notification etc., Customs Tariff Heading. This Bill of Entry is subject to verification by the proper officer of Customs (under self assessment scheme) and may be reassessed if declarations are found to be incorrect. Normally import declarations made are scrutinized without prior examination of goods with reference to documents made available and other information about the value/ classification etc. It is at the time of clearance of goods that these are examined by the Customs to confirm the nature of goods, valuation and other aspects of the declarations. In case no discrepancies are observed at the time of examination of goods, 'Out of Charge' order is issued and thereafter the goods can be cleared. Similarly, Customs clearance formalities for goods meant for export have to be fulfilled by presenting a Shipping Bill and other related documents. These documents are verified for correctness of assessment and after examination of the goods, if warranted, 'Let Export Order' is given on the Shipping Bill.

question_text: How should additional services be handled under a lump‑sum contract to regulate payment
answer:
**Handling Additional Services under a Lump‑Sum Contract**  
*Step‑by‑Step Instructional Guide for Procurement Officers (mid‑level)*  

---

### 1. Identify the Need for Additional Services  
- Review the original scope of work and deliverables.  
- Determine whether any new tasks or outputs are required that were not covered in the initial lump‑sum agreement.  
- Document the specific nature of the extra services (e.g., additional field surveys, supplemental data analysis, extra reporting).  

### 2. Assess Impact on Scope and Cost  
- Estimate the additional effort, time, and resources required.  
- Calculate the projected cost increase as a percentage of the original contract price.  
- Verify that the estimated increase falls within the allowable range for lump‑sum contracts (generally **not more than 10‑15 %**).  

### 3. Prepare a Contract Variation Request  
- Draft a formal variation request that includes:  
  - Description of the extra services.  
  - Revised deliverables and milestones.  
  - Updated cost breakdown showing the increase.  
  - Justification for why the amendment is necessary.  
- Attach any supporting documents (e.g., revised work plan, cost estimates).  

### 4. Submit the Variation to the Procuring Entity  
- Forward the variation request to the procuring entity’s designated contract officer.  
- Ensure submission occurs **timely**, before any work on the extra services begins, to avoid disputes over payment.  
- Keep a record of the submission date and any acknowledgment received.  

### 5. Obtain Approval and Amend the Contract  
- Await formal approval from the procuring entity.  
- Once approved, execute a contract variation that:  
  - Incorporates the additional services into the scope of work.  
  - Adjusts the contract price to reflect the agreed increase.  
  - Updates any relevant schedules (e.g., reporting dates, payment milestones).  
- Ensure both parties sign the variation and retain copies in the contract file.  

### 6. Monitor Implementation and Payment  
- Track progress of the newly added services against the updated schedule.  
- Verify that stage payments are released only after the quality of draft reports or deliverables has been checked, as required for lump‑sum contracts.  
- Confirm that the cumulative increase does not exceed the 10‑15 % limit; if it does, initiate a further variation or seek alternative funding.  

---

#### Practical Example  
A consultancy contract for a city‑wide traffic study originally includes data collection at 20 intersections. Mid‑project, the client requests counts at five additional intersections. The procurement officer:  

1. Identifies the extra five intersections as additional services.  
2. Estimates the extra work will raise the contract price by 12 %.  
3. Prepares a variation request detailing the new intersections, revised deliverables, and cost increase.  
4. Submits the request to the procuring entity before fieldwork begins.  
5. Receives approval, signs the variation, and updates the contract price accordingly.  
6. Monitors the extra fieldwork, ensuring payments are tied to satisfactory draft reports and that the total increase stays within the 12 % (≤15 %) threshold.  

#### Common Pitfalls to Avoid  
- **Delaying the variation request** – starting extra work before approval can lead to non‑payment or disputes.  
- **Exceeding the allowable increase** – going beyond 10‑15 % without a new variation breaches contract terms and may trigger claims.  
- **Failing to document the amendment** – undocumented changes create ambiguity and complicate audit or close‑out processes.  
- **Neglecting quality checks** – releasing stage payments without verifying draft reports can result in rework and disputes after task completion.  

By following these steps, procurement officers can ensure that additional services under a lump‑sum contract are properly incorporated, payments are regulated, and the risk of disputes is minimized. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 62)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: when a lump‑sum contract is in place and extra work shows up, how do we make sure that payment for that extra work is properly controlled and does not lead to disputes. The core of a lump‑sum agreement is that the price is fixed for a defined set of deliverables, so any change to that set must be reflected in the contract itself; otherwise the provider could perform work without a clear basis for payment, and the procuring entity could be unwilling to pay. 

Next, I think about the conditions that trigger this situation. The extra work must be something that falls outside the original scope—new tasks, additional deliverables, or extra effort that was not priced in the original lump sum. Because the contract price is tied to output, the only way to regulate payment is to formally adjust the contract to incorporate those new outputs and to adjust the price accordingly. 

From there, I reason that the first practical step is to recognize and document exactly what the additional services are. I would review the original scope, list the new items, and describe them in enough detail that both parties understand what is being added. Once I have that description, I need to estimate how much effort, time, and resources the new work will require and translate that into a cost impact. Since lump‑sum contracts usually allow only a modest adjustment for changes, I would check that the estimated increase stays within the generally accepted band of roughly ten to fifteen percent of the original price; if it exceeds that, a different approach might be needed, but for now I assume it falls within the limit.

Having quantified the change, the next logical move is to prepare a formal contract variation. This variation should contain a clear description of the extra services, the revised deliverables and milestones, an updated cost breakdown showing the increase, and a justification explaining why the amendment is necessary. I would attach any supporting sketches, work plans, or cost estimates that make the request transparent. 

After the variation is drafted, I would submit it to the procuring entity’s contract officer promptly—ideally before any work on the extra services begins. Timing matters because starting the work without approval risks creating a situation where the provider has performed but has no contractual basis for payment, which can lead to claims. I would keep a record of the submission date and any acknowledgment to demonstrate that the request was made in good faith. 

Once the procuring entity reviews the request, I would await formal approval. Upon receiving it, I would execute the variation: both parties sign the document, the additional services are incorporated into the scope of work, the contract price is adjusted to reflect the agreed increase, and any related schedules—such as reporting dates or payment milestones—are updated. I would make sure copies of the signed variation are filed with the original contract so that the amendment is part of the official record. 

With the contract now updated, I turn to monitoring implementation. I would track progress of the newly added services against the revised schedule, ensuring that stage payments are released only after the quality of draft reports or deliverables has been checked, as is customary for lump‑sum contracts where payment is tied to output verification. I would also keep a running total of the cumulative increase to confirm it does not surpass the ten‑to‑fifteen percent ceiling; if it ever looks like it might, I would prepare another variation or seek alternative funding before proceeding further. 

To illustrate, imagine a traffic‑study contract that originally covered twenty intersections. Mid‑project the client asks for counts at five more intersections. I would note those five as additional services, estimate that they raise the price by about twelve percent, draft a variation describing the new intersections and the cost increase, submit it before fieldwork starts, get approval, sign the variation, and then monitor the extra fieldwork, releasing payments only after satisfactory draft reports are verified and confirming the total increase stays within the twelve‑percent limit. 

Finally, I reflect on common missteps that could undermine this process: delaying the variation request and starting work early, exceeding the allowable increase without a new amendment, failing to document the change which creates ambiguity, and releasing payments without verifying draft reports, which can lead to rework and disputes. By avoiding those pitfalls and following the outlined steps, the additional services are properly incorporated, payment is regulated, and the risk of conflict is minimized. 

This line of reasoning naturally leads to the step‑by‑step guide for handling additional services under a lump‑sum contract that regulates payment.
chunk_content:
## 8.5 Reporting of Progress
The timing, nature, and number of reports that the consultant/ service provider should provide are normally contained in the Consultancy and other services contract. If the assignment is of a routine nature over a long period (for example, implementation supervision), then monthly, quarterly, and annual progress reports may be required. On the other hand, if the assignment is to prepare a study or to implement a particular task, a more specific type of reporting may be required.

## 8.6 Monitoring a Time-based Contract
As indicated earlier, the performance of a time-based contract may depend on the progress in other contracts (for example, the progress of a construction supervision contract depends on the progress of a construction contract). In such situations, the mobilisation and demobilisation of resources/ key experts and time employed by them should be mobilised and monitored carefully as it is possible that the contract period and the total amount under the contract are spent fully and construction work being supervised is not even half complete. These situations could lead to claims and disputes.

## 8.7 Monitoring a Lump-sum Contract
As Lump-sum contract is based on output and deliverables, it is important that the quality of draft reports is checked carefully before release of stage payment as subsequent dispute after completion of the task could lead to disputes. In this form of contract, if there are extra additional services, there should be timely amendment to the contract to reflect these increases and to regulate payment. In general, in a lump-sum contract, the increase should not be more than 10-15 (ten to fifteen) per cent.

## 8.8 Unsatisfactory Performance
Poor performance may involve one or more particular staff from the consultant/ service provider's team, or the whole team or non-participation by the main qualifying JV member. Based on the provisions of the contract, the Procuring Entity will advise the consultant/ service provider to take the necessary measures to address the situation. Poor performance should not be tolerated; therefore, the consultant/ service provider should act quickly to comply with a reasonable request to improve the performance of the team or to replace any particular staff member who is not performing adequately. If the consultant/ service provider fails to take adequate corrective actions, the Procuring Entity may take up the issue with the top management of the consultant/ service provider and issue notice to rectify the situation and finally consider terminating the contract.

## 8.9 Delays
Consultancy and other services may be delayed for a variety of reasons. The consultant/ service

provider should notify the Procuring Entity and explain the causes of such delays. If corrective action requires extra work and the delay cannot be attributed to the consultant/ service provider, the extra work should be reimbursed in accordance with the contract.

## 8.10 Issuing Contract Variations
8.10.1 The formal method of making and documenting a change in the Consultancy and other services contract is through a contract variation.

Contract variations are issued when there are agreed-upon changes in the scope of work, personnel inputs, costs, timing of the submission of reports, or out-of-pocket expenditures. There are few Consultancy and other services contracts of any type that do not require a contract variation at one time or another. Normally, these relate to changes that have a cost implication, but when there is a significant change in the timing of an activity or a particular output, these should also be recorded through a contract variation. Normally, the request for contract variation is prepared by the consultant/ service provider or Consultancy/ service provider firm and submitted to the Procuring Entity.

question_text: From whom are responses evaluated in the second stage of a two stage bid
answer: - Responses are evaluated from the shortlisted qualified bidders (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 73).
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants to know who supplies the responses that are evaluated during the second stage of a two‑stage bid.  
Thinking about how a two‑stage bidding procedure works, the first stage is usually a prequalification or expression of interest step designed to weed out unsuitable bidders and leave only those who meet the basic qualification criteria.  
Because the purpose of that initial stage is to create a shortlist of competent bidders, the second stage does not open the floor to everyone; it is limited to those bidders who have already been deemed qualified after the first stage.  
Consequently, the responses that are examined in the second stage come solely from this group of shortlisted, qualified bidders.  
The description of the two‑stage process notes that after the PQB/EOI stage (the first stage) has been evaluated, the second stage focuses on evaluating the responses to the second‑stage multiple envelopes from those shortlisted qualified bidders.  
Putting these points together, the answer is clear: the responses evaluated in the second stage of a two‑stage bid are those submitted by the shortlisted qualified bidders.
chunk_content:
### 5.4.4 Clarification of Bids/ Shortfall Documents
During evaluation and comparison of bids, the Procuring Entity may, at his discretion, ask the bidder for clarifications on the bid. The request for clarification shall be given in writing by e-mail / through e-tendering portal, and so on, asking the tenderer to respond by a specified date, and also mentioning therein that, if the tenderer does not comply or respond by the date, his tender will be liable to be rejected. Depending on the outcome, such tenders are to be ignored or considered further. No change in prices or substance of the bid including specifications, shall be sought, offered or permitted. No post-bid clarification at the initiative of the bidder shall be entertained. The shortfall information/ documents should be sought only in case of historical documents which pre-existed at the time of the tender opening and which have not undergone change since then.

(Example: if the Permanent Account Number, GSTN number has been asked to be submitted and the tenderer has not provided them, these documents may be asked for with a target date as above). So far as the submission of documents is concerned with regard to qualification criteria, after submission of the tender, only related shortfall documents should be asked for and considered. For example, if the bidder has submitted a contract without its completion/ performance certificate, the certificate can be asked for and considered. However, no new contract should be asked for so as to qualify the bidder.

If the bidder cites any reference of a job executed for NRL and the bidder is not able to furnish documentary evidence, the internal records of shall be considered.

## 5.5 Evaluation of Responsive Bids
In case of single stage single envelope bidding, the evaluation of qualification of bidders,

technical, commercial and financial aspect is done simultaneously. In single stage multiple envelopes, initially only the techno-commercial bids would be opened and evaluated for bids which successfully meet the qualification criteria and techno-commercial aspects. Financial bids of such successful bidders only would be opened for selecting the L1 bidder (the lowest evaluated, substantially responsive, technically- suitable bid from eligible and qualified bidder) among these and in case of manual tenders, financial bids of techno-commercially unsuccessful bidders would not be opened or be returned unopened to them. In two stage bids, the PQB/ EOI stage would have already been evaluated as detailed in Chapter 3 and this second stage is for evaluation of responses to the Second Stage multiple envelopes from the shortlisted qualified bidders. Evaluation of techno-commercial and financial aspects are, however, discussed separately below.

question_text: What steps are recommended to avoid disputes before they escalate
answer:
**A:** Parties should make reasonable efforts to deal with problems as they arise, working together on a mutually constructive basis; this may include actions such as repatriating consultant/service‑provider staff or changing the Procuring Entity’s CMC/EIC personnel if needed.  
**Rationale:** Addressing issues early and cooperatively helps prevent them from developing into formal disputes. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 63)
cot: First, I consider what usually turns a minor disagreement into a formal dispute – it’s when problems are left unattended or handled adversarially. Then, I look for ways to stop that progression: the most direct is to address each issue as soon as it appears, before it can grow. Next, I think about how the parties should engage when they do address an issue; a mutually constructive approach keeps the conversation focused on solutions rather than blame, which reduces the chance of hardening positions. After that, I ask what concrete measures can support that constructive stance; if the problem stems from personnel mismatches or unavailable expertise, bringing in the right people or, conversely, sending home unsuitable staff can restore alignment, and similarly adjusting the client’s project‑management team can improve communication. Finally, I synthesize these points: to keep disputes from escalating, parties ought to make reasonable efforts to tackle problems promptly, work together constructively, and, when needed, adjust staff or personnel on either side.
chunk_content:
## 8.13 Disputes and Conflicts
8.13.1 Disputes between the consultant/ service provider and the client may arise for a number of reasons. This could relate to technical and administrative matters such as interpretation of contract, payment for services or substitution of key experts - all of which should be dealt with promptly and amicably between the contracting parties in terms of contract provisions. These may be the result of delays prompted by weaknesses on the part of the consultant/ service provider or the Procuring Entity; by a lack of funds; by delays in getting key approvals, data, or information; or by causes beyond anyone's control such as natural disasters. These may be the result of deviations from the Scope of Work or work plan by the consultant/ service provider or out-of-course requests for deviations by the Procuring Entity.

8.13.2 All reasonable efforts should be made to avoid disputes in the first place; both parties should attempt to deal with problems as they arise, on a mutually constructive basis. (This may include the repatriation of consultant/ service provider staff if necessary or a change in the personnel of the Procuring Entity's CMC/EIC) If this is not possible, GCC sets clear procedures for dealing with disputes. This entails provision of a notification of dispute by one party to the other, and provision for a mutual resolution at higher levels of authority within the consultant/ service provider and the Procuring Entity. Finally, if the dispute cannot be amicably settled between the consultant/ service provider and the Procuring Entity, then provision is made for arbitration under the Arbitration Clause. The award decreed by arbitration tribunal is binding.

For further details please refer section 6.10.1 and 6.10.2 of the “Manual for Procurement of Works”

## 8.14 Force Majeure
8.14.1 A Force Majeure (FM) means extraordinary events or circumstance beyond human control such as an event described as an act of God (like a natural calamity) or events such as a war, strike, riots, rebellion or sabotage, lockouts, crimes, hostility, acts of public enemy, civil commotion, fires, explosions, floods, earthquakes, epidemics, quarantine restrictions and freight embargoes (but not including negligence or wrong-doing, predictable/seasonal rain and any other events specifically excluded in the clause). An FM clause in the contract frees both parties from contractual liability or obligation when prevented by such events from fulfilling their obligations under the contract. An FM clause does not excuse a party's non-performance entirely, but only suspends it for the duration of the FM. The firm has to give notice of FM as soon as possible and it cannot be claimed ex-post facto. There may be a FM situation affecting the purchase organisation only. In such a situation, the purchase organisation is to communicate with the supplier along similar lines as above for further necessary action. If the performance in whole or in part or any obligation under this contract is

prevented or delayed by any reason of FM for a period exceeding 90 (ninety) days, either party may at its option terminate the contract without any financial repercussion on either side.

8.14.2 Any delays in or failure of the performance of either party hereto shall not constitute default hereunder or give rise to any claims for damages, if any, to the extent such delays or failure of performance is caused by force majeure.

question_text: What information is shown on the checklist that I return to the exporter/CHA after the Customs Officer's review
answer:
The checklist you return to the exporter/CHA after the Customs Officer’s review includes the following information:

- The custodian’s endorsement confirming that the goods have been received at the dock.  
- Any other declarations that were submitted with the shipment.  
- A record of the original documents you presented – typically the commercial invoice, packing list, AR‑4 form and similar paperwork.  
- After verifying the quantity received, the Customs Officer writes their name on the checklist and indicates which packages, if any, are selected for further examination.

All of these details are entered on the same checklist that you hand back to the exporter/CHA so they can see what was verified and what, if anything, still needs to be looked at. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 226)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know what details appear on the checklist that is handed back to the exporter or CHA after the Customs Officer has finished reviewing the export goods.  

Next, I recall the part of the procedure that describes the handling of that checklist. When the goods arrive at the dock, the exporter/CHA presents the checklist together with the custodian’s endorsement, any other declarations, and the original documents such as the invoice, packing list and AR‑4 form.  

Then, the Customs Officer checks the quantity of the goods actually received, records that verification in the system, and afterwards hands the original documents to the Dock Appraiser. ## Classification/Assessment of Projects Imports, Baggage and Postal imports


### 1. Project imports:
1.1 'Project Imports' is an Indian innovation to facilitate setting up of and expansion of industrial projects. Normally, imported goods are classified separately under different tariff headings and assessed to applicable Customs duty, but as a variety of goods are imported for setting up an industrial project their separate classification and valuation for assessment to duty becomes cumbersome. Further, the suppliers of a contracted project, do not value each and every item or parts of machinery which are supplied in stages. Hence, ascertaining values for different items delay assessment leading to demurrage and time and cost overruns for the project. Therefore, to facilitate

smooth and quick assessment by a simplified process of classification and valuation, the goods imported under Project Import Scheme are placed under a single Tariff Heading 9801 in the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. The Central Government has formulated the Project Import Regulations, 1986 prescribing the procedure for effecting imports under this scheme.

1.2 The Project Import Scheme seeks to achieve the objective of simplifying the assessment in respect of import of capital goods and related items required for setting up of a project by classifying all goods under heading 9801 of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and prescribing a uniform Customs duty rate for them even though other headings may cover these goods more specifically. Thus, a number of notifications have been issued notifying a large number of projects for assessment under Tariff Heading 9801, which may have to be referred for availing the scheme.

question_text: How many copies of the tender should I prepare and how should they be labeled
answer:
You should prepare as many copies as the tender notice indicates – for example, if it asks for a duplicate set you need one original and one copy; if it asks for a triplicate set you need one original and two copies, and so on.  

Each copy (including the original) must be placed in its own sealed envelope and clearly marked on the front as “Original”, “Duplicate”, “Triplicate”, etc. In addition, every envelope must show the purchase office’s address and the tender reference number.  

After sealing and labeling the individual envelopes, put them all inside a larger outer envelope. Seal the outer envelope and mark it in the same way (original/duplicate/etc.), again printing the purchase office address and the tender reference number on it.  

If the outer envelope is not sealed and marked correctly, the purchaser will not assume responsibility for any misplacement, premature or late opening of your tender.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 96)
cot:
First, I need to see what the tender notice itself says about how many sets are required—whether it calls for a duplicate, a triplicate, or some other number. That statement tells me the total number of tender sets I have to submit.  

From that, I can figure out how many copies I actually need: if the notice asks for a duplicate set, I need one original plus one copy; if it asks for a triplicate set, I need one original plus two copies; in general, the number of copies equals the indicated number of sets minus one.  

Each of those sets—the original and every copy—has to go into its own sealed envelope. On the front of each envelope I must clearly label which set it is (“Original”, “Duplicate”, “Triplicate”, etc.) and also print the purchase office’s address and the tender reference number.  

After all the individual envelopes are ready, I put them together inside a larger outer envelope. I seal that outer envelope and mark it in the same way—using the same “Original/Duplicate/Triplicate” designation—and again I print the purchase office address and the tender reference number on it.  

Finally, I check that the outer envelope is properly sealed and marked; if it isn’t, the purchaser will not assume responsibility for any misplacement, premature opening, or late opening, so getting this step right is essential to ensure my tender is handled correctly.

After that, I focus on the specific limitation attached to this concession. The bonded‑warehouse labelling facility is allowed only for goods that cannot be easily labelled at ports, CFSs or ICDs, taking into account their size and other factors like sensitivity to temperature and dust.

question_text: If I haven’t delivered anything and the contract is cancelled, can I still be charged late delivery fees?
answer: No. If you haven’t delivered any goods and the contract is cancelled, the buyer cannot charge you late‑delivery fees. They may only recover the actual loss they suffered because of the cancellation; liquidated damages for delayed delivery do not apply when no supplies have been made. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 150)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is really asking: whether a buyer can still impose late‑delivery penalties when the seller has not delivered anything and the contract has been terminated.  

The core of the issue hinges on how liquidated damages for late delivery are defined and when they become applicable. I recall that liquidated damages are only triggered when there is actually a delay in the supply of goods; they accrue “only in case of delayed supplies.” If nothing has been supplied, there is no delay to speak of, so the basis for charging those penalties does not exist.  

Next, I consider what happens when a contract is cancelled before any delivery occurs. In such a situation, the buyer may recover only the loss occasioned by the cancellation itself, not the liquidated damages that would have applied to delayed delivery. Even if the buyer had previously granted extensions with a reservation of the right to claim liquidated damages, those rights disappear once no supplies have been made and the contract is ended.  

Putting these points together, if no goods have been delivered, there is no delayed supply, and therefore no liquidated damages can be levied. The buyer’s remedy is limited to compensating for the actual loss suffered because the contract was cancelled, not to imposing a penalty for lateness that never occurred.  

Finally, synthesizing the analysis: the absence of any delivery means the condition for liquidated damages is not met, and cancellation limits recovery to actual loss only. Hence, the seller cannot be charged late‑delivery fees under these circumstances. The answer follows naturally: no, late‑delivery fees are not recoverable when nothing has been delivered and the contract is cancelled.

### 9.7.8 Quantum of LD
While granting extension of the delivery period, where the delivery of stores or any instalment thereof is accepted after expiry of the original delivery period, the buyer may recover from the vendor, as agreed, the LD a sum equivalent to 0.5% (half percent) of the prices of any portion of stores delivered late, for each week or part thereof of delay. The total damages shall not exceed 5% (five percent) of the value of delayed goods. The LD cannot exceed the amount stipulated in the contract.

LR date will be considered as delivery completion date for calculation of price reduction in the case of delivery on ex works contract. Date of receipt of materials at owner's premises shall be considered for calculation of price reduction for F.O.R destination contract.

Where or in so far as no supplies have been made under a contract, upon cancellation, recovery of only the loss occasioned thereby can be made, notwithstanding the fact that prior to the cancellation one or more extensions of the delivery period with reservation of the right to LD are granted.

Government establishments/Departments, as distinct from PSUs, that execute contract work should not be dealt with as ordinary contractors and not generally be penalised for late delivery and claims for loss on risk-purchase should not be enforced against them. question_text: What documentation is required before a negotiation meeting can commence
answer:
Before a negotiation meeting can begin, the procuring authority must:

- Send the selected bidder a formal invitation letter using the format specified in **Annexure 4**; and  
- Obtain a signed declaration from the negotiating contractor, also as outlined in **Annexure 4**.  

(Procurement of Works Manual, p. 78)
cot:
I start by asking what has to happen before the parties can sit down to negotiate. The trigger is the procuring authority’s decision to invite a particular bidder to the table, so the first thing to check is what the authority must do to make that invitation official.  

Looking at the steps that follow the decision to call a bidder, I see that the bidder must be contacted in a specific way—using the letter format set out in Annexure 4. This isn’t just a courtesy; it locks in the original quoted rates so they remain available if the talks fall through.  

Next, the guidance notes that the meeting cannot actually begin until the bidder has supplied a signed declaration, also prescribed in Annexure 4. That declaration serves as the bidder’s acknowledgment that they are entering the negotiation under the terms outlined in the invitation.  

Both pieces—the invitation letter and the signed declaration—are explicitly linked to the same annexure, which tells me they are the two distinct documents the authority must have in hand before any negotiation session can start.  

Putting it together, the required pre‑meeting documentation is the Annexure 4 invitation letter sent to the selected bidder and the Annexure 4 signed declaration obtained from that bidder.

cot: I need to determine who pays for the sample and its shipping when I bid on catalysts, chemicals, or blend components. The procurement notes point out that for these materials even slight variations in properties can greatly affect the quality of the finished product, so it is common practice to request samples from bidders and evaluate them against predefined test parameters. question_text: For what purpose is the consolidated liabilities information submitted to the Budget Division
answer: The consolidated liabilities information is submitted to the Budget Division so that it can be suitably reflected in the Budget Estimates for the relevant financial year and incorporated into the Medium Term Expenditure Framework (MTEF) (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 88).
cot:
First, I need to figure out why the consolidated liabilities information is being sent to the Budget Division. The question is asking for the purpose, so I should start by thinking about what the Budget Division does and what it needs liabilities data for.

The Budget Division is part of the Ministry of Finance and is responsible for preparing the government’s budget. To do that, it has to know how much money the government has already committed to spend in the coming years, not just what is planned for a single year. If there are liabilities that will stretch over multiple years—like ongoing contracts or multi‑year procurement commitments—the Budget Division must see them to avoid double‑counting or under‑funding.

The liabilities in question arise from procurement activities on the GeM portal. After a purchase is made, the government incurs a commitment to pay the supplier, and these commitments can extend beyond the current financial year. The Programme Division or Administrative unit reviews these liabilities regularly, often with the help of the Financial Adviser, to keep track of what is owed and when.

The Financial Adviser then takes the reviewed information and puts together a consolidated picture—total committed liabilities broken down year by year. This consolidated view is what the Budget Division needs, because it allows the division to see exactly how much of the upcoming budget is already spoken for by existing commitments.

With that year‑wise liability picture in hand, the Budget Division can adjust the Budget Estimates for the relevant financial year, ensuring that the estimates reflect not only new proposals but also the money that must be set aside to meet those existing obligations. At the same time, the same information feeds into the Medium Term Expenditure Framework, which looks at spending plans over a three‑year horizon and requires a clear view of ongoing liabilities to be realistic and sustainable.

So, the reason the consolidated liabilities information is sent to the Budget Division is so that it can be suitably reflected in the Budget Estimates for the relevant financial year and incorporated into the Medium Term Expenditure Framework. That matches the answer: the information is used to reflect liabilities in the budget and the MTEF.

question_text: What must an MSE bidder do in their original offer to ensure they can choose between PP-LC and PPP-2012, and what restriction applies if they later wish to change that choice?
answer: To be able to elect either PP‑LC or PPP‑2012, an MSE bidder must **state their chosen preference policy in the original offer**. Once that option is declared, **no change is permitted later**; if the bidder omits the choice, the evaluator will treat PPP‑2012 as the default option. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 32)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the bidder has to do up front to keep the option open between the two purchase‑preference schemes. The question is asking for a condition in the original offer and a limitation on later changes.  

The MSE bidder can only use one of the two policies, PP‑LC or PPP‑2012, and must explicitly indicate which one they want to avail. This indication has to be made in the original bid.  

Once that choice is made, it is locked in—no alteration of the option is allowed after the offer is submitted.  

There is also a consequence for failing to make that declaration: if the bidder does not specify a preference even though they qualify for both, the evaluator will automatically treat PPP‑2012 as the selected option.  

Putting these pieces together, the bidder must state their chosen preference policy in the original offer to retain the ability to pick either PP‑LC or PPP‑2012. ## 1.5 Fundamental Principles of Public Procurement
Over and above the basic aims of procurement, the obligations of procuring authorities can be grouped into following five fundamental principles of public procurement, which all procuring authorities must abide by and be accountable for:

- i) Transparency principle;
- ii) Professionalism principle;
- iii) Broader obligations principle;

*(For more details on principles of procurement, please refer to Chapter 1 of the Manual for Procurement of Goods 1).*

## 1.6 Standards (Canons) of Financial Propriety
Public Procurement like any other expenditure in Government must conform to the Standards (also called Canons) of Financial Propriety.

*"Standards of financial propriety: Every officer incurring or authorizing expenditure from public moneys should be guided by high standards of financial propriety. Every officer should also enforce financial order and strict economy and see that all relevant financial rules and regulations are observed, by his own office and by subordinate disbursing officers. Among the principles on which emphasis is generally laid are the following:-*

- i) *Every officer is expected to exercise the same vigilance in respect of expenditure incurred from public moneys as a person of ordinary prudence would exercise in respect of expenditure of his own money.*
- ii) *The expenditure should not be prima facie more than the occasion demands.*
- iii) *No authority should exercise its powers of sanctioning expenditure to pass an order which will be directly or indirectly to its own advantage.*
- iv) *Expenditure from public moneys should not be incurred for the benefit of a particular person or a section of the people, unless -*
  - i) *a claim for the amount could be enforced in a Court of Law, or*
  - ii) *The expenditure is in pursuance of a recognized policy or custom.*
- v) *The amount of allowances granted to meet expenditure of a particular type should be so regulated that the allowances are not on the whole a source of profit to the recipients.*
- vi) *While discharging the duties of financial concurrence of any public expenditure, such authorities subsequent to such decision, shall not be involved in any future audit responsibilities which may create conflict of interest.*

## 1.7 Public Procurement Infrastructure at the Centre


### i) Procurement Policy Division
Procurement Policy Division (PPD) in Department of Expenditure; Ministry of Finance has been created to encourage uniformity and harmonisation in public procurement processes by setting guidelines, dissemination of best practices, providing guidance, oversight and capacity building and issuing of procurement manuals. However, Centralisation of procurement or involvement in procurement processes is not the intended purpose of creation of PPD.

### ii) Central Public Procurement Portal
Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP) has been designed, developed and hosted by National Informatics Centre (NIC, Ministry of Electronics & Information Technology) in association with Dept. of Expenditure to ensure transparency in the public procurement process. The primary objective of the Central Public Procurement portal is to provide a single point access to the information on procurements made across various Ministries and the Departments. The CPPP has e-publishing and e-procurement modules. It is mandatory for all Ministries/ Departments of the Central Government, Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and Autonomous and Statutory Bodies to publish on the CPPP all their tender enquiries and information about the resulting contracts.

question_text: How does the auto‑extension rule work when a bid is placed in the final five minutes of the online reverse auction?
answer:
The auto‑extension provision is designed to preserve competitive tension while protecting the auction schedule.  

- **Trigger:** A bid submitted in the final five minutes of the reverse auction must be accepted as the lowest offer.  
- **Effect:** When triggered, the auction clock is reset and an additional five minutes are added, measured from the moment that qualifying bid is received.  
- **Non‑trigger scenarios:** If the bid is not the lowest, or if no bid is received in the last five minutes, the auction closes automatically without any extension.  

This mechanism ensures that only genuinely competitive, low‑value bids can extend the process, supporting timely procurement outcomes and reducing the risk of unnecessary delay. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 264)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is asking: it wants a clear description of the auto‑extension mechanism that kicks in when a bid appears in the final five minutes of an online reverse auction.  

Looking at the rule, the core idea is that the auction clock is not fixed; it can be stretched if certain conditions are met during that closing window.  

So I start by identifying the trigger condition: a bid must be submitted within the last five minutes before the scheduled close, and that bid has to be accepted as the lowest offer at that moment.  

If that condition is satisfied, the effect is that the auction duration is reset—specifically, an additional five minutes are added, and the new closing time is calculated from the exact moment the qualifying bid was received.  

Next, I consider what happens when the trigger is not met. If the bid arrives in the last five minutes but is not the lowest, the rule does not apply and the auction proceeds to close at the original time. Similarly, if no bid is placed in that final window, there is nothing to extend, so the auction ends as scheduled.  

Finally, I reflect on why the rule is structured this way. By allowing extensions only for genuinely competitive, low‑value bids, the process keeps pressure on suppliers to improve their offers while preventing the auction from lingering indefinitely due to trivial or non‑winning bids. This balances the need for a fair, competitive outcome with the desire to finish the procurement in a timely manner.  

Putting these pieces together gives a complete picture of how the auto‑extension rule operates when a bid is placed in the final five minutes of the online reverse auction.

question_text: If no domestic bidders are present, what basis can be used for comparing offers in GTE tenders and why
answer:
- **Comparison basis:** When no domestic bidders participate, offers in GTE tenders are compared on the basis of CIF (Cost, Insurance, Freight) or landed cost.  
- **Rationale:** All other cost elements—freight, insurance, port handling, customs duties, inland freight, taxes, etc.—are identical for every foreign bidder; therefore, evaluating the CIF/landed cost provides an apples‑to‑apples assessment that ensures transparency, delivers value for money, and supports risk‑aligned procurement decisions.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 124)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: when there are no domestic bidders in a GTE tender, on what basis should the foreign offers be compared, and what justifies that basis.  

I recall that GTE tenders require all price elements to be expressed in a common currency for evaluation, and that the evaluation distinguishes between costs incurred before the goods arrive at the port and those incurred after arrival. The pre‑arrival costs include the product price, freight, and insurance (i.e., the CIF components), while the post‑arrival costs cover port handling, customs duties, inland freight, taxes, and any LC‑related charges.  

If domestic bidders were present, the comparison would have to include the full FOR/FOT destination cost because Indian bidders would not incur the international freight and insurance leg, making a CIF‑only comparison unfair. However, the scenario specifies that there are no domestic bidders, meaning every participant is a foreign supplier facing exactly the same set of post‑arrival charges at the point of entry.  

Since those post‑arrival elements—port handling, customs, countervailing duties, inland freight, octroi/entry tax, and LC charges—are identical for all foreign bidders (they depend only on the destination port and the applicable regulations, not on the supplier), they cancel out when comparing offers. Consequently, the only differentiating factor among the bids lies in the CIF/landed cost, which encompasses the product price, freight, and insurance.  

Using CIF/landed cost as the comparison basis therefore provides an apples‑to‑apples assessment: it isolates the variable portion of the offer while holding the constant portion steady. This approach ensures transparency, allows the procuring entity to see which supplier truly offers the lowest landed price, and supports a value‑for‑money decision that is aligned with risk, because any differences in freight or insurance are already reflected in the CIF figure.  

Thus, when no domestic bidders are present, the appropriate basis for comparing offers in GTE tenders is the CIF (or landed) cost, and the rationale is that all other cost elements are uniform across foreign bidders, making a direct comparison of CIF/landed cost both fair and informative.

#### GTE Tenders
Special aspects of evaluation of the financial offer in GTE tenders are:

#### i) Currency of Tender
In GTE tenders, the price in the quotation could be in US Dollar or Euro or Pound Sterling or Yen or in currencies under the RBI's notified basket of currencies, in addition to the Indian Rupees, except for expenditure incurred in India (including agency commission if any) which should be stated in Indian Rupees. All offers are to be converted to Indian Rupees based on the "Bill currency selling" exchange rate on the date of tender opening (Techno- commercial offer) from a source as specified in the tender document [usually TT selling rates of exchange as quoted by authorised exchange bankers approved by RBI].

#### ii) Currency of Payment
The contract price will be normally paid in the currency/currencies in which the price is stated in the contract.

#### iii) Evaluation of Offers
As per Government policy, Ministries/Departments/Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) should ensure imports on FOB/FAS basis failing which a No Objection Certificate (NOC) should be obtained from the Ministry of Surface Transport (Chartering Wing).

The foreign bidders are normally asked, in the bid documents, to quote both on FAS/FOB basis and also on Cost and Freight (CFR)/CIF basis duly indicating the break-up of prices for freight, insurance, and so on, with purchasers reserving the right to order on either basis.. In the case of FAS/FOB offers, the freight and insurance shall be (after ascertaining, if not quoted) added to make up the CIF cost. To arrive at the Free On Rail (FOR) cost, one per cent shall be added over and above CIF as port handling charges, custom duty, countervailing duty and surcharges, as applicable on the date of opening of the tender, as well as clearing agency charges, inland freight and Octroi/entry tax, as assessed, may be added to make it a FOR/Free On Truck (FOT) destination. The FOR/FOT destination price for domestic offers may be calculated as in OTE tenders. For bids with Letter of Credit (LC) payment, the likely LC charges (as ascertained from Procuring Entity's bankers) should also be

loaded.

In case both Indian and foreign bidders have quoted in the tender, the comparison of the offers would be done on the basis of FOR/FOT destination including all applicable taxes and duties (on the principle of the total outgo from Procuring Entity's pockets). In case there are no domestic bidders, a comparison of offers can be made on the basis of CIF/landed costs since the rest of costs would be same for all bidders.

## 7.5 Deliberations for Award of Contract.


### 7.5.1 Timely Processing of Tenders
Delays in finalising procurement deprive the public of the intended benefits and results in lost revenues and cost over-run. Award of contract should be completed within the original bid validity. Accordingly, a suitable clause should be included in the NIT for information of bidders. Every official in the chain of the procurement operation is accountable for taking action in a specified time so that the tender is finalised on time. question_text: What documentation should an auditor review to confirm that the fall clause provisions have been correctly communicated to parallel rate contract holders?
answer:
To verify that the fall‑clause provisions have been properly communicated to parallel rate‑contract holders, the auditor should examine the following documentation:

1. **Notice of reduced price** issued to each parallel rate‑contract holder informing them of the price reduction triggered by the fall clause.  
2. **Sealed covers** received from the parallel rate‑contract holders containing their revised prices (if any) submitted within the stipulated seven‑day period.  
3. **Record/minutes of the public opening** of the sealed covers on the specified date and time, evidencing that the opening was conducted transparently.  
4. **Amended rate contract** (or formal amendment) reflecting the reduced price that took effect from the date of the price reduction, showing that the contract was updated accordingly.  
5. **Correspondence or log** confirming that the seven‑day response period was granted and that any revised prices were considered in accordance with standard practice.  

Reviewing these items provides objective evidence that the fall‑clause communication requirements were fulfilled as outlined in the manual. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 138)
cot:
First, I need to picture exactly what the fall‑clause procedure requires when a rate‑contract holder lowers its price. The clause says the holder must inform every parallel rate‑contract holder of the new, lower price, give them seven days to decide whether they want to match that price, collect any revised offers in sealed covers, open those covers publicly on a set date and time, and then amend the rate contract to reflect the reduced price if it stands.  

With that process in mind, the auditor’s job is to check that each of those steps actually happened and was properly documented. So I start by asking what proof would show that the initial notification was sent out to all parallel holders. That points to a copy of the notice or communication that conveyed the reduced price and the seven‑day response window.  

Next, I consider how to verify that the parallel holders actually received the notice and had the chance to respond. The natural evidence would be the sealed covers they returned, each containing their revised price (or a statement that they chose not to change it), together with a record that they were received within the seven‑day period.  

Then I think about the public opening of those sealed covers. To confirm it was done transparently and on the agreed date and time, the auditor would look for the minutes or a record of that opening session, showing who was present, what time it started, and that the covers were opened in public.  

After the opening, the contract itself must be updated to reflect the new price that took effect from the date of the reduction. Therefore, the auditor needs to see the amended rate contract or a formal amendment that shows the revised price and the effective date.  

Finally, to tie the timeline together and prove that the seven‑day window was respected and any revised prices were handled according to standard practice, the auditor would examine any correspondence, log, or tracking sheet that notes when the notice was sent, when the covers were received, and how the responses were processed.  

Putting those pieces together—notice of the price cut, the sealed covers received, the record of their public opening, the amended contract, and the correspondence/log confirming the seven‑day period—gives the auditor objective evidence that the fall‑clause provisions were properly communicated to all parallel rate‑contract holders.

question_text: What is the purpose of the "Rate of GST" column in the priced bid opening table?
answer: The “Rate of GST” column is included to capture the applicable goods and services tax rate for each bidder’s quoted price (which is presented exclusive of GST). By recording this rate, the opening sheet enables the calculation of the GST amount and the total price inclusive of tax, thereby supporting accurate financial evaluation of bids and ensuring compliance with tax‑related procurement requirements. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 120)
cot:
I’m looking at the table that records the priced bid opening and I see a column labeled “Rate of GST” right next to the “Total Quoted Price (Excl. GST)”. The question asks why that column is there. 

First, I notice that the quoted price is explicitly marked as exclusive of GST, which means the amount bidders have entered does not yet include any tax. If we only had that figure, we wouldn’t know what the actual outflow would be once the tax is applied, and we couldn’t compare bids on a like‑for‑like basis because different bidders might be subject to different GST rates depending on their location or the nature of the supplies.

Next, I think about what is needed to turn an exclusive‑of‑GST price into a total cost that can be evaluated financially. The missing piece is the applicable GST rate; multiplying the exclusive price by that rate gives the GST amount, and adding it to the exclusive price yields the price inclusive of tax. 

So the column must be there to capture exactly that rate for each bidder. By recording it alongside the exclusive price, the opening sheet provides all the data required to compute the GST component and the final total price for every bid. 

Having those totals allows the procurement team to perform a proper financial evaluation—ranking bids by their true cost to the organization—and also ensures that the tax treatment is transparent and compliant with relevant regulations. 

Putting it together, the purpose of the “Rate of GST” column is to record the applicable goods and services tax rate so that the GST amount and the total price inclusive of tax can be calculated, enabling accurate bid evaluation and tax‑related compliance.

question_text: How is the Surety's liability limited in the Bank Guarantee agreement
answer:
The Surety’s liability under the Bank Guarantee is expressly limited in the following ways:

1. **Monetary cap** – The Surety’s obligation to pay is restricted to a fixed sum of Rs. .... (Rupees ..... only) (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 251).  
2. **Time bound** – The guarantee remains in force only until a specified date (​till .....​) and, in the first instance, remains effective up to a further date (​upto .....​) (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 251).  
3. **Extension provision** – If the contract for which the guarantee is given is not completed or fully performed, the Surety (Bank) agrees to extend the guarantee until such time as is required to fulfill the contract (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 251).  
4. **Non‑discharge clause** – The Surety cannot be released or discharged from the guarantee by any arrangement between the Company and the Supplier, alteration of the parties’ obligations, or any indulgence or forbearance regarding payment or time performance (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 251).  

These provisions together define the Surety’s liability as limited to a specified monetary amount, confined to a defined period (with possible extension), and protected from release through contractual modifications or indulgence.
cot:
First, I need to grasp what the question is asking: it wants to know the ways in which the Surety’s responsibility under the Bank Guarantee is curtailed.

The Bank Guarantee agreement includes a clause that binds the Surety to pay only up to a certain sum if the Supplier fails to perform. This indicates a hard ceiling on how much the Surety can be called upon to pay.

The agreement also specifies the guarantee’s duration. The Surety’s liability is restricted to that sum, and the guarantee remains in force only until a specified date, and in the first instance, it is effective up to another date. This shows the liability is not only capped in amount but also limited in time.

There is a provision that deals with what happens if the underlying contract isn’t finished. The Surety agrees to extend the guarantee for as long as needed to fulfill the contract. So while the guarantee has an initial expiry, it can be prolonged, but only to cover the actual performance period of the contract.

Finally, the agreement contains a non‑discharge clause. It makes clear that the Surety cannot be released from the guarantee by any arrangement between the Company and the Supplier, by changes to the parties’ obligations, or by any indulgence or forbearance regarding payment or timing. This protects the Surety from being let off the hook through side agreements or leniency.

Putting these observations together, the Surety’s liability is limited by a fixed monetary ceiling, by a defined time frame (with a possible extension tied to contract completion), and by a guarantee that cannot be voided through mutual arrangements, alterations, or indulgence. These four elements together define the extent of the Surety’s exposure under the Bank Guarantee.

question_text: Are there any cases where I do not have to provide a warranty or performance bank guarantee?
answer:
Yes, there are specific situations where a warranty or performance bank guarantee is not required. You do not need to submit one if:

- You are supplying materials and the value of each individual contract is Rs 5 lakh or less.  
- You are supplying spares or proprietary materials that come directly from the original equipment manufacturer (OEM), its sole selling agent, an authorized dealer, or when you are providing services.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 105)
cot:
First, I consider what triggers the need for a warranty or performance bank guarantee – it is tied to the nature of the contract and its value, as outlined in the security provisions.  
Then, I scan for any explicit carve‑outs that relieve a supplier of that obligation, focusing on the sections that discuss when the guarantee is not mandatory.  
I notice a provision stating that for the procurement of materials where each individual contract does not exceed Rs 5 lakh, the submission of a performance bank guarantee is waived.  
Next, I see another exemption covering spares or proprietary items sourced directly from the original equipment manufacturer, its sole selling agent, or an authorized dealer, as well as pure service contracts.  
Putting these observations together, it becomes clear that there are indeed defined situations – low‑value material supplies, OEM‑origin spare parts, and service‑only engagements – where a warranty or performance bank guarantee is not required.  
Therefore, the answer to the question is affirmative, with the specific cases being exactly those identified.

# Chapter 6: Forms of Securities, Payment Terms and Price Variations


## 6.1 Forms of Security


### 6.1.1 Bid Security
Bid security [EMD] may not be sought in tenders for procurement of goods.

### 6.1.2 Contract Performance Security:
Contract Performance Security within specified period of placement of LOA/PO may be sought from the contractor on case to case basis. Such condition and rates shall be specified in the NIT/ITB.

### 6.1.3 Warranty / Performance Bank Guarantee
In case of works and capital equipment, there is usually a defect liability/warranty clause against defects arising from design, material, workmanship or any omission on part of the vendor/contractor during a specified period of months from the date of commissioning or from the date of dispatch in case of goods - whichever is earlier. In such cases, Warranty /Performance Bank Guarantee of 10 (ten) per cent of the value of the goods is required to be submitted in prescribed format in the currency of the contract, valid for 06 months (claim period) beyond the Warranty period. [The value has been reduced to three (3) percent till 31.03.2023]. In case, PBG is not provided by the vendor, 10% of the basic value shall be retained in lieu of PBG, till the expiry of guarantee and claim period.

Unless otherwise specified, submission of PBG is not necessary for following types of contract:

- Procurement of Materials upto individual contract Value Rs 5 lakh
- Procurement of Spares, materials of proprietary nature from OEM, sole selling agent of OEM, authorized dealer and services.

### 6.1.4 Verification of Bank Guarantees
Bank guarantees submitted by the tenderers/suppliers as Performance Bank Guarantee need to be immediately verified from the issuing bank before acceptance. There may not be any need to get the Bank Guarantee vetted from legal/ finance authority if it is in the specified format. Guidelines for verification of BGs submitted by the bidders/ contractors against performance bank guarantee /advance payments and for various other purposes are as follows:

- i) BG shall be as per the prescribed formats. Modification(s), if requested by any bidder, shall be forwarded to Legal dept. for confirmation.
- ii) The BG contains the name, designation and code number of the Bank officer(s) signing the guarantee(s);
- iii) The address and other details (including telephone no.) of the controlling officer of the bank are obtained from the branch of the bank issuing the BG (this should be included in all BGs);
- iv) Bank guarantee should be routed through SFMS platform (necessary instructions to bidder to be included in the tender document / order). Alternatively, the

confirmation from the issuing branch of the bank is obtained in writing through registered post/speed post/courier/e-mail. The bank should be advised to confirm the issuance of the BGs specifically quoting the letter of Procurement Entity on the printed official letterhead of the bank indicating address and other details (including telephone nos.) of the bank and the name, designation and code number of the officer(s) confirming the issuance of the BG;

- v) Pending receipt of confirmation as above, confirmation can also be obtained with the help of responsible officer at the field office, which is close to the issuing branch of the bank, who should personally obtain the confirmation from issuing branch of the bank and forward the confirmation report to the concerned procurement entity.
