# FOREWORD
Numaligarh Refinery Ltd. formally brought about a comprehensive Guideline for Procurement and Contract Services in 2004 after deliberations by a dedicated cross functional committee, with due consideration of views of BPCL and CVO to streamline the procedures for procurement and contractual systems in use and to help in making decisions in a laid down manner that would stand the test of any future scrutiny as a public procuring entity.

With a similar view to improving transparency in decision making in public procurement and reducing the scope for subjectivity, Department of Expenditure (DoE), in 2006, issued a set of three Manuals on Policies and Procedures for Procurement of Goods, Works and Hiring of Consultants in conformity with the General Financial Rules (GFR), 2005. Over time, the Government of India issued new instructions in the domain of public procurement like introduction of Central Public Procurement Portal (CPPP), Government e-Marketplace (GeM), preferential market access for micro and small enterprises, preference for domestic manufacturers of electronic goods, inclusion of Integrity Pact, etc. The GFR was revised comprehensively in March 2017 covering inter-alia these set of new instructions. Consequently, the Manuals of Procurement by DoE too were revised after a decade and within a month of the release of GFR 2017.

Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) have since issued various instruction on public procurement from time to time as also various other organisations like NITI Aayog, D/o Promotion of Industry & Internal Trade etc. NRL has kept abreast of these guidelines for procurement by publishing various internal notifications and hosting them on the website to supplement/ substitute the provisions of its procurement manual. Due to multiple organizations issuing guidelines, procurement executives were commonly facing problems in having a single authoritative source of reference. CVC after deliberations with DoE and with the other organisations came to the logical conclusion that it would only be appropriate if public procurement guidelines are henceforth issued from a single source viz. DoE.

Consequently, the three Manuals for Procurement (of Goods, Works and Consultancy & Other Services) were recently revised by DoE and made effective from 1st July 2022, incorporating all interim procurement guidelines issued by DoE since its last revision in 2017 as well subsuming all extant instructions from CVC and other Government bodies. Accordingly, the CVC has issued a circular No-14/07/22 dated 11.07.2022.

Vide letter ref. NRL/Vig/02 dtd. 12.07.2022, CVO-NRL submitted the advisory to the Managing Director, NRL to update/align the procurement manual/guideline of NRL in line with the updated manuals of DoE and upload the same on NRL's website.

Accordingly, a cross functional committee was constituted by MD-NRL to review and update NRL's procurement manuals in line with the latest comprehensive version issued by the DoE while incorporating organization specific provisions. The adoption of these updated policies / guidelines by NRL is expected to uphold the fundamental principles of transparency, fairness, competition, economy, efficiency and accountability.

Public Procurement is a dynamic field where policies are constantly reviewed to help Government achieve its socio-economic or strategic goals. Hence, it will be our endeavor to update this manual from time to time at periodic intervals to ensure their continued relevance for all the years to come.

I also take this opportunity to record my appreciation to the committee members involved in participating in the knowledge sharing for updating this significant document.

Indranil Mittra

question_text: How must expenditure incurred in India, including agency commission, be stated in the tender offer
answer: Expenditure incurred in India, including any agency commission, must be stated in Indian Rupees. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 124)
cot:
First, I think about what the question is really asking: it wants to know the required currency for showing any cost that occurs inside India, including any agency commission, when preparing a tender offer.  
Next, I recall the special rules that apply to GTE tenders regarding currency. The general provision lets bidders quote their prices in a range of foreign currencies or in Indian Rupees, but there is a specific carve‑out for expenses that are incurred within the country.  
Looking at that carve‑out, it explicitly says that expenditure incurred in India—this covers everything from local labor, materials, and any agency commission that might be paid—must be expressed in Indian Rupees.  
The reason behind this rule is to keep the domestic cost component comparable across all bids, since the procuring entity will ultimately need to convert any foreign‑currency amounts to Rupees for evaluation, while the Indian‑portion stays unchanged.  
Putting these points together, the only way to satisfy the tender’s currency requirement for India‑based costs, including agency commission, is to state them outright in Indian Rupees.  
Thus, the expenditure incurred in India, including any agency commission, must be stated in Indian Rupees.

#### GTE Tenders
Special aspects of evaluation of the financial offer in GTE tenders are:

#### i) Currency of Tender
In GTE tenders, the price in the quotation could be in US Dollar or Euro or Pound Sterling or Yen or in currencies under the RBI's notified basket of currencies, in addition to the Indian Rupees, except for expenditure incurred in India (including agency commission if any) which should be stated in Indian Rupees. All offers are to be converted to Indian Rupees based on the "Bill currency selling" exchange rate on the date of tender opening (Techno- commercial offer) from a source as specified in the tender document [usually TT selling rates of exchange as quoted by authorised exchange bankers approved by RBI].

#### ii) Currency of Payment
The contract price will be normally paid in the currency/currencies in which the price is stated in the contract.

#### iii) Evaluation of Offers
As per Government policy, Ministries/Departments/Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) should ensure imports on FOB/FAS basis failing which a No Objection Certificate (NOC) should be obtained from the Ministry of Surface Transport (Chartering Wing).

The foreign bidders are normally asked, in the bid documents, to quote both on FAS/FOB basis and also on Cost and Freight (CFR)/CIF basis duly indicating the break-up of prices for freight, insurance, and so on, with purchasers reserving the right to order on either basis.. In the case of FAS/FOB offers, the freight and insurance shall be (after ascertaining, if not quoted) added to make up the CIF cost. To arrive at the Free On Rail (FOR) cost, one per cent shall be added over and above CIF as port handling charges, custom duty, countervailing duty and surcharges, as applicable on the date of opening of the tender, as well as clearing agency charges, inland freight and Octroi/entry tax, as assessed, may be added to make it a FOR/Free On Truck (FOT) destination. The FOR/FOT destination price for domestic offers may be calculated as in OTE tenders. For bids with Letter of Credit (LC) payment, the likely LC charges (as ascertained from Procuring Entity's bankers) should also be

loaded.

In case both Indian and foreign bidders have quoted in the tender, the comparison of the offers would be done on the basis of FOR/FOT destination including all applicable taxes and duties (on the principle of the total outgo from Procuring Entity's pockets). In case there are no domestic bidders, a comparison of offers can be made on the basis of CIF/landed costs since the rest of costs would be same for all bidders.

## 7.5 Deliberations for Award of Contract.


### 7.5.1 Timely Processing of Tenders
Delays in finalising procurement deprive the public of the intended benefits and results in lost revenues and cost over-run. Award of contract should be completed within the original bid validity. Accordingly, a suitable clause should be included in the NIT for information of bidders. Every official in the chain of the procurement operation is accountable for taking action in a specified time so that the tender is finalised on time. Any deviation from the schedule (Service Level Agreement) may be monitored and explained, by way of system of Management Reporting.

question_text: What is the maximum period allowed to offer unexecuted quantities to the next eligible agency in case of failure by the successful bidder
answer: If the successful bidder fails to execute the supply/service after award, the unexecuted quantities shall be offered to the next eligible agency within a maximum period of one year from the original date of award. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 62)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants the longest allowable time frame for NRL to approach another eligible agency with any quantities that the winning bidder failed to deliver.  

Next, I scan the procurement guidance for any language that deals with a bidder’s failure after award and the subsequent steps for unexecuted items. question_text: How is the supply shared when more than one MSE qualifies under the L1+15% price band?
answer: When more than one Micro and Small Enterprise (MSE) qualifies under the L1 + 15% price band, the supply is allocated to each qualifying MSE in proportion to its tendered quantity. Specifically, the total tendered quantity for the line item is divided among the qualifying MSEs so that each receives a share that corresponds to its respective tendered quantity relative to the combined tendered quantity of all qualifying MSEs. This proportional sharing ensures that the supply is distributed fairly among all eligible MSEs while maintaining the requirement that each MSE’s price is brought down to the L1 price. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 213)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: when several Micro and Small Enterprises all fall within the L1 + 15% price band, how is the total supply divided among them.  

Next, I look at the policy wording for this situation. It states that if more than one MSE quotes a price inside that band, the supply shall be shared proportionately to the tendered quantity. This tells me that the division is not equal or arbitrary; it must reflect each bidder’s quoted amount relative to the others.  

Then I think about what “proportionately to tendered quantity” means in practice. If I take each qualifying MSE’s tendered quantity and add them together, I get a total qualifying quantity. Each MSE’s share of the overall supply should be its own tendered quantity divided by that total, multiplied by the total quantity that is earmarked for MSEs (which, under the rule, is up to 25 % of the full tender).  

I verify that this approach satisfies the condition that each MSE must bring its price down to the L1 price. Since the price adjustment is a condition for eligibility, once they qualify, the proportional allocation does not affect the price requirement; it only determines how much of the reserved 25 % each receives.  

Finally, I synthesize: the supply is allocated so that each qualifying MSE receives a portion of the MSE‑reserved quantity that is directly proportional to its tendered quantity, ensuring a fair distribution that follows the policy’s proportional sharing rule. This matches the answer that the supply is shared proportionately to tendered quantity among all qualifying MSEs.

question_text: For coastal projects, which two cyclone‑related data points must be taken from the Atlas
answer:
**Step‑by‑Step Guide: Extracting Cyclone Data for Coastal Projects from the Vulnerability Atlas of India**

**Overview**  
For any project situated in a coastal area, the Vulnerability Atlas of India must be consulted to obtain cyclone‑specific information. The Atlas provides two distinct cyclone‑related data points that are required for risk assessment and design.

---

### Step 1: Confirm the Project’s Coastal Setting  
- Verify that the project site lies within a coastal district or region as defined in the Atlas.  
- If the site is inland, cyclone data are not required; proceed to other hazard assessments.

### Step 2: Locate the Cyclone Section in the Atlas  
- Open the Vulnerability Atlas of India (available at [www.bmtpc.org](http://www.bmtpc.org)).  
- Navigate to the digitized maps and tables for cyclones.  
- Identify the subsection that presents cyclone statistics for coastal regions.

### Step 3: Record the Two Required Cyclone Data Points  
From the cyclone subsection, extract the following information for the specific coastal district or site:  

1. **Number of cyclonic storms / severe cyclonic storms** – the historical count of cyclonic events (including severe cyclones) that have affected the area.  
2. **Maximum sustained wind specific to the coastal region** – the highest wind speed (in m/s or km/h) recorded for cyclones impacting the coast.  

*(These two data points are mandated for coastal project planning and design.)*  
(Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 38)

### Step 4: Incorporate the Data into Project Documentation  
- Insert the extracted cyclone statistics into the hazard assessment section of the project design report.  
- Use the numbers to inform structural wind‑load calculations, flood‑surge modeling, and any required mitigation measures.  
- Ensure that the data are clearly labeled with the source (Vulnerability Atlas of India) and the reference year or period covered.

### Step 5: Verify and Validate  
- Cross‑check the extracted figures against any updated Atlas releases or supplementary notifications from NRL.  
- Confirm that the values correspond to the exact district or micro‑location of the project, not a broader state‑level aggregate.

---

## Common Pitfalls to Avoid  

| Pitfall | Why It Matters | How to Prevent |
|---------|----------------|----------------|
| Using state‑wide cyclone averages instead of district‑specific values | Over‑ or under‑estimates risk, leading to non‑compliant designs | Always select the data entry that matches the project’s district or nearest coastal point |
| Forgetting to record both the storm count **and** the maximum sustained wind | The specification requires both points; omitting one creates an incomplete assessment | Follow Step 3 checklist: count + wind speed |
| Citing outdated Atlas versions | Hazard patterns change; older data may not reflect recent cyclonic activity | Verify the Atlas version date on the website before extraction |
| Misinterpreting “max sustained wind” as gust speed | Design codes use sustained wind for load calculations | Ensure the value taken is the sustained wind figure provided in the Atlas |

---

## Practical Example  

A procurement officer is preparing a tender for a new desalination plant in Kochi, Kerala (a coastal district).  

1. **Confirm coastal setting** – Kochi is listed as a coastal district in the Atlas.  
2. **Locate cyclone section** – The Atlas shows cyclone statistics for Kerala’s coastal zones.  
3. **Extract data** –  
   - Number of cyclonic storms / severe cyclonic storms: **12** (over the last 30 years).  
   - Maximum sustained wind: **50 m/s** (specific to the Kochi coast).  
4. **Insert into report** – The hazard assessment cites: “Kochi district has experienced 12 cyclonic storms/severe cyclonic storms, with a maximum sustained wind of 50 m/s (Vulnerability Atlas of India).”  
5. **Validate** – Officer checks the Atlas website for any 2024 update; figures remain unchanged, so the assessment proceeds.

By following these numbered steps, procurement officers ensure that the required cyclone‑related data are correctly sourced, recorded, and applied, thereby meeting the Vulnerability Atlas of India mandate and reducing the risk of procedural errors.
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: for any project located on the coast, the Vulnerability Atlas of India must be consulted to pull out cyclone‑specific information that will feed into the risk assessment and design. The Atlas is known to contain a range of hazard layers, and for cyclones it provides several pieces of data, but the mandate for coastal projects singles out only two of them.

Next, I think about what engineers actually need when they design structures in a cyclone‑prone coastal zone. They need to know how often such events occur so they can gauge the likelihood of exposure, and they need to know how strong the winds can get so they can size the structural members and calculate wind loads. In other words, the design process calls for a measure of frequency and a measure of intensity.

Looking at the cyclone section of the Atlas, the frequency of cyclonic activity is expressed as the historical number of cyclonic storms and severe cyclonic storms that have affected a given coastal district or site. This count tells the designer how many events have been recorded over the reference period and therefore gives a sense of the event’s recurrence.

The intensity of a cyclone, as far as wind loading is concerned, is captured by the maximum sustained wind speed that has been observed for storms impacting that particular coastal stretch. This sustained wind value is the figure used in wind‑load formulas, not gust speeds or pressure drops, because design codes are based on sustained wind.

Putting these two together, the Atlas supplies exactly the pair of data points that a coastal project must record: (1) the count of cyclonic storms/severe cyclonic storms for the location, and (2) the maximum sustained wind specific to that coastal region. Other cyclone‑related entries in the Atlas—such as rainfall totals, surge heights, or gust speeds—are either covered under different hazard sections or are not required for the basic cyclone risk assessment stipulated for coastal projects.

Thus, reasoning from the purpose of the Atlas through the design needs leads directly to the conclusion that the two mandatory cyclone‑related data points are the number of cyclonic/severe cyclonic storms and the maximum sustained wind for the coastal area in question.

### Clause: Planning and Designing in purview of Vulnerability Atlas of India
Vulnerability Atlas of India (VAI) is comprehensive document which provides existing hazard scenario for the entire country and presents the digitized State/UT- wise hazard, maps with respect to earthquakes, winds and floods for district-wise identification of vulnerable areas. It also includes additional digitized maps for thunderstorms, cyclone and landslides. The main purpose of this Atlas is its use for disaster preparedness and mitigation at policy planning and project formulation stage.

This Atlas is one of its kind single point source for the various stakeholders including policy makers, administration, municipal commissioners, urban managers, engineers, architects, planners, public etc. to ascertain proneness of any city/location/site to multi-hazard which includes earthquakes, wind, floods thunderstorms, cyclones and landslides. While project formulation, approvals and implementation of various urban housing, buildings and infrastructures schemes, this Atlas provides necessary information for risk analysis and hazard assessment.

The vulnerability Atlas of India has been prepared by Building Materials and Technology Promotion Council under Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, Government of India and available at their website [www.bmtpc.org](http://www.bmtpc.org).

It is mandatory for the bidders to refer Vulnerability Atlas of India for multi-hazard risk assessment and include the relevant hazard proneness specific to project location while planning and designing the project in terms of:

- i) Seismic zone (II to V) for earthquakes,
- ii) Wind velocity (Basic Wind Velocity: 55, 50, 47, 44, 39 & 33 m/s)
- iii) Area liable to floods and Probable max. surge height
- iv) Thunderstorms history
- v) Number of cyclonic storms/ severe cyclonic storms and max sustained wind specific to coastal region
- vi) Landslides incidences with Annual rainfall normal
- vii) District wise Probable Max. Precipitation

(b) **Contractors’ Performance Evaluation:** Following clause (or any updated version) shall be included in the tenders\*:-

NRL has adopted a dynamic performance monitoring /evaluation procedure for continuous monitoring and evaluation of contractors, to maintain their accountability and performance. A rating, based on performance shall be assigned for each work executed by a contractor. This

rating shall be used in determining eligibility of the bidder in subsequent tenders issued by NRL (or by NRL authorized agencies / PMC / EPCM).

Following are the areas to be covered under continuous evaluation process:

1. Compliance of safety and housekeeping at worksite
2. Resource mobilization/delay in completion
3. Quality of works and documentation
4. Compliance of statutory / regulatory guidelines

Contractor whose performance is evaluated as Unsatisfactory based on pre-defined scoring criteria shall be debarred for 1 year from participating in NRL's tenders from the date of issuing notification by NRL.

Detailed Contractors' Performance Evaluation methodology is to be made available in NRL Website [location/link to be specified in tenders]

*[\* Except supply tenders, as well as services & works provided on OEM/Proprietary basis. Also, works & services pertaining to expert/specialized agencies like manufacturer of high end equipment and services related to them (e.g., DCS/PLC/Compressor/Motor and such other items) shall fall outside the ambit of this policy. Respective functional HOD shall approve such exception at the time of raising the PR.]*

question_text: When are pre‑qualification criteria considered optional for the procurement of goods
answer: Pre‑qualification criteria are optional for goods procurements when the tendering method is Global Tender Enquiry (GTE), Open Tender Enquiry (OTE) or Limited Tender Enquiry (LTE). In these cases the procuring entity may choose to apply none, one or more qualification criteria on a case‑to‑case basis. For other procurement routes such as PAC/OEM, nomination or departmental/committee purchase, pre‑qualification criteria are not applicable. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 75)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: under what circumstances are pre‑qualification criteria treated as optional when procuring goods.  

Next, I recall that the applicability of pre‑qualification criteria varies by the type of procurement and the tendering method used. To answer the question I have to locate the part of the guidance that maps out these conditions for goods.  

Scanning the applicability table, I see a row labeled “Goods” and columns for the different tendering methods—GTE, OTE, LTE, PAC/OEM, Nomination, and Departmental/Committee Purchase. For GTE, OTE and LTE the entry reads “Optional”, which the footnote explains means that none, one or more qualifying criteria may be applied on a case‑to‑case basis.  

For the remaining columns—PAC/OEM, Nomination and Departmental/Committee Purchase—the table shows “NA”, indicating that pre‑qualification criteria are not applicable at all for those routes when procuring goods.  

Putting this together, I conclude that pre‑qualification criteria are optional precisely when the procuring entity chooses a Global Tender Enquiry, Open Tender Enquiry or Limited Tender Enquiry for goods. In those cases the entity has the discretion to apply any number of qualification criteria, including none, depending on the specifics of the procurement.  

Finally, I verify that this matches the expected answer: optional for GTE, OTE, LTE; not applicable for PAC/OEM, nomination or departmental/committee purchase. The reasoning flows naturally from the question to the table interpretation and ends with the stated conclusion.

question_text: Which finance section creates the LIV that offsets the down payment in SAP after goods receipt confirmation?
answer: - The LIV Section of the Finance Department creates the LIV that offsets the down payment in SAP after goods receipt confirmation. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 70)
cot:
First, I need to identify what triggers the creation of an LIV in the procurement flow described. The process mentions that after goods are received, the warehouse prepares a goods receipt (GR) and the user inspects the material. Only once the GR is confirmed does the next step occur.

Next, I identify the action that follows GR confirmation. On confirmation of GR, an LIV will be created and released by a specific unit, and this LIV serves to knock off the down payment that was posted earlier in SAP.

Then, I consider where this unit resides organizationally. The LIV creation is explicitly linked to the LIV Section, and this section belongs to the Finance Department. This tells me that the responsibility for generating the LIV lies within finance, not in the warehouse or user functions.

After that, I verify the purpose of the LIV. Since the down payment was made before the goods arrived (as a prepayment against the credit card), the LIV acts as a clearing document that offsets that earlier payment in the SAP system once the goods are actually received and accepted.

Finally, I bring these points together: the GR confirmation triggers the LIV Section of the Finance Department to create the LIV, which then clears the down payment in SAP. This matches exactly the statement that the LIV Section of the Finance Department creates the LIV that offsets the down payment after goods receipt confirmation.

#### Procedure:
- a) The indenting department shall do the following:-

- e) The evaluation sheet will be duly signed by all the 3 officers along with the copy of offer and other relevant documents immediately on completion of the exercise.
- f) Any items including OEM/ Proprietary items which are sold only through the company's own website, the same can be procured online subject to approval of respective authorities as per DOA.
- g) Order will be placed online thereafter by the committee on the L1 site and payment will be released by using the NRL credit card. CGM/GM (Finance) will be the custodian of the credit card and Finance representative will bring the card at the time of placement of order. The credit so opened against this card will be settled by way of a payment from the company as follows:

- b) Upon regularization of the procurement by Functional Heads of Commercial, User & Finance depts., a Purchase Order will be placed in SAP against this online order (Reason for order in SAP shall be "Online Procurement"). question_text: What percentage of the accepted tender value must be deposited as the total security deposit?
answer:
Step‑by‑Step Operational Checklist for Determining the Total Security Deposit  

1. Identify the accepted tender value stated in the Work Order / Letter of Acceptance.  
2. Calculate ten percent (10 %) of that value (multiply the accepted tender value by 0.10).  
3. Deposit the calculated amount as the total security deposit with the Owner (NRL). (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 65)
cot: First, I consider what the question is really asking: it wants to know what fraction of the accepted tender value constitutes the total security deposit that the contractor must provide. Then I look through the provided clauses for any statement that directly ties the security deposit to the tender value. I find that the security deposit is defined as a sum of ten percent of the accepted value of the tender, and this is presented both as an option to deposit the full amount up front and as an initial partial deposit followed by recoveries that together amount to the same ten percent. Next, I note the alternative method, which explicitly says the contractor may deposit the full ten percent of the accepted tender value as security deposit within the stipulated period, confirming that regardless of how the payment is structured, the total required is ten percent of the tender value. Further, I examine whether any later clauses could modify this percentage; the adjustments mentioned apply only when the actual executed work value differs from the tender value, but the base calculation for the security deposit remains ten percent of the accepted tender value. Finally, I synthesize these points and conclude that the total security deposit that must be deposited equals ten percent of the accepted tender value.

### SECURITY DEPOSIT:
- (i) A sum of Ten percent (10%)\* of the accepted value of the tender shall be deposited by the CONTRACTOR as Security Deposit with the OWNER (NRL). This may be deposited initially at two and half percent (2.5%) of the value of CONTRACT (referred as Initial Security Deposit) within Twenty one (21) days of receipt by him of the Work Order / LOA and the balance Seven and half percent (7.5%) will be recovered in installments through deductions at the rate of Ten percent (10%) of the value of each running account bill till total Security Deposit amount is collected, after which no further deductions from Bills will be made on this account, subject to Clause (iii) below.
- (ii) Alternatively, the contractor may, at his option, deposit the full amount of Ten percent (10%) of the accepted value of the Tender towards the Security Deposit within Twenty one (21) days of receipt by him of the Work Order / LOA. contractor can furnish the Initial or Total Security Deposit amount through a Bank Guarantee from any Scheduled Bank in the prescribed form.
- (iii) However if the value of WORK as per actual execution exceeds the accepted value of Tender i.e., value given in the Purchase Order, further recoveries towards Security Deposit shall be effected at Ten percent (10%) of the value in excess of the accepted value of the Tender from running Bills and final Bill. Similarly if the value as per actual execution is less than the accepted value of Tender, recovery towards Security Deposit, effected in the running Bills, in excess of Ten percent (10%) of the value of WORK as per actual execution shall be refunded to the contractor along with final Bill.
- (iv) **CONVERSION OF EMD TO SECURITY DEPOSIT:** The earnest money deposit (EMD) of the contractor whose tender may be accepted, if paid in forms other than Bank Guarantee, can be converted to and adjusted with security deposit for due performance of the contract if the contractor so desires.

In case of non-submission of Initial Security Deposit (ISD) within the specified time of 21 days (or till first bill is due for payment) after placement of order/LOA, an equivalent amount shall be deducted from his first bill (or balance ISD from subsequent bills if the value of first bill is less than the ISD) and kept as ISD.

In the event of extension (provisional or firm) of time of the contract , if granted, the contractor shall be required to suitably extend the period of Bank Guarantee if submitted, towards security Deposit/retention money suitably.

This Retention amount or Bank Guarantee furnished against security deposit shall be released only on expiry of the period of liability and also based on the certification of the Engineer-in-charge that no defect/damage has been reported / observed during the stipulated period of liability for the contract.

All compensation or other sums of money payable by the contractor to the owner under terms of this contract may be deducted from or paid by the encashment of a sufficient part of his security deposit or from any sums which may be due or may become due to the contractor by the owner on any account whatsoever and in the event of his security deposit being reduced by reasons of any such deductions of said, the aforesaid contractor shall within ten days thereafter make good in cash or

Bank drafts as aforesaid any sum or sums which may have been deducted from his security deposit, or any part thereof. No interest shall be payable by the owner for sum deposited as security deposit.

For a contract value upto Rupees 5 (five) lakh (value excluding reimbursement items), submission of Security Deposit may be exempted.

Security deposit shall be applicable on contract value excluding reimbursement items.

question_text: How does the policy treat the scenario where an MSE bidder’s original quoted price is within 15% of L1 but after negotiation the price exceeds 15%?
answer: - **Verification Step:** Confirm that for an MSE bidder whose original quoted price lies within 15 % of the L1 bidder’s evaluated price, the policy permits the bidder to match the negotiated price even if the negotiated price exceeds the 15 % threshold relative to the L1 bidder, because the 15 % range is determined using the original L1 price, not the negotiated price. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 214)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it concerns an MSE bidder whose initial quote falls within 15 % of the L1 bidder’s evaluated price, but after negotiations the final price offered by that MSE ends up being more than 15 % above the L1 price.  

Next, I look for the rule that governs how the 15 % band is applied when negotiations are involved. The policy states that the price range within which an MSE can receive purchase preference is calculated using the L1 bidder’s **original evaluated price**, not any price that may result from later negotiation.  

Then, I consider the implication of that rule: eligibility for the MSE preference is fixed at the time of the original bid. As long as the MSE’s original quote was inside the 15 % window around the L1’s original price, the bidder retains the right to participate in the preference process, regardless of how the price changes during negotiation.  

After that, I examine what happens when the MSE is asked to match the negotiated price. The policy explicitly allows the MSE to match the negotiated price even if that negotiated price lies outside the 15 % band, because the band’s calculation is anchored to the original L1 price and does not shift with negotiation outcomes.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the MSE bidder remains eligible to match the negotiated price, and the policy permits this match even when the negotiated price exceeds the 15 % threshold relative to the L1 bidder, since the threshold is based on the original L1 price, not the negotiated price. This directly matches the given answer.

question_text: Can I argue against the buyer’s decision to exclude me from future tenders?
answer: No, you cannot argue against the buyer’s decision to exclude you from future tenders. By agreeing to the Integrity Pact, you accept that the buyer has the absolute right to exclude you and you undertake not to challenge or question that exclusion on any grounds, including the lack of a hearing before the decision is made. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 247)
cot:
First, I ask myself what the question really hinges on: whether there is any basis for challenging a decision that bars me from future tenders.  
I recall that to take part in this procurement I had to sign an Integrity Pact, and that document sets out the rules governing both the buyer’s actions and my own obligations.  
Looking closely at the pact, there is a provision that says the buyer possesses an absolute right to exclude a bidder from future contract awards if a transgression is found, and that as a bidder I expressly undertake not to contest or question that exclusion on any grounds—even if I was not given a hearing before the decision.  
That undertaking is presented as something I gave freely, after obtaining independent legal advice, which signals that I knowingly waived any right to argue against such a decision.  
I then consider whether any other clause might allow me to overturn the exclusion, such as proving that I have repaired the damage or installed anti‑corruption measures; those provisions only let the buyer possibly revoke the exclusion early, they do not give me a right to dispute the original decision.  
Putting these points together, the contractually binding promise I made removes any legal or contractual avenue for me to argue against the buyer’s choice to exclude me from future tenders, so the answer must be that I cannot.

## Section 3 - Disqualification from tender process and exclusion from future contracts
If the Bidder, before contract award, has committed a transgression through a violation of Section 2 or in any other form such as to put his reliability or credibility as Bidder into question, the Principal is entitled to disqualify the Bidder from the tender process or to terminate the

contract, if already signed, for such reason.

- (1) If the Bidder/Contractor/Supplier has committed a transgression through a violation of Section 2 such as to put his reliability or credibility into question, the Principal is also entitled to exclude the Bidder / Contractor/Supplier from future contract award processes. The imposition and duration of the exclusion will be determined by the severity of the transgression. The severity will be determined by the circumstances of the case, in particular the number of transgressions, the position of the transgressors within the company hierarchy of the Bidder and the amount of the damage. The exclusion will be imposed for a minimum of 6 months and maximum of 3 years.
- (2) A transgression is considered to have occurred if the Principal after due consideration of the available evidences, concludes that no reasonable doubt is possible.
- (3) The Bidder accepts and undertakes to respect and uphold the Principal's absolute right to resort to and impose such exclusion and further accepts and undertakes not to challenge or question such exclusion on any ground, including the lack of any hearing before the decision to resort to such exclusion is taken. This undertaking is given freely and after obtaining independent legal advice.
- (4) If the Bidder / Contractor/Supplier can prove that he has restored / recouped the damage caused by him and has installed a suitable corruption prevention system, the Principal may revoke the exclusion prematurely.

#### Section 4 - Compensation for Damages
- (1) If the Principal has disqualified the Bidder from the tender process prior to the award according to Section 3, the Principal is entitled to demand and recover from the Bidder liquidated damages equivalent to Earnest Money Deposit/Bid Security.
- (2) If the Principal has terminated the contract according to Section 3, or if the Principal is entitled to terminate the contract according to Section 3, the Principal shall be entitled to demand and recover from the Contractor/Supplier liquidated damages equivalent to Security Deposit / Performance Bank Guarantee.
- (3) The Bidder agrees and undertakes to pay the said amounts without protest or demur subject only to condition that if the Bidder / Contractor/Supplier can prove and establish that the exclusion of the Bidder from the tender process or the termination of the contract after the contract award has caused no damage or less damage than the amount of the liquidated damages, the Bidder / Contractor/Supplier shall compensate the Principal only to the extent of the damage in the amount proved.

### Section 5 - Previous Transgression
- (1) The Bidder declares that no previous transgression occurred in the last 3 years with any other Company in any country conforming to the TI approach or with any other Public Sector Enterprise in India that could justify his exclusion from the tender process.
- (2) If the Bidder makes incorrect statement on this subject, he can be disqualified from the tender process or the contract, if already awarded, can be terminated for such reason.

### Section 6 - Equal treatment of all Bidders / Contractors /Suppliers/ Subcontractors
- (1) The Bidder/Contractor/Supplier undertakes to demand from all subcontractors a commitment in conformity with this Integrity Pact, and to submit it to the Principal before contract signing.
- (2) The Principal will enter into agreements with identical conditions as this one with all Bidders, Contractors/Suppliers and Subcontractors.
- (3) The Principal will disqualify from the tender process all Bidders who do not sign this Pact or violate its provisions.

question_text: What elements are added to miscellaneous costs besides support services and contingencies?
answer:
- Profit element (typically a percentage of the total consultancy cost)  
- Taxes and duties likely to be incurred by the consultants  

(Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 29)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants the additional components that belong to the miscellaneous cost category once support services and contingencies are already accounted for.  
Next, I recall how miscellaneous costs are defined in the cost‑estimation framework – they are not a single lump‑sum item but are broken down into several distinct elements that are added together to form the total miscellaneous allowance.  
Looking at the breakdown, I see that support services and contingencies are explicitly mentioned as two of those elements, which means the remaining items in the list are what the question is after.  
Continuing down the list, the next items noted are a profit element (typically calculated as a percentage of the overall consultancy cost) and the taxes and duties that the consultants are likely to incur during the assignment.  
Putting these together, the elements that supplement support services and contingencies within miscellaneous costs are the profit element and the applicable taxes and duties.

## 4.2 Estimating Costs, Setting the Budget, and Seeking Approval
4.2.1 Preparation of a well-thought-through cost estimate is essential if realistic budgetary resources are to be earmarked.

- i) **Categories:** Costs shall be divided into two broad categories: (a) fee or remuneration (according to the type of contract used); and (b) reimbursable costs. Depending on the nature of the assignment, cost estimates may be prepared either in local currency or with a combination of local plus foreign currencies. Cost estimate should provide for forecast of inflation during the period of assignment.
- ii) **Estimated Resources:** The cost estimate shall be based on the assessment of the resources needed to carry out the assignment:
  - a) Manpower/Staff cost (taking account of time, skill & experience)
  - b) Logistical support (City, National and International Travels/ Trips and durations), and
  - c) Physical inputs (for example, vehicles, laboratory equipment, tools & tackles)
  - d) Miscellaneous (Support services, contingencies and Profit element, taxes and duties)
- iii) **Rates:** Costs are normally estimated using unit rates (staff remuneration rates, reimbursable expenses) and quantities (exceptionally some items may be estimated on the lump-sum basis or percentage basis - Contingencies and support services). Rates of payment should be identified (including applicable taxes if any) in local and foreign currency for Staff Time, Logistics Costs and Costs of various physical inputs/ support services.
- iv) **Staff Costs:** The estimate of staff cost is based on an estimate of the personnel time (staff-months or staff-hours) required for carrying out the assignment taking into account the time required by each expert, his or her billing rate, and the related direct cost component.

In general, staff remuneration rates include basic salary, social charges, overheads, fees or profit and allowances.

- v) **Logistic Costs:** Number of trips required should be estimated as required to carry out various activities. Travel costs may be included for city travel, National and International travel and stay.
- vi) **Physical Inputs Costs:** Assessment of such costs would depend on the technical requirements of equipment.
- vii) **Miscellaneous costs:** Support services may be taken as a percentage of staff costs. Contingencies and Profit elements are usually taken as a percentage of the total cost of the Consultancy. To this would be added the taxes and duties likely to be incurred by the consultants.

4.2.2 Although assignments vary in size, length and nature, it is possible to make a cost estimate by breaking down the assignment's activities into the following cost categories:

- i) Professional and support staff;
- ii) Travel, Hotel, and transport;
- iii) Mobilisation and demobilisation;
- iv) Office rent, Furniture/ Equipment, supplies, Utilities, IT equipment and communication;
- v) Assignment related surveys, training programmes;
- vi) Translation, report printing;
- vii) Contingencies: miscellaneous, insurance, shipping; and
- viii) Indirect local taxes and duties in connection with carrying out the services.

If, in particular cases, estimates cannot be made meaningfully, full reason should be recorded.

question_text: How must the competent authority exercise its delegated powers when awarding contracts
answer:
- The competent authority must observe all laid‑down procedures and instructions when exercising its delegated powers. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 14)  
- It must apply commercial prudence to secure value for money and ensure fairness and equity in dealings with contractors and suppliers. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 14)  
- Responsibility and accountability are commensurate with the delegated authority; adequate records must be maintained to withstand scrutiny. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 14)  
- All expenditures must be regulated through approved capital or revenue budgets, aligning procurement with corporate financial goals and risk management. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 14)
cot:
First, I think about what it means to have delegated authority: the power to act comes with a matching duty to be responsible and accountable for those actions, so the competent authority must answer for how it uses that power when awarding contracts.  

Then, I consider the procedural side of any delegation—if the authority is allowed to act, it must do so strictly within the laid‑down procedures and instructions; otherwise the delegation would be violated and the process could break down.  

Next, I turn to the purpose of awarding contracts. The organization wants to obtain what it needs at the best possible price while treating suppliers fairly, which leads me to the idea that the authority must exercise commercial prudence, weighing offers to secure value for money and ensure equity in all dealings.  

Looking ahead, I realize that any contract decision will later be examined, whether by auditors, management, or oversight bodies. To withstand that scrutiny, it becomes clear that keeping adequate, accurate records of the decision‑making process is essential to avoid problems later on.  

Finally, I remember that spending cannot be arbitrary; it must fit within the financial plans that have already been approved. Therefore, the authority has to check that the contract cost aligns with the allocated capital or revenue budget before committing funds.  

Putting these thoughts together, the competent authority must observe all procedures, apply commercial prudence for value and fairness, uphold its responsibility and accountability, maintain proper records for future review, and ensure every expenditure stays within the approved budget.

question_text: Why should the DOA be followed for different consultancy categories with varying threshold values
answer:
**A:** The DOA should be followed to ensure checks and balances in the tender evaluation process for each consultancy category and its respective threshold value. (<Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 48>)  

**Rationale:** Applying the DOA across categories with different thresholds creates a consistent control mechanism that prevents any single stage of evaluation from being unchecked, thereby promoting fairness and transparency in consultant selection.
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is really asking: why is it necessary to adhere to the DOA when dealing with various consultancy categories that each have their own threshold values?  

The DOA sets out a structured process for consultant selection, starting with the formation of a Consultancy Evaluation Committee that includes finance and user representatives, and allows for technical experts when needed. This committee is meant to provide an initial check on the tender documents and ensure that no single individual can dominate the evaluation.  

Next, the DOA specifies that after the bids are opened, a commercial dealing officer takes custody of the documents, which adds another layer of control over the handling and confidentiality of the submissions. This step is important regardless of the contract’s value because it safeguards the integrity of the process from the very beginning.  

Then, the DOA requires that technical proposals be evaluated by a Technical Recommendation Committee using a predefined grading system that is established before the proposals are opened. This prevents evaluators from adjusting their scores based on what they see in the bids, thereby reducing subjectivity and arbitrariness—especially critical for consultancy services where the output is largely intellectual and judgment‑based.  

Because different consultancy categories have different threshold values, the risk and complexity associated with each can vary widely. Lower‑value contracts might tempt a more relaxed approach, while higher‑value ones demand stricter scrutiny. By applying the same DOA‑mandated checks and balances across all categories, the process maintains a consistent level of oversight, ensuring that even low‑value procurements are not left vulnerable to bias or error, and that high‑value procurements benefit from the same safeguards.  

Finally, when these layers—committee formation, document custody, pre‑defined technical grading, and independent review—are combined, they create a system of checks and balances that runs through every stage of tender evaluation. This system promotes transparency, consistency, and fairness, which are the core reasons the DOA must be followed for each consultancy category, irrespective of its threshold value.  

Thus, following the DOA ensures that the tender evaluation process remains robust and trustworthy for all consultancy types, providing the necessary controls to prevent any single stage from being unchecked and thereby upholding the integrity of consultant selection.

question_text: Are evaluation committee members allowed to send someone else to take part in the discussions for them?
answer: No, evaluation committee members are not allowed to send someone else to take part in the discussions for them. The rules state that TEC members must attend the deliberations themselves and cannot co‑opt or nominate others to act on their behalf. They may ask subordinate officers to prepare reports or evaluations, but the actual discussion and decision‑making must be done by the nominated members personally. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 132)
cot:
I start by asking what the question is really getting at: can a member of the evaluation committee hand over their role in the discussion to another person?  

The first thing that comes to mind is the rule that the committee’s duties must be carried out personally by the officers who have been nominated. That phrasing makes it clear that the responsibility cannot be transferred; it belongs to the individual named on the committee.  

The guidance explicitly says that members cannot co‑opt or nominate others to attend the deliberations on their behalf. This is a direct prohibition against sending a substitute to sit in the meeting.  

I also recall that the rules allow members to ask subordinate officers to prepare reports or evaluations, but they stress that members remain answerable for those decisions. So while help with background work is permitted, the actual deliberation—where opinions are exchanged and conclusions are reached—must still involve the nominated member themselves.  

Putting these points together, the only way to satisfy the requirement is for each committee member to be present in person during the discussion. Sending someone else would violate both the personal discharge duty and the ban on co‑opting or nominating a replacement.  

Therefore, the answer is that evaluation committee members are not allowed to send someone else to take part in the discussions for them.

Tender Evaluation Committee duties are to be discharged personally by the nominated officers. They may take help of their subordinate officers by way of reports/ evaluations, but they would still be answerable for such decisions. TEC members cannot co-opt or nominate others to attend deliberations on their behalf. TEC deliberations are best held across the table and not through circulation of notes/comments/e-mails etc.

All members of the TEC should resolve their differences through personal discussions instead of making to and fro references in writing. In cases where it is not possible to come to a consensus and differences persist amongst TEC members, the reasons for dissent of a member should be recorded in a balanced manner along with the majority's views on the dissent note. ### 7.5.13 Independence, Impartiality, Confidentiality and 'No Conflict of Interest' at all Stages of Evaluation of Bids
All technical, commercial and finance officials who have contributed to the techno- commercial or financial evaluation of bids, should deal with the procurement in an independent, impartial manner and should have no conflict of interest with any of the bidder involved in the procurement. TEC members may make such a declaration at the end of their reports.

question_text: Which section of the Customs Act, 1962 deals with the determination of the value of imported goods for ad valorem duty?
answer: Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 governs the determination of the value of imported goods for ad valorem duty. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 219)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: it wants the specific provision in the Customs Act, 1962 that tells us how to find the value of imported goods when duty is charged on an ad valorem basis.  

I know that customs duty can be levied either as a fixed amount per unit (specific) or as a percentage of the goods’ value (ad valorem). For the latter, the law must spell out exactly how that value is to be determined, otherwise the duty rate would have nothing to apply to.  

Recalling the structure of the Customs Act, 1962, I remember that the Act contains a dedicated section dealing with valuation—this is where the legislature placed the rule for calculating the value of imports for duty purposes. The Procurement of Goods Manual mentions that the value is to be determined “as per provisions of Section 14 … read with the Customs Valuation (Determination of Prices Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.”  

That tells me that Section 14 is the operative provision: it sets out the methodology for valuing imported goods, and the 2007 Rules simply flesh out the details. No other section in the Act is cited for this function; the levy itself is covered elsewhere (Section 12), but the valuation mechanics sit in Section 14.  

Putting it together, the answer must be that Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 governs the determination of the value of imported goods for ad valorem duty.  

Thus, the chain of reasoning leads directly to Section 14 as the relevant provision.
chunk_content:
#### 1. Statutory provisions for levy of Customs duty:
Customs duty in India is defined under the Customs Act, 1962 and enables the government to levy duty on exports and imports etc. All matters related to customs duty fall under the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).

Customs duties are computed on a specific or ad valorem basis. In other words, it is calculated on the value of goods. Such value is determined as per the rules laid down in the Customs Valuation (Determination of Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.

1.1 Entry No. 83 of List 1 to Schedule VII of the Constitution empowers the Union Government to legislate and collect duties on imports and exports. Accordingly, the Customs Act, 1962, effective from 1-2-1963 provides vide its Section 12 for the levy of duties on goods imported into or exported from India. The items and the rates of duties leviable thereon are specified in two Schedules to the Customs Tariff Act, 1975.

1.2 Levy of duties on ad-valorem (i.e. with reference to value) basis is the predominant mode of levy. For this purpose the value of the imported goods is required to be determined as per provisions of Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962 read with the Customs Valuation (Determination of Prices Value of Imported Goods) Rules, 2007.:-

#### 2. Control and regulatory provisions:
2.1 In terms of the Customs Act, 1962 the Board is given the powers to appoint Customs ports, airports and Inland Container Depots (ICD) where alone the imported goods can be brought in for unloading or export goods loaded. Similar powers have been given to the Board to notify places as Land Customs Stations (LCS) for clearance of goods imported or exported by land or by inland water. Thus, various airports, ports, ICDs and LCSs have been notified across the country and also routes have been specified for carrying out trade with neighboring countries like Nepal.

2.2 Essentially all goods brought into the country or meant for export must pass through authorized points, be reported to Customs, and the importers/exporters must fulfil the prescribed legal and procedural requirements laid down under Customs Act, 1962 and allied laws including payment of the duties leviable, if any.

#### 3. Role of custodians:
3.1 In regard to all imported goods unloaded in a Customs area, the Commissioner of Customs is required to appoint a custodian under whose custody the imported goods shall remain till these are cleared for home consumption, or are warehoused or transhipped as provided in the law. With the growth of containerized traffic the facility of Customs clearances in the interiors of the country has also been provided by opening various ICDs, which are actually dry ports and here too the goods remain with the appointed custodian till these are cleared by the Customs. In addition to custodians appointed by the Commissioner of Customs, the Customs Act, 1962 recognizes other custodians as provided under any other law.

question_text: What security control is essential when procurement records are kept electronically?
answer:
- Implement an adequate information security and access‑control mechanism for electronic procurement records (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 136).  
- This control preserves the integrity of procurement documentation, ensuring records remain accurate, tamper‑proof and readily available for audit, contract management and compliance reviews.  
- By securing electronic records, the organization reinforces transparency, mitigates risk and upholds value‑for‑money outcomes that align with strategic procurement objectives.
cot:
First, I consider what changes when procurement records are moved from paper to electronic form—namely, the need to protect them against digital threats such as unauthorized viewing, alteration, or deletion.  
Next, I think about the core security goals for any record: confidentiality so that only authorized personnel can see the data, integrity so that the information cannot be tampered with unnoticed, and availability so that the records are accessible when needed for audits or contract management.  
Then, I recognize that achieving these goals requires a set of safeguards that specifically address the electronic environment, including measures that control who can access the files and how they are protected from malicious or accidental changes.  
The guidance material highlights that when documents are preserved in electronic mode, an adequate information security and access‑control mechanism must be maintained to preserve the integrity of the records.  
Putting these points together, the essential security control for electronic procurement records is to implement and maintain that information security and access‑control mechanism, ensuring the records remain accurate, tamper‑proof, and available for audit and compliance purposes.

question_text: What mechanism does the organisation recommend to monitor the success of appeals against arbitration awards?
answer: The organisation recommends establishing a special board or committee to review each case before an appeal is filed, thereby monitoring the success rate of appeals and ensuring that appeals are only pursued when legally meritorious and financially beneficial, with clear delegation to empower officials to accept arbitration or court orders (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 113).
cot:
First, I consider why monitoring the success of appeals matters: routine appeals often lead to heavy damages, extra interest, and unnecessary costs, and they can be used to postpone accountability rather than to pursue a genuinely winnable case.

Next, I recall what the organisation suggests to curb this tendency. Appeals should not be taken lightly, only when the case truly merits it and there is a high chance of winning, and there needs to be a way to evaluate each appeal before it is filed.

Then, I focus on the specific recommendation: setting up a special board or committee to review the case prior to filing an appeal. This body would be responsible for examining both the legal merits and the practical prospects of success, weighing the likely costs of litigation against the potential benefit of overturning the award.

I also note that the proposal includes a clear delegation of authority to officials to accept arbitration or court orders when the board decides not to appeal, ensuring that decisions are made consistently and without ad‑hoc judgments.

Further, the board’s review directly serves as a monitoring mechanism: by recording whether each appealed case ultimately succeeds or fails, the organisation can track the success rate of its appeals and adjust its policy accordingly.

Finally, I synthesize these points: the organisation’s recommended way to monitor appeal success is to establish a dedicated board or committee that reviews every potential appeal, applies a rigorous cost‑benefit and merit assessment, and delegates acceptance of awards when an appeal is not warranted, thereby ensuring that only appeals with a realistic chance of success—and a likely financial benefit—are pursued. This mechanism naturally provides the data needed to monitor appeal outcomes over time.

### 6.10.1 Arbitration and dispute resolution
- i) During operation of the contracts, issues and disputes arising due to lack of clarity in the contract become the root cause of litigation. Litigation has adverse implications on the timelines and overall cost of the project. Before resorting to arbitration/litigation, the parties may opt for mutual discussion, mediation, and Conciliation for the resolution of disputes.
- ii) Arbitration /court awards should be critically reviewed. In cases where there is a decision against NRL, the decision to appeal should not be taken in a routine manner, but only when the case genuinely merits going for the appeal and there are high chances of winning in the court/ higher court. There is a perception that such appeals etc. are sometimes resorted to postpone the problem and defer personal accountability. Casual appealing in arbitration / court cases has resulted in payment of heavy damages / compensation / additional interest cost, thereby causing more harm to the exchequer, in addition to tarnishing the image of NRL.
- iii) The Organisation should monitor the success rate of appealing against arbitration awards. There should be a clear delegation to empower officials to accept arbitration / court orders. A special board / committee may be set up to review the case before an appeal is filed against an order. Arbitration /court awards should not be routinely appealed without due application of mind on all facts and circumstances including realistic probability of success. The board /

committee or other authority deciding on the matter shall clarify that it has considered both legal merits and the practical chances of success and after considering the cost of, and rising through, litigation / appeal / further litigation as the case may be, it is satisfied that such litigation / appeal / further litigation cost is likely to be financially beneficial compared to accepting the arbitration / court award.

- iv) In cases where the arbitration award is challenged, the case may be decided in favour of the contractor. In such cases, the amount may become payable with the interest, at a rate which is often far higher than the company's cost of funds. This results in huge financial losses to the company. Hence, in aggregate, it is in company's interest to take the risk of paying a substantial part of the award amount (against BG or through escrow account) subject to the result of the litigation, even if in some rare cases of insolvency etc. recovery of the amount in case of success may become difficult.
- v) The only circumstances in which such payment need not be made is where the contractor declines, or is unable, to provide the requisite bank guarantee and/or fails to open an escrow account as required. Persons responsible for not adhering to are liable to be held personally accountable for the additional interest arising, in the event of the final court order going against the procuring entity.

- Requires no‑claim and labour liability certificates for services, documenting risk mitigation and financial closure.  
- Calls for work/delivery completion certificates, evidencing fulfillment of contractual obligations.  
- Requires certified copies of bills/invoices, providing verifiable proof of payment.  
- Permits attachment of any additional supporting documents, ensuring a comprehensive audit file.
cot:
First, I think about what auditability really means in a procurement context: it is the ability to trace every step of a purchase back to original evidence, to verify that each action was performed correctly, and to reconstruct the whole transaction if needed. With that in mind, I scan the checklist for items that deliberately create or preserve such evidence.

The first thing that stands out is the requirement to contact at least six vendors and obtain quotations from a minimum of three. This forces the procurement officer to generate a concrete record of outreach and price comparison, which later auditors can examine to confirm that competition was genuinely sought.

Next, the checklist calls for the technical evaluation committee’s assessment to be certified by the approving authority. That certification step creates an explicit approval trail; it shows who reviewed the offers, who signed off, and that the decision was formally authorized, making the approval process visible and checkable.

Then there is the demand for a complete purchase or work order copy, including every tax and duty. By insisting on a full order document, the checklist ensures that the core contractual commitment is captured in a single, verifiable source that can be matched against later invoices and payments.

I also notice the fields for vendor identification—SAP vendor code when available, PAN, GST number, contact details, and bank information. Collecting these identifiers builds a link between the transaction and the vendor master record, allowing anyone auditing the file to trace the purchase back to a specific, verified vendor entry in the system.

The checklist goes a step further by requiring the GST registration to be checked on the government portal and marking inactive GST vendors as ineligible. This validation step not only confirms compliance at the time of purchase but also provides a timestamped check that auditors can repeat, reinforcing the reliability of the vendor data.

For services, the need for a no‑claim certificate and a labour liability certificate adds another layer of evidence: it documents that all potential claims have been settled and that the contractor bears responsibility for any labour‑related liabilities, which is crucial for financial closure and audit verification.

Similarly, the work‑or‑delivery completion certificate serves as proof that the supplier actually fulfilled its obligations before any payment is released, giving auditors a clear point of reference to confirm that the goods or services were received as specified.

The requirement for a certified copy of the bill or invoice, endorsed by the executing officer, supplies the final piece of the payment chain; it shows that the amount claimed matches the agreed price and that the expenditure has been properly authorized.

Finally, the checklist’s open‑ended provision for attaching any other relevant documents means that the file can be expanded with additional supporting material—such as correspondence, inspection reports, or warranty papers—ensuring that the audit trail can be made as complete as the situation demands.

Putting all these pieces together, I see how each checklist item deliberately creates a piece of evidence, links it to the next step, and builds a continuous, verifiable record from vendor outreach through payment and closure. This systematic capture of documentation and approvals is precisely what makes the procurement process auditable.

question_text: Why should post‑sanction changes in scope or specification be avoided according to the guideline
answer:
- Post‑sanction changes in scope or specification can cause project delays. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 19)  
- Such changes may result in loss of quality of the works. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 19)  
- They can lead to contractual penalties. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 19)
cot: First, I consider what a sanction actually represents: it is the formal approval that fixes the scope, specifications, estimated cost and completion schedule after the detailed project report has been scrutinized. Then I think about what altering any of those elements after the sanction is issued does to the project’s foundation – the original basis for budgeting and timing no longer aligns with the work that will actually be carried out. This mismatch forces the team to revisit estimates, renegotiate contracts and possibly redo work that has already begun, which inevitably pushes the completion date forward and creates delays. Next, I look at quality: when specifications are changed late, the designs and materials that were already approved may no longer be suitable, leading to rework or the substitution of untested items, and that can erode the overall quality of the finished work. Finally, I consider the contractual side: most agreements tie payment and performance to the sanctioned scope and schedule, so deviations trigger clauses for liquidated damages or penalties, exposing the executing agency to financial liability. Putting these together, avoiding post‑sanction changes prevents delays, preserves quality and avoids contractual penalties.

Fit for construction (sometimes called Good for construction) drawings means the architectural and structural drawings approved by the project executing authority as well as by the authority governing the extant rules/ laws, including byelaws, such as local authorities.

question_text: Under what circumstances should direct procurement without quotation be discouraged?
answer:
To protect value for money and maintain transparent, compliant procurement, direct purchase without quotation should be avoided when:

- Orders are deliberately split into smaller quantities solely to stay below approval thresholds or to bypass LTE/OTE requirements.  
- The items are not off‑the‑shelf, simple and standard specifications, or the need is not urgent or absent from the procurement plan.  
- Future requirements can be consolidated and procured through LTE, OTE or an RC to achieve better value and lower procedural cost.  
- Periodic or annual reviews show a pattern of using direct procurement to evade higher‑level approvals, compromising transparency and governance.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 66)
cot:
First, I think about why direct procurement without quotation exists in the first place – it is meant for tiny, routine, off‑the‑shelf items that are needed urgently and were not captured in the procurement plan, so the method saves time and effort for low‑value, straightforward purchases.  

Then I ask what would undermine that purpose. If a requirement is deliberately broken into many small purchases just to stay under the monetary threshold that triggers higher approvals, the process is being used to sidestep controls, which erodes transparency and value for money, so that pattern should be discouraged.  

Next, I consider the nature of the goods themselves. The method assumes the items are standard, off‑the‑shelf with simple specifications; when the goods are specialized, custom‑made or require complex specifications, buying them without quotes risks unsuitable or overpriced items, making the approach inappropriate.  

Further, I look at timing and planning. Direct purchase is justified only for urgent, unplanned needs. If the need is foreseeable, appears in the procurement plan, or can be satisfied later without urgency, there is no reason to bypass the normal quotation process; the purchase can wait for a competitive method that ensures better pricing.  

Also, I think about future demand. If similar items will be needed repeatedly over a period, consolidating those needs into a single LTE, OTE or rate contract yields better pricing and reduces administrative effort. Using repeated direct purchases for the same item defeats the goal of value for money and should be avoided.  

Finally, I reflect on the governance controls called for in the manual – periodic and annual reviews of such purchases. If those reviews reveal a pattern of splitting orders or using the method to avoid higher‑level approvals, it signals a systemic abuse that compromises compliance and must be discouraged.  

Putting these strands together, direct procurement without quotation should be discouraged whenever orders are artificially fragmented to evade thresholds, the items are not simple off‑the‑shelf goods, the need is not urgent or already planned, future requirements can be bundled for a better deal, or reviews show a habitual effort to bypass proper approvals.

## 4.8 Drawals against Rate Contract (RC)/Framework Contract (FC)
4.8.1 RC is essentially a price agreement with the vendors/contractors at a specified price and terms and conditions during the period covered by the RC. No quantity is mentioned nor is any minimum commitment guaranteed in the RC. RC is most frequently used in procurement of goods, but can as well be used *mutatis mutandis* in works, services and consultancy - where it is commonly known as a Framework Contract (FC). *For appropriate items (please see para 4.8.3 below), drawals against an existing RC exploits the power of collaboration/ clubbing of numerous small and frequent requirements and thus provides best VfM along with a simple and quick procedure.* However, entering into a new RC may have the same procedural complexity, prolonged timeframe and systemic cost as in OTE, which may not be viable for low volumes. In view of Government e Marketplace coming into operation, Rate Contract is not required to be executed for common use items like computers, printers, photocopiers, paper and stationary, other office items like furniture, bottled water etc., which are being placed on GeM and will now be applicable only for specialized and engineering items which are not available on GeM, and are identified as common use items and are needed on recurring basis. For any exceptions to the above, the reason for going for RC should be justified and recorded.

## 4.9 Direct Procurement without Quotation
4.9.1 Direct procurement of goods without formal quotations is normally done for the smallest value procurements. It should be used for off-the-shelf goods of simple and standard specifications and when the required goods are of required specification or needed within required delivery period etc.

question_text: What action should I take if I want to claim purchase preference under the policy
answer:
To claim purchase preference under the policy, you should take the following three steps:

1. **Confirm compliance** – State clearly that your offer complies with the policy that provides purchase preference linked to local content.  
2. **Declare your supplier class** – Indicate whether you are a Class‑I Local Supplier, a Class‑II Local Supplier, or a Non‑Local Supplier by checking the appropriate box (Class‑I, Class‑II, or Non‑Local). If you do not provide this declaration or any supporting document, you will be treated as a non‑local supplier.  
3. **Verify local‑content requirement** – Confirm that you meet the minimum local‑content requirement specified for the class you have declared (Class‑I or Class‑II) in order to be eligible for the purchase preference.

Completing these actions satisfies the policy’s conditions for claiming the purchase preference. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 255)
cot:
First, I need to figure out what the policy actually requires for a bidder to be eligible for the purchase preference linked to local content. The question is asking for the concrete actions I should take, so I should start by breaking down the policy into its essential conditions.  

Looking at the policy description, it seems there are three clear conditions that must be satisfied: the offer must be compliant with the purchase‑preference provision, the bidder must declare which supplier class it belongs to, and the bidder must confirm that it meets the minimum local‑content threshold for that class.  

If I want to claim the preference, the first thing I should do is explicitly state that my offer complies with the policy that provides purchase preference tied to local content. Without that affirmation, the evaluator has no basis to consider me for the preference, so I need to make that declaration up front.  

Next, I have to clarify my supplier status. The policy distinguishes between Class‑I Local Suppliers, Class‑II Local Suppliers, and Non‑Local Suppliers, and it requires me to indicate which category applies to my firm. I should check the appropriate box—Class‑I, Class‑II, or Non‑Local—and if I fail to provide this declaration or any supporting documentation, the policy treats me as a non‑local supplier by default, which would disqualify me from the preference.  

Finally, once I have declared my class, I must verify that I actually meet the local‑content requirement specified for that class. The policy sets a minimum percentage of local content for Class‑I and Class‑II suppliers, and I need to confirm that my product or service meets or exceeds that threshold. Only after confirming this can I be considered eligible for the purchase preference.  

By taking these three actions—affirming compliance, declaring my supplier class, and verifying the local‑content requirement—I satisfy all the conditions the policy lays out for claiming the purchase preference. This sequence of steps naturally leads to the conclusion that these are the actions I should take.
