question_text: Why is it recommended to purchase steel or structural items in units of weight rather than length?
answer: Steel or structural items should be purchased in units of weight because their weight per unit length is subject to tolerance; procuring by length may result in receiving less weight than anticipated, which disadvantages the buyer, whereas weight‑based purchasing aligns with the unit of manufacture, ensuring transparency and standardization. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 37)
cot:
First, I think about what makes a procurement specification effective: it has to be unambiguous and tied to how the item is actually produced, otherwise you open the door to misunderstandings and potential losses.  

Next, I consider steel and structural shapes. Even though we often talk about them in terms of length—meters of beam, feet of pipe—they are actually made and sold by the manufacturer in units of weight, such as metric tons or pounds.  

Then I recall that the weight of a given length of steel isn’t fixed; there’s a tolerance built into the rolling process. A piece that is nominally one meter long might weigh a little more or a little less than the theoretical value, depending on the exact cross‑sectional thickness and density variations.  

If I were to buy by length, I would be paying for a assumed weight per meter. Because of that tolerance, the actual weight I receive could be lower than what I paid for, meaning I get less steel for the same cost—a clear disadvantage to the buyer.  

On the other hand, purchasing directly in weight eliminates that uncertainty: the quantity I pay for is exactly what I receive, irrespective of how the length varies. This aligns the buying unit with the manufacturing unit, which promotes transparency, makes it easier to compare bids, and keeps the process standardized across suppliers.  

Putting these points together, the recommendation to buy steel or structural items by weight rather than by length stems from the need to avoid the shortfall caused by weight‑per‑length tolerance, to protect the buyer from receiving less material than expected, and to ensure the procurement unit matches the unit of manufacture for clarity and fairness.
chunk_content:
**2.1.1** Procurements should be initiated only based on an indent from the user Department. The authority in the user Department initiating the indent for procurement shall first determine the need (including anticipated requirement) for the subject matter of the procurement. Description and Specification of Need assessment is of fundamental importance in ensuring value for money, transparency, competition and level playing field in procurement. The user Department shall maintain all documents relating to the determination and technical/financial/budgetary approvals of the need for procurement. During need assessments, the following matters are decided to comply with the 'Procurement Guidelines':

- i) **The expression/description of the need** keeping in view the Value for Money (VfM) and to ensure wide competition. Therefore to the extent practicable it should be:
  - a) Unambiguous, complete, using common terminology prevalent in relevant trade;
  - b) In accordance with the guidelines prescribed if any in this regard;
  - c) Except in case of proprietary purchase from a selected single source, reference to brand names, catalogue numbers or other details that limit any materials or items to specific manufacturer(s) should be avoided as far as possible. Where unavoidable, such item descriptions should always be followed by the words "or substantially equivalent".
- ii) **Method of satisfying it** (owning/leasing/hiring/outourcing and so on) may be determined as per policies declared in this regard or based on a techno-economic evaluation (using life cycle cost, if feasible) of various alternative methods of satisfaction of the need and compatibility and inter-operability with existing infrastructure or systems.
- iii) The quantity of the subject matter of procurement, commensurate with economy:
  - a) Care should be taken not to make unnecessary procurements much in advance of actual requirements, if such procurement is likely to be unprofitable to the company, coupled with unwarranted inventory-carrying cost. Where sales, consumption or usage limits of requirements have been laid down by the Competent Authority (CA), the officer signing the indent should also certify that the prescribed scales or limits are not exceeded. The authority preparing the indent shall neither package nor divide its procurement or take any other action so as to limit competition among potential bidders or to avoid its obligations under 'Procurement Guidelines'. Provided that in the interest of efficiency, economy, timely completion or supply, wider competition or access to MSEs, a indenting or procuring authority may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, divide its procurement into appropriate packages, or club requirements of other users for procurement. Some requirements e.g. IT Systems may have elements of Goods, Works and Services. It could be either sliced into Goods, Works and Services elements or combined into a package. Such decisions for slicing or packaging should be based on technical and VfM considerations. It is also necessary to round off the calculated quantity to the nearest wagon load/truck load/package to economise on transportation; and
  - b) Units of quantity are a very important parameter. Some items may be manufactured in metric tons but may be used in units of numbers or units of lengths (for example, steel

sheets/structural). For the sake of transparency, it is important to buy an item in units of manufacture. For example, it is better to buy steel/structural in units of weight since it has a tolerance in weight per unit of length; this usually works to the disadvantage of the buyer if it is bought in units of length. The buying and issuing units of an item may be different - but should be standardised.

question_text: What additional details may be required for key professionals or a Project Manager in the Labour/Personnel Activity Schedule?
answer: - Qualification and experience required for any key professionals or Project Manager must be specified in the Labour/Personnel Activity Schedule. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 70)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: it wants to know what extra information should be included for key professionals or a Project Manager when they appear in the Labour/Personnel Activity Schedule.  

Next, I think about what the Labour/Personnel Activity Schedule normally covers. It is used to quantify how personnel are deployed—specifying where they work, what shifts they cover, and how often they are needed.  

Then, I recall that the schedule also addresses situations where specialized staff are involved. When a key professional or a Project Manager is required, the guidance indicates that their specific qualifications and the relevant experience they must possess should be spelled out in the schedule.  

Following that, I consider why those details matter: they allow the bidder to understand the level of expertise needed and to price the service accordingly, while ensuring that any relievers or leave reserves are already factored into the rate and not listed separately.  

Finally, synthesizing these points, the additional detail that must be provided for any key professional or Project Manager in the Labour/Personnel Activity Schedule is their required qualification and experience. This directly matches the answer.

Consistent with these requirements, the layout and content of the Activity Schedule should be as simple and brief as possible. All information relevant for the bidder to quote a price may be included e.g. -the frequency and quantum and time-frame/ duration of completion of activities to be performed. statutory and contractual obligations must be listed, so that price implications and compliance is taken care of by the bidder. question_text: What happens to packets inside letter mail bags that are found to contain dutiable goods
answer: When a letter‑mail bag is opened and a packet inside is found to contain dutiable goods, the packet is **detained** and handed over to the Customs Appraiser together with the letter‑mail bill and the assessment memos. The Appraiser examines the packet, records the description, quantity and value of its contents in the bill, works out the applicable duty rate and amount, notes that rate and amount against the item in the bill, and copies the same information onto the assessment memos that travel with the packet. After this assessment the packet can be released once the duty is paid. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 235)
cot:
First, I picture the scene: a letter‑mail bag is opened and inside one of the packets there are goods that attract duty. The immediate question is what the postal authority does with that packet.  

Then I recall the handling rule for letter‑mail bags: the postmaster must open the bag under customs supervision and look specifically for packets that contain dutiable articles. Any packet that meets that description is not allowed to continue on its normal route; it is set aside for further action.  

Next, I think about what happens to a detained packet. It is not simply left in the bag; it is taken out and handed over to the Customs Appraiser together with the paperwork that travels with the mail – the letter‑mail bill and the assessment memos that have been prepared for the bag. This ensures the customs officer has all the reference details needed to assess the packet.  

Looking at the appraiser’s role, the next step is the actual examination. The appraiser opens the packet, notes down a full description of its contents, the quantity and the declared value, and enters those particulars into the letter‑mail bill. From that information the applicable duty rate is determined, the amount of duty is calculated, and both the rate and the amount are recorded against the item in the bill. The same figures are then copied onto the assessment memos that accompany the packet so that the postmaster later knows what duty must be paid.  

Finally, once the assessment is complete the packet remains in customs custody until the duty is settled. After the addressee (or their agent) pays the assessed duty, the packet is released and can proceed to normal delivery.  

Putting those steps together gives the full picture: the packet is detained, presented to the Customs Appraiser with the letter‑mail bill and assessment memos, examined and valued, duty is calculated and noted in both documents, and the packet is forwarded for delivery only after the duty is paid.

6.1 Rules Regarding Postal Parcels and Letter Packets from Foreign Ports in/out of India prescribe procedure for landing and clearing at notified ports/airports/ LCSs of parcels and packets forwarded by foreign mails or passenger vessels or airliners. The procedure broadly is as under:

(a) The boxes or bags containing the parcels shall be labeled as "Postal Parcel", "Parcel Post", "Parcel Mail", "Letter Mail" and will be allowed to pass at specified the Foreign Parcel Department of the Foreign Post Offices and Sub Foreign Post Offices.

(b) On receipt of the parcel mail, the Postmaster hands over to the Customs the following documents:

- (i) A memo showing the total number of parcels received from each country of origin;
- (ii) Parcel Bills in sheet form (in triplicate) and the senders' declarations (if available) and any other relevant documents that may be required for the examination, assessment etc. by the Customs Department;
- (iii) The relative Customs Declarations and dispatch notes (if any); and
- (iv) Any other information required in connection with the preparation of the Parcel Bills which the Post Office is able to furnish.

(c) On receipt of the documents, the Customs Appraiser shall scrutinize the particulars given in the Parcel Bill and identify the parcels to be detained for examination either for want of necessary particulars or defective description or suspected misdeclaration or under-valuation of contents. The remaining parcels are to be assessed by showing the rates of duty on the declarations or Parcel Bill, as the case may be. For this purpose, the Appraisers are generally guided by the particulars given in the Parcel Bill or Customs declarations and dispatch notes (if any). When any invoice, document or information is required to ascertain the real value, quantity or description of the contents of a parcel, the addressee may be called upon by way of a notice to produce or furnish such invoice, document and information.

(d) Whenever necessary, the values from the declarations are entered into the Parcel Bill and after conversion into Indian Currency at the ruling rates of exchange, the amount of duty is calculated and entered. The relevant copies of Parcel Bills with the declarations so completed are then returned to the Postmaster.

(e) Duty is calculated at the rate and valuation in force on the date that the postal authorities present a list of such goods to the Customs. In case the parcels are brought through a vessel and postal authorities present list of goods before arrival of the vessel, the rate of duty and tariff value shall be the date on which Inward Entry is granted to the vessel.

(f) All parcels marked for detention are to be detained by the Postmaster. Rest of the parcels will go forward for delivery to the addressee on payment of the duty marked on each parcel.

(g) The detained parcels are submitted together with the Parcel Bill to the Customs. After examining them and filling in details of contents of value in the Parcel Bills, Customs Appraiser notes down the rate and amount of duty against each item. The remark "Examined" is then entered against the entry in the Parcel Bill relating to each parcel examined by the Customs Appraiser and the Postmaster's copies will be returned by the Customs.

(h) In the case of receipt of letter mail bags, the Postmaster gets the bags opened and scrutinized under the supervision of the Customs with a view to identify all packets containing dutiable articles. Such packets are to be detained and presented in due course to the Customs Appraiser with letter mail bill and assessment memos for assessment. After examining them and filling the details of contents of value in the bill, the Customs Appraiser will note the rate and amount of duty against each item. He will likewise fill in these details on the assessment memos to be forwarded along with each packet.

question_text: What warranty obligation does the supplier have regarding defective equipment, machinery, or components
answer:
- Supplier must repair or replace, at no cost, any equipment, machinery, parts or components found defective due to workmanship, faulty material or inferior manufacture.  
- This warranty applies for the period specified in the order (measured from either commissioning/installation or delivery), protecting procurement investments and reducing risk of defective performance.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 251)

First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the agreement says about the supplier’s responsibility when equipment turns out faulty. The Procurement of Goods Manual includes a section on the Warranty and Guarantee Clause of the Order, which directly addresses defects in equipment, machinery, parts or components.  

The clause makes it clear that the supplier must take action at no charge to the buyer if any of those items are found defective because of poor workmanship, substandard material, or an inferior manufacturing process. In other words, the burden of fixing or swapping out the faulty item falls entirely on the supplier, and the buyer should not incur any cost for repairs or replacements.  

Next, I consider the time frame during which this obligation is valid. The warranty is tied to a specific period that starts either from the date the equipment is commissioned and installed or from the date it is delivered, whichever is relevant. This means the supplier’s liability to repair or replace is limited to that window, after which the warranty expires.  

Putting these points together, the supplier’s warranty obligation can be summarized as a promise to repair or replace, free of charge, any equipment, machinery, parts or components that prove defective due to workmanship, faulty material, or inferior manufacture, and this promise holds for the stipulated period measured from commissioning/installation or delivery.  

Finally, I verify that this interpretation captures both the substantive duty (free repair/replacement) and the temporal limitation (the defined warranty period), which matches the answer provided. The reasoning flows naturally from identifying the clause, extracting the supplier’s duty, noting the cost‑free aspect, specifying the defect triggers, and anchoring the obligation in the stated time frame. This yields a complete and coherent explanation of the supplier’s warranty responsibility.

The wording makes it clear that this is not an optional suggestion but a required clause for all contracts covering the supply of goods.  

Since the question seeks the mandatory right that must be reserved, the only right that matches this description is the right to reject non‑conforming goods.  

Putting it together, the right that must be reserved in all contracts for the supply of goods is the right of the procuring entity to reject goods that do not conform to the specifications.

- i) Any agreement shall be issued strictly as per approval of TEC. The terms of contract must be precise, definite and without any ambiguities. The terms should not involve an uncertain or indefinite liability, except in the case of a cost plus contract or where there is PVC in the contract. In other words, no contract involving an uncertain or indefinite

liability or any condition of an unusual character should be entered into without the previous consent of the CA

- ii) All contracts shall contain a provision for
  - a) Recovery of liquidated damages (LD) for delay in performance of the contract on the part of the contractor;
  - b) A warranty clause/defect liability clause should be incorporated in contracts for plant and machinery, requiring the contractor to, without charge, replace, repair or rectify defective goods/ works/services;
- iii) All contracts for supply of goods should reserve the right of the procuring entity to reject goods which do not conform to the specifications;
- iv) Payment of all applicable taxes by the contractor or supplier; and
- v) When a contract is likely to endure for a period of more than two years, it should, wherever feasible, include a provision for an unconditional power of revocation or cancellation by the procuring entity at any time on the expiry of six months' notice to that effect, subject to inclusion of such provision in the tender/RfP document.
- vi) Standard forms of contracts should be invariably adopted, except in following cases:
  - a) Departmental procurement, Spot procurement, Online procurement.
  - b) In cases where standard forms of contracts are not used or where modifications in standard forms are considered necessary in respect of individual contracts, legal and financial advice should be taken in drafting the clauses in the contract and approval of CAs is to be obtained; and

### 7.6.5 Procurement Records
The Procurement file should start with the Indent and related documents. All subsequent documents relating to procurement planning; Copy of Bid Document and documents relating to its formulation, publishing and issue/ uploading; Bid Opening; Bids received; Correspondence and documents (including Technical Evaluation and TEC report) relating to pre-qualification, evaluation, Award of Contract; and finally the Contract copy, should be kept on the file. In case of bulky Bids received, all bids received may be kept in a separate volume, with a copy of accepted bids later being put on the main volume. To maintain integrity of the records relating to Procurement, these files should be kept secure and for contract management a new volume of file may be opened to obviate frequent exposure of sensitive procurement file. In contract management volume, copies of successful bid, Tender Committee Report, Contract may also be kept for ready reference, besides correspondence and documents relating to Contract Management and its closure. In case the documents are preserved in electronic mode adequate information security & access control mechanism should be maintained.

question_text: When is it appropriate to hire an individual consultant instead of a consulting firm
answer:
**Answer:**  
Hire an individual consultant when the work does not require a full team—such as for project‑implementation supervision, training, providing specific expert advice on a highly technical subject, offering policy guidance, conducting special studies, performing compliance supervision, or monitoring implementation—and when the task is either a simple project preparation that repeats an existing successful effort or involves no more than three experts.

**Rationale:**  
The manual explains that individual consultants are recruited for the same kinds of activities as consulting firms when a full team is not considered necessary, and that assignments needing more than three experts should normally be undertaken by a firm‑based team. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 18)
cot: When I think about the choice between an individual consultant and a consulting firm, the first thing that comes to mind is what the work actually requires in terms of manpower and expertise. If the assignment can be handled by a single expert or a very small group, there’s no reason to bring in a whole team from a firm. I then consider what kinds of tasks are typically given to individuals: they are often asked to oversee project implementation, run training sessions, give focused advice on a technical niche, shape policy, carry out special studies, check compliance, or monitor how implementation is progressing. These are the same activities firms perform, but they don’t demand a full crew. Next, I remember the limits placed on individual consultants—project preparation is usually reserved for firms unless the project is straightforward and merely repeats a proven model, and any need for more than three specialists pushes the work toward a firm‑based team. Putting those pieces together, it makes sense to hire an individual consultant when the job matches one of those specific expert‑type activities and either involves no more than three experts or is a simple repeat of an existing successful project. That reasoning leads directly to the conclusion that an individual consultant is appropriate under exactly those conditions.

### 2.1.3 Individual consultants/ service providers
Individual consultants or service providers are recruited for similar activities as Consultancy/ Service providing firms when a full team is not considered necessary. They may be independent experts not permanently associated with any particular firm, or they may be employees of a firm recruited on an individual basis. They may also be employees of an agency, institution, or university. They are normally recruited for project implementation supervision, training, provision of specific expert advice on a highly technical subject, policy guidance, special studies, compliance supervision, or implementation monitoring. Individual consultants/ service providers are not normally recruited for project preparation unless the proposed project is simple and, generally, a repeat of an already established and successful project. If more than three experts are required, then the assignment should normally be undertaken by a team from a firm. As with firms, individual consultants/ service providers are classed as either international or national, depending on their level of expertise and their international experience and exposure.

Specialized agencies or institutions (including Government/ Semi-Government agencies, universities and professional institutions) may also from time to time be recruited to provide Consultancy/ other services. These services may be provided by individuals (as discussed above) or by teams. Nonetheless, there are at times distinct advantages to using such agencies. Experts and teams from such agencies and institutions may undertake a variety of roles across the whole field of possible Consultancy and other services. These may range from project preparation through project supervision and policy advice to project benefit monitoring and evaluation.

question_text: What is the preferred mode of invoicing to enable faster processing of payments?
answer: E‑invoices or digitally signed invoices are the preferred mode of invoicing to enable faster processing of payments (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 116).
cot:
First, I consider what makes payment processing fast: the sooner the invoice can be matched to a purchase order and approved, the quicker the funds can be released, so any step that reduces manual handling or delays is valuable.  

Next, I look at how invoices are traditionally handled—paper or PDF copies that need to be printed, mailed, scanned, and entered manually into accounting systems—each of those actions adds latency and introduces the chance for errors that require rework.  

Then, I think about electronic alternatives: if the invoice is sent in a structured digital format, it can be imported directly into the buyer’s ERP or financial system, allowing automatic validation against contracts and purchase orders without human intervention.  

Further, I note that adding a digital signature to that electronic invoice guarantees its integrity and authenticity, which removes the need for separate verification steps and enables straight‑through processing from receipt to payment.  

Putting these points together, the mode that eliminates paper handling, enables instant data capture, and assures authenticity is the use of e‑invoices or digitally signed invoices, which is therefore the preferred way to speed up payment processing.  

E‑invoices or digitally signed invoices are the preferred mode of invoicing to enable faster processing of payments.

This will be done as per the existing law in force during the currency of the contract.

## 6.12 Payment against Time Barred Claims
Ordinarily, all claims are time barred after a period of three years calculated from the date when the payment falls due unless the payment claim has been under correspondence. However, the limitation is saved if there is an admission of liability to pay, and fresh period of limitation starts from the time such admission is made. The paying authority is to ensure that no payment against such time barred claim is made till a decision has been taken in this regard by the CA.

# Chapter 7: Evaluation of Bids and Award of Contract


## 7.1 Tender Evaluation
7.1.1 The evaluation of tenders is one of the most significant areas of purchase management and the process must be transparent. All tenders are to be evaluated strictly on the basis of the terms and conditions incorporated in the tender document and those stipulated by the tenderers in their tenders. The Contracting Authority may include quality, price, technical merit, aesthetic and functional characteristics, environmental characteristics, running costs, cost-effectiveness, after-sales service and technical assistance, delivery date and delivery period or period of completion etc. No criteria shall be used for evaluation of tenders that cannot be verified. No hearsay information or hitherto undeclared condition should be brought in while evaluating the tenders. Care should be taken that preferences provided to any category of bidders on certain specified grounds should not result in single vendor selection. Similarly, no tender enquiry condition (especially the significant/essential ones) should be overlooked/ relaxed while evaluating the tenders. The aim should be ensure that no tenderer gets undue advantage at the cost of other tenderers and/or at the cost of Procuring Entity. Information relating to evaluation of tenders and the Tender Evaluation Committee's (TEC's) deliberations should be confidential and not be shared with persons not officially connected with the process. TEC should normally comprise of members including Finance and a representative of the user as per DOA in order to carry out evaluation of the tenders. TEC should not be very large as it may slow down the evaluation process. However, suitable domain/ technical experts may be included in the committee to render assistance in evaluation of the bids. The dealing officer of the proposal will work as a convenor of the TEC. No member of the tender committee should be reporting directly to any other member of such committee The process of tender evaluation is described in the subsequent paras.

question_text: What occurs if the MSE bidder (L3) matches the L1 evaluated price in a non-divisible procurement
answer: - When the MSE bidder (L3) matches the L1 evaluated price for a non‑divisible item, the order is placed directly with that MSE bidder. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 32)
cot:
First, I need to picture what a non‑divisible procurement looks like: the item cannot be split, so the whole quantity must go to a single bidder.  
Next, I recall the purchase‑preference hierarchy that applies when the lowest evaluated bidder (L1) is neither an MSE nor a Class‑I local supplier. In that case the MSE bidder (L3) is given the first chance to match the L1 evaluated price.  
If L3 actually matches that price, the rule says the order shall be placed on him because he has satisfied the preference condition.  
Since the item is non‑divisible, there is no remainder quantity to allocate to any other bidder; the entire award therefore goes to the MSE bidder who matched L1.  
Putting it together, when the MSE bidder (L3) matches the L1 evaluated price for a non‑divisible item, the order is placed directly with that MSE bidder.

###### Examples of Purchase Preference:


###### Non divisible item
L1 bidder is non MSE or other than class-I local supplier

L2 bidder is Class-I local supplier (within 20%)

L3 bidder is MSE bidder (within 15%)

MSE bidder shall be given preference to match the L1 evaluated price. If L3 bidder matches the L1 evaluated price, order shall be placed on him, otherwise, option for matching the L1 price shall be given to L2 bidder (Class-I local supplier).

###### Divisible item
L1 bidder is non MSE or other than class-I local supplier

L2 bidder is Class-I local supplier (within 20%)

L3 bidder is MSE bidder (within 15%)

MSE bidder shall be given preference to match the L1 evaluated price. If bidder matches the L1 price, order shall be placed on him for the quantity specified in the bidding document (i.e., 25% of

the quantities against the item(s) of MR). For the balance quantity (i.e. 50% of tendered quantity / value) option for matching the L1 evaluated price shall be given to L2 bidder (Class-I local supplier). Balance quantity (i.e., 25% of the quantities against the item(s) of MR) shall be awarded to natural lowest bidder.

In above case, if there will be 2 or more MSE bidder within 15%, then 25% quantity shall be distributed proportionately / equally among the MSEs who have agreed to match the L1 prices.

- C. In case lowest bidder is a MSE bidder, the entire work shall be awarded to him without resorting to purchase preference to bidders complying with Local Content.
- D. In case lowest bidder is a Class-I local supplier, purchase preference shall be resorted to MSE bidder as per provisions specified in the enquiry document w.r.t. PPP-2012 only.

###### a) LC of goods
- (i) LC of goods shall be computed on the basis of the cost of domestic components in goods, compared to the whole cost of product.
- (ii) The criteria for determination of the local content cost in the goods shall be as follows:

question_text: Which identifier must be used for all Purchase Orders to avoid an 'Unknown' account assignment, and what should never appear in the account assignment field
answer: All Purchase Orders must be created using an appropriate Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) or Cost Centre that has the required funds assigned. The account assignment field must never contain the value “Unknown”. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 71)
cot:
First, I need to understand what the question is asking: it wants to know which identifier must be used on every Purchase Order to prevent an “Unknown” account assignment, and what value should never appear in that field.  

The discussion around purchase orders emphasizes that proper budgeting and cost tracking are essential before any procurement action. It notes that a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) or a Cost Centre must have the required funds assigned before a PO can be raised, and that the system will book costs to the general ledger only when a valid account assignment is present.  

The Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual explicitly states that an appropriate WBS or Cost Centre having the required fund has to be used in all POs, and that no PO should be issued with an “Unknown” account assignment. This directly ties the identifier to the WBS/Cost Centre and warns against leaving the field blank or filling it with “Unknown”.  

Putting these points together, the identifier that guarantees a valid account assignment is the WBS or Cost Centre code that is linked to funded budget. Consequently, the account assignment field must never contain the placeholder “Unknown”, because doing so would bypass the required budget check and lead to untracked expenses.  

Thus, the reasoning leads to the conclusion that every Purchase Order must be created using an appropriate WBS or Cost Centre with allocated funds, and the account assignment field must never show “Unknown”.

### 9.9.2 **Estimating Costs, Setting the Budget, and seeking Approval.**
Preparation of a well-thought-through cost estimate is essential if realistic budgetary resources are to be earmarked. The cost estimate shall be based on the Procuring Entity's assessment of the resources needed to carry out the assignment: managerial and staff time and physical inputs (for example, materials, consumables, tools and machines). Costs shall be divided into three broad categories:

- i) Remunerations for Personnel deployed;
- ii) Reimbursable: (Travel, logistics, Consumable, Material, Tools, Hiring of third party services etc.);
- iii) Administrative and Miscellaneous (Mobilisation, demobilisation, Temporary Structures, Administrative expenses, office and IT equipment, contingencies, financing costs, Costs for hiring/ depreciation/ financing of machinery and equipment etc).

### 9.9.3 **Final Administrative and Budgetary Approvals**
The Activity Schedule shall be compatible with the available budget. The most important step is to determine whether all tasks required to achieve the desired output have been included. The next step is to determine whether adequate budget has been allocated to implement the assignment as designed. Procurement should be initiated only after such approvals and budgetary provisions.

Appropriate WBS / Cost Centre having required fund has to be used in all POs. No PO should be issued with "Unknown" account assignment.

Services are procured against Cost Centre (K) and Project (P) and procurement budget is required during creation of PR and PO. Cost is booked in GL as soon as SES (Service Entry Sheet) is made and accepted in system.

For ARCs (outline agreement) adequate fund will be required only at the time of issuing Release Order.

## 9.11 Procedure for Small Value and emergency Procurements of Other (Non-consultancy) Services
In many small value procurements of other services, the service provider may neither be capable of handling the bidding process, nor would this be a cost-effective process for the Procuring Entity. The 'Direct Procurement without Quotation' mode of procurement used in Procurement of goods may very well be utilised in such cases. question_text: What specific functionalities are available on the GeM portal that support the procurement of other (non‑consultancy) services
answer:
**Step‑by‑Step Instructional Guide: Using GeM Portal Functionalities for Procurement of Other (Non‑consultancy) Services**  

**Purpose:** This guide shows mid‑level procurement officers how to apply the specific GeM portal functionalities—listing of products, terms and conditions, online bidding, reverse auction, demand aggregation, and call‑centre support—to procure services such as taxi hire, cleaning, maintenance, or any other non‑consultancy requirement.

---

### 1. Access the GeM Portal  
- Open a web browser and navigate to **https://gem.gov.in**.  
- Log in with your official user ID and password; if you do not have an account, complete the registration process using your organization’s credentials.  

### 2. Prepare a Service Listing (Product Listing)  
- Select the **“List Products/Services”** option.  
- Enter a clear, concise description of the service (e.g., “Daily office cleaning – 8 hr shift, 5 days/week”).  
- Include relevant specifications such as service frequency, duration, location, and any required qualifications or certifications.  
- **Pitfall to avoid:** Vague or incomplete descriptions can lead to non‑responsive bids; ensure all essential details are captured before publishing.

### 3. Define Terms and Conditions  
- Use the **“Terms and Conditions”** template to outline payment schedule, penalties for non‑performance, service level expectations, and confidentiality clauses.  
- Attach any annexes (e.g., safety standards, equipment lists) that bidders must acknowledge.  
- **Pitfall to avoid:** Overly complex or contradictory clauses may disqualify otherwise eligible bidders; keep language plain and consistent with the service description.

### 4. Publish the Tender with Online Bidding  
- Choose **“Create Tender”** and attach the service listing and terms and conditions.  
- Set the bid submission deadline and enable the **online bidding** feature so suppliers can submit their financial and technical proposals directly through the portal.  
- **Pitfall to avoid:** Failing to set a realistic deadline may rush suppliers or cause delays; allow sufficient time for bidders to prepare quality offers.

### 5. Conduct a Reverse Auction (if price is the primary criterion)  
- After the initial bid opening, select the **“Reverse Auction”** option for lots where lowest price (L‑1) is the deciding factor.  
- Schedule the auction, notify pre‑qualified bidders, and monitor the live price‑dropping process.  
- **Pitfall to avoid:** Using a reverse auction for services where quality or technical capability is critical can lead to awarding to an unsuitable provider; reserve this function for purely price‑driven procurements.

### 6. Leverage Demand Aggregation  
- If multiple departments require the same service (e.g., monthly pest control across several offices), use the **“Demand Aggregation”** tool to combine requirements into a single tender.  
- This can increase buying power and often results in better rates.  
- **Pitfall to avoid:** Aggregating dissimilar services (different scopes or service levels) may confuse bidders; ensure aggregated items are truly comparable.

### 7. Utilize Call‑Centre Support  
- Throughout the process, access the **call‑centre** (via the portal’s help icon or the toll‑free number) for clarification on portal functions, bid submission issues, or technical difficulties.  
- Keep a record of the ticket number and resolution for audit purposes.  
- **Pitfall to avoid:** Relying solely on self‑service when encountering persistent errors can cause missed deadlines; timely escalation prevents process delays.

### 8. Evaluate Bids and Award the Contract  
- After bid closure, download the submitted proposals, verify technical responsiveness, and compare financial offers (or auction results).  
- Document the evaluation rationale in accordance with your organization’s procurement policy.  
- Issue the award notice through the portal and proceed to contract signing.  

---

#### Quick Reference Checklist  

| Step | Action | Key Output | Common Pitfall |
|------|--------|------------|----------------|
| 1 | Login to GeM | Authenticated session | Forgotten credentials → delay |
| 2 | List service | Detailed service description | Vague specs → non‑responsive bids |
| 3 | Set terms & conditions | Clear contractual clauses | Contradictory/overly complex terms |
| 4 | Publish tender with online bidding | Open bid submission window | Unrealistic deadline |
| 5 | Run reverse auction (if applicable) | Live price‑dropping event | Misuse for quality‑sensitive services |
| 6 | Aggregate demand (if needed) | Combined tender for multiple units | Mixing incomparable services |
| 7 | Call‑centre support | Issue resolution ticket | Ignoring portal errors |
| 8 | Evaluate & award | Signed contract / award notice | Inadequate documentation of evaluation |

By following these numbered steps and watching for the noted pitfalls, procurement officers can effectively harness the GeM portal’s listed functionalities to procure other (non‑consultancy) services efficiently and in compliance with procedural requirements.
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really asking: it wants to know which specific features of the GeM portal can be used when buying services that are not consultancy‑type, such as taxi hire, cleaning or maintenance.  

The One Stop Government e‑Marketplace (GeM) provides detailed instructions for a handful of core activities—listing of products or services, setting out terms and conditions, conducting online bidding, running reverse auctions, aggregating demand, and offering call‑centre support. Those are the exact tools that a procurement officer would need to run a tender for any kind of service, and they are available on the GeM portal.  

Next, I consider how those tools fit together in a typical procurement cycle for non‑consultancy services. To start, I would have to create a clear description of the service I want to buy; that matches the “listing of products/services” function. After the service is defined, I need to lay out the contractual rules—payment milestones, penalties, service levels—which corresponds to the “terms and conditions” template.  

Once the description and rules are ready, I must open the opportunity for suppliers to respond. The portal lets me publish a tender and enables suppliers to submit their technical and financial proposals online, which is the online bidding facility. If price is the main driver and the service is straightforward, I can then trigger a reverse auction to let bidders compete on cost in real time.  

Often, several departments need the same service, so combining their requirements into a single tender can improve leverage. The demand aggregation tool on GeM lets me do exactly that, turning multiple similar needs into one larger lot.  

Throughout the process, I might run into portal‑related questions or technical hiccups. A call‑centre is available via the portal’s help icon or a toll‑free number, giving me a way to get quick assistance and keep the timeline on track.  

Finally, after bids are in—or after the auction closes—I evaluate the offers, check technical responsiveness, compare prices (or auction results), document the decision, and issue the award through the portal.  

Putting those pieces together, I can lay out a numbered‑style guide that walks a procurement officer through each GeM functionality in the order they would be used, highlights the key output of each step, and warns about common pitfalls such as vague service descriptions, contradictory terms, unrealistic deadlines, misusing reverse auctions for quality‑sensitive work, aggregating incomparable services, ignoring portal errors, or failing to document the evaluation.  

This reasoning leads directly to the step‑by‑step instructional guide that lists the specific GeM portal functionalities—listing of products/services, terms and conditions, online bidding, reverse auction, demand aggregation, and call‑centre support—and shows how they are applied to procure other (non‑consultancy) services.

**6.8.1** Normally, there should not be any scope for dispute between the Procuring Entity and contractor after entering into a mutually agreed valid contract. The party initiating conciliation shall send a written invitation to the other party to conciliate and

question_text: Under what circumstances can missing pages or illegible documents be overlooked without affecting tender ranking
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: under what conditions can a tender that has missing pages or illegible documents still be considered valid without changing the order in which tenderers are ranked.  
I start by recalling how tenders are initially screened – they are examined for basic compliance, and anything that fails to meet the essential requirements is labeled unresponsive and set aside.  
From that screening perspective, missing pages or illegible text could lead to a tender being deemed unresponsive only if those deficiencies affect a core requirement, such as omitting a mandatory schedule, a required price breakdown, or a critical certification.  
If the missing or unreadable parts do not touch any of those essential elements, the deficiency is not a material deviation; it is merely a superficial flaw.  
Next, I think about the practical consequences of such a flaw. Even if it is not material, I must check whether it introduces any financial ambiguity – for instance, if the missing page contained a price or a quantity that would alter the bid amount. When the absent information has no bearing on the calculated price or any cost‑related obligation, the financial impact is nil.  
Finally, I examine the effect on ranking. Ranking depends on the substantive comparison of bids; if the irregularity does not change any evaluative criterion – price, technical compliance, delivery schedule – then the relative standing of the tenderers remains the same.  
Putting these three observations together, I conclude that missing pages or illegible documents can be overlooked only when they satisfy all three conditions: they are not a material deviation from the bid specifications, they cause no financial change, and they do not prejudice or affect the tenderers’ ranking order.  
When the procuring entity finds such a minor issue, it may seek clarification from the bidder; if the bidder fails to respond appropriately, the tender can then be rejected, but as long as the conditions hold, the oversight does not disturb the tender ranking.

question_text: How can publishing a tentative time schedule in the Bid Documents contribute to timely procurement?
answer:
In the spring of 2024, the Northern Roads Authority (NRA) initiated a project to rehabilitate the aging pavement on State Highway 12. The procurement team began by drafting the tender documents, keeping in mind the manual’s guidance on timely processing. Recognising that a clear timeline would help keep the process on track, they decided to publish a tentative time schedule for award of contract and for the subsequent site hand‑over directly in the Bid Documents, as the manual recommends (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 76).

When the bid documents were released, prospective contractors saw not only the technical requirements but also a calendar that showed the NRA aimed to open tenders on 1 May, complete evaluation and award the contract within 60 days, and hand over the site for work to start by 1 July. This upfront visibility set a shared expectation: every official involved—from the tender opening officer to the finance reviewer and the user department representative—knew exactly when their actions were needed to keep the schedule intact.

Because the schedule was explicit, the NRA established an inter‑departmental Service Level Agreement (SLA) that outlined each role holder’s responsibilities and the allowable time frame for each activity, exactly as suggested in the manual. The tender evaluation committee (TEC) began meeting shortly after the tender opening, using the published schedule as a reference point to resolve any questions quickly. When a minor clarification was needed from a bidder, the TEC referred back to the timeline, issued a prompt request, and received the response within the allotted window, preventing any drift.

As the evaluation progressed, the NRA’s monitoring mechanism kicked in. Any deviation from the published dates—such as a delay in receiving the financial clearance—was immediately flagged and explained through an internal review of the responsible function. This accountability meant that the procurement team could take corrective action before the slippage accumulated, keeping the overall decision period within the targeted 60 days.

When the contract was finally awarded on 28 June—well within the 60‑day window—the site hand‑over occurred on 30 June, allowing the contractor to mobilise equipment and begin work on 1 July as planned. The project proceeded without the costly delays that often accompany uncertain timelines, and the completed pavement was opened to traffic three months ahead of the original fiscal year target.

By publishing a tentative time schedule in the Bid Documents, the NRA turned a procedural guideline into a practical tool: it created clear expectations, enabled an SLA‑driven workflow, made every stakeholder accountable for timely action, and provided a basis for monitoring and quick corrective measures. The result was a procurement process that stayed on schedule, demonstrating how the manual’s provision can be applied in real‑world projects to achieve timely outcomes.
cot:
First, I think about why procurement often drags on—usually because nobody knows exactly when each step should happen, so actions get postponed and the whole process slips.  
Then I notice that putting a tentative time schedule straight into the bid documents fixes that problem by laying out the target dates for contract award and site hand‑over where every bidder and every internal official can see them.  
With those dates visible, everyone involved—from the tender opening officer to the finance reviewer and the user‑department representative—gets a clear picture of when their own contribution is needed, turning a vague expectation into a concrete deadline.  
That shared understanding makes it natural to draw up an inter‑departmental service level agreement that spells out each role’s responsibilities and the allowable time frame for each activity, because the schedule already gives the reference points the agreement needs.  
Once the SLA is in place, any departure from the published dates—say a delay in getting financial clearance—can be spotted right away; the monitoring mechanism flags the deviation, triggers an internal review of the responsible function, and prompts corrective action before the slip turns into a larger delay.  
Because the schedule is constantly used as a benchmark, the evaluation committee can meet promptly, resolve queries quickly, and keep the decision period within the targeted window, leading to an award and hand‑over that occur exactly as planned.  
Seeing how the explicit timetable drives expectations, enables accountability, supports monitoring, and facilitates timely corrections shows that publishing a tentative time schedule in the bid documents is a practical way to keep procurement on schedule and avoid the costly overruns that come from uncertainty.

### 5.5.4 Selection Through Lottery:
Selection of successful bidder(s) among multiple L1 bidders shall be determined through lottery in the following circumstances:-

- (i) Vehicle tenders where detailed estimate is displayed considering the bidder's capital and operational expenditure and margin.
- (ii) Manpower oriented tenders with displayed estimates.
- (iii) Other tenders with displayed estimates based on approved SOR.
- (iv) Other than above scenarios, where the prices of multiple L1 bidders remain same even after submission of revised priced bid / discount because of tie in the original prices.

The methodology for conducting lottery shall be specified in the tender documents. Commercial department shall conduct the lottery in presence of representatives from Finance and User department. The concerned bidders shall be invited to witness the lottery.

It may also be decided that in case the L1 agency selected through lottery refuses or fails to execute the job, the job (or balance part of the job) may be subsequently offered to any of the other L1

agencies (not selected for award so far), adopting appropriate selection process by NRL like lottery among the remaining interested agencies. Alternatively, a process for selection of wait listed L1 agency(ies) may be appropriately specified. Such conditions should be specified in the tender documents.

- In case of “refusal”, subsequent award to next eligible agency shall be done within original or extended offer validity.
- In case of “failure”, unexecuted quantities shall be offered to the next eligible agency within maximum one year from the original date of award.

Defaulting supplier/contractor shall be subject to penalties as per procedure.

## 5.6 Deliberations by the Tender Evaluation Committee


### 5.6.1 Timely Processing of Tenders
- i) Delays in finalising procurement deprive the public of the intended benefits and results in lost revenues and cost over-run. Currently, the contracts are generally awarded in 90 days from the date of tender opening. In order to further shorten the period for award of contract, the procuring entity should try to shorten the procurement decision period to 60 days from the date of opening of the tenders wherever possible. However, in exceptional cases, like two packet/two stage bidding, the period may be extended. To achieve the target of shorter processing period, an inter- departmental Service Level Agreement (SLA) may be accorded. The SLA should include responsibilities of all respective role holders along with activity wise allowable time frame.

Tentative time schedule of award of contract and tentative site hand over for start of work should be published in the Bid Documents. Every official in the chain of the procurement operation is accountable for taking action in a specified time so that the tender is finalised on time. Any deviation from the schedule may be monitored and explained, by way of internal review of respective functions.

- ii) It has been also noted that delay in decision making after opening of certain tenders is taking place because the Tender Committee (TEC), wherever in place, are not meeting frequently. In order to ensure that most of the tenders are decided as per the timelines as indicated in para above, the concerned TEC should meet to resolve issues if any at the earliest.

### 3. Procedure for clearance of import goods:
3.1 For facilitating Customs clearance, the goods imported by courier are divided into the following categories:

(a) Documents that include any message, information or data recorded on paper, cards or photographs having no commercial value, and which do not attract any duty or subject to any prohibition/restriction

on their import or export;

(b) Samples - any bonafide commercial samples and prototypes of goods supplied free of charge of a value not exceeding Rs.50,000/- for exports and Rs.10,000/- for imports which are not subject to any prohibition or restriction on their import or export and which does not involve transfer of foreign exchange.

(c) Free gifts - any bonafide gifts of articles for personal use of a value not exceeding rupees 25,000/- for a consignment in case of exports and Rs.10,000/- for imports which are not subject to any prohibition or restriction on their import or export and which do not involve transfer of foreign exchange.

(d) Low value dutiable or commercial goods - goods having a declared value of upto Rs.1,00,000/-; and

(e) Dutiable or commercial goods - goods having a declared value of more than Rs.1,00,000/-.

3.2 Different Customs declaration forms have been prescribed under the Courier Regulations for manual mode and electronic mode. Under the manual mode, simplified Bills of Entry have been specified, as mentioned below, for the clearance of goods. The goods are assessed to duty on merits like any other imported goods, and exemption, wherever available, is allowed to such imports when claimed.

(a) Courier Bill of Entry-III for documents,

(b) Courier Bill of Entry-IV for samples and free gifts, and

(c) Courier Bill of Entry-V for commercial shipments upto a declared value of Rs. One lakh.

3.3 The courier regulations for the manual mode stipulate that for certain categories of imports, a regular Bill of Entry prescribed in the Bill of Entry (Forms) Regulations, 1976 is to be filed. These include, (a) goods imported under EOU scheme; (b) goods imported under DEPB, DEEC and EPCG schemes; (c) goods imported against the license issued under the Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation), Act, 1992; (d) goods imported by a related person defined under the Customs Valuation Rules, 1988 (e) goods in respect of which the proper officer directs filing of a Bill of Entry; and (f) goods having a declared value of more than Rs. One Lakh.

3.4 Under the courier regulations for the electronic mode the forms prescribed for filing Customs declarations are:

(a) Courier Bill of Entry-XI (CBE-XI) for documents in Form B,

(b) Courier Bill of Entry-XII (CBE-XII) for free gifts and samples in Form C,

(c) Courier Bill of Entry-XIII (CSE-XIII) for low value dutiable consignments in Form D and

(d) Courier Bill of Entry-XIV (CBE-XIV) for other dutiable consignments in Form E for import consignments.

#### vi) **Sealing and Marking of Tenders (other than e-Tender)**
The tender document is to indicate the total number of tender sets (for example, in duplicate or in triplicate, and so on) required to be submitted. The tenderer is to seal the original and each copy of the tender in separate envelopes, duly marking the same as "original", "duplicate," and so on, and also printing the address of the purchase office and the tender reference number on the envelopes. Further, the sentence "NOT TO BE OPENED" before (due date and time of tender opening) is also to be printed on these envelopes. The inner envelopes are then to be put inside a bigger outer envelope, which will also be duly sealed marked, and so on, as above. If the outer envelope is not sealed and marked properly as above, the purchaser will not assume any responsibility for its misplacement, premature opening, late opening, and so on. All the above instructions are to be suitably incorporated in the tender documents.

#### vii) **Withdrawal, Substitution and Modification of Tenders**
The tenderer, after submitting the tender, is permitted to withdraw, substitute or modify the tenders in writing without forfeiture of Bid Security/ EMD, provided these are received duly sealed and marked like the original tender, up to the date and time of receipt of the tender. Any such request received after the prescribed date and time of receipt of tenders will not be considered. No bid may be withdrawn in the interval between the deadline for submission of bids and expiration of the period of bid validity. Withdrawal of a bid during this period will result in forfeiture of the bidder's bid security (EMD) and other sanctions.

#### viii) **Eligibility / Evaluation / Qualification Criteria**
If it is intended to use eligibility/evaluation/qualification criteria to evaluate a tender and determine whether a tenderer has the required qualifications, this point may be clearly specified in NIT, ITB/AITB or as a separate section of the tender document. The bidder has to ensure that he provides convincing proof of having fulfilled these criteria. *Any criteria not specified in the tender cannot be used for evaluation or qualification.*

The condition of prior turnover and prior experience may be relaxed for Startups (as defined by Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion) subject to meeting of quality & technical specifications and making suitable provisions in the bidding document. As per Department of Expenditure's OM No.F.20/2/2014-PPD dated 20.09.2016, relaxation regarding the prior turnover and prior experience is applicable only to all startups recognized by Department of Industry & Internal Trade (DPIIT) subject to meeting of quality and technical specifications. Point iii, as listed among the responsibilities of the CA (TEC) in the Procurement of Works Manual, requires that the price of the offer must be reasonable and consistent with the quality required. This tells me right away that the check is not a single test but has two aspects—one about the price’s reasonableness and another about how that price aligns with the quality that the contract demands. 

Next, I break down what each aspect entails in practice. To judge reasonableness, the CA would need to consider whether the price fits within expected market rates and the scope of work, ensuring it is neither excessively high nor suspiciously low. To assess consistency with quality, the CA would compare the offered price against the quality specifications laid out in the tender, confirming that the price reflects the level of performance, materials, or standards required. 

Putting these two verification steps together, the natural outcome is a concise operational checklist: first, confirm that the offered price is reasonable; second, confirm that the offered price is consistent with the quality required for the contract. This matches exactly what point iii obliges the CA (TEC) to do.

question_text: How can a purchaser’s reference sample be used during the tender process without violating sample‑evaluation rules?
answer:
- Display the purchaser’s reference sample to tenderers only to illustrate indeterminable characteristics such as shade, finish, or workmanship; the sample is not used for evaluating bids. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 42)  
- Base bid evaluation solely on detailed specifications and drawings; do not call for or assess the sample alongside the bids. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 42)  
- If indeterminable characteristics must be verified, stipulate that successful bidders submit a pre‑production sample matching the purchaser’s reference sample before bulk production clearance. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 42)  
- This use of the reference sample supports transparency, ensures value‑for‑money, and reduces the risk of non‑conforming outputs, thereby aligning procurement with corporate goals and risk‑management objectives. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 42)
cot:
First, I think about what a purchaser’s reference sample is really meant to convey – it captures those hard‑to‑specify traits like shade, finish or workmanship that drawings alone cannot describe.  
Then, I remember the procurement rule that a sample must not be called for or evaluated alongside the bids; the decision has to rest solely on the detailed specifications and drawings supplied in the tender documents.  
Next, I consider how to still show those indeterminable characteristics to potential suppliers without breaking that rule: the purchaser can simply display the reference sample to tenderers as an illustration, making it clear that the sample is for informational purposes only and will not factor into bid scoring.  
Further, if the buyer needs assurance that the successful supplier can actually reproduce those qualities, the tender can stipulate that the winning bidder must submit a pre‑production sample matching the reference before any clearance for bulk production is granted.  
Finally, by keeping the sample out of the evaluation stage, using it only for illustration, and requiring a matching pre‑production sample when needed, the process stays transparent, protects against non‑conforming outputs, supports value‑for‑money, and aligns with the buyer’s risk‑management and corporate objectives.

question_text: In clause 4, what specific rights does the Contractor NOT have regarding the site, structures, and materials brought onto the site, unless they belong to the Contractor?
answer: The Contractor shall have no right, title or interest in (i) the site made available by the Owner for execution of the works; (ii) any building, structures or works executed on that site by the Contractor; and (iii) goods, articles, materials or other items brought onto the site, unless those items specifically belong to the Contractor. Furthermore, the Contractor shall not possess or be deemed to possess any lien arising from unpaid bills and is not entitled to assume or retain possession or control of the site or the structures erected thereon. These limitations are expressly stated in clause 4 of the manual (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 140).
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what clause 4 actually says about the contractor’s entitlements concerning the site, the works erected there, and any materials that are brought onto the site. The question is asking for the specific rights that the contractor does **not** have, with the exception that anything that truly belongs to the contractor is excluded from those restrictions.

I start by reading the clause carefully. It opens with a clear statement that the contractor shall have no right, title or interest in three distinct categories: the site made available by the owner, any building, structures or works executed on that site by the contractor, and the goods, articles, materials or other items brought onto the site. The parenthetical note immediately clarifies that this blanket prohibition does not apply if those items specifically belong to the contractor.

Next, the clause adds another limitation: the contractor shall not have, nor be deemed to have, any lien arising from unpaid bills. This means that even if the contractor has not been paid, they cannot claim a security interest over the site or the structures as a way to retain possession.

Following that, the clause explicitly states that the contractor is not entitled to assume or retain possession or control of the site or the structures erected thereon. In other words, the contractor cannot simply stay on the premises or keep hold of the work after the contract ends or if payment is withheld.

Finally, the clause reinforces the owner’s position by saying the owner shall have an absolute and unfettered right to take full possession of the site and to remove the contractor, their servants, agents, and any materials that belong to the contractor and are lying on the site. This underscores that the contractor’s lack of rights is not merely a passive absence but is backed by the owner’s active authority to reclaim the site.

Putting these pieces together, the specific rights the contractor does not have—unless the items in question are the contractor’s own property—are: (1) any right, title, or interest in the site itself; (2) any right, title, or interest in the buildings, structures, or works erected on that site; (3) any right, title, or interest in the goods, articles, materials, or other items brought onto the site; (4) any lien arising from unpaid bills; and (5) the entitlement to assume or retain possession or control of the site or the structures. The owner, conversely, retains the absolute right to take possession and to remove the contractor and their belongings. This synthesis matches exactly what the question asks for.

question_text: How often should price adjustment bills be submitted for supplies made during a quarter
answer: - Price adjustment bills must be submitted **quarterly** for supplies made during the quarter. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 208)
cot:
First, I need to pin down exactly what the question is asking: it wants to know the timing or interval for submitting price adjustment bills when the supplies in question have been made during a quarter.  
Next, I recall the contractual rule that governs how these adjustments are handled—payments are first made at the base price, and the adjustment bill is not to be sent arbitrarily; it is prescribed that the bill should be submitted only quarterly for the supplies made during the quarter.  
This wording ties the submission directly to the quarterly period: you gather all the supplies that occurred in a given three‑month span, compute any price variation, and then issue a single adjustment bill covering that entire span.  
Because the rule says “only quarterly,” it precludes more frequent submissions (such as monthly) and also precludes waiting longer than a quarter (such as semi‑annual or annual), unless there is simply no variation to report.  
The additional condition that no adjustment is payable when the variation is two percent or less does not change the timing; it merely determines whether a bill actually needs to be prepared, but whenever a bill is required it must still follow the quarterly schedule.  
Putting these points together, the only frequency that satisfies the contract’s instruction is once per quarter for the supplies made during that quarter.  
Therefore, price adjustment bills must be submitted quarterly for supplies made during the quarter.

question_text: How is the quantity handled if 50% of an item results in a fractional amount under the divisible procurement procedure
answer:
- When 50 % of an item results in a fractional quantity, the policy treats the fraction as the next higher whole unit; the eligible Class‑I local supplier is invited to match the L1 price for that rounded‑up amount.  
- If the item cannot be split at all, the entire quantity is awarded to the lowest evaluated bidder (L1).  

This approach maintains transparency, safeguards value for money, and reduces procurement risk by avoiding ambiguous partial awards. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 31)
cot:
First, I focus on the core of the question: it asks what happens when the 50 % share of a divisible item works out to a fractional amount under the procurement procedure.  
I recall that the policy for divisible items specifies a special treatment for exactly this situation – it does not allow the contract to be split into a partial unit.  
So, I think through the logic: if the calculated 50 % yields, say, 3.2 units, awarding only 3.2 would leave an ambiguous remainder that cannot be fulfilled as a whole item.  
To avoid that ambiguity, the rule states that the fraction is rounded up to the next whole unit; the eligible Class‑I local supplier is then asked to match the L1 price for that rounded‑up quantity.  
Next, I consider the alternative case where the item itself cannot be divided at all – for example, a single piece of equipment that must be delivered whole.  
In that scenario, there is no meaningful way to award only a portion, so the policy directs that the entire quantity be awarded to the lowest evaluated bidder (L1).  
I then reflect on why the policy adopts these approaches: rounding up guarantees a clear, whole‑unit award, which keeps the process transparent and prevents disputes over partial deliveries, while awarding the full amount to L1 when splitting is impossible preserves value for money and minimizes procurement risk by avoiding uncertain partial contracts.  
Finally, bringing these points together, I conclude that the quantity is handled by treating any fractional 50 % as the next higher whole unit for the Class‑I local supplier’s price‑matching invitation, and if the item cannot be split, the full quantity goes to L1 – exactly the outcome described in the answer.

question_text: Which organisations are required to establish a GeM Pool Account under the given instructions
answer:
All organisations that do not use the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) for their payment transactions are required to establish a GeM Pool Account. This includes, but is not limited to, Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), municipalities, educational institutions, autonomous bodies, societies, and any other Government of India departments or entities that operate their own payment system for purchases made through GeM.  

(Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 88)
cot:
I need to figure out which organisations are obliged to set up a GeM Pool Account. The core idea behind the account is to guarantee timely payment to sellers when a buyer does not use the government’s Public Financial Management System (PFMS) for its transactions. Therefore, the requirement must hinge on whether an entity routes its payments through PFMS or relies on its own payment mechanism.

Looking at the description of a Non‑PFMS Agency/Entity (NPAE), it is defined as any Government of India body that does not use PFMS for payments and maintains its own payment system for purchases made via GeM. The guidance explicitly states that every such NPAE must open and operate a special purpose account called the GeM Pool Account for all its procurement activities.

Since the instruction then broadens the scope to cover all organisations and departments—including Central Public Sector Undertakings, municipalities, educational institutions, autonomous bodies, societies and similar entities—that are not operating through PFMS, it follows that the pool account is mandatory for every GoI organisation that falls outside the PFMS framework.

The account’s purpose is independent of the value of the procurement; it is required for any transaction conducted through GeM by these non‑PFMS users. Consequently, the set of organisations that must establish a GeM Pool Account comprises precisely those Government of India entities that do not utilise PFMS for their payment transactions, which includes, but is not limited to, CPSUs, municipalities, educational institutions, autonomous bodies, societies and any other GoI departments or bodies that run their own payment system for GeM purchases.

question_text: When procuring divisible items, what action should auditors confirm if L1 is a Class I local supplier
answer: Auditors should confirm that, when the lowest evaluated bid (L1) is submitted by a Class I local supplier for divisible items, the contract for the full quantity is awarded directly to that L1 bidder without requiring price matching or quantity splitting. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 31)

First, I need to pinpoint exactly what the question is asking: when buying items that can be split into smaller lots, what should auditors check if the lowest evaluated bid comes from a Class I local supplier.  

Next, I recall the rule that governs procurement of divisible goods. It says that among all qualified bids, the lowest bid is labeled L1, and if that L1 bidder is a Class I local supplier, the contract for the entire quantity goes straight to that bidder.  

Then I consider what happens in the alternative scenario—if L1 were not a Class I local supplier. In that case the policy would require price‑matching invitations to Class I suppliers and possibly splitting the quantity, but that pathway is irrelevant here because the premise already states L1 is a Class I supplier.  

Because the policy awards the full quantity directly to L1 when it meets the Class I condition, there is no need for auditors to look for any price‑matching exercise, quantity‑splitting, or further negotiations; the contract is already finalized at that point.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: auditors should confirm that, under the condition of a Class I L1 bid for divisible items, the contract for the full quantity is awarded outright to that L1 bidder, with no additional steps such as price matching or lot splitting required. This matches the expected action auditors must verify.

question_text: What constitutes "Outsourcing of Services" under the policy, and what is the minimum duration for such arrangements?
answer:
- Outsourcing of Services is defined as the deployment of outside agencies on a sustained long‑term basis (for one year or more) to perform services that were traditionally carried out in‑house, such as security, horticultural, janitorial/cooking/catering, hostel/guest‑house management, cleaning/housekeeping, and errand/messenger services. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 13)  
- The policy requires that such arrangements have a minimum duration of one year or more to qualify as outsourcing of services. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 13)
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is asking: it wants the policy’s definition of “Outsourcing of Services” and the specific time threshold that such arrangements must meet to be considered outsourcing.  

Turning to the policy text, I see that the term is explicitly defined as the deployment of outside agencies on a sustained long‑term basis to perform services that were traditionally handled in‑house. The wording emphasizes that the arrangement must be ongoing and not merely a one‑off task.  

Scanning the definition further, the policy lists concrete examples—security, horticultural, janitorial/cooking/catering, hostel/guest‑house management, cleaning/housekeeping, and errand/messenger services—to illustrate the types of work that fall under this category when performed by external providers.  

The definition also includes a parenthetical qualifier that specifies the duration: “for one year or more.” This qualifier is attached directly to the phrase “sustained long‑term,” indicating that the policy treats any arrangement shorter than a year as a short‑term stand‑alone service rather than outsourcing.  

Putting these pieces together, the policy’s concept of outsourcing of services consists of two essential elements: (1) the use of external agencies to carry out functions that were previously done internally, and (2) a minimum engagement period of one year or longer to qualify as a sustained, long‑term arrangement.  

Therefore, the answer is that outsourcing of services means deploying outside agencies on a sustained long‑term basis (one year or more) to perform traditionally in‑house services such as security, horticulture, janitorial/cooking/catering, hostel/guest‑house management, cleaning/housekeeping, and errand/messenger services, and the policy requires that such arrangements last at least one year to be classified as outsourcing.
