question_text: Are the payment terms flexible for contracts that involve a lot of installation work
answer: Yes, the payment terms can be made flexible for contracts that involve a lot of installation work. The buyer can set up configurable milestone‑based payments. For example, an initial payment of 80 % to 90 % of the basic price (which can be lowered further if the installation scope is very extensive) is made after delivery of the goods and generation of a delivery receipt. The remaining balance—typically 10 % to 20 % of the basic price plus 100 % of the installation, testing, commissioning and other charges, with GST applied accordingly—is paid after installation, testing, commissioning and final acceptance, once an installation acceptance certificate is generated. The buyer also has the ability to define the exact percentage linked to delivery, and any recoveries for short supply, liquidated damages or similar issues can be deducted from the payments due under these milestones (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 83).
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: whether the payment schedule can be adjusted when a contract contains a substantial amount of installation work.  
Next, I think about the type of contract that would involve such work—those that cover not just the supply of goods but also their installation, testing, commissioning and sometimes training.  
For contracts of that nature, the guidance explains that the buyer must be able to set up payment terms that are configurable and tied to specific milestones, rather than a single lump‑sum payment.  
Looking at the first milestone, it shows that an initial payment can be made upon delivery of the goods, typically ranging from 80 % to 90 % of the basic price, and importantly the buyer has the option to reduce this share further if the installation scope is especially extensive.  
Then the second milestone covers the balance: after installation, testing, commissioning and final acceptance, the remaining 10 % to 20 % of the basic price plus the full amount for installation, testing, commissioning and any associated charges is paid, with any recoveries for short supply, liquidated damages or similar issues deducted from this amount.  
Because the buyer can define the exact percentage linked to delivery and can lower that initial share when installation work is heavy, the payment structure can be adapted to match the installation intensity of the contract.  
Putting these points together, it follows that payment terms are indeed flexible for contracts that involve a lot of installation work.

question_text: What factors influence the choice of bidding system for a procurement
answer: **A:** The choice of bidding system depends on the complexity and criticality of the technical requirements, the technical and financial capability of the source of supply, and the value of the procurement. It also considers the need to balance right quality, right source and right price, and whether detailed specifications and a schedule of quantities can be readily prepared. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 30‑31)
cot:
First, I consider what the question is really asking: it wants to know what drives the decision‑making process when picking a bidding system for a procurement effort.  

Next, I think about the procurement context. Bidding systems are meant to strike a balance among three competing goals—getting the right quality, the right source, and the right price—and the appropriate system varies with how complex or critical the technical work is, how important the supplier’s capability is, and how large the purchase is in monetary terms.  

Then, I break those ideas down into concrete factors. If the technical requirements are simple or moderate and the supplier’s technical or financial strength isn’t a major concern, a straightforward single‑stage approach works fine. Conversely, when the specifications are intricate, the work is high‑risk, or the contract value is substantial, the procurement team needs a more rigorous system that can evaluate both technical and financial qualifications separately.  

After that, I reflect on the practical side of preparing bid documents. The ability to draw up a clear schedule of quantities and detailed specifications influences whether a single‑envelope, single‑stage method can be used; if those documents can’t be readily prepared, a more elaborate bidding process is warranted to avoid ambiguity and ensure comparability of offers.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the choice hinges on the technical complexity and criticality, the supplier’s technical and financial capability, the procurement’s value, the overarching need to balance quality, source, and price, and the feasibility of preparing detailed specifications and quantity schedules. This combination of considerations naturally leads to the answer that the bidding system is selected based on those factors.

### 3.2.6 Public Private Partnership (PPP)
PPP means an arrangement between a government/ statutory entity/ government owned entity on one side [Sponsoring (PPP) authority - or simply the Authority] and a private sector entity (a legal entity in which 51% or more of equity is with the private partner/s - concessionaire) on the other, for the creation and/ or management of public assets and/ or public services, through investments being made and/ or management being undertaken by the concessionaire, for a specified period of time (concession period) on commercial terms, where there is well defined allocation of risk between the concessionaire and the Authority; and the concessionaire (who is

chosen on the basis of a transparent and open competitive bidding), receives performance linked payments that conform (or are benchmarked) to specified and pre-determined performance standards, measurable by the Authority or its representative. For further information, PPP instructions issue by Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), Ministry of Finance from time to time, may be referred.

## 3.3 Bidding Systems, Pre-Qualification Criteria
Bidding systems are designed to achieve an appropriate balance between the countervailing needs for Right Quality, Right Source and the Right Price under different complexities/ criticality of Technical requirements and value of procurements. In certain critical and complex requirements, the technical and financial capability of Source of supply becomes an important determinant for value for money. Depending on the complexity and criticality of Technical requirement, Criticality of capability of Source and value of procurement, following types of bidding systems may be used.

### 3.3.1 Single Stage Bidding System
In single stage bidding, all bids are invited together in a single envelope or in multiple envelopes system. This bidding system is suitable where technical requirements are simple or moderate; capability of source of supply is not too crucial and the value of procurement is not too high;

### 3.3.2 Single Stage Single Bid/ Envelope System (1S1E)
Where it is feasible to work out the schedule of quantities and to formulate detailed specifications for Works and capability of contractor isn't critical and value of procurement is low or moderate, the single envelope system may be adopted, where eligibility, technical/ commercial and financial details are submitted together in the same envelope. This is the simplest and the quickest bidding system. The lowest responsive priced bid that meets the eligibility criteria, technical and commercial requirements laid down in the bid documents is declared as successful and awarded the contract.

question_text: How should government establishments or departments be treated regarding liquidated damages and risk‑purchase claims compared with ordinary contractors?
answer:
Government establishments and departments are to be handled differently from ordinary contractors when it comes to liquidated damages (LDs) and risk‑purchase claims. They should not be subjected to the standard penalties that apply to regular suppliers; instead, exemptions are granted unless a serious default occurs, in which case the issue must be escalated to the relevant head of department or government authority.  

- **Liquidated damages:** Generally not levied on government establishments/departments for delayed delivery; only serious defaults warrant notice to the HOD or department (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 150).  
- **Risk‑purchase claims:** Not enforced against these entities; enforcement is reserved for serious cases that should be referred to the appropriate government authority (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 150).  
- **Public sector undertakings (PSUs):** Do not receive automatic waiver; each case is assessed on merit for LD relief or risk‑purchase recovery (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 150‑151).  
- **Approval process:** Any waiver of LDs or risk‑purchase expenditure requires merit‑based approval, with consultation of Finance and the Contracting Authority where needed (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 150).  

This approach preserves transparency, protects value for money, and aligns procurement practices with broader risk‑management objectives while ensuring that only genuine breaches trigger corrective action.
cot:
Initially, I focus on what the question is really asking: it wants to know how the rules for liquidated damages and risk‑purchase claims differ when the supplier is a government establishment or department rather than an ordinary contractor.  

Next, I look for the core principle that governs this distinction. The guidance makes it clear that government establishments and departments are not to be treated the same way as regular suppliers; they are given a special status that shields them from the routine application of penalties.  

Then I break down what that special status means in practice. For liquidated damages, the default position is that no penalty is imposed for late delivery; the supplier is not dealt with as an ordinary contractor and therefore does not incur the standard LD charges unless the default is serious enough to warrant escalation.  

Moving on to risk‑purchase claims, the same logic applies: the loss that would normally be recovered from a contractor through a risk‑purchase action is not pursued against a government establishment or department, again except in cases of serious default where the matter must be raised with the head of the department or the relevant government authority.  

After establishing the baseline treatment for government entities, I consider how public sector undertakings (PSUs) fit into the picture. The guidance notes that the relaxations granted to government departments do not automatically extend to PSUs; each PSU case must be examined on its own merits before deciding whether to waive LDs or risk‑purchase recovery.  

Finally, I reflect on the procedural safeguards that surround any exception. Even when a waiver is contemplated—whether for a government establishment, a department, or a PSU—the decision must be merit‑based, involve consultation with finance, and receive approval from the contracting authority. This ensures that exemptions are not granted arbitrarily and that value for money is protected.  

Putting these pieces together, the conclusion is that government establishments and departments should be handled differently from ordinary contractors: they are generally exempt from liquidated damages and risk‑purchase claims, with only serious defaults triggering notice to the appropriate authority; PSUs do not receive automatic exemptions and each case is judged on merit, with any waiver requiring proper approval and financial consultation. This reasoning aligns precisely with the answer provided.

question_text: Why should appeals against arbitration awards not be pursued as a routine practice
answer: Appealing arbitration awards should not be pursued as a routine practice because it often leads to unnecessary financial harm and reputational damage. Routine appeals can result in heavy damages, compensation and additional interest costs that outweigh any benefit, and they may be used merely to delay resolving the issue or avoid personal accountability. Appeals should only be pursued when a careful review shows the case has genuine merit and a high likelihood of success, after weighing legal merits, practical chances of success and the expected costs of litigation against the award. (Procurement of Works Manual, p. 113)
cot:
First, I consider what it means to treat an appeal against an arbitration award as a routine step—essentially, filing an appeal whenever the award is unfavorable without much thought.  
Then I ask why an organization might be tempted to do that: it could be a way to buy time, to shift blame, or to hope that a higher court will overturn the decision in its favor.  
Looking at the practical effects, I notice that each appeal adds layers of litigation—court fees, lawyer costs, and, if the appeal fails, the original award often comes with interest that can far exceed the company’s cost of funds, turning a manageable payment into a heavy financial burden.  
Beyond the money, there is a reputational risk; repeatedly challenging awards can be seen as a tactic to avoid accountability, which erodes trust with partners and regulators.  
Because of these downsides, the decision to appeal should hinge on a careful appraisal: does the case have real legal merit, and is there a strong likelihood of success? Only when both are true, and after weighing the expected litigation expenses against the award amount, does an appeal make sense.  
Putting it together, routine appeals are ill‑advised because they usually generate unnecessary costs and damage credibility, while appeals reserved for genuinely strong cases, evaluated on merit, success probability, and cost‑benefit, serve the organization’s true interests.

question_text: What does the Delegation of Authority impose on the various levels of the organization
answer: The Delegation of Authority imposes commensurate responsibility and accountability on the various levels of the organization. This means that as authority is delegated, each level must also take on matching duties and be answerable for its actions (Procurement of Consultancy & Other Services Manual, p. 9).
cot:
First, I consider what the phrase “Delegation of Authority” actually means in an organizational context: it is the process by which higher‑level managers transfer decision‑making power to lower‑level units or individuals.  

Next, I think about the practical implications of giving someone authority without also giving them the means to answer for how that authority is used. If authority were handed out alone, people could act without any obligation to justify their actions, which would undermine control and create risk.  

Then, I recall that a sound delegation system must balance the power given with the obligations that come with it. The only way to keep the organization functioning properly is to require that whoever receives authority also assumes a matching level of responsibility for the outcomes and is held accountable for their decisions.  

Building on that, I reason that this balance is what the Delegation of Authority “imposes” on each level: as authority flows down, each level must take on duties that are proportional to the authority they receive, and they must be prepared to answer for how they exercise it.  

Finally, I synthesize these points: the imposition is commensurate responsibility and accountability—meaning that responsibility and accountability increase in step with the authority delegated, ensuring that every level is both empowered and answerable for its actions. This matches the answer that the Delegation of Authority imposes commensurate responsibility and accountability on the various levels of the organization.

question_text: Do I need to use an outer envelope for my tender submission, and how should it be handled
answer: Yes, you must use an outer envelope for your tender submission. Place each sealed and marked inner envelope (original, duplicate, etc.) inside a larger outer envelope. The outer envelope also needs to be sealed and marked in the same way – show the words “original”, “duplicate”, etc., print the purchase office address and the tender reference number on it, and add the line “NOT TO BE OPENED” before the due date and time of tender opening. If the outer envelope is not properly sealed and marked, the purchaser will not assume responsibility for any misplacement, premature or late opening. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 96)
cot:
First, I think about what the tender instructions require for each copy of the bid – they must be sealed in separate envelopes and clearly labeled as “original,” “duplicate,” etc., with the purchase office address, tender reference number and the warning “NOT TO BE OPENED” before the opening date and time.  
Next, I recall that after those inner envelopes are prepared, the directions say they are to be placed inside a larger outer envelope. This outer envelope is not just a casual wrapper; it too must be sealed and marked in the same way – bearing the same labels, address, reference number and the “NOT TO BE OPENED” note.  
Then I consider why this extra step matters: the Procurement of Goods Manual warns that if the outer envelope is not properly sealed and marked, the purchaser will not take responsibility for any misplacement, premature or late opening. That makes it clear that the outer envelope is part of the formal submission package, not an optional extra.  
Putting those points together, I conclude that yes, an outer envelope is mandatory for a tender submission. To handle it correctly, I would seal each inner envelope (original, duplicate, etc.), mark them as required, place all of them inside a bigger envelope, seal that outer envelope, and replicate the same labeling – “original,” “duplicate,” the office address, the tender reference number and the “NOT TO BE OPENED” line before the due date and time.  
Finally, I check that this matches the guidance: the outer envelope must be treated exactly like the inner ones, and failure to do so relieves the purchaser of liability, confirming that the outer envelope is indeed required and must be handled as described.

#### vi) **Sealing and Marking of Tenders (other than e-Tender)**
The tender document is to indicate the total number of tender sets (for example, in duplicate or in triplicate, and so on) required to be submitted. Further, the sentence "NOT TO BE OPENED" before (due date and time of tender opening) is also to be printed on these envelopes. If the outer envelope is not sealed and marked properly as above, the purchaser will not assume any responsibility for its misplacement, premature opening, late opening, and so on. All the above instructions are to be suitably incorporated in the tender documents.

#### vii) **Withdrawal, Substitution and Modification of Tenders**
The tenderer, after submitting the tender, is permitted to withdraw, substitute or modify the tenders in writing without forfeiture of Bid Security/ EMD, provided these are received duly sealed and marked like the original tender, up to the date and time of receipt of the tender. Any such request received after the prescribed date and time of receipt of tenders will not be considered. No bid may be withdrawn in the interval between the deadline for submission of bids and expiration of the period of bid validity. Withdrawal of a bid during this period will result in forfeiture of the bidder's bid security (EMD) and other sanctions.

If it is intended to use eligibility/evaluation/qualification criteria to evaluate a tender and determine whether a tenderer has the required qualifications, this point may be clearly specified in NIT, ITB/AITB or as a separate section of the tender document. The bidder has to ensure that he provides convincing proof of having fulfilled these criteria. *Any criteria not specified in the tender cannot be used for evaluation or qualification.*

question_text: What is the legal basis for the Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises, 2012
answer: The Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises, 2012 was notified by the Government of India exercising the powers conferred in Section 11 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006. (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 26)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the question is really after: the legal authority that allowed the government to issue the Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises, 2012.  
Then I think about how such policies are normally grounded—they are usually issued under a specific provision of a parent act that grants the government rule‑making power.  
Next, I recall that the policy was notified by the Government “in exercise of the powers conferred in Section 11 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006.”  
This tells me that Section 11 of the MSMED Act, 2006 is the provision that confers the necessary authority, so it must be the legal basis for the policy.  
To be thorough, I consider whether any other section or act is referenced in connection with the policy’s issuance, and I do not have the detail on any alternative legal foundation.  
Finally, I bring the pieces together: the Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises, 2012 derives its legal validity from Section 11 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006, which is exactly the basis the answer states.
chunk_content:
- i) From time to time, the Government of India (Procuring Entity) lays down procurement policies to help inclusive national economic growth by providing long-term support to micro, small and medium enterprises and disadvantaged sections of society. The Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises, 2012 [amended 2018 and 2021] has been notified by the

Government in exercise of the powers conferred in Section 11 of the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act, 2006. Details of the policy along with the amendments issued in 2018 and 2021 are available on the MSME website.

- ii) Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) registered under Udyam Registration are eligible to avail the benefits under the policy.
- iii) The Policy is applicable to all the Central Government Ministries/ Departments/ CPSUs. However, the policy is presently not applicable to State Government Ministries/ Departments/ PSUs.
  - 1) To reduce transaction cost of doing business, MSEs will be facilitated by providing them tender documents free of cost, exempting MSEs from payment of earnest money deposit, adopting e-procurement to bring transparency in tendering process. However, exemption from paying Performance Bank Guarantee is not covered under the policy. MSEs may also be given relaxation in prior turnover and prior experience criteria during the tender process, subject to meeting of quality and technical specifications. However, there may be circumstances (like procurement of items related to public safety, health, critical security operations and equipment, etc.) where procuring entity may prefer the vendor to have prior experience rather than giving orders to new entities.
  - 2) Chapter V of the MSMED Act, 2006 also has provision for ensuring timely payments to the MSE suppliers. The period agreed upon for payment must not exceed forty-five days after the supplies. For delays in payment the buyer shall be liable to pay compound interest to the supplier on the delayed amount at three times of the bank rate notified by the Reserve Bank. For arbitration and conciliation regarding recovery of such payments and interests, Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council has been setup in states.
  - 3) In tender, participating Micro and Small Enterprises (MSE) quoting price within price band of L1+15 (fifteen) per cent shall also be allowed to supply a portion of requirement by bringing down their price to L1 price in a situation where L1 price is from someone other than a MSE and such MSE shall be allowed to supply up to 25(twenty five) per cent of total tendered value. The 25(twenty five) per cent quantity is to be distributed proportionately among these bidders, in case there are more than one MSEs within such price band.
  - 4) Within this 25% (Twenty Five Percent) quantity, a purchase preference of four (4) per cents reserved for MSEs owned by Scheduled Caste (SC)/ Scheduled Tribe (ST) entrepreneurs and three (3) percent is reserved for MSEs owned by women entrepreneur (if they participate in the tender process and match the L1 price). However, in event of failure of such MSEs to participate in tender process or meet tender requirements and L1 price, four percent sub-target for procurement earmarked for MSEs owned by SC/ST entrepreneurs and three (3) percent earmarked to women entrepreneur will be met from other MSEs. MSEs would be treated as owned by SC/ ST entrepreneurs:
    - a) In case of proprietary MSE, proprietor(s) shall be SC /ST;
    - b) In case of partnership MSE, the SC/ ST partners shall be holding at least 51% (fifty-one percent) shares in the unit;
    - c) In case of Private Limited Companies, at least 51% (fifty-one percent) share shall be held by SC/ ST promoters.
- iv) If subcontract is given to MSEs, it will be considered as procurement from MSEs.

Then I recall that the policy’s very purpose is to support enterprises that fall within the micro and small category, so the eligible group must be a subset of those defined as micro or small enterprises.  

Next, I think about how the government currently identifies micro and small enterprises: they are required to be registered under the Udyam Registration system, which replaced the earlier Udyog Aadhaar and serves as the official recognition of an enterprise’s size and status.  

Looking at the policy details, it explicitly states that only those Micro and Small Enterprises that have completed Udyam Registration are entitled to the benefits such as free tender documents, exemption from earnest money deposit, and relaxation in turnover or experience criteria.  

Combining these points, I conclude that the enterprises eligible to avail the benefits under the Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises are precisely the Micro and Small Enterprises that are registered under Udyam Registration.

question_text: Has it been verified that startups eligible for turnover/experience relaxation may be either MSMEs or non‑MSMEs?
answer: Yes, startups eligible for turnover/experience relaxation may be either MSMEs or non‑MSMEs (Procurement of Goods Manual, p. 28).
cot:
First, I need to clarify what the question is really asking: it wants confirmation that the turnover‑and‑experience relaxation granted to startups is not limited to only those that are MSMEs, but also extends to startups that are not classified as MSMEs.  

Next, I recall the criteria that define a startup under the DPIIT framework—incorporation within ten years, turnover below ₹100 crore, innovative or scalable business, and formal DPIIT recognition—and I note that the relaxation of prior turnover and experience is expressly tied to meeting those startup conditions and to satisfying quality and technical specifications.  

Then I look at the provision that governs the relaxation itself: it states that the benefit applies to *all* startups recognized by DPIIT, provided they meet the quality and technical requirements, and it does not impose any additional filter based on MSME status.  

After that, I see the explicit clarification that follows the rule: “Startups may be MSMEs or otherwise.” This sentence directly tells us that the category of eligible startups includes both MSME‑registered entities and those that fall outside the MSME definition.  

Putting these points together, the relaxation mechanism is open to any DPIIT‑recognized startup irrespective of whether it is an MSME, which means the policy deliberately covers both groups.  

Therefore, the verification requested in the question is affirmative: startups eligible for turnover/experience relaxation may indeed be either MSMEs or non‑MSMEs.

question_text: Besides equipment specification, what else must be ensured for critical equipment according to the essential equipment schedule
answer: Besides specifying the equipment’s details, the essential equipment schedule also requires that competent operators for the critical equipment be identified and listed as key personnel. This ensures that the service provider has qualified personnel to operate the equipment safely and effectively, meeting both operational and compliance requirements. (Procurement of Consultancy and Other Services Manual, p. 70)
cot:
First, I need to pinpoint what the essential equipment schedule demands beyond just describing the equipment itself.
The essential equipment schedule requires that any essential equipment be listed together with its specification, capacity, age, and similar technical details.
Additionally, the schedule includes a separate clause that follows the equipment details: it stresses that competent operators for such critical equipment must be mentioned as key personnel.
This means that, in addition to the equipment’s technical specs, the schedule requires the service provider to identify and list qualified operators who will handle the equipment.
Putting those two points together, the extra condition that must be ensured is the inclusion of competent operators as key personnel for the critical equipment.
This reasoning leads directly to the answer: besides specifying the equipment’s details, the essential equipment schedule also requires that competent operators for the critical equipment be identified and listed as key personnel.

question_text: What is the Vulnerability Atlas of India and why was it created?
answer: **A:** The Vulnerability Atlas of India is a comprehensive document that provides existing hazard scenarios for the entire country, presenting digitized State/UT‑wise hazard maps for earthquakes, winds, and floods, plus additional maps for thunderstorms, cyclones, and landslides to identify vulnerable areas at the district level. It was created to serve as a single‑point source for policy makers, administrators, engineers, architects, planners, and the public to ascertain multi‑hazard proneness of any location and to support disaster preparedness, mitigation, risk analysis, and hazard assessment during policy planning and project formulation. (Procurement of Works Manual, pp. 51-52)
cot:
I start by asking myself what the question is really after: a clear description of the Vulnerability Atlas of India and the reason it came into existence.  

First, I think about what kind of object would be called an “atlas” in this context. It must be a collection of maps or spatial information that covers the whole country. The Procurement of Works Manual describes it as a comprehensive document that presents existing hazard scenarios for India and provides digitized, state‑wise maps for several natural hazards—earthquakes, wind, floods, thunderstorms, cyclones and landslides—so that vulnerable areas can be identified at the district level. That paints the picture of a multi‑hazard atlas rather than a single‑hazard map.  

Next, I consider why such a detailed, nationwide hazard compilation would be useful. If planners, engineers or policy makers are about to approve a housing project, a road or any infrastructure, they need to know what dangers the site might face. Without a single source that brings together earthquake zones, wind speeds, flood‑prone areas, storm histories and landslide incidence, they would have to hunt through disparate reports, which is inefficient and prone to gaps. The Procurement of Works Manual notes that the atlas is meant to be a “single point source” for various stakeholders—policy makers, administrators, municipal commissioners, urban managers, engineers, architects, planners and the public—to quickly ascertain how prone any location is to multiple hazards.  

I then look at the stated purpose in the Procurement of Works Manual: the main purpose of the atlas is disaster preparedness and mitigation at the policy planning and project formulation stage. question_text: What must a bidder include in the financial bid to ensure that all duties, taxes, and other levies payable under the contract are accounted for
answer: To ensure that all duties, taxes, and other levies payable under the contract are accounted for, a bidder must include every such charge—calculated as of the month prior to the bid submission deadline—in the total bid price submitted. This requirement ensures full compliance with NRL’s procurement expectations and avoids disqualification for unresponsive bidding. (Procurement of Consultancy Other Services Manual, p. 76)

First, I need to grasp what the question is really asking: it wants to know what a bidder must put into the financial bid so that every duty, tax, or other levy that the contractor will have to pay under the contract is already covered in the bid amount.

From that, I deduce that if a bidder omits a particular charge—say, a tax or levy—then that item would effectively have no price attached, and the procuring entity would not compensate for it later.  

Therefore, to avoid that situation, the bidder must explicitly account for every such charge somewhere in the bid. The only place where a single, all‑inclusive figure is expected is the total bid price that sums up all the priced items.

This ensures that the bid reflects the actual cost the contractor will face at the time of contract execution.  

Putting it together, the bidder must take the applicable duty, tax, and levy rates from the month before the deadline, compute the total amount that will be payable under the contract, and roll that sum into the overall bid price.

### 9.15.7 Liquidated Damages for Delay in Performance and Incentives/ Bonus:-
**Liquidated Damages:** Compensation of loss on account of late delivery (actually incurred as well as notional) where loss is pre-estimated is termed as LD. Recovery of such pre-estimated loss is allowed provided such a term is included in the contract. There is no need to establish actual loss due to late delivery. Price reduction clause (PRC) for late delivery shall convey the same meaning as Liquidated Damages (LD).

The Contractor is liable to pay Liquidated Damages for per day of delay beyond the specified date of completion, an amount equal to 0.5% for every week or part thereof, subject to the total amount of Damages not exceeding 5% (five per cent) of the Contract Price. However, the Contractor is entitled to time extension arising out of delays on account of change of scope and force majeure or delays caused by or attributable to NRL. The Procuring Entity may deduct liquidated damages from payments due to the service provider. Payment of liquidated damages shall not affect the service provider's liabilities.

Normally, tenders shall be invited with reference to a pre-determined period of completion of services. Provision of incentives for completion of service before schedule should be sparingly made after careful assessment of tangible benefits there from and disclosed in the tender documents in clear monetary terms.

Incentives/ Bonus (e.g. one percent of the contract value per month subject to a maximum of five percent of contract value) for early completion and penalties for delay should, therefore, be built into the contract very judiciously. To avail of the incentive clause, it shall be mandatory on the part of the contractor to report the actual date of completion to the concerned Engineer (Engineer herein refers

to EIC). To implement a bonus clause in any tender, prior administrative approval of CFD shall be obtained by indenting/user department.

**9.15.8 Penalty for non-performance:** If the service provider has not corrected a Defect within the time specified in the Procuring Entity's notice, a penalty for Lack of performance will be paid by the service provider. The amount to be paid will be calculated as a percentage of the cost of having the Defect corrected, as assessed by EIC or as described in SCC/GCC.

**9.15.9 Filling up the Financial Bid by the Bidders:** The Bidder should be asked to fill in rates and prices for all items of the Services described in the Activity Schedule. Items for which no rate or price is entered by the Bidder will not be paid for by the Procuring Entity when executed and shall be deemed covered by the other rates and prices in the Activity Schedule. The priced Activity Schedule contains sections on Remuneration for Staff deployed, Reimbursable Expenses and Miscellaneous Expenses. All duties, taxes, and other levies payable by the service provider under the Contract, or for any other cause, as in the month prior to the month of the deadline for submission of bids, should be included/indicated in the total Bid price submitted by the Bidder. Bidding Documents should include a clause that **"if a firm quotes NIL charges/consideration, the bid shall be treated as unresponsive and will not be considered"**. In case of e-tendering, the soft copy BOQ (priced bid format) should be free of ambiguity and user friendly. All necessary information should be provided in the BOQ format to guide the bidder for correct uploading of their quoted price; further, if any formula is used to arrive at the total quoted price from the unit prices entered by the bidder, the formula should be made known to the bidder.

### 4.4.1 (B) Minimum Response in Open/Limited Tenders:
1. **"Minimum Response"** shall be considered as under, and no separate approval note to be processed for un-priced bid opening:
  - i. Where the enquiry is issued on open tender basis, the minimum response shall be 03 (three) bids.
  - ii. Where the enquiry is issued on limited tender basis, the minimum response shall be 03 (three) bids. Wherever limited tender is issued to two parties only, minimum response shall be two.
2. Respective purchase officer shall suitably extend the bid due date in either of the following two situations:
  - i) Where Minimum response is not obtained, Purchase officer can give first extension of up to one week but subsequent extensions shall require Commercial HOD's consent. Indentor and HOD of user dept. is to be notified about such extensions.
  - ii) Where Minimum response is obtained but one or more of the vendors have requested for extension by the due date. In such a cases, user dept HOD's prior consent shall be obtained.
3. Normally two extensions shall be given to any enquiry. In case, even after two bid due date extension(s), minimum response is not obtained, whatever bids are received, may be opened. In the case of no response, refloating may be done only in consultation with user department.
4. Where extension is required for any reason(s) beyond two extensions, Commercial HOD's prior consent shall be obtained. Reason for such extensions should be recorded.

## 4.5 Eligibility and Qualifications of Bidders


### 4.5.1 Eligibility of Bidders
- i) All eligible bidders meeting the eligibility criteria as defined in ITB can participate in the

tender. The bidder should be a private or government-owned legal entity.

- ii) Bidder should have valid registration with Employees Provident Fund organization under 'EPF and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952', wherever applicable.
- iii) Tenders where Joint Ventures / LLPs (limited liability partnerships) are allowed, all the partners shall be jointly and severally liable (as applicable) for the successful completion of the work.
- iv) A firm that has been engaged by the procuring entity to provide consultancy services for the preparation or implementation of a project, and any of its affiliates (associates, subsidiary, JV partner), shall not be eligible for subsequently providing goods or works (other than a continuation of the firm's earlier consultancy services) for the same project.
- v) A firm determined non-performing by the Procuring Entity shall not be eligible to bid during the period so determined.

### 4.5.2 Qualification of Bidders
Qualification of bidders is done on Pre-qualification Bidding basis (refer Para 3.3.6, PQB) or on post-qualification basis (refer Para 3.3.4, single stage multiple envelope system). In both cases Qualification criteria needs to be laid down in the Bid Document (refer para 3.3.6 iii). It is of utmost importance to develop new contractors and also to provide avenues to Sub-contractors executing NRL contracts, since they may not get opportunities to accumulate the required credentials to compete in normal tenders. To enable a window of entry for such Start-ups and sub-contractors, in small value contracts (e.g. repair contracts upto Rs.30 lakh) the requirements regarding, Past Experience may not be insisted upon provided the bidders fulfil other criteria regarding Financial/ Personnel/ Equipment capabilities. However to avoid overstretching of their resources, no such contractors may be allowed to hold more than 2 contracts under relaxed credentials, at any given time. Documentary proof of being sub-contractor of NRL jobs endorsed by NRL EIC should be furnished.
